question: According to Figure 3 in the LBNF Neutrino Beam document, which neutrino processes are shown in the top and bottom panels?
reference_answer: The top panel shows νₑ appearance and the bottom panel shows ν_μ disappearance.
evidence_quote: FIG. 3: _νe_ appearance (top) and _νµ_ disappearance (bottom) spectra in the LBNF _ν_ (left) and _ν_ ¯ (right) beams.

Figure 3 displays the predicted energy spectra of the two key oscillation channels:

* **Top panel:** νₑ **appearance** spectra (the rate at which electron‑neutrinos appear in a muon‑neutrino beam).  
* **Bottom panel:** ν_μ **disappearance** spectra (the depletion of muon‑neutrinos from the original beam).

These spectra are shown for both the neutrino (ν) and antineutrino ( ν̅ ) running modes and for two different target‑horn configurations.

Box 500, Batavia, IL 60510-0500, USA_ _on behalf of the DUNE Collaboration_ (Dated: January 20, 2016) > _‡_ Operated by Fermi Research Alliance, LLC under Contract No. De-AC02-07CH11359 with the United States Department of Energy 1 _NuFact15 - Rio de Janeiro, Brazil - August 2015_ 2 # Abstract The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment is a worldwide effort to build a next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiment with a neutrino beam and near detector at Fermilab and a far detector at the Sanford Underground Research Facility 1,300 km from Fermilab. It is a merger of previous efforts and other interested parties to build, operate and exploit a staged 40-kt liquid argon detector and a high precision near detector exposed to a high-power, broad-band neutrino beam. The goals of the experiment are precision oscillation measurements, including CP violation and neutrino mass hierarchy determination, search for nucleon decay, and neutrino astrophysics, as well as precision neutrino physics at the near site. ## **INTRODUCTION** The DUNE Collaboration[1] plans to address a number of the fundamental open questions in particle physics and astroparticle physics utilizing a massive liquid argon time-projection chamber (LAr TPC) located at a depth of 4,300 meters water equivalent at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, South Dakota; a high-power, broad band, sign-selected _νµ_ beam at Fermilab with a baseline distance from source to detector of 1,300 km; and a precision neutrino detector located on the Fermilab site[2]. The primary science objectives[3] include: neutrino oscillation physics to search for CP is violation in the leptonic sector, determine the ordering of the neutrino mass eigenstates, make precision measurements of oscillation parameters, test the three-neutrino paradigm; searches for baryon number violating processes (nucleon decay); and neutrino astrophysics, most notably precision measurements of neutrinos from a core-collapse supernova within the Galaxy, should one occur during the multi-decade lifetime of the experiment. DUNE is a newly formed international collaboration, with strong representation from the previous LBNE, LBNO and other collaborations. As of the time of _NuFact15_ , DUNE had 776 collaborators from 144 institutions located in 26 different countries on five continents. The DUNE Collaboration will design, build, commission and operate the near and far detectors[4] and is responsible for carrying out the scientific program utilizing them. Facilities necessary to mount this experiment[5], including the neutrino beam[6], the cryostats and cryogenics systems to house the LAr TPC far detector, and conventional facilities at both Fermilab and SURF will be designed, built and commissioned by the Long- _NuFact15 - Rio de Janeiro, Brazil - August 2015_ 3 Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) Project. A new, broad-band and tunable neutrino beam is being designed, optimized for the Fermilab-SURF baseline. It will be driven by a 1.2 MW proton beam provided by the PIP-II upgrade[7], and is designed to accommodate future beam power upgrades to 2.4 MW. The design of the beam is still being optimized, and physics results are presented below for different options currently under study. LBNF is a U.S. Project based at Fermilab with contributions from a number of international partners. ## **THE DUNE DETECTORS** The far detector[4] is a 40 kt fiducial mass ( _∼_ 70 kt total mass) LAr TPC, located deep underground at SURF. The detector is divided into four independent 10 kt modules, each housed in its own cavern, as shown in Fig. 1. The detectors are placed in cryostats each of inner dimension 15 m wide _×_ 14 m high _×_ 62 m long. This arrangement allows for a staged construction and gives flexibility for evolution of the LAr TPC technology. While the cryostats will be identical, the LAr TPC detectors may not be, allowing lessons learned from the construction of the first module or information gleaned from the DUNE or other R&D programs to be incorporated in subsequent modules. The reference design is a single-phase LAr TPC, which is an evolution of the successful ICARUS design[8] and in which alternating anode and cathode planes divide the liquid volume into four 3.6 m drift regions. The reference design is supported by development programs at Fermilab (the DUNE 35 t prototype, MicroBooNE[9], the Fermilab Short-Baseline Neutrino Program[10], and LArIAT[11]) and at CERN (ICARUS/WA104[12] and the DUNE Single-Phase Prototype[13]). Dual-phase readout technology, which is being developed by the WA105 Collaboration[14], is a potential alternate design that if demonstrated could form the basis for the second or subsequent 10 kt modules. The DUNE near detector must constrain the systematic uncertainties for the oscillation analysis, which requires it to have the capability to precisely measure exclusive neutrino interactions of all four species in the beam: _νµ,_ ¯ _νµ, νe_ , and _ν_ ¯ _e_ . This naturally results also in a self-contained non-oscillation neutrino physics program that exploits the intense LBNF beam. The reference design is a NOMAD-inspired[15] Fine-Grained Tracker (FGT)[4] illustrated in Fig. 2. It consists of a central straw-tube tracker with embedded nuclear targets, including high-pressure argon-filled tubes and calcium (A=40) targets, and a lead-scintillator _NuFact15 - Rio de Janeiro, Brazil - August 2015_ 4 #2

Further details about the DUNE near detector can be found in [16]. _NuFact15 - Rio de Janeiro, Brazil - August 2015_ 5 ## **THE DUNE SCIENCE PROGRAM** The primary scientific program of LBNF/DUNE addresses key science questions highlighted in the P5 report[17]. This program focuses on three areas: 1) Neutrino oscillation physics to probe CP violation (CPV) in the leptonic sector, determine the neutrino mass hierarchy (MH), and make precision measurements of oscillation parameters to test the threeneutrino paradigm; 2) Search for nucleon decay, particularly in modes such as _p → K_+ _ν_ ¯ which are difficult for existing experiments to access; and 3) Supernova burst physics, exploiting the sensitivity of an LAr TPC to _νe_ (as opposed to _ν_ ¯ _e_ ). Any of these would represent a major discovery. It is these science objectives that drive the design of LBNF and DUNE. In addition, there is a high-priority ancillary science program that is enabled by the intense LBNF beam, the very long baseline, and the precision DUNE detectors. This program includes: 1) Other oscillation physics with beyond-the-Standard-Model sensitivity such as non-standard neutrino interactions, sterile neutrinos, or measurements of _ντ_ appearance; 2) Oscillation physics with atmospheric neutrinos; 3) Neutrino physics with the near detector such as neutrino cross-sections, electroweak physics, nuclear and QCD physics; and 4) Searches for signatures of dark matter. DUNE will exploit the high-intensity, broad-band LBNF neutrino beam and the 1,300 km baseline to make a comprehensive set of neutrino oscillation measurements to determine the MH, probe CPV, determine the _θ_ 23 octant, test the 3-flavor paradigm, and search for _ν_ non-standard interactions in a single experiment. The long-baseline and wide-band beam allow measurement of oscillation effects over a broad range of energies, covering more than one full oscillation cycle as illustrated in Fig. 3. With a 1,300 km baseline, matter effects are at the 40% level, which allows for an efficient determination of the mass ordering and clean separation of CP violating effects from the matter effect. Sensitivities for determining oscillation parameter are evaluated using a fast Monte Carlo[18], GLoBES[19] and GENIE[20]. The fast MC simulates detector response by smearing energies and angles at the final-state particle level based on measurements by ICARUS[8] and ArgoNeuT[21]. It ”reconstructs” the neutrino energy, uses a kNN-based multivariate technique for _νe_ ”reconstruction,” and generates parameterized efficiencies for input to GLoBES. Examples of the fast MC results are shown in Fig. 4. LIST OF FIGURES Figure 3-1 NSCF+B within the overall Project management 8 Figure 3-2 NSCF+B Subproject Organization 10 Figure 4-1 Work Breakdown Structure for NSCF+B Subproject 16 NSCF+B Subproject Introduction The LBNF/DUNE Project is the construction project to create both the experiment and the facility as a global endeavor. The LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan (PMP) describes the project management, high-level governance, and oversight structures; responsibilities, systems, project management documents, and processes used for managing the LBNF/DUNE enterprise to achieve its scientific, technical, cost, and schedule objectives for the construction project. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) project that supports this is the LBNF/DUNE-US Project (“Project”). The Project scope and lower-level management is done in five subprojects, and the management of each is described in separate appendices to the PMP, as follows: Far Site Conventional Facilities Excavation (FSCF-EXC): Appendix A Far Site Conventional Facilities Buildings and Site Infrastructure (FSCF-BSI): Appendix B Near Site Conventional Facilities and Beamline (NSCF+B): Appendix C Far Detectors 1 and 2 and Cryogenics (FDC): Appendix D Near Detector (ND): Appendix E The NSCF+B subproject is responsible to plan, design, and construct the Conventional Facilities and the Primary and Neutrino Beamlines located at the Near Site (Fermilab). The NSCF+B subproject is specifically responsible for planning and executing the Beamline Complex, which houses and supports the Primary and Neutrino Beamlines, and the Near Detector Complex, which houses and supports the Near Detector. The overall management of the LBNF/DUNE Project is described in the Project Management Plan, including the project oversight, high-level governance structure, project management documents and systems which apply across all subprojects. This Appendix C outlines the management of the NSCF+B subproject. Section 2 lists the institutions and laboratories that are participants and stakeholders for NSCF+B and references the PMP, which describes the management and agreements relevant to its development, supporting organizations from each institution, and key team members as they relate to it. Advisory boards are also described in the PMP. The NSCF+B subproject team and descriptions of their roles and responsibilities appear in Section 3. NSCF+B Subproject Partners The PMP describes the Project partners and their roles. The following are the partners that interact with NSCF+B: DUNE Collaboration (PMP Section 1.4.1) Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (PMP Section 1.3.7) Fermilab Director (PMP Section 1.3.7.2) Fermilab Organizations (PMP Section 1.4.2): Finance Section, Fermilab Divisions/Sections/Centers (D/S/C), Chief Project Officer (CPO), Human Resources Section. Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, India (BARC) Science and Technology Facilities Council as part of the United Kingdom Research and Innovation (STFC UKRI) BARC is providing primary beamline dipole and quadrupole magnets, which have specific Beamline requirements. STFC UKRI is providing the target, target exchange system, horn-protection baffle and carrier, and design of the helium cooling system, which have specific Beamline requirements. Close coordination with BARC and STFC UKRI is managed through systems engineering processes and regular meetings to ensure the completed work scope will meet Beamline requirements. NSCF+B Subproject Management The subproject is overseen and supported by the Project’s senior management, as described in the Project Management Plan [1] and depicted in Figure 3-1. Figure 3-1 NSCF+B within the overall Project management NSCF+B Management The subproject team is led by the NSCF+B Subproject Manager and overseen directly by the Deputy Project Director for Facilities. The roles and responsibilities are described below. Deputy Project Director for Facilities The Deputy Project Director for Facilities (DPD-Fac) is responsible for the successful execution of the conventional facilities and beamline subprojects for the LBNF/DUNE-US Project, providing programmatic leadership, strategic planning, and general oversight of design and construction of the conventional facilities and beamline. The DPD-Fac is appointed by and reports directly to the LBNF/DUNE-US Project Director (PD) who holds primary responsibility for FRA’s management oversight of the LBNF/DUNE-US Project. The PD has delegated certain responsibilities and authorities to the DPD-Fac who holds primary responsibility for FRA’s management oversight of the conventional facilities for the LBNF/DUNE-US Project. The DPD-Fac is the primary point of contact for the facilities with Fermilab Directorate, DOE Program Manager and Federal Project Director, the rest of the LBNF/DUNE Project and DUNE collaboration leadership and external institutions engaged in the Project. Within the subproject, the DPD-Fac is responsible for Providing the primary point of contact for the subproject with Fermilab Directorate and the rest of the LBNF/DUNE Project and DUNE collaboration leadership and external institutions engaged in the Project; Coordinating a subproject funding profile consistent with overall project funding after consultation and guidance from the LBNF/DUNE-US FPD, Program Manager and Project Office; Ensuring that required and effective project management and control systems developed, deployed and implemented by the Joint Project Office are used to successfully manage and assess the subproject performance; Requesting and coordinating internal and external peer reviews of the subproject; Securing all resources (management, design, and construction staffing resources) as required by the subproject; Working closely with other elements of LBNF/DUNE Project and DUNE collaboration leadership on mutual issues and concerns; Ensuring interfaces and schedule dependencies between subprojects are understood and incorporated in the plan; Providing periodic reports to the Collaboration to ensure good communication; represent the subproject’s facilities to the broader physics community; Confirming final acceptance of major systems and facilities; approve the start of operations; Assuring safety, security, and administrative performance of the subproject; Participating in the Integrated Subproject Team; Coordinating closely with the FPD on all aspects of planning, budgeting, and project execution for the subproject; Providing direct supervision of the Subproject Manager; Managing all human resources actions for the assigned area including hiring, training, promotions, performance and merit reviews, disciplinary actions and terminations, as may be appropriate; Managing staffing selection for the Subproject Managers in conjunction with the LBNF/DUNE Project Director and others as appropriate; Approving baseline changes with authority level described in the Systems Engineering Management Plan. NSCF+B Subproject Manager NSCF+B Subproject Manager (NSCF+B-SPM) reports to the DPD-Fac. The NSCF+B-SPM has the responsibility and authority to manage the subproject to the approved scope, cost, and schedule. The DPD-Fac has delegated certain responsibilities and authorities to the NSCF+B-SPM who holds primary responsibility for the management of the NSCF+B Subproject. The definition of the project, control of its scope, proposals for allocation of project contingency within bounds established in the PEP are the responsibility of the NSCF+B-SPM. The NSCF+B-SPM manages the team responsible for the design and construction of the Near Site Conventional Facilities and Beamline. The NSCF+B-SPM is responsible for: Managing the execution of the subproject to ensure that the project is completed within approved performance baseline (cost, schedule, and technical scope); Leading the subproject project team, including the NSCF Project Manager and Beamline Project Manager; Communicating resource needs to the DPD-Fac; Implementing and deploying all necessary project management and control systems to successfully manage and report the project performance; Ensuring ESH&Q responsibilities and requirements are integrated into all stages of the subproject; Serving as Control Account Manager for the subproject PM WBS, providing status and reporting as required; Providing the primary point of contact for the subproject with the FPD; Approving baseline changes with authority level described in the Systems Engineering Management Plan. The NSCF+B-SPM has delegated certain responsibilities and authorities to the NSCF-PM who holds primary responsibility for the management of the NSCF. The NSCF-PM manages the team responsible for the design and construction of the NSCF scope of work to support the Beamline and Near Detector. The NSCF-PM is responsible for: Leading the NSCF project team, including the construction manager, design manager, project engineers, and construction coordinators; Identifying resource needs and communicating them to the NSCF+B-SPM; Overseeing and coordinating external requirements (cryogenic infrastructure, detector equipment, etc.) with the Near Detector subproject, interacting regularly with appropriate managers and the project system engineers to assure requirements are incorporated into NSCF design and construction, and to verify progress and resolve issues; Ensuring ESH&Q responsibilities and requirements are integrated into all stages of the subproject; Overseeing execution of all subcontracts for the NSCF construction, including the Construction Manager as Advisor (CMa) subcontract, Beamline Complex subcontract, Near Detector Complex subcontract, and A/E; Serving as Control Account Manager for the NSCF PM WBS, providing status and reporting as required; Managing NSCF risks and representing the NSCF on the project risk management board; Preparing and providing NSCF change control proposals; Approving final acceptance of NSCF major systems and facilities; verify the readiness for start of operations. Beamline Project Manager The Beamline Project Manager (B-PM) reports to the NSCF+B-SPM. The NSCF+B-SPM has delegated certain responsibilities and authorities to the Beamline PM who holds primary responsibility for the management of the Beamline. The Beamline PM manages the team responsible for the design and construction of the Beamline scope of work. The B-PM is responsible for: Leading the Beamline project team; Identifying resource needs and communicating them to the NSCF+B-SPM; Ensuring ESH&Q responsibilities and requirements are integrated into all stages of the subproject; Overseeing execution of all subcontracts for the Beamline construction; Serving as Control Account Manager for the Beamline PM WBS, providing status and reporting as required; Managing Beamline risks and representing the Beamline on the project risk management board; Preparing and providing Beamline change control proposals; Approving final acceptance of Beamline major systems and facilities; verify the readiness for start of operations. NSCF Design Manager The NSCF Design Manager (NSCF-DM) is responsible for design management including changes to design during construction. The NSCF-DM reports to the NSCF-PM. The NSCF-DM is responsible for: Reporting status and issues to the NSCF-PM; Performing as Control Account Manager for subproject design activities and completing the assigned scope within agreed cost and schedule parameters; Administering the technical terms of the design subcontracts, including coordinating with procurement specialists to assure that all design subcontractors and vendors perform in accordance with the terms of their subcontracts and purchase orders; Acting as the primary technical point of contact for the A/E team; Coordinating design with existing Fermilab facilities and requirements as well as Near Detector requirements; Participating in the weekly construction meetings with the CMa and NSCF construction team; Coordinating with the Construction Manager on construction quality assurance, testing, commissioning, and startup of NSCF; Leading the NSCF design and engineering team, including engineers and A/E to assure the implementation of QA and ES&H requirements; Reviewing and approving design subcontractor payment requests to verify completed scope; Managing the efforts of the A/E firm to perform design and construction-phase services, including changes to the design resulting from user requirements, changed conditions or other construction-period issues; Resolving any engineering design or technical issues in consultation with the Project Engineer, Construction Manager, the A/E and other stakeholders; Participating in the subcontractor submittal review and change order processes as it pertains to the design documents or changes to such; Reporting status and issues to the NSCF-PM and providing input to periodic project reporting. The current revision is maintained in the LBNF/DUNE Document Management System (DocDB 117) where internal Project document approvals are managed. DocDB can be accessed through the web by authorized users (https://docs.dunescience.org/). This document can be identified by the revision date as indicated in the Version Control Table below. The six subprojects are outlined in blue. The Joint Project Office (JPO), shared among the overall LBNF/DUNE construction project, is shown in purple. 2-9 Figure 4: Work Breakdown Structure to WBS Level 2 4-24 Acronyms and Abbreviations Introduction The experiment – the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) - at the facility – the Long Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) - was borne out of the 2014 U.S. Particle Physics Project Prioritization Panel (P5) recommendations. The recommendations called for formation of a truly international collaboration for constructing a US-based long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment with a powerful neutrino beam (~MW scale) and a massive liquid argon TPC (40 kt fiducial volume) sited deep underground to unambiguously determine the neutrino mass ordering, search for CP violation in the lepton sector, search for proton decay, and observe neutrinos from core collapse supernova explosions. This program consolidates a variety of previous efforts in the U.S. (LBNE), Europe (LBNO), and other parts of the world focusing on this immensely important science program. The LBNF/DUNE-US Project is the construction project to create the facility and contribute US scope to the international DUNE Collaboration. This LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan (PMP) describes the project management structure, responsibilities, systems, and processes used for managing the LBNF/DUNE enterprise to achieve its scientific, technical, cost, and schedule objectives for the construction project. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) project that supports this is the LBNF/DUNE-US Project. The major participants in the overall LBNF/DUNE enterprise are the international DUNE collaboration, the LBNF/DUNE-US construction project, the DOE, international funding agencies, Fermilab (in Batavia, Illinois) as the host laboratory and the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF, in Lead, South Dakota) as the far site. Overview of Project Structure Modeled after the project structure of traditional accelerator-based particle physics experiments, such as the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC, the LBNF/DUNE construction project (the “Project”) includes The LBNF/DUNE-US Project (the “US Project”) to design and build the conventional and beamline facilities and the DOE contributions to the detectors; it is organized as a DOE/Fermilab project and incorporates contributions to the facilities from international partners. It also acts as host for the installation and integration of the detectors. Projects funded by multiple international partners for the detectors to design, build, and install the detector components; the deliverables from projects are collectively organized and coordinated by the International DUNE collaboration with oversight provided by Fermilab on behalf of all stakeholders; this effort is described in the DUNE Management Plan . The US Project is divided into six subprojects: Far Site Conventional Facilities Excavation (FSCF-EXC) Far Site Conventional Facilities Buildings and Site Infrastructure (FSCF-BSI) Near Site Conventional Facilities (NSCF) Beamline First two Far Detector modules and Cryogenics (FDC) Near Detector (ND) Fermilab as host is directly responsible for providing the facilities and provides oversight of the international DUNE detector construction effort and of the integration and installation of the detectors. It is responsible to the participating funding agencies through the DOE for the successful management and execution of all LBNF/DUNE construction project efforts. As the new Management and Operating (M&O) contractor for Fermilab as of January 2025, Fermi Forward Discovery Group, LLC (FermiForward) will be accountable to DOE for carrying out the remainder of the US Project. The Fermi Research Alliance, LLC (FRA) preceded FermiForward as Fermilab’s M&O contractor. Fermilab has established the LBNF/DUNE-US Project team, including the six subproject teams, that are responsible for all research and development (R&D); conceptual, preliminary, and final design; fabrication; installation; inspection; commissioning; and overall day-to-day management of the US Project, in close cooperation and partnership with the DUNE Collaboration, and SURF for those activities occurring at the Far Site. Top-Level Organization, Management, Roles and Responsibilities A set of structures is established to provide coordination among the participating funding agencies, oversight of the projects, and coordination and communication between the projects. These structures and the relationships among them are shown in Figure 2-1 and described in the following sections. Figure : Top-level organization and advisory structure for oversight of the LBNF/DUNE project and the (separate) PIP-II Project. Solid lines indicate organizational structure; dashed lines indicate advisory relationships. International Neutrino Council (INC) The International Neutrino Council (INC), which is composed of representatives from participating regions and partners such as CERN, and representatives of funding agencies making major contributions to the LBNF/DUNE facilities infrastructure or to PIP-II (which is a separate project building a proton accelerator upstream of the LBNF/DUNE beamline), acts as the highest-level international advisory body to the US DOE. The INC is the forum for status and issue resolution for PIP-II and LBNF. It is chaired by the DOE Office of Science Associate Director for High Energy Physics and includes the Fermilab Director in its membership. The DUNE Co-Spokespersons and/or other participants within the Fermilab neutrino program are invited to sessions of the INC as needed. Council membership may increase as additional funding agencies from other geographic regions make major contributions to LBNF/DUNE facilities and detectors as well as PIP-II. Resources Review Board (RRB) The DUNE Resources Review Board (RRB) is part of the international project governance structure for DUNE. It was established as a forum to provide coordination among funding partners and oversight of DUNE. It is comprised of representatives of all funding agencies that sponsor DUNE, and of Fermilab management. In addition, parties that have not yet committed their contributions to DUNE may be invited to attend as observers. The RRB provides monitoring and oversight of the DUNE Collaboration, and receives updates on the progress of LBNF, PIP-II, and SBN. The RRB receives periodic reports from both the Long-Baseline Neutrino Committee (LBNC) and the Neutrino Scope Group (NSG), which are review committees for DUNE charged by and reporting to the Fermilab Directorate. The LBNC reviews DUNE from a technical perspective, and the NSG reviews DUNE from a cost and schedule perspective. The roles of the RRB include: Monitoring and oversight of DUNE technical progress and costs, supported by reports and recommendations from the LBNC and the NSG. Monitoring international commitments secured by the DUNE Collaboration, in timeframes necessary to support the projects. Approving DUNE common fund contributions (including any annual common fund budgets) as appropriate. Assisting the DOE, DUNE management, and the FNAL Directorate with resolving issues regarding contributions to DUNE. Neutrino Scope Group (NSG) The Neutrino Scope Group (NSG) is part of the international governance and oversight structure for DUNE. Its purpose is to review the scope completeness, the availability and sufficiency of resources to complete the scope on schedule, identify any non-technical risks, and review the Common Funds associated with the DUNE program. The primary responsibilities of the NSG include: Evaluating the completeness of the DUNE scope necessary to deliver the detectors, the complete mapping onto the DUNE partners, and verifying there are no scope gaps. Assessing the credibility of the schedule for DUNE, major milestones, and coordination with the LBNF/DUNE-US project schedule. Assessing the appropriateness of the estimate of available resources, including staffing resources and M&S funding for the DUNE experiment, including computing. Reviewing the performance and plans of the collaboration’s Common Fund spending in the construction and operations eras. Reviewing non-technical risks for DUNE, such as supply-chain issues, including proposed levels of cost realism and schedule contingency to address identified strategies for mitigation of those risks. Monitoring DUNE progress against the scope and schedule associated with the Technical Design Reports. Coordinating and receiving input from the LBNC on the overall scientific and technical status of DUNE program. The Chair of the NSG is appointed by and reports to the Fermilab Director. Long-Baseline Neutrino Committee (LBNC) The Long-Baseline Neutrino Committee (LBNC) is composed of internationally prominent scientists with relevant expertise. The LBNC provides external scientific peer review and monitors the technical progress of the International DUNE collaboration and those aspects of the facility construction that have direct impact on the DUNE experiment. It acts effectively as an adjunct to the Fermilab Physics Advisory Committee (PAC), meeting on a more frequent basis than the PAC. The LBNC may employ Scrutiny Groups for more detailed reports and evaluations. The LBNC members are appointed by the Fermilab director. Selected LBNC members are also members of the Fermilab PAC. LBNF/DUNE-US Strategic Project Advisory Committee (SPAC) The Strategic Project Advisory Committee (SPAC), through its charter , provides expert, independent advice on significant issues and strategies related to project organization, management, and risks; how to optimize successful execution of LBNF/DUNE-US within DOE-approved budget profiles, plans, and baselines; paths to reduce perceived risks and build sponsor buy-in for innovative strategies, including procurement approach; and the formulation, development, and sustainment of partnerships with national and international institutions, agencies, and countries. The committee meets annually or more frequently and is comprised of members of the scientific and project management communities, appointed by the Fermilab Director in consultation with the LBNF Project Director (PD). It provides reports to the Fermilab Director after each meeting. Fermilab Role as Host lab DOE has assigned Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) the responsibility to plan, execute and manage all LBNF/DUNE-US efforts within an agreed-to scope, cost, and schedule in a safe and responsible manner. Fermilab leads a partnership of national laboratories and universities in the execution of the US Project and provides access to resources, systems, and other capabilities required in the execution of this Project. The laboratory’s responsibilities fan out to many areas. Fermilab works with all stakeholders, including international funding agencies, the DUNE Collaboration, the LBNF/DUNE-US Project, the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority (SDSTA), and state and local governments, as appropriate, to put in place the strategies, collaboration and communication required for success of the overall LBNF/DUNE enterprise. Areas of responsibility include: International agreements with the US DOE as the lead, Interfaces between agencies and entities, Advocacy on behalf of LBNF/DUNE, Identifying needs and securing the needed resources, ES&H, Consistency in lab operations and schedules vis-à-vis LBNF/DUNE and PIP-II needs, and Solicitation of and response to input and advice from review bodies. Fermilab is directly responsible for the design, construction, installation, commissioning, and operation of the facilities and infrastructure that support the entire LBNF/DUNE program as well as integration of the facilities with the detectors and oversight of the international DUNE effort. Although SDSTA owns and operates the LBNF/DUNE Far Site at SURF, Fermilab serves as the single point of contact for the DUNE collaboration on all matters pertaining to the Far Site. Fermilab works with international partners in designing and building these facilities, and with the DUNE collaboration to ensure that the facilities are optimized to achieve the science goals of the experimental program. Fermilab, as host lab, provides oversight of the DUNE collaboration and detector construction project through: Regular meetings with the collaboration leadership Approving the selection of collaboration Spokespersons Jointly with DUNE collaboration co-spokespersons, appoints Technical and Resource Coordinators. The LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan (PMP) describes the project management, high-level governance, and oversight structures; responsibilities, systems, project management documents, and processes used for managing the LBNF/DUNE enterprise to achieve its scientific, technical, cost, and schedule objectives for the construction project. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) project that supports this is the LBNF/DUNE-US Project (“Project”). The FSCF-EXC subproject is specifically responsible for planning and executing the Reliability Projects, Pre-excavation, and Excavation scopes of work. FSCF-BSI provides the surface, shaft, and underground utilities and infrastructure to support the detectors. The overall management of the LBNF/DUNE Project is described in the Project Management Plan, including the project oversight, high-level governance structure, project management documents and systems which apply across all subprojects. This Appendix A describes the management of the FSCF-EXC subproject. Sanford

> U.S. DEPARTMENT OF Office of ENERGY Science ### **International Particle Physics Community Steps toward LBNF/DUNE** - 2013: European Strategy for Particle Physics updated - Endorsed high priority of neutrino physics - Bottom line: CERN should help the European neutrino community participate in a long-baseline program outside of Europe European Strategy for Particle Physics - 2014: P5 Plan Building for Discovery Strategic Plan for U.s.Particle Physics in the Global Context - A strategic plan for U.S. particle physics maximizing opportunities for breakthrough science - Explicit prioritization, hard choices made within realistic budget scenarios - Particle physics community unified behind the plan: 2,331 signatures on letter sent to DOE Secretary Moniz **2** 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview **LBNF** ### **P5 Mandate: a new international collaboration** • P5 recommendation 13: “Form a new international collaboration to design and execute a highly capable Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) hosted by the U.S. To proceed, a project plan and identified resources must exist to meet the minimum requirements in the text [of the report]. LBNF is the highestpriority large project in its timeframe” - Basically asks Fermilab to do for neutrinos what CERN did for the Higgs, involving the worldwide community - The science from DUNE will be game changing for particle and astro-particle physics and will be in all the textbooks. Building for Discovery Strategic Plan for U.S. Particle Physics in the Global Context E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview **LBNF** **3** 08.11.15 ### **P5 Mandate: Scope of LBNF/DUNE based on science requirements** - “For a long-baseline oscillation experiment, based on the science drivers and what is practically achievable in a major step forward, we set as the goal a mean sensitivity to CP violation of better than 3σ over more than 75% of the range of possible values of the unknown CP-violating phase δCP.” - “With a wideband neutrino beam produced by a proton beam with power of 1.2 MW, this … implies a far detector with fiducial mass of more than 40 kilotons of liquid argon and a suitable near detector.” - This is the scope of the LBNF/DUNE project. E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview **LBNF** 08.11.15 **4** ### **DUNE is a discovery science program….science requirements drive the scope and design** - Determine if neutrinos violate leptonic CP and by how much - Extract multiple detailed properties of neutrinos in a single experiment to test the current 3-flavor paradigm - Look for surprises - Search for nucleon decay - Detect thousands of neutrinos from galactic supernova explosions - And more E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview **LBNF** 08.11.15 **5** ### **Facility and Experiment as separate major subprojects** - The facility, LBNF, is treated as a separate project from the experiment, “DUNE”, but with a single Federal Project Director....this facilitates CERN as facility partner - DUNE Collaboration comprises 776 members from 26 countries and 144 institutions (~ half international) - DUNE has brought together the world liquid argon TPC neutrino community, as well as an underground neutrino particle astrophysics community - Collaboration has come together faster than even the optimistic schedule considered by P5….an indication of intense interest in this science and the perception that the DOE is prepared to host an ambitious world class neutrino facility E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview **LBNF** **6** 08.11.15 ### **LBNF/DUNE Partners** - Strong domestic and international scientific and funding partners are key to LBNF/DUNE success. - CERN is a major partner in facility infrastructure at both Fermilab and SURF (such as cryostats) who will also facilitate European engagement. - UK, Switzerland, Italy, India are showing strong leadership and support - Groups from France, Poland, Spain, Brazil, Netherlands… campaign soon to begin to engage all 26 countries involved - Agreements with individual countries will take 3-4 years, once DOE commits to the project. - And of course, South Dakota, where more than $100M has been invested in the facility to date. 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview **LBNF** **7** ### **P5 “Minimum to Proceed”** - It will take considerable time to secure the international agreements needed for full scope of LBNF/DUNE - Recognizing this, P5 defined a “minimum to proceed”: - “The minimum requirements to proceed are the identified capability to reach an exposure of at least 120 kt*MW*yr by the 2035 timeframe, the far detector situated underground with cavern space for expansion to at least 40 kt LAr fiducial volume, and 1.2 MW beam power upgradable to multi-megawatt power.” - Non-DOE contributions to the LBNF/DUNE project can thus be divided into those needed for the minimum to proceed, and those additional contributions needed to reach the full scope E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview **LBNF** **8** 08.11.15 **LBNF AND DUNE** ### **LBNF/DUNE Scope** - LBNF will provide facilities at Fermilab and at SURF to enable the scientific program of DUNE. - These facilities are geographically separated into - Near Site Facilities, those to be constructed at Fermilab - Far Site Facilities, those to be constructed at SURF. - The DUNE detectors will be installed at SURF (the far site) and FNAL (the near site) will enable the scientific program of DUNE. - Scope is detailed in 4 CDR volumes with individual annexes

For some beam conditions, the muon distribution is clearly driven by the absorber geometry and not the beam - Reliably measuring the centroid, intensity, width will be difficult in these cases 18 6/2/2016 Absorber Design & Muons # A Bit on Flux Measurements - DUNE proposes to measure NC elastic scattering on electrons in the ND to get absolute flux - The claim is that absolute flux measurements are important for some of the physics - CC interactions measure (flux)*(cross section) for oscillations not flux and xs separately - Several possible issues: - NCE on e- produces only ~10-20 events / 10^20 POT / ton argon (not including detector effects) - Will take some time to get a good measurement - There could be a gap between beam & FD being ready and ND being ready 19 6/2/2016 Absorber Design & Muons # More on Flux - Also, ND-only physics cannot make as much use of flux constraints as oscillation physics - (Again – may take a while to get enough NCE on e- events) - Shared systematics - Current absorber (both nominal and “simplified” models used here) – Muons need 8-10 GeV to reach alcove - An absorber this thick will likely make it difficult to measure the flux over the whole range of energies interesting for neutrino physics - If flux measurements not possible, could delay DUNE making competitive measurements for a long time if the ND isn’t ready right away 20 6/2/2016 Absorber Design & Muons # Conclusions - The current absorber geometry clearly has significant influence on the shape of the particle distributions in the muon alcove - Already clear just by altering a couple absorber features - Have also looked at only a limited number of beam conditions, more issues may arise as more simulations are done - Will be difficult to reliably reconstruct beam parameters (centroid, intensity, width, etc) - Will make monitoring much more challenging, less sensitive to beam changes - Absorber size may preclude making good flux measurements (limited phase space) – Still need some more studies here 21 6/2/2016 Absorber Design & Muons # Backups 22 6/2/2016 Absorber Design & Muons # Beam Y Position Scan 20

PD Status – June 12, 2015 Norm Buchanan Colorado State University ### Colorado State University - Director’s Review Review took place at FNAL from June 2-4 • There was an FD overview talk by Jim and no L3-specific talks – i.e. no PD talk - The PD schedule/budget was not selected for “drill-down”. The TPC and Installation were chosen for this. - One recommendation pertained to photon system… <u>Full review report: http://www.fnal.gov/directorate/OPMO/Projects/LBNF-DUNE/DirRev/ 2015/20150602/review.htm</u> Feb 6, 2015 2 Photon Detector Meeting ## Colorado State University Recommendation related to PD system: Seriously consider inclusion in the “reference design” of the photon detector scheme presently considered as “alternative” to allow a better reach in supernova neutrino physics (low energy ~10 MeV). This should be done as quickly as possible. Feb 6, 2015 3 Photon Detector Meeting ## Colorado State University # Next steps • CD1R Review § Delayed by 1 week (now July 14-16) § Similar format as Director’s review - CERN Prototype proposal § Submitted June 8<sup>th</sup> § Presentation to SPSC June 23<sup>rd</sup> Feb 6, 2015 Photon Detector Meeting 4 ## Colorado State University Tallbo Test – IU/CSU/LSU prototype comparison test _(from Denver)_ “TallBo is filled and the LAr level has been stable for two days now. Source: docdb Title: Photon Detector System Update for May 29, 2015 PD Status – May 29, 2015 Norm Buchanan Colorado State University ###### Colorado State University # Technical Review FD Design Independent Review -May 19-20th Close out report circulated via email - Executive Summary: "The purpose of the review was to evaluate the DUNE project's technical progress and readiness to proceed to CD-1 - Refresh. The Committee found that the DUNE project design is sufficiently advanced and that several promising alternative design options were actively being pursued. The Committee was very impressed with the progress made in the LBNE transition to DUNE and encourages a timely advance from prototypes to the industrial production needed to construct and mount the large and complex DuNE as to fully optimize the DUNE experiment. Three areas were considered; TPC and Installation,PhotonDetection and Electronicsand DAQ." ·Very successful -Thanks again to everyone involved Feb 6, 2015 2 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 1 The simulation does not yet allow for the effects of Ar39 decay, cross talk, dark counts or other SIPM effects. What is the plan to incorporate these issues? - 39 Ar Decay: - A radiological “generator” has been written by Tom Junk, we need to turn it on and study the output in the photon detectors. - The tools are ready, we just need (a person) to do the study. - Once we have an estimate of the rate, we can either turn on the simulation all the time, or just increase the effective dark rate to compensate. DUNE FD Technical Review – May 19-20, 2015 3 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 1 - Electronics response: - The following effects have already been implemented in the simulation: - Dark rate - Cross talk - Cable noise - The following are still in the works - Afterpulsing - Saturation - Performance studies with realistic electronics - Need reconstruction to evaluate performance with these effects. - Have prototypes, but not ready for performance studies yet - Have some ideas on how to get to “good enough” to get started - Have a Duke grad student working on these issues now - Hope to have working tools in a few weeks. - Then we just need manpower to do the studies it enables. DUNE FD Technical Review – May 19-20, 2015 4 ###### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 2 The SIPM spec cannot be fully determined (for example cross talk) without knowledge based on simulation. What is the plan for formalizing the SIPM spec? In terms of providing timing for the events – the primary purpose of the PD system – the effect of the SiPM specs are the following: Cross talk Only affects the measured energy of an event – in time with the initial signal After-pulsing More significant issue as it can provide false coincidences giving incorrect timing – but the rate is low (< 10Hz). This is covered by the dark rate spec. S Title of Review – Review Date 5 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 2 Dark Rate ~10 Hz at bias voltage of 24.5 V The simulation to confirm these requirements would be to generate a series of test event samples, scanning over possible values of the cross-talk, after pulsing, etc., and see how the reconstruction performance changes. Timing resolution, fake rate, and reco. efficiency are the obvious metrics. S Title of Review – Review Date 6 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 3 SIPMs have not been extensively used in cryogenic envirnments and may experience effects like premature aging or other issues. What is the plan to qualify the SIPMs for safe operation in this environment. What is an acceptable failure rate in the full detector? How will you know that the chosen SIPM will satisfy this rate? (The Dune electronics group has worried about electronics lifetimes at LAr temperature. Is any of this relevant.) The plan to qualify the SiPMs for cold operation is to both thermally cycle a population of the devices and subject another population to a long term test at cryo temperature. Both of these tests are happening now with small populations. We still need to understand what size of samples is needed to give confidence in device qualification and to project failure rates. Title of Review – Review Date 7 ### Photon Detector Question 3 An example of a study to look at longevity is being carried out at IU. Six devices are being operated (biased) in LN2 for an extended period. Three of the devices are being operated with an increased bias voltage to stress them. Gain Slope @ 24.5 V, SiPMs 4-6

More work is needed to ensure we understand the anticipated failure rate – or the limit on this rate. Title of Review – Review Date 9 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 4 What are the criteria for the optical detector down-select (in addition to the Tallbo cosmic ray test)? 1. The primary criteria is relative performance – coupled with cost. (We have other tests planned for the CSU 500 liter dewar – one just completed with the CSU and LSU alternatives). 2. We will have simulation and reconstruction at the level to allow us to compare relative simulated performance between designs. PDK kaons (200 MeV) as well as SN interactions of 5 MeV and 10 MeV would be good signals to use for the comparison. 3. Complexity of production and handling will also be considered for the down selection. Title of Review – Review Date 10 ##### Colorado State University Executive Summary for Photon Detection System The requirements and documentation of the conceptual design are in place and at the appropriate level for CD-1. However, the reference design has difficulties reaching the performance required to meet the physics goals, specifically the signal to noise. The ability to determine to is a desirable capability for both the proton decay and the supernova physics goals of Dune. Several alternatives were presented that should meet the specification. It would be useful to rapidly choose a reference design that meets the stated goals of Dune with some headroom. Prototype results will soon aid in choosing. In addition, better simulation is needed to evaluate the alternative designs. Extended experience of SiPM in a LAr environment would also help quantify the requirements. Feb 6, 2015 11 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University #### Recommendations for Photon Detection System 1. Develop a requirement for SiPM reliability and develop a plan for verifying that SiPMs can achieve this reliability while operating in LAr. 2. Complete the simulation and reconstruction development and use these tools to better define the requirements on the PD. 3. Continue on the path to make a down-select in the fall. The team should consider the feasibility of continuing low level R&D on a backup as well. 4. Complete a test of the electronics with baseline configuration of 3 SiPMs ganged on a 40m cable. Feb 6, 2015 12 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University ## Summary Overall the review was very successful and when I talked to two of the reviewers after the review they re-iterated that they were very impressed with what the group has accomplished and fully believe that we will be able to deliver a system that will meet the DUNE requirements (which do still need to be optimized with collaboration). The recommendations will figure into prioritization of PD tasks going forward. Director’s review is next week. It depends on a number of things: - Off-project involvement (esp. with international partners) - • Funding levels (expected to be reduced) - Ensuring medium term priorities are met I will keep people informed as I become informed to avoid last minute surprises. question: According to the presentation "SiPM Coupling R&D at UTA", what radius was used for the concave configuration that gave a much more uniform response than the square gap?

generated_answer: The concave configuration used a **3.4 mm radius** to achieve the much more uniform response compared with the square gap.

Title: SiPM Coupling R&D at UTA

UTA DUNE SiPM Coupling R&D J. Yu (A. Brandt, A. White, A. Chaterjee, R. Musser & E. Amador) June 12, 2015 June 12, 2015 DUNE SiPM R&D @ UTA, J. Yu 1 Introduction Our R&D on SiPM scintillator coupling studies began with ORKA Range Stack detector which consists of Scintillator-SiPM + GEM tracking layers Essential for P-ID between K and π High precision position and energy measurements essential The mechanical stability and transmission efficiency of the coupling scheme between scintillation counters and SiPM of critical importance No matter how good the other parts of the detector are, if the coupling is inefficient or mechanically unstable, the light output will be compromised This is especially true for DUNE since it will be under LAr temperature June 12, 2015 DUNE SiPM R&D @ UTA, J. Yu 2 Integrated RS Scintillator and SiPM Readout Scheme SiPM June 12, 2015 DUNE SiPM R&D @ UTA, J. Yu The team Consists of 3 faculty: A. Brandt (TBC), A White and J. Yu One postdoc: Animesh Chaterjee (limited time commitment) Three UG students on this project Ron Musser: Lab Manager LabView software set up, GosSiP SiPM response simulations, data taking, response characterization and data analyses Josh Medford: Deputy Lab manager Assists the lab manager, experimental set up, SiPM data taking Eric Amador : SiPM visual inspection, data taking, response characterization and data analyses June 12, 2015 DUNE SiPM R&D @ UTA, J. Yu 4 SiPM R&D Plans We obtained some funds for photon detector coupling R&D Establish multi-channel desktop SiPM DAQ system Based on NI and LabView DAQ software Now ANL SSP is in play Determine optimal number of SiPM’s to readout the long scintillators to meet the physics requirements Single side vs Double side readout Number of SiPM’s Characterize various SiPM’s with Scintillators Hamatsu? SenSL? How do their performance compare attached to a scintillator Study optimal mating scheme between SiPM and Scintillators Direct coupling versus using (multiple?) wavelength shifting fibers Cold temperature stability June 12, 2015 DUNE SiPM R&D @ UTA, J. Proposal for Contributions to the Development of a photon detector system for the DUNE Liquid Argon TPC Detector for the Period February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016 Overview This statement of work provides details of funding for R&D and design tasks related to the development of a photon detector (PD) sub-detector for the DUNE far detector (FD). Members of the NIU team involved in this effort are: professors Gerald Blazey, Michael Eads and Vishnu Zutshi (PI), senior research scientist Alexander Dyshkant, senior technician Kurt Francis, students and electrical and mechanical machine shops. Funds are requested here to: Set up infrastructure for the evaluation, characterization and long-term performance of Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) in a cryogenic environment Study SiPM parameters and performance in warm and cold conditions Initiate the development of a quality assurance plan and procedure for SiPM qualification for LAr TPC prototypes under the following scheduled activities: 13122.05.290 Test passive ganging of 3 SiPMs 13122.05.300 Test passive ganging of 6 SiPMs 13122.05.310 Prepare final report on passive SiPM ganging The period of execution of these tasks is February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016. The tasks will be executed in coordination with existing members of the PD group especially CSU and Caltech. Statement of Work During FY2016, the NIU group will contribute in the following areas: Initiate SiPM characterization in warm (room temperature) conditions. The test stand will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, x-talk, after-pulsing etc.) using DUNE electronics. Of particular interest will be characterization of ganged sensors. Studies will initially look at performance of three ganged sensors and then explore the possibility of ganging six of them. This task will primarily involve Francis and a student with oversight by Zutshi and assistance from Gary Drake (ANL). Setup cryogenic test-stand for SiPM characterization and qualification. Once the test stand is setup it will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, x-talk, after-pulsing etc.) using DUNE electronics. Ganging studies will be extended to this realm. Failure modes, both electrical and mechanical will be explored. This task will primarily involve Dyshkant, Francis and NIU machine & electrical shops with oversight by Blazey and Zutshi. Detailed comparisons of sensor parameters in warm and cold environments to understand the performance correlations and dependencies. This will be used to demonstrate how well the determination of sensor parameters in the warm environment can be extrapolated to LAr temperatures. This task will primarily involve a student with oversight by Eads. Initiate development of a work plan and procedure for quality control and assurance of SiPMs for the LAr TPC prototypes under design or construction. This should be considered as the first step in the development of long-term (~30 years) qualification procedures for the SiPMs. This task will primarily involve Francis and a student with oversight by Eads and Zutshi. Cost Proposal for Brookhaven National Laboratory N.B. The NIU Division of Research and Innovation Partnerships has approved a cost share of up to $13K.

Proposal for Contributions to the Development of a photon detector system for the DUNE Liquid Argon TPC Detector for the Period February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016 Overview This statement of work provides details of funding for R&D and design tasks related to the development of a photon detector (PD) sub-detector for the DUNE far detector (FD). Members of the Caltech team involved in this effort are: Professor Ryan Patterson, Scientist Leon Mualem, a future Postdoctoral Researcher, Engineer Jason Trevor, and students as needed. Funds are requested here to: Set up infrastructure for the evaluation, characterization and long-term performance of Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) in a cryogenic environment Study SiPM parameters and performance in warm and cold conditions Begin perform long-term testing of a large number, O(200), SiPMs at cryogenic temperatures to monitor for any performance degradation or instability with exposure to significant DC light in the cryogenic fluid. Develop acceptance tests for commercially produced SiPM with sufficient sensitivity to quantify the operating characteristics for operation in the Single-Phase ProtoDUNE detector at the CERN neutrino platform. Coordinate efforts with NIU for development of tests in order to ensure reproducibility and reliability of the testing procedures by repeating measurements and measuring independently with a DC characterization program. The period of execution of these tasks is February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016. The tasks will be executed in coordination with existing members of the PD group especially CSU and NIU. Statement of Work During FY2016, the Caltech group will contribute in the following areas: (1) Setup cryogenic test-stand for SiPM characterization and qualification. Once the test stand is setup it will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, etc.) using commercial test equipment and custom electronics. Failure modes, both electrical and mechanical will be explored. This task will primarily involve Mualem and Trevor and students. (2) Detailed studies of sensor performance of a large number of devices over time while subjected to cold environment to determine if there is any degradation due to exposure to light and cold. This task will primarily involve Mualem and students (3) Develop a DC measurement technique for measuring the characteristics of the DUNE photodetectors to be used as an efficient acceptance and QA test of incoming components for the detectors. This task will primarily involve Mualem and students. (4) As needed work with NIU in understanding the reproducibility of tests done with DUNE electronics, and how it correlates with tests done measuring DC characteristics of the sensors. This task will primarily involve Mualem and students Cost Proposal

Title: Project Management Plan

Level 3 WBS corresponds to major equipment items or technical support activities within subproject systems’ elements. The work at this level has been divided so that, to the extent possible, the responsibility for each subtask can be assigned to a Control Account Manager (WBS 131.xxxx.xx.xx). Due to the breadth of the scope of some subprojects, this is achieved one level down further, at WBS L4. A WBS and WBS dictionary giving a detailed description of each WBS task is presented as a standalone document and is shown graphically in Figure 3. The WBS and Dictionary are controlled documents; changes must be approved by the LBNF PM and DUNE TC, as appropriate. Figure : Work Breakdown Structure to WBS Level 2 Decision Process for Issues that Affect All Project Elements Interface Control LBNF/DUNE uses a system for Interface Control to identify the connections between project elements. The Systems Engineering Manager is responsible to implement a configuration management system, including Interface Control. The Systems Engineering Management Plan describes the interface control system that accounts for interfaces between all deliverables to the combined Projects. This system consists of a complete list of deliverables and associated interface matrices that point to Interface Control Documents (ICD). An ICD describes the multitude of physical and programmatic interfaces between two deliverables or between a deliverable and the existing and/or transitional Near Site or Far Site facilities. The combination of the deliverables list, the matrices, and ICDs represent the full scope of LBNF/DUNE. Changes in One Project Affect Others Major LBNF/DUNE Project interfaces exist at both the Near Site and Far Site. Each major project element has defined scope and cost, and the project schedules are entirely integrated. Therefore, proposed changes may cross project element boundaries. The Systems Engineer Management Plan identifies a Change Control process that includes the EFIG for instances of Change Requests in which one project impacts the scope, cost, and/or schedule of the other, as well as control of certain higher-level milestones. The LBNF/DUNE-US Project Director has approval at specified thresholds for changes to the DOE Project. Lower-level changes can be implemented through the Change Control process at appropriate LBNF/DUNE management levels as defined in the Systems Engineering Management Plan. Project Technical Baseline The LBNF/DUNE Project scope is developed in response to the mission need as documented in project requirements. Design alternatives explored during the conceptual design phase culminated in a reference design configuration at the DOE CD-1 milestone, also known as the preferred alternative. The preliminary design advances until the expected performance is mature, understood, and documented such that it can be baselined with specific performance parameters. After this point, the technical baseline is placed under configuration management in accordance with project procedures, and changes to the baseline at specific thresholds must be approved. As the design is finalized post-baselining, it is documented and reviewed in preparation for fabrication and construction. With construction/fabrication approval, facilities and technical components can be fabricated, constructed, and installed, after which verification that requirements have been satisfied occurs. Design Maturity Assessment Process The US Project defines design maturity based on completion of design reviews at specific points in the design process, which are expected to have specific deliverables completed with each review. Assessment of design maturity also uses cost weighting of project scope including subsystems in the assessment. Design Maturity Calculation Approach Subproject Managers are responsible to assess the overall design maturity periodically as the subproject progresses. Title: Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report

LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report (PSVAR) [lbne-doc-10768] 23 June 2015 Approvals and Signatures Change Log This version of the document may not be the current or approved revision. The current revision is maintained in the former LBNF/DUNE’s document Management system (DocDB) where all internal Project document approvals are also managed. DocDB can be accessed through the web by authorized users (http://lbne2-DocDB-.fnal.gov/) and this document can be identified by the document and version number as indicated in the Version Control Table below. Note: The version number in the table below and DocDB may not match. The current approved version is always available in DocDB. Abbreviations and Acronyms Overview The LBNF/DUNE Project is designed to support the Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science (SC) mission as described in the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF)/ Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) Mission Need Statements. The DOE Mission Need for the LBNF/DUNE Project proposes the following major elements: A neutrino beamline, produced from a primary proton beam, aimed at a far detector site A neutrino detector located at the Far Detector site The LBNF/DUNE Project scope includes construction of experimental systems and facilities at two separate geographical locations. The reference design is planned to achieve the Project's mission in which a proton beam extracted from the Fermilab Main Injector (MI) is used to produce a neutrino beam. The neutrino beam travels through the Earth's mantle to a Far Detector located 1,300 km away in the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF), the site of the former Homestake Mine in Lead, South Dakota. The 1,300-km separation between the sites presents an optimal baseline for LBNF's neutrino-oscillation physics goals. The main scope elements on the Fermilab site, also referred to as the Near Site, include: Magnets and support equipment to transport the extracted protons to the target, where they interact, producing pions and kaons A target and target hall Magnetic focusing horns to direct the pions and kaons into a decay tunnel A decay tunnel where these particles decay into neutrinos A beam absorber at the end of the decay tunnel to absorb the residual secondary hadronic particles Conventional Facilities at Fermilab to support the technical components of the primary proton beam, the neutrino beam and the near detectors. The main scope elements at the Far Site include: The Far Detector Caverns Central Utility Cavern Access/Egress Drifts Cryogenic Compressor Building Ross Dry Building Infrastructure required for the Far Detector Purpose The purpose of this Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report (PSVAR) is to identify the security requirements and integrate these requirements into the LBNF/DUNE Project at the early design phase of the Project’s life cycle. In addition the implementation of those requirements is assessed throughout the Project. Scope The PSVAR evaluates the potential security risk to employees, the public, and the environment at Fermilab during the design, construction, and operational phases of the LBNF/DUNE Project. The PSVAR also develops the effective protection strategies that will be implemented during the Project’s different phases. The successful protection of security interests requires that effective protection strategies and procedures are developed and implemented. The Protection strategy for an asset will include consideration of the threat to the asset as a fundamental part of the design process. Establishing and integrating security requirements early in the projects lifecycle is necessary for project planning, cost estimating, facilities requirements, and to prevent project impacts that can arise when safeguards and security requirements are identified late into the design process, construction, or as part of the operational readiness review. Additionally, due to potential conflicts in meeting site security requirements and the requirements of other critical disciplines such as, safety, the integration of all requirements is critical to developing the best overall cost effective solution for the Project. Objectives The objectives of the PSVAR are as follows: To provide site security advice to Federal Project Directors (FPD) and Federal program/site office managers (contractors and subcontractors as applicable) in identifying and implementing key safeguards and security components of their projects and integrating site security consideration into each acquisition management phase (initiation, definition, execution and transition/closeout). To define security features and functions as developed or required by the security program or security policy, which minimizes impact on operations. To identify the function of the federal site security program representative who serves as security design point of contact for security features and is a member of the Integrated Project Team (IPT) as appropriate during the entire Project cycle. To facilitate communication and interaction between the site security professionals, other integrated project teams and the members of the Project design team. Target Identification and Description The PSVAR for the LBNF/DUNE Project is developed to evaluate the potential risk to employees, the public, and the environment at Fermilab during Project design, construction and operation phases. The Project will not change the site security requirements at Fermilab. The site is designated as a Class PP (Property Protection) facility with nuclear materials graded Category IV, Attractiveness Level E. No sensitive or classified research is conducted by Fermilab. Currently the entry gates provide perimeter access control and basic visitor services and traffic management. The Sanford Underground Research Facility presently has no DOE security classification, as the facility is managed outside of the DOE complex. This classification for the LBNF/DUNE leased space at SURF is presently being studied. Project Facilities The Conventional Facilities scope includes the construction of new structures and modifications to existing structures and laboratory “system-wide” services. Modifications include demolition of structures to clear the way for new construction. The LBNF/DUNE is a particle physics research project. Fermilab researchers have proposed to send a neutrino beam generated by Fermilab to SURF. The LBNF/DUNE Near Site Facilities will be constructed at the Fermilab site located in an area west of Kautz Road and south of Giese Road. In general terms, a proton beam will be extracted from the existing Main Injector, directed north and west towards new below grade enclosures housing the LBNF Target Hall, Absorber Hall, and Near Detector Hall. The proposed Far Detector (FD) and associated Conventional Facilities will be constructed at the SURF. The LAr far detector has a total fiducial mass of 40 kilotons of high purity LAr and will be located underground at the 4850 level in close proximity to the Ross shaft. Near Site Facility Descriptions The LBNF Near Site Facilities consist of the following eight (8) functional areas: Beamline Extraction Enclosure and Primary Beam Enclosure (below grade) Primary Beam Service Building (LBNF 5) (above grade) Target Hall Complex (LBNF 20) (above grade, in fill) Decay Pipe (below grade, in soil and bedrock) Absorber Hall, Muon Alcove and support rooms (below grade, in soil and bedrock) Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30) (above grade) Near Detector Service Building (LBNF 40) (above grade) Near Detector Hall (below grade) This section provides a description of each functional area. Note: All dimensions indicated here are based upon planning that existed at a single point in the conceptual design. These dimensions and other units of measure may change as the Project design continues to evolve. Beamline Extraction Enclosure and Primary Beam Enclosure The first underground functional area is the Beamline Extraction Enclosure and Primary Beam Enclosure. This area, consisting of the upstream Beamline Extraction Enclosure and the downstream Primary Beam Enclosure are required to allow the beam to be extracted from the Main Injector and transported 328 m (1,078 ft) to the LBNF Target Complex. The construction of the upstream portion of this area will consist of a cut-and-cover below-grade section. The downstream portion of this area includes a transition from the below-grade section to an above-grade section located within an embankment. Some of these areas will be constructed using cast-in-place concrete sections and other areas will be pre-cast concrete enclosure sections. The 778-ft long Primary Beam Enclosure will start at the end of the extraction enclosure and continue along a 15% incline into and through the above-grade embankment, and then at a 10% decline to and through the Target Hall. The depth of the enclosure will be 36.5 ft from the top of the soil shielding fill to the invert/floor. This will provide a minimum of 25 ft of soil and concrete shielding (measured from the center of the beamline) for both the 1.2-MW and 2.3-MW beam power levels. The apex of the embankment over the Primary Beam Enclosure will be approximately 70 ft above existing grade. With the required minimum 25 ft of soil and concrete shielding, the apex of the beamline will be 45 ft above existing grade. The Primary Beam Enclosure has interior dimensions measuring 10 ft wide and 8 ft high. Primary Beam Service Building (LBNF 5) One of four at-grade service buildings is the Primary Beam Service Building (LBNF 5). The function of LBNF 5 is to provide housing for primary beam support equipment and utilities, and access for personnel and light equipment to the Primary Beam Enclosure below. This single-story, steel-framed, metal-sided service building will have approximately 3,600 ft2 of floor space (60 ft by 60 ft), with a minimum 12-ft interior clear height. The building will be positioned off center and right of the beamline and will have a corridor (conduits, Gerardi Coffin, and penetrations) for technical and conventional utilities routing to the Primary Beam Enclosure. Target Hall Complex (LBNF 20) The Target Complex (LBNF 20) will be a 22,200 ft2 near-surface facility constructed in the engineered fill embankment, that combines the Target Hall, corresponding beam-on and beam-off support rooms (power supply, remote crane controls, piped system carrying radioactive water (RAW), and air handling rooms), and the Target Hall service rooms (two truck bays with lay down/staging areas, morgue area, maintenance cell, mechanical/utilities rooms, and rest room). Beam-on spaces are accessible by personnel while the beam is energized, and beam-off spaces are only accessible when the beam is not energized. These support and service rooms accommodate the support equipment and utilities and provide access needed to assemble and operate the equipment and conventional and programmatic/technical components for the Target Hall. Decay Pipe The LBNF Decay Pipe begins at the downstream end of the target chase in the Target Hall and continues 668 ft (204 m) at a decline of approximately 10% to the Absorber Hall, which is approximately 94 ft below grade. The Decay Pipe consists of two concentric pipes; the inner pipe is a 13-ft 2-in (4-m) diameter pipe and the outer pipe is a 14-ft 5-in (4.4-m) diameter pipe. Both pipes are ½-inch thick steel pipes surrounded by the required 18-ft 0.5-in (5.5m) cast-in-place concrete shielding. The direction of supply airflow for Decay Pipe cooling is down through the 20-cm annulus between the two concentric decay pipes and returns through the inner decay pipe for the air-cooling of the beam heat load deposited in the steel and concrete shielding surrounding the decay pipe. Absorber Hall The Absorber Hall will be approximately 94 ft below existing grade. The Absorber Hall will house the concrete-shielded hadron absorber and monitor, the Muon Alcove, and the absorber support rooms, all constructed in an open cut soil excavation to bedrock and then a drill-and-blast rock excavation to the base of the underground facility. A water barrier system will be included between the soil and rock excavation and the internal concrete structure to seal the facility from groundwater infiltration. This underground facility will be a two-level cast in place concrete structure. The lower level of the Absorber Hall will house the Absorber, Muon Alcove, sump and pump systems, and will provide the base of the egress shaft. The middle level of this underground facility will house the top of the absorber, and the RAW room the upper level will house the instrumentation room. The roof/ceiling of the underground portion of the facility will serve as the floor of the above ground Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30). Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30) The Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30) consists of the 53-ft wide by 62-ft long above-grade building to accommodate the support equipment and access needed for the assembly and operation of
