LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan [dune-doc-82] October 2019 Approvals and Signatures Change Log This version of the document may not be the current or approved revision. The current revision is maintained in the former LBNF/DUNE’s document Management system (DocDB) where all internal Project document approvals are also managed. DocDB can be accessed through the web by authorized users (http://docs.dunescience.org/) and this document can be identified by the document and version number as indicated in the Version Control Table below. Note: The version number in the table below and DocDB may not match. The current approved version is always available in DocDB. List of Figures Figure 4-1: A Sample Interface Control Matrix 14 Figure 5-1: LBNF/DUNE Change Control Process 19 List of Tables Table 5-1 DOE-Funded Project Change Control Thresholds and Authorities 17 Table 5-2 DUNE Change Control Thresholds and Authorities 18 Abbreviations and Acronyms Overview This Configuration Management Plan (CMP) describes the configuration management (CM) responsibilities and processes that support the design and implementation of the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF), Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), and Integration project elements. The purpose of this CMP is to identify the organization providing the configuration control, describe the change control process, and identify the plan for configuration status accounting and verification. It is a living document that is developed and maintained by the combined efforts of the Projects. LBNF, DUNE, and Integration are separate organizational entities with correlated objectives. Management of these entities is defined in the LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan (PMP) and its Appendices and the DUNE Management Plan (DMP). Roles and responsibilities of management groups and individuals are defined in these management documents. This CMP does not attempt to duplicate information in the PMP or DMP; rather, it defines roles and responsibilities of groups and individuals for Configuration Management and refers to those defined in the PMP and DMP by title only. Due to the differences in the management structures of LBNF and DUNE, it is necessary to distinguish the Projects clearly in this document: LBNF/DUNE is used in reference to the combined and coordinated efforts of the project elements, including Integration LBNF/DUNE-US is used in reference to practices that are applicable to the LBNF, DUNE, & Integration scope funded by DOE LBNF and DUNE is used in reference to efforts undertaken independently by each project toward a common goal (e.g., CM processes unique to each Project that result in the combined LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management) Either LBNF or DUNE or Integration is used in reference to efforts unique to project elements, particularly when the DUNE Collaboration structure dictates a separate process. Purpose This CMP is designed to ensure that: LBNF/DUNE configuration documentation is identified, released and controlled The LBNF/DUNE Configuration Control Manager (CCM) position is established, including definition of roles and responsibilities Processes are established in LBNF and DUNE, and within the LBNF/DUNE global enterprise, by which Configuration Changes are proposed, controlled, managed, approved, implemented and tracked Change Control Boards (CCB) are established and function according to the CMP guidelines Configuration status accounting is implemented This Configuration Management Plan provides for implementation of a system of management and engineering controls that are necessary for effective execution of the Projects. Plan Overview A CMP is employed to identify and control relationships during design and construction at both the Near Site and the Far Site. It is important to maintain clear, concise, and accurate records to remain within cost & schedule boundaries and minimize interface issues. This CMP has been established to ensure that the Projects’ organizations are aware of their roles and responsibilities during the design, construction, and testing phases of the Projects. The main goal of the LBNF/DUNE CMP is to prevent unauthorized or uncontrolled changes to engineering design or analysis, hardware, controlled documents, and controlled software. The plan integrates the various Configuration Management (CM) control systems. It is also meant to focus on the control of active documents and not on longer-term records management, retention, or archiving. The key elements of CM are Configuration Identification, Change Control, Configuration Status Accounting, and Configuration Verification. Configuration Identification defines the system through Computer-Aided Design (CAD) models, drawings, interface and requirements documents that specify the system components in terms of functional and physical characteristics, as well as how they are to be manufactured and tested. All Project elements utilize a single Change Control process as the vehicle by which proposed changes are reviewed and approved. It ensures that the science, technical scope, cost and schedule impacts of each major change are considered before approval is granted. Configuration control is the means to track configuration information and relay it to key personnel in order to support management decisions and ensure that all work is performed according to the current approved design. The Configuration Verification process ensures that the current engineering, facilities, hardware, software and requirements configurations match the intended design by verifying the implementation of each approved change and by conducting periodic configuration audits. Definitions Approval Thresholds – All proposed changes to Project documentation are assigned approval thresholds as per Table 5-1 and Table 5-2 in this CMP and per the draft DOE Project Execution Plan (draft PEP) . Baseline – The point at which requirements and design are formally recorded as a starting point for change control, and after which all changes must be tracked and approved. Change Classification - All proposed Project changes submitted to the Change Control Board for consideration are assigned a “type” and “category” in the Fermilab Baseline Change Request Tool. Configuration changes may affect multiple project WBS elements and may be a combination of cost, schedule or technical change. Change Control Board (CCB) – A board composed of technical and administrative representatives who recommend approval or disapproval of proposed changes to the Projects approved configuration. These are currently considered to be the LBNF Project Management Boards (PMB) and the DUNE Technical Board/Executive Board (TB/EB). Change Request – A proposal to change the preliminary baseline or configuration baseline (defined in Section 3) of the LBNF or DUNE Project. Configuration Management (CM) – The systematic control and evaluation of all changes to the configuration that affect deliverables that have been baselined. Documentation - The controlled data that define the current configuration and controlled changes (both proposed and approved). Interface Control Document – A document that records technical and programmatic interfaces between at least two systems or project elements. An ICD can exist in many different formats such as documents or drawings. Pending Changes - Pending changes are those for which conceptual design has been approved, those that have been approved for implementation, or those that are approved and unincorporated and that have been implemented in the field, but for which the document revision has not been completed. Requirements – A statement of what a sub-system component needs to do in order to meet the science goal of the project Technical Design Report (TDR)– Defines the technical specifications, physical characteristics, and functional operating parameters of the various technical systems and facilities of the LBNF and DUNE projects. Scope and Applicability Scope The scope of the LBNF/DUNE Project encompasses the fabrication and construction of components, systems and facilities for LBNF/DUNE. List of Figures Figure 3-1: High Level View of LBNF/DUNE Near Site Facilities 3-15 Figure 3-2: LBNF/DUNE Near Site at Fermilab 3-16 Figure 3-3: SURF Site in Lead, South Dakota 3-26 Figure 3-4: SURF 4850L Campus Site Plan 3-27 Figure 3-5: Far Detector Configuration 3-27 List of Tables Table 4-1: LBNF/DUNE Conceptual Design Baseline Hazards List 4-30 Table 6-1: Risk Assessment Summary 6-52 Table 8-1: Risk Assessment Summary for Construction Hazards 54 Table 8-2: Risk Assessment Summary for Natural Phenomena Hazards 55 Table 8-3: Risk Assessment Summary for Environmental Hazards 56 Table 8-4: Risk Assessment Summary for Waste Hazards 57 Table 8-5: Risk Assessment Summary for Fire Hazards 58 Table 8-6: Risk Assessment Summary for Electrical Hazards 59 Table 8-7: Risk Assessment Summary for Noise Hazards 60 Table 8-8: Risk Assessment Summary for Cryogenic Hazards 61 Table 8-9: Risk Assessment Summary for Confined Space Hazards 62 Table 8-10: Risk Assessment Summary for Ionizing RAD Inside Accelerator 62 Table 8-11: Risk Assessment Summary for Chemical & Hazardous Material 64 Table 8-12: Risk Assessment Summary for Accelerator/Beamline Hazards 65 Table 8-13: Risk Assessment Summary for Ionizing Radiation Hazards 66 Table 8-14: Risk Assessment Summary for Non-Ionizing Radiation Hazards 67 Table 8-15: Risk Assessment Summary for Material Handling Hazards 68 Table 8-16: Risk Assessment Summary for Experimental Hazards 68 Table 8-17: Risk Consequence Classification 70 Table 8-18: Risk Probability Classification 70 Table 8-19: Risk Category Classification 71 Abbreviations and Acronyms Overview The Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) has been classified as an accelerator facility, subject to the requirements of the Department of Energy (DOE) Accelerator Safety Order, DOE Order 420.2B Safety of Accelerator Facilities. According to the requirements of DOE O 420.2B, a Safety Assessment Document (SAD) is to be developed and an Accelerator Safety Envelope (ASE) established before operations begin. In addition, as the development of a new capital asset, the LBNF/DUNE Project is subject to DOE O 413.3B Program and Project Management for the Acquisition of Capital Assets which requires the development of a Hazard Analysis Report (HAR). This document will address both of these requirements. Given the preliminary nature of the Project, this document will be referred to as a Preliminary Hazards Analysis Report (PHAR). The conceptual design for the LBNF/DUNE has been defined, the proposed facility and experimental layouts have been determined and the reconfiguration of the accelerator has been established. This document establishes the process that will be followed by the LBNF/DUNE Project to identify hazards encountered in the design, construction, commissioning and operation of the facility. Since the LBNF is similar in concept to the existing NuMI facility at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab), this PHAR has a firm basis from recent and relevant experience. Generally, the hazards and risks anticipated to be encountered at LBNF are typical of those previously encountered within the accelerator community. The LBNF/DUNE design team has experience developing safety controls and also has access to the Safety Assessment Documents and Hazards Analysis Reports of recently completed facilities at Fermilab, within the DOE complex, and throughout international accelerator and experimental neutrino facilities. Table 6-1 summarizes the risk categories of identified hazards and their pre-mitigation and post-mitigation conditions. Currently nine of the risk categories have been mitigated to “Low or below” and seven remain at a “Moderate” level. The latter include construction, electrical, chemical, ionizing radiation inside/outside, cryogenics, material Handling and experimental Operations. It is the LBNF/DUNE design objective to reduce hazards to no more than minor on-site and negligible off-site impacts to people and the environment during construction and operations. Introduction The hazards analysis process begins at the conceptual design stage of a project to assure that identified hazards are mitigated early in the evolution of the design. The LBNF/DUNE PHAR will analyze the risks within the Project. The Hazard Analysis process began concurrent at the conceptual design stage to assure that identified hazards are mitigated early in the evolution of the design. A Baseline Hazards List (BHL) was developed as the first step in identifying the potential hazards. This list utilized the best available information, encompassing data from the LBNF/DUNE conceptual design, existing safety basis documentation, subject matter expertise [with conventional facilities, accelerator system, and Environment, Safety & Health (ES&H)] and lessons learned from the DOE accelerator community covering design criteria, regulatory requirements, and related occurrences. It also included a preliminary (pre-mitigation) risk assessment at the subsystem level that identified a risk category before incorporating the ES&H related design and operational controls that are postulated to mitigate those risks. The identified hazards then were further developed in this PHAR where the proposed ES&H design enhancements were taken into consideration. The PHAR re-analyzed the risks including these enhancements and, in certain cases, operational controls to establish a post-mitigation risk category. This category affords a realistic assessment of the residual ES&H risks posed by the LBNF/DUNE facility and is input to the conceptual design. The LBNF/DUNE PHAR will analyze the risks within the Project and details of the Preliminary Hazard Analysis (PHA) process will be further addressed in Chapters 4 and 5 of this document. LBNF/DUNE Background The global neutrino physics community is developing a multi-decade physics program to measure unknown parameters of the Standard Model of particle physics and search for new phenomena. The program will be carried out as an international, leading-edge, dual-site experiment for neutrino science and proton decay studies, which is known as the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). The detectors for this experiment will be designed, built, commissioned and operated by the international DUNE Collaboration. The facility required to support this experiment, the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF), is hosted by Fermilab and its design and construction is organized as a DOE/Fermilab project incorporating international partners. Together LBNF and DUNE will comprise the world's highest-intensity neutrino beam at Fermilab, in Batavia, IL, a high-precision near detector on the Fermilab site, a massive liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) far detector installed deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) 1,300 km away in Lead, SD, and all of the conventional and technical facilities necessary to support the beamline and detector systems. The strategy for executing the experimental program presented in this Conceptual Design Report (CDR) has been developed to meet the requirements set out in the P5 report and takes into account the recommendations of the European Strategy for Particle Physics. It adopts a model where U.S. and international funding agencies share costs on the DUNE detectors, and various international participants provide in-kind contributions to the supporting infrastructure of LBNF. LBNF and DUNE will be tightly coordinated as DUNE collaborators design the detectors and infrastructure that will carry out the scientific program. The scope of the LBNF covers the following components: An intense neutrino beam aimed at the far site. Conventional facilities at both the near and far site. Cryogenics infrastructure to support the DUNE liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) detectors at SURF. The DUNE detectors include a fine-grained neutrino detector and beamline monitoring system located a few hundred meters downstream of the neutrino source a massive LArTPC neutrino detector located deep underground at the far site With the facilities provided by LBNF and the detectors provided by DUNE, the DUNE Collaboration proposes to mount a focused attack on the puzzle of neutrinos with broad sensitivity to neutrino oscillation parameters in a single experiment. The focus of the scientific program is the determination of the neutrino mass hierarchy and the explicit demonstration of leptonic CP violation, if it exists, by precisely measuring differences between the oscillations of muon-type neutrinos and antineutrinos into respectively electron-type neutrinos and antineutrinos. Siting the far detector deep underground will provide exciting additional research opportunities in nucleon decay, studies utilizing atmospheric neutrinos, and neutrino astrophysics, including measurements of neutrinos from a core-collapse supernova should such an event occur in our galaxy during the experiment’s lifetime. Description of the Site, Facility and Operations Characterization of the LBNF/DUNE Site Locations Figure -: High Level View of LBNF/DUNE Near Site Facilities Description of the Fermilab and SURF Sites The Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) is operated by Fermi Research Alliance (FRA) for the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science. In the 1960’s, Fermilab was dedicated to research in experimental and theoretical particle physics using high energy particle accelerators. The Fermilab mission is to advance the understanding of the fundamental nature of matter and energy by providing leadership and resources for qualified researchers to conduct basic research at the frontiers of high energy physics and related disciplines. The proposed LBNF/DUNE Far Site location is presently operated by the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority (SDSTA). The Sanford Underground Research Facility at Homestake (SURF) has been operating since March 2008 with both re-opening activities and early science experimental program active on multiple levels of the facility to the 4850L. Figure -: LBNF/DUNE Near Site at Fermilab Site Locations The LBNF/DUNE is a high energy physics research project. Fermilab researchers have proposed to send a neutrino beam generated by Fermilab to the Sanford Underground Research Facility. The LBNF/DUNE Near Site Facilities will be constructed on the Fermilab site located in an area west of Kautz Road and south of Giese Road, see Figure 3-1. In general terms, a proton beam will be extracted from the existing Main Injector, directed north and west towards new below grade enclosures housing the LBNF/DUNE Target Hall and Absorber Hall. The LBNF/DUNE Beamline complex at Fermilab will be designed to provide a neutrino beam of sufficient intensity and energy to meet the goals of the LBNF/DUNE experiment with respect to long baseline neutrino-oscillation physics. The design is a conventional, horn-focused neutrino beamline. The components of the beamline will be designed to extract a proton beam from the Fermilab Main Injector (MI) and transport it to a target area where the collisions generate a beam of charged particles. This secondary beam, aimed toward the far detector, is followed by a decay-pipe where the particles of the secondary beam decay to generate the neutrino beam. At the end of the decay pipe, an absorber pile absorbs the residual energy from uninteracted protons and the secondary particles (hadrons) that do not decay. The facility is designed for initial operation at proton beam power of 1.2 MW, with the capability to support an upgrade to 2.4 MW. In the reference design, extraction of the proton beam occurs at MI-10, a new installation. After extraction, this primary beam establishes a horizontally straight compass heading west-northwest toward the far detector, but will be bent upward to an apex before being bent downward at the appropriate angle, 101 milliradians, as shown in Figure 3-2 . The primary beam will be above grade for 500 feet; this design minimizes expensive underground construction and significantly enhances capability for ground water radiological protection. The design requires, however, construction of an earthen embankment, or hill, whose dimensions are commensurate with the bending strength of the dipole magnets required for the beamline. The embankment will need to be approximately 950 feet long and 58 feet high above grade at its peak. The Beam Loss Monitor will be located in the region of the Absorber Complex at the downstream end of the decay region to measure the muon fluxes from hadron decay. The Near Detector Hall is located near the west Fermilab site boundary east of Kirk Road, approximately 200 ft underground. The reference design is a straw-tube tracker. Refer to DUNE CDR Volume 4 for additional information.

The SEMP supports and is subordinate to the LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan (PMP), and the DUNE Management Plan. The SEMP defines the technical management across the LBNF/DUNE teams to provide the specific processes required to manage the systems engineering effort, while the other documents describe other project management systems for the DOE Project, LBNF/DUNE-US and DUNE. This group is responsible for assuring that the subprojects are integrated and meet their overall objectives. The members work closely together through a variety of communication methods outlined later in this document, section 11.1. Figure 2: LBNF/DUNE Systems Engineering Responsibilities The system engineering organization has responsibilities for the design development process in three ways. First, it supports project-wide and subproject trade studies and value engineering analyses. Second, it supports integrated technical analyses of the facilities and detectors. Third, system engineering maintains the design baselines by handling configuration management for project and subproject-level configuration items, and the mechanisms whereby technical baselines are modified, and designs implemented. Other responsibilities of the Systems Engineering Manager include: Ensure that all project elements are identified and controlled. Scope and Applicability Scope The scope of the LBNF/DUNE Project encompasses the fabrication and construction of components, systems, and facilities for LBNF/DUNE/Integration. Configuration Management Overview Configuration Management (CM) is employed to identify and control relationships during design and construction at both the Near Site and the Far Site. It is important to maintain clear, concise, and accurate records to remain within cost & schedule boundaries and minimize interface issues. This document has been established to ensure that the Projects’ organizations are aware of their roles and responsibilities during the design, construction, and testing phases of the Projects. One of the main goals of LBNF/DUNE CM is to prevent unauthorized or uncontrolled changes to engineering design or analysis, hardware, controlled documents, and controlled software. Source: docdb Title: The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment # **The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE)** Maury Goodman, _Argonne National Lab for the DUNE Collaboration_ 2 November 2015 ## **Abstract** The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment is a worldwide effort to construct a next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiment based at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory. It is a merger of previous efforts and other interested parties to build, operate and exploit a staged 40-kt Liquid Argon detector at the Sanford Underground Research Facility 1300 km from Fermilab, and a high precision near detector, exposed to a 1.2 MW, tunable _ν_ beam produced by the PIP-II upgrade by 2024, evolving to a power of 2.3 MW by 2030. The neutrino oscillation physics goals and the status of the collaboration and project are summarized in this article. # **1 Introduction** The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) has been established as an international partnership to fulfill the goals established by the Particle Physics Program Prioritization Panel in the United States [1]. The design, goals and status of the collaboration, experiment and project have been recently described in detail in a Conceptual Design Report (CDR) [2] written for a “CD-1 Refresh” review that took place in July 2015 for the U.S. Department of Energy. Members of the international neutrino community broadly agree on the goals for study to remove gaps in our understanding of the neutrino sector in the current Standard Model of Particle Physics: - Determination of the Mass Ordering between the normal mass ordering ( _m_ 3 _> m_ 1; NO) and the inverted ordering ( _m_ 1 _> m_ 3; IO)1 - Determination of the value of the CP(Charge Parity)-violation phase _δ_ - Determination of the octant of _θ_ 23 - More precision in the determination of the values of the mixing angles and ∆ _m_2 values - Search for new physics beyond the three neutrino paradigm - Determination of the overall mass scale - Determination whether the the neutrino is Dirac or Majorana. The first five issues can be addressed with precise new accelerator experiments with detectors located near and far from the proton target. One requires a deep underground location to reduce backgrounds in the search for neutrinoless double beta decay. Through the first > 1A common notation is to call these the normal hierarchy (NH) and inverted hierarchy (IH), but for the case of non-hierarchical degenerate neutrino mass, there is still sensitivity to the ordering, so this paper uses the slightly more precise notation NO and IO. 1 two decades of the 21st century, a large variety of experiments have been proposed to accomplish this program. Since the scale in size and cost is larger than previous neutrino experiments, a large variety of solutions in terms of baseline, location, overburden, detector size, detector design and beam energy spectrum have been investigated to achieve an optimum program. Many of the advocates of these programs have coalesced into a new international collaboration based on two facilities: the Fermilab accelerator complex that will host the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF), and the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) located 1300 km away in South Dakota. LBNF will be operated as a fully international facility hosted by Fermilab. The detectors, totaling 40 kt fiducial mass of Liquid Argon will be designed, built, commissioned and operated by the international DUNE collaboration. The scope of LBNF includes an intense on-axis neutrino beam aimed at the far site, the conventional facilities at both the near and far sites, and the cryogenic infrastructure needed to support the DUNE detector at the far site. The DUNE detectors include a high-performance near neutrino detector, a beamline measurement system, and a massive liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) for use as a neutrino detector deep underground at SURF. DUNE and LBNF encompass an ambitious and long-term program to improve our knowledge of neutrino physics and particle astrophysics. They represent what will be a significant investment by the world’s high energy physics community. The goals of the program will not be accomplished in a single phase. A partially applicable analogy is to look at the tremendous success of the LHC program as of 2015, even though it has not yet run at its design energy of 14 TeV. At the same time that the DUNE physics program is ambitious, the facility and detectors are also flexible in their ability to adapt to changing understanding of the neutrino sector or any new and unexpected physics beyond the three neutrino paradigm that might be uncovered in the coming decade. A previous look at potential future experiments and facilities, including the LBNE program in the United States and the Hyper-Kamiokande program in Japan, is provided in the last special issue on neutrino oscillations in reference [3]. A more detailed look at the science opportunities for LBNE were given in [4]. As this special issue focuses on neutrino mass and oscillations, in this paper I will cover only the oscillation physics of DUNE, and the status of the collaboration. In section 2 I summarize DUNE’s beam physics program. In section 3 some complementary measurements using atmospheric neutrinos are discussed. Other physics capabilities, including nucleon decay, astrophysical neutrinos and neutrino physics in the near detector are covered extensively in references [2] and [4]. I will not review the current design of the 1.2 MW beamline and the other facilities that are described in volume 3 of the CDR or describe in any detail the design for the 40-kt (fiducial volume) LArTPC that can be found in volume 4 [2]. In section 4 I will summarize the current status and timeline for DUNE and LBNF. # **2 Neutrino Oscillation Physics Capabilities using the NuMI beam** SURF is located 1300 km from Fermilab. A study of baseline optimization for the measurement of CP violation, mass ordering, and _θ_ 23 octant in a long-baseline experiment concluded that a detector at a baseline of at least 1000 km in a wide-band _νµ_ beam is the optimal configuration [5]. SURF well satisfies this requirement and as the site of the original Davis 2 solar neutrino experiment, and thoroughly investigated as as a candidate site for a Deep Underground Science and Engineering Lab, it is well suited for a large scientific endeavor. Briefly the optimization comes from the fact that CP violation and matter effects, which are sensitive to the mass ordering, both cause a difference in the rate of neutrino and antineutrino oscillation events. But those differences are different. The size of the asymmetry from the matter effect grows with increasing baseline, and dominates for a baseline over 1000 km. The oscillation probabilities for _νe_ ~~(~~ _~~ν~~ e_ ) appearance in a _νµ_ ~~(~~ _~~ν~~ µ_ ) beam at the Fermilab/SURF distance are shown in Fig. 1 as a function of neutrino energy for several possible values of the CP phase parameter _δCP_ . These curves illustrate the choice of a broadband beam that can not only measure the rate of _νe_ and _~~ν~~ e_ appearance but can also map out the spectrum down to energies of 500 MeV. Figure 1 also informs the decision about beam optimization, such as the choice of proton momentum. That choice involves tradeoffs in secondary particle production, cycle time and beam power, all of which affect the integrated flux. The reference design in Chapter 3 of the CDR [2] has chosen a proton beam energy of 80 GeV, a beam power (after the PIP-II upgrades) of 1.07 MW, a graphite target, a horn current of 230 kA, and a 4 m diameter decay pipe that is 204 m long. Further optimizations of these parameters are continuing and some improvements in sensitivity can be expected as reflected in the curves labeled “optimized design” in some of the sensitivity plots in this paper. The 1300-km baseline allows the neutrino and antineutrinos in the NuMI beam to travel through enough matter to be affected by the MSW effect. This leads to a large asymmetry in the _νµ → νe_ versus _~~ν~~ µ →_ _~~ν~~ e_ oscillation probabilities, the sign of which depends on the mass ordering. There are only two possible values of the ordering, and the asymmetry in the region of the peak flux for DUNE is _±_ 40%, larger than the maximal possible asymmetry due to CP violation. Figure 4 shows how well the mass ordering (called the mass hierarchy in the figures) can be measured as a function of _δCP_ using beam neutrinos. The areas of lower sensitivity are for values of the ordering and _δCP_ where the total asymmetry is smaller, and the better sensitivity happens where the total asymmetry is larger. The value of _θ_ 23 is important, affecting both the statistics and the sensitivity (in opposite directions) to the ordering and to CP violation. Nevertheless, DUNE will be able to unequivocally measure the mass ordering in the three neutrino paradigm for any values of neutrino oscillation parameters. Source: docdb Title: Photon Detector System Update for May 29, 2015 PD Status – May 29, 2015 Norm Buchanan Colorado State University ###### Colorado State University # Technical Review FD Design Independent Review -May 19-20th Close out report circulated via email - Executive Summary: "The purpose of the review was to evaluate the DUNE project's technical progress and readiness to proceed to CD-1 - Refresh. The Committee found that the DUNE project design is sufficiently advanced and that several promising alternative design options were actively being pursued. The Committee was very impressed with the progress made in the LBNE transition to DUNE and encourages a timely advance from prototypes to the industrial production needed to construct and mount the large and complex DuNE as to fully optimize the DUNE experiment. Three areas were considered; TPC and Installation,PhotonDetection and Electronicsand DAQ." ·Very successful -Thanks again to everyone involved Feb 6, 2015 2 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 1 The simulation does not yet allow for the effects of Ar39 decay, cross talk, dark counts or other SIPM effects. What is the plan to incorporate these issues? - 39 Ar Decay: - A radiological “generator” has been written by Tom Junk, we need to turn it on and study the output in the photon detectors. - The tools are ready, we just need (a person) to do the study. - Once we have an estimate of the rate, we can either turn on the simulation all the time, or just increase the effective dark rate to compensate. DUNE FD Technical Review – May 19-20, 2015 3 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 1 - Electronics response: - The following effects have already been implemented in the simulation: - Dark rate - Cross talk - Cable noise - The following are still in the works - Afterpulsing - Saturation - Performance studies with realistic electronics - Need reconstruction to evaluate performance with these effects. - Have prototypes, but not ready for performance studies yet - Have some ideas on how to get to “good enough” to get started - Have a Duke grad student working on these issues now - Hope to have working tools in a few weeks. - Then we just need manpower to do the studies it enables. DUNE FD Technical Review – May 19-20, 2015 4 ###### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 2 The SIPM spec cannot be fully determined (for example cross talk) without knowledge based on simulation. What is the plan for formalizing the SIPM spec? In terms of providing timing for the events – the primary purpose of the PD system – the effect of the SiPM specs are the following: Cross talk Only affects the measured energy of an event – in time with the initial signal After-pulsing More significant issue as it can provide false coincidences giving incorrect timing – but the rate is low (< 10Hz). This is covered by the dark rate spec. S Title of Review – Review Date 5 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 2 Dark Rate ~10 Hz at bias voltage of 24.5 V The simulation to confirm these requirements would be to generate a series of test event samples, scanning over possible values of the cross-talk, after pulsing, etc., and see how the reconstruction performance changes. Timing resolution, fake rate, and reco. efficiency are the obvious metrics. S Title of Review – Review Date 6 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 3 SIPMs have not been extensively used in cryogenic envirnments and may experience effects like premature aging or other issues. What is the plan to qualify the SIPMs for safe operation in this environment. What is an acceptable failure rate in the full detector? How will you know that the chosen SIPM will satisfy this rate? (The Dune electronics group has worried about electronics lifetimes at LAr temperature. Is any of this relevant.) The plan to qualify the SiPMs for cold operation is to both thermally cycle a population of the devices and subject another population to a long term test at cryo temperature. Both of these tests are happening now with small populations. We still need to understand what size of samples is needed to give confidence in device qualification and to project failure rates. Title of Review – Review Date 7 ### Photon Detector Question 3 An example of a study to look at longevity is being carried out at IU. Six devices are being operated (biased) in LN2 for an extended period. Three of the devices are being operated with an increased bias voltage to stress them. Gain Slope @ 24.5 V, SiPMs 4-6

Simulation Review Follow-up: Photons from 39Ar Tolerable SiPM Failure Rate Alex Himmel DUNE Photon Detector Meeting Friday, May 29th, 2015 1 Photons from 39Ar 39Ar β decays, ~500 keV endpoint 12,000 photons Energy is low, but visible if close to the PDs 3.5 γ’s if decay is close to the PDs geo ε = 10% geo, det. ε = 0.3% A potentially significant background rate 1.01 Bq/kg Study the effect using Tom Junk’s radiological generator Simulated events throughout 4APA geometry – active and passive Ar 39Ar Spectrum 2 Radiological Simulation At right is 1 OpDet in a 6.4 ms event Assuming IU radiator design ~0.3% det. efficiency True photons – no dark noise Usually see a low rate of single hits Occasionally see a correlated burst of 3 or 4 hits Possibly 39Ar decay close to a PD surface 3 Total Rate Total expected rate is large relative to our dark noise (x50) Assumes IU radiator design 0.32% average det. efficiency. Better detectors make this background worse. 4 Coincidence Rate Observed rate of 2-γ coincidences is much higher than expected from Poisson statistics Likely source, decays close to the PDs with noise on SiPMs ~negligible unless malfunctioning May have implications for data rate Correlated hits are a much larger problem SN event rates are ~100 Hz, overwhelmed by 330 kHz Potential mitigation with selection cuts A 2-hit SN event is likely far from the APA Hits on multiple PDs A 2-hit 39Ar event is likely close to the APA All hits on a single PD A potential selection: exclude small flashes Title: DUNE Governance Document

Governance of the DUNE Collaboration The DUNE Collaboration DUNE-docdb-1 Version 10, approved on 25-July-2026 Table of Contents Preamble Preparation, Approval and Amendments of the Agreement Collaboration membership Institutional Board Co-Spokespersons Deputy Spokesperson Executive Board Collaboration General Assembly Young DUNE Physics, Technical and Resource Coordinators Other Management Structures Dissenting opinions and Procedure to Appeal Attachments Records of drafts and amendments Preamble The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a multi-purpose neutrino and nucleon decay experiment that will use the Fermilab accelerator complex, a neutrino beam line, a near detector complex, and a far detector composed of a set of large liquid argon TPC’s situated deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, Lead, South Dakota, U.S.A. The DUNE experiment will be designed and constructed by the collaborating institutions (The DUNE Collaboration). This document, “Governance of the DUNE Collaboration” (GDC) provides a formal framework of the governance of the DUNE Collaboration. The participating institutions and collaborators recognize that the DUNE experiment is an exciting and important experiment that must be designed, constructed, operated and completed successfully. The DUNE Collaboration recognizes the core values of international scientific collaboration across borders as a driver for peace. We work together in the spirit of peaceful collaboration, and we are unified in support of fundamental human rights. Thus, all participants agree that they will do their best to collaborate in a congenial and constructive manner beyond the language of this document for the ultimate success of the experiment. The relationship between the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) and the DUNE collaboration as well as their respective roles are described in the DUNE/LBNF Project Management Plan (See Attachment A.1). Article 1 Amendments of the Agreement Amendments to this document can be made as needed by a 2/3 majority vote by the DUNE Institutional Board (IB), which is defined in Article 3. The proposed amendments must be announced at least two weeks ahead of an IB meeting and the outcome will be determined by a vote. Article 2 Collaboration Membership § 2.1 Membership of the DUNE Collaboration Members of the DUNE collaboration must be affiliated with collaborating institutions. The IB representative for an institution has the following responsibilities: determination of the list of DUNE members at the institution; notifying the IB Chair of any changes to institutional membership; ensuring that members of the institution fulfill agreed commitments to DUNE. (The different types of members and their responsibilities are defined in attachment A.6.) Through their membership of the DUNE collaboration, collaborators agree to abide by the DUNE Community Agreement (see attachment A.5). Membership in the DUNE collaboration may be restricted, suspended or revoked for serious violations of the DUNE Community Agreement or the general principles stated in this document, as determined by the procedures provided in that document. Restrictions may include qualifications or limits to the privileges of membership. Collaborators whose membership has been revoked may not reapply for membership. The DUNE Collaboration recognizes that collaborating institutions or their funding agencies may sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with relevant parties that defines in whole or in part their contribution to the experiment. § 2.2 Admission of New Institutions and New Senior Members to DUNE A prospective new institution, after conferring with the Co-Spokespersons, will submit a written application to the IB Chair and to the Co-Spokespersons at least two weeks prior to the meeting of the IB at a scheduled IB meeting. The application will include a proposal stating the intended contributions that the prospective institution is proposing to make to the experiment and a well thought out plan for the group’s effective participation in the experiment, and include CV’s and past research experience of the proposed senior members (faculty or equivalent) from the institution. For a successful application, there must be at least one senior member in the institution who proposes to join. The IB Chair will circulate the application materials to the IB members prior to the meeting and put consideration of the application on the agenda of the IB meeting, which may include a presentation by the prospective institution. The IB may ask for verbal or written clarifications of items in the application. The IB may: (1) approve the proposal and formally admit the institution to the Collaboration, (2) request written clarifications to be considered at the next IB meeting, or (3) reject the proposal. IB approval should be sought if new persons of rank equivalent to faculty at a member institution wish to join the collaboration. The IB will attempt to make decisions on admission of new institutions or new members by consensus. If consensus is not possible, an open vote will be taken on admission. Admission will require a 2/3 majority vote, in favor of the application, of those representatives with the right to vote present and voting (an abstention is not a vote for this purpose). Existing senior members of the collaboration who move to a different collaborating institution should notify the IB Chair and Co-Spokespersons but do not require IB approval to change their DUNE institutional affiliation. § 2.3 Associate Membership The collaboration may decide to admit associate institutions. The type of membership must be specified during the application process. Associate Institutions will join the collaboration for an initial period of 2 years, which can be extended by application to the IB. The purpose of this limited membership is either to prepare an intuition for full membership or for it to make time- or subject-limited contributions to the experiment, which do not justify full membership. IB representatives of associate institutions can attend IB meetings but not vote (see § 3.3). § 2.4 Secession from DUNE An institution may leave the collaboration by notification to the IB chair. However, the items contributed to the experiment by the out-going institution that are not covered by any relevant MOUs may not be removed without an approval by the IB. § 2.5 Removal of Institutions from DUNE Removal of an institution from DUNE can be proposed by any IB or Executive Board member for actions by the institution that are judged to be gravely detrimental to the experiment, against the spirit of peaceful collaboration laid out in this document, or for no activity in the experiment by the institution for more than one year. An open vote will be taken on removal. Removal will require a 2/3 majority vote, in favor of the removal, of those representatives with the right to vote present and voting (an abstention is not a vote for this purpose). Details of the procedure are specified in attachment A.7 and A.8. Article 3 Institutional Board § 3.1 Role of the Institutional Board In general, the Institutional Board (IB) is responsible for establishing governance rules of the DUNE collaboration and regulating the governance related issues. The responsibilities of the IB include but are not limited to: admission of new collaborating institutions and members; oversight of Co-Spokesperson election process; approval of common funds assessments; establishment and governance of detector operations shifts; and establishment of procedures for publication of scientific results and authorship rules. The IB can request presentations on and discussion of specific issues relating to the collaboration or the experiment. The results of such discussions may be recorded and passed to the Co-Spokespersons as formal advice. § 3.2 Membership of the Institutional Board All collaborating institutions except the host lab will be given one seat in the IB regardless of their varying sizes. Fermilab will be given two seats to reflect the lab’s large DUNE membership as well as its role as the host lab of the DUNE experiment. Each institution designates its IB representative. § 3.3 IB Voting In general, the IB will attempt to make decisions by consensus. If consensus is not reachable, the IB can have open or secret votes on various issues. Normally, IB votes will be open votes and each IB member’s vote will be counted as one vote regardless of the number of collaboration members they represent. On issues deemed to be sensitive the IB can decide to have a secret vote, which can be triggered by a motion by any IB member. The IB will then decide whether to have a secret vote or not on the issue by an open vote. Even for secret votes, the “one IB representative, one vote” principle will normally apply. For exceptional cases, the IB can decide to have a secret vote that is weighted by the number of collaboration members (eligible voters for general election) each IB member represents, following the procedure described above. Any IB representative that attends an IB meeting physically or virtually will be considered present for that meeting. For votes conducted during a scheduled IB meeting, representatives of the IB must be present at the time of the vote to vote and, when required, to count toward quorum; if unable to attend, a member may designate another collaboration member from their institution to attend by notifying the IB chair prior to the start of the meeting. # **Governance of the DUNE Collaboration** ## **The DUNE Collaboration** ## **DUNE-docdb-1** ## **Version 10, approved on 25-July-2026** ## **Table of Contents** Preamble - 1 Preparation, Approval and Amendments of the Agreement - 2 Collaboration membership - 3 Institutional Board - 4 Co-Spokespersons - 5 Deputy Spokesperson - 6 Executive Board - 7 Collaboration General Assembly - 8 Young DUNE - 9 Physics, Technical and Resource Coordinators - 10 Other Management Structures - 11 Dissenting opinions and Procedure to Appeal - 12 Attachments Records of drafts and amendments 1 ## **_Preamble_** The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a multi-purpose neutrino and nucleon decay experiment that will use the Fermilab accelerator complex, a neutrino beam line, a near detector complex, and a far detector composed of a set of large liquid argon TPC’s situated deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, Lead, South Dakota, U.S.A. The DUNE experiment will be designed and constructed by the collaborating institutions (The DUNE Collaboration). This document, “Governance of the DUNE Collaboration” (GDC) provides a formal framework of the governance of the DUNE Collaboration. The participating institutions and collaborators recognize that the DUNE experiment is an exciting and important experiment that must be designed, constructed, operated and completed successfully. The DUNE Collaboration recognizes the core values of international scientific collaboration across borders as a driver for peace. We work together in the spirit of peaceful collaboration, and we are unified in support of fundamental human rights. Thus, all participants agree that they will do their best to collaborate in a congenial and constructive manner beyond the language of this document for the ultimate success of the experiment. The relationship between the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) and the DUNE collaboration as well as their respective roles are described in the DUNE/LBNF Project Management Plan (See Attachment A.1). ## **_Article 1_** ## **_Amendments of the Agreement_** Amendments to this document can be made as needed by a 2/3 majority vote by the DUNE Institutional Board (IB), which is defined in Article 3. The proposed amendments must be announced at least two weeks ahead of an IB meeting and the outcome will be determined by a vote. ## **_Article 2_** ## **_Collaboration Membership_** ## § 2.1 Membership of the DUNE Collaboration Members of the DUNE collaboration must be affiliated with collaborating institutions. The IB representative for an institution has the following responsibilities: 1. determination of the list of DUNE members at the institution; 2. notifying the IB Chair of any changes to institutional membership; 3. ensuring that members of the institution fulfill agreed commitments to DUNE. (The different types of members and their responsibilities are defined in attachment A.6.) Through their membership of the DUNE collaboration, collaborators agree to abide by the DUNE Community Agreement (see attachment A.5). Membership in the DUNE collaboration may be restricted, suspended or revoked for serious violations of the DUNE Community Agreement or the general principles stated in this document, as determined by the procedures provided in that document. Restrictions may include qualifications or limits to the privileges of membership. Collaborators whose membership has been revoked may not reapply for membership. The DUNE Collaboration recognizes that collaborating institutions or their funding agencies may sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with relevant parties that defines in whole or in part their contribution to the experiment. 2 ## § 2.2 Admission of New Institutions and New Senior Members to DUNE A prospective new institution, after conferring with the Co-Spokespersons, will submit a written application to the IB Chair and to the Co-Spokespersons at least two weeks prior to the meeting of the IB at a scheduled IB meeting. The application will include a proposal stating the intended contributions that the prospective institution is proposing to make to the experiment and a well thought out plan for the group’s effective participation in the experiment, and include CV’s and past research experience of the proposed senior members (faculty or equivalent) from the institution. For a successful application, there must be at least one senior member in the institution who proposes to join. The IB Chair will circulate the application materials to the IB members prior to the meeting and put consideration of the application on the agenda of the IB meeting, which may include a presentation by the prospective institution. The IB may ask for verbal or written clarifications of items in the application. The IB may: (1) approve the proposal and formally admit the institution to the Collaboration, (2) request written clarifications to be considered at the next IB meeting, or (3) reject the proposal. IB approval should be sought if new persons of rank equivalent to faculty at a member institution wish to join the collaboration. The IB will attempt to make decisions on admission of new institutions or new members by consensus. If consensus is not possible, an open vote will be taken on admission. Admission will require a 2/3 majority vote, in favor of the application, of those representatives with the right to vote present and voting (an abstention is not a vote for this purpose). Existing senior members of the collaboration who move to a different collaborating institution should notify the IB Chair and Co-Spokespersons but do not require IB approval to change their DUNE institutional affiliation. ## § 2.3 Associate Membership The collaboration may decide to admit associate institutions. The type of membership must be specified during the application process. Associate Institutions will join the collaboration for an initial period of 2 years, which can be extended by application to the IB. The purpose of this limited membership is either to prepare an intuition for full membership or for it to make time- or subject-limited contributions to the experiment, which do not justify full membership. IB representatives of associate institutions can attend IB meetings but not vote (see § 3.3). ## § 2.4 Secession from DUNE An institution may leave the collaboration by notification to the IB chair. However, the items contributed to the experiment by the out-going institution that are not covered by any relevant MOUs may not be removed without an approval by the IB. ## § 2.5 Removal of Institutions from DUNE Removal of an institution from DUNE can be proposed by any IB or Executive Board member for actions by the institution that are judged to be gravely detrimental to the experiment, against the spirit of peaceful collaboration laid out in this document, or for no activity in the experiment by the institution for more than one year. An open vote will be taken on removal. Removal will require a 2/3 majority vote, in favor of the removal, of those representatives with the right to vote present and voting (an abstention is not a vote for this purpose). Details of the procedure are specified in attachment A.7 and A.8. 3 ## **_Article 3 Institutional Board_** ## § 3.1 Role of the Institutional Board In general, the Institutional Board (IB) is responsible for establishing governance rules of the DUNE collaboration and regulating the governance related issues. The responsibilities of the IB include but are not limited to: admission of new collaborating institutions and members; oversight of Co-Spokesperson election process; approval of common funds assessments; establishment and governance of detector operations shifts; and establishment of procedures for publication of scientific results and authorship rules. The IB can request presentations on and discussion of specific issues relating to the collaboration or the experiment. The results of such discussions may be recorded and passed to the Co-Spokespersons as formal advice. ## § 3.2 Membership of the Institutional Board All collaborating institutions except the host lab will be given one seat in the IB regardless of their varying sizes. Fermilab will be given two seats to reflect the lab’s large DUNE membership as well as its role as the host lab of the DUNE experiment. Each institution designates its IB representative. ## § 3.3 IB Voting In general, the IB will attempt to make decisions by consensus. If consensus is not reachable, the IB can have open or secret votes on various issues. Normally, IB votes will be open votes and each IB member’s vote will be counted as one vote regardless of the number of collaboration members they represent. On issues deemed to be sensitive the IB can decide to have a secret vote, which can be triggered by a motion by any IB member. The IB will then decide whether to have a secret vote or not on the issue by an open vote. Even for secret votes, the “one IB representative, one vote” principle will normally apply. Title: Minutes of the DUNE Institutional Board, 5 June 2015

Minutes of the DUNE institutional board meeting by telephone of 5 June 2015, 9:00 am U.S. Central Time Approved 14 August 2015 Present: The meeting was called to order by IB chair Maury Goodman 1. Minutes The minutes of the first official DUNE institutional board meeting of 18 April 2015 were approved. DUNE-docdb-14. Minutes were also included for the ELBNF institutional board meetings of 22 January 2015, 20 February 2015, 6 March 2015 and 13 March 2015, in which many of the DUNE structures were established. They are all included in docdb-14. 2. Discussion of Election Procedures During the spokesperson elections and the executive committee elections, there were a couple of complaints that the ballots were made by email and weren't strictly secret ballots. The committee(s) running the elections investigated numerous voting systems and did not (yet) find one that prevented the person from running the election from finding out how people voted if he/she chose to do so. We only want valid voters to vote but we aren't together in person. For both the spokesperson and executive committee elections there was one instance of an ineligible voter submitting a vote (just due to misunderstanding - nothing nefarious). Maury plans to investigate a "token" system. Alternative suggestions are welcomed. In the meantime, such as for the approval of appointed EC nominees, votes will be done by email with the counting done by a secretary who doesn't know or care who votes for whom. 3. Need for a governance amendment - IB vice chair The IB chair was thinking of appointing Lisa Whitehead from Houston as a deputy, to run meetings in his absence, and to distribute applications for membership in DUNE when we get them. Alfons Weber, who had helped to draft the governance rules, pointed out that this wasn't covered under those rules and an amendment to the rules would be needed. A governance amendment will be considered at a later date. 4. Approval of DUNE logo The result of the logo contest was a preference for a design that had been made by Louisa Castomonte, the wife of Cesar Castromonte from Goias. The logo was tuned by the Fermilab Media Services Department and this process iterated a few times with communication between that department and the designer. The result is 6 versions of the logo, with two layouts (vertical and horizontal) and three color patterns (colored, black on white, and white on black). There was considerable discussion, particularly about the ability to distinguish the two neutrinos which make up the N in the black on white and white on black versions. Maury will ask Media Services if they can solve this problem with a thin line or a greyscale. The IB chair asked for the following motion which was made and seconded: The IB approves the logo as submitted by FNAL and authorizes the IB chair to thank: Louisa Castromonte (wife of Cesar Castromonte from Goias) for creating the winning design Diana Brandonisio (FNAL) for tweaking the design and for vectorizing it (not yet done) Dan Cherdack (Col State) for running the elections The motion passed on a voice vote. The logos are available in docdb-4 5. Appointment of member to the executive committee There are two slots on the executive committee to be filled by Spokesperson nomination and IB ratification (Section 6.3 of the governance document). At this time, the spokespersons were nominating Bonnie Fleming for one of the two positions. A vote was taken by email to dune-election@fnal.gov, and the nomination was accepted unanimously. 6. September collaboration meeting It was previously decided that the September collaboration meeting would be in Fermilab or South Dakota. Attempts were made to plan the meeting in Deadwood, but they did not work out, in part because of the 75th Sturgiss motorcycle rally a month earlier was keeping all of the hotels filled. We also investigated holding the meeting in Rapid City SD, and that possibility existed, but we were told that good hotel prices and availability would be limited for the same reason. So the decision was made to go to Fermilab, with Deadwood and Rapid City meetings in the future. A doodle poll was taken between 2-5 September and 9-12 September and the clear preferences was 2-5 September. 7. Future collaboration meetings The January 2016 meeting should be held in a warm U.S. location. Initial conversations have been held with collaborators from University of Texas at Arlington, and Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge. Maury was asked to conduct a doodle poll of these two locations with possible dates. A possible future meeting schedule of May 2016 in Deadwood, September 2016 at Fermilab, and January 2017 in CERN was mentioned. Chris Mauger pointed out that we had skipped July this year due to the CD1-refresh, and that would be a good month for a meeting. The EC will be asked to consider a March-July-November schedule along with a January-May-September rotation. 8. Establishment of a committee to establish procedures for a DUNE speaker's committee When a new chair is appointed for the DUNE speaker's committee, a set of SC procedures will be drafted to be discussed by the executive committee and approved by the IB. Respectively Submitted Maury Goodman

Discussion of the White Paper on International Governance (WLIG) prepared by a committee chaired by Joe Lykken, (available at https://indico.fnal.gov/getFile.py/access?resId=0&materialId=0&confId=9209) Question: Should the Technical Coordinator be a lab employee? they are reporting to the spokespeople on a daily basis. they play the role of providing an interface for connected areas. The Memorandum of Collaboration, prepared by a subcommittee of the iIEB chaired by Chang Kee Jung and Stefan Soldner-Rembold and available at https://indico.fnal.gov/internalPage.py?pageId=2&confId=9209 Sergio started with the voting system for spokespersons. Question: Are all elections (IB chair, WG leaders, etc.) to be done the same way? There were discussions of pros and cons. It was pointed out the MOC was a limited document just to get the collaboration started. Question: Do people sign the MOC? Answer: No. It is not an MOU nor a legal document. The collaboration will be built from institutions that sign the LOI. There was an issue raised about the definition of an experimental physicist. After an extended discussion, a motion was made to clarify by adding language to "a faculty member or equivalent" to be "who makes a contribution to the experiment". That motion was passed. The vote to adopt the MOC was passed apparently unanimously. 3. Formation of co-Spokespersons election committee (SEC) This will be approximately 3 people. Send nomination of candidate members, including self-nomination, to sergio.bertolucci@cern.ch by this weekend. Question: Does it need to be an IB member? There was discussion on both sides of this issue. The timing of notification of candidates to the Fermilab Director was discussed. 4. Formation of Collaboration governance document. Proposal for about 5 members. Send nomination of candidate members, including self-nomination, to sergio.bertolucci@cern.ch by this weekend. For this committee, Sergio will propose names and they will be approved at the next IB meeting. Comment: There needs to be a process defined to approve any by-laws. Comment: When draft by-laws are written, there needs to be a significant comment period and process for incorporating comments. 5. Order of business The following schedule was worked out and approved for the spokesperson election cycle: 25 Jan Sunday - nominations for election committee 3 names to Sergio.bertolucci@cern.ch 28 Jan Wednesday - circulate list of committee; IB should endorse SEC will ask for spokesperson nominations from IB members and collect names by Sunday 1 February and stay open for one week, no later than 8 February The committee meets, checks with nominees within 5 days by Friday 13 February Friday 27 February the nominees post statements/bios Voting 27 Feb to 6 March, SEC announces 7 March 6. Working Groups (WG) Sergio proposed to nominate five members to the interim Experimental Facility Interface Group (iEFIG): Mark Thomson Marzio Nessi Andre Rubbia David Lissauer Jim Stewart This was approved. There was discussion of the Facility Project input to this group, and Jim Strait, Elaine McCluskey and Mike Headley were mentioned. Sergio proposed that the IB vote on the interim WG leaders. As discussion progressed, this changed to a proposal that Sergio propose the interim leaders and they be endorsed by the IB. The IB voted for this idea with no apparent opposition. There was some discussion of the role of the CDR and TDR. 7. Collaboration name People are asked to suggest collaboration names by sending the name and a short explanation to maury.goodman@anl.gov by 1 February. Dan Cherdack will use these to organize a naming contest. There was a consensus that this vote should be left to the full collaboration but would need to be endorsed by the IB. 8. Next meeting dates After discussion, three dates in March/April will be sent to the IB for a doodle poll. Starting next week, there will be weekly one hour meetings of the whole collaboraiont at 9:00 am Central Time on Fridays. Sergio will set the agenda. 9. Random discussion There was a question what the charge for the WGs was. The goal is to establish content for the CDR and start progress toward the TDR. The CDR would have the physics scope and options. The meeting was adjourned respectfully submitted Maury Goodman

Such interim action may not modify this governance document; change authorship rights; impose new common funds assessments; or establish continuing institutional obligations. Interim action expires after 90 days or at the next IB meeting whichever occurs earlier. ## § 3.4 Chair and vice-chair of the Institutional Board The IB Chair is elected by the IB for a two-year term. The term is renewable. The IB Chair election process should commence in March in the election year. The IB Chair election will be carried out by an IB-appointed ad hoc three-member election committee. The election committee members may not stand for the election. The committee will receive up to three nominations from each IB representative. The committee will contact all nominees with three or more nominations to ascertain their willingness to stand for the election. The election will be held electronically by using the Preferential Voting System (PVS) in which an IB member submits a fully ranked list of the candidates. In the case of a single candidate, the voting procedure will be a simple Yes or No on the appointment of the candidate as IB Chair; a simple majority of Yes votes is required to elect the candidate. The IB chair may appoint a vice-chair with the same term, subject to the approval of the IB. The IB chair will only vote in the case of a tie; the vice-chair will vote as a regular IB representative. If the IB Chair cannot complete the full two-year term, a new IB Chair will be elected immediately according to the procedures described above, except that the IB will decide when the special election should commence. The newly elected IB Chair will serve the remainder of the term of the replaced IB Chair in addition to the nominal two-year term. The IB chair can be removed at any time by the IB by a secret ballot of at least 2/3 of those present at a scheduled IB meeting. The quorum for the vote is 2/3 of the entire IB membership. A two-week notice is required for a vote for removal, and such a vote will be taken if at least five IB members propose such a vote to the Co-Spokespersons. One of the Co-Spokespersons will 5 conduct the vote. In the event of a removal, the open position will be filled following the procedure described above. The newly elected IB Chair will have a term that includes the remaining term of the removed IB Chair in addition to the nominal two-year term. ## § 3.5 IB Meetings The IB meets at every collaboration meeting normally in person. In addition, the IB Chair may call an IB meeting by video/phone. Every IB meeting should have a well-defined agenda and a preliminary agenda will be distributed to the IB at least two weeks ahead of the IB meeting. In particular, any agenda items containing proposals that require voting by IB should be presented to the IB along with any supporting materials at the time of distribution of the preliminary agenda. The preliminary agenda will identify any proposed vote as routine, major collaboration-wide policy, or governance, and will state any applicable quorum and majority requirements. If, before the meeting begins, at least five IB members request the IB Chair that an item be treated as a higher category, the item will be classified accordingly. An item identified as major collaboration-wide policy or governance may not be downgraded. ## § 3.6 IB Committees The IB or its Chair may establish various committees as needed. ## **_Article 4_** ## **_Co-Spokespersons_** Considering the international nature of the project, it is generally desirable to have one CoSpokesperson from US institutions and the other from non-US institutions. ## § 4.1 Number of Co-Spokespersons and their Role There will be two equal Co-Spokespersons of the collaboration. The Co-Spokespersons are the scientific leaders and representatives of the collaboration. The Co-Spokespersons will equally share leadership, authority and responsibilities. The longest serving of the Co-Spokespersons serves as the Executive Board Chair, and the shortest serving of the Co-Spokespersons serves as the Collaboration General Assembly Chair. The Co-Spokespersons are responsible for preparing agendas for collaboration meetings. The Co-Spokespersons will work very closely with the Executive Board on all major collaboration matters, seek advice from the Institutional Board, and bring major issues to the Collaboration General Assembly for discussions. The Co-Spokespersons will also work closely with the host lab Director and the LBNF management team. The CoSpokespersons will bear authority and responsibilities for the day-to-day matters of the collaboration. ## § 4.2 Election Procedure and Terms The Co-Spokespersons will serve two-year terms, staggered so that one new Co-Spokesperson is elected each year. The term of a Co-Spokesperson is renewable, but it is only renewable once. The Co-Spokesperson election process should commence around December every year, and the new Co-Spokesperson should start his or her term on April 1. The IB Chair will initiate the election process by establishing a Co-Spokesperson Search Committee (CSSC). The composition of the search committee will be proposed by the IB chair and will be approved by the IB. The CSSC members may not stand for the election. The committee will choose its own chair. CSSC will then receive nominations from all eligible voters (up to three nominations per nominator). The committee will contact all nominees with three or more nominations to produce an initial list of candidates who are willing to stand for the election. The committee will then interview the candidates and produce a short list of candidates able to serve as co-spokesperson (normally no 6 more than 5 candidates). The chair of the CSSC will inform the host lab director of the proposed slate of candidates. The slate of candidates will then be presented to the collaboration for a general election. The election will be held electronically by using the Preferential Voting System (PVS) in which a voter submits a fully ranked list of the candidates. In the case of a single candidate, the voting procedure will be a simple Yes or No on the appointment of the candidate as co-spokesperson; a simple majority of Yes votes is required to elect the candidate. All voting collaborators as defined in attachment A6, who have been the members of the DUNE collaboration for at least one year prior to the election opening date, will be eligible to vote. Further requirements for voter eligibility may be imposed by the IB. In case of a tie, the following sequence of events will be followed 1. A rerun of the original election with the top two candidates. 2. If this results in a tie, the IB will vote on the candidates (without the chair having the deciding vote). 3. If this results in a tie, the IB chair will flip a coin. If one of the Co-Spokespersons cannot complete the full two-year term, a new Co-Spokesperson will be elected using the procedure described above, except that the IB Chair will decide when the special election should commence and when the new Co-Spokesperson should start his or her term. The newly elected Co-Spokesperson will serve the remainder of the term of the replaced Co-Spokesperson in addition to the nominal two-year term. If the IB chair is a candidate for co-spokesperson (i.e., appears on the election slate), the last serving, non-candidate chair of the IB will serve as IB chair until the election concludes. ## § 4.3 Removal of a Co-Spokesperson Any of the Co-Spokespersons can be removed at any time by the IB by a secret ballot of at least 2/3 of those present at a scheduled Institutional Board meeting. The quorum for the vote is 2/3 of the entire IB membership. A two-week notice is required for a vote for removal and such a vote will be taken if at least five IB members propose such a vote to the Chair. In the event of a removal, the open position will be filled following the procedure described above, except that the IB Chair will decide when the special election should commence and when the new CoSpokesperson should start his or her term. The newly elected Co-Spokesperson will have a term that includes the remaining term of the removed Co-Spokesperson in addition to the nominal twoyear term. ## **_Article 5_** ## **_Deputy Spokesperson_** ## § 5.1 Selection of Deputy Spokesperson The Deputy Spokesperson position in the DUNE collaboration is an optional position. If the elected Co-Spokespersons see a need for such a position, they can nominate a person to fill the position with specified roles that are agreed between the Co-spokespersons and the nominee. After a brief presentation of the nominee to the IB by the Co-spokespersons, the IB will confirm or reject the nomination with a secret vote. The confirmation will require a simple majority vote of the IB members voting. The term of the Deputy Spokesperson is one year and renewable. § 5.2 Removal of the Deputy Spokesperson 7 The Deputy Spokesperson can be removed at any time by the IB by a secret ballot of at least 2/3 of those present at a scheduled Institutional Board meeting. A two-week notice is required for a vote for removal and such a vote will be taken if at least five IB members propose such a vote to the Chair. In the event of a removal, the open position will be filled following the procedure described above. The term of the newly appointed Deputy Spokesperson will be the remaining term of the removed Deputy Spokesperson. ## **_Article 6_** ## **_Executive Board_** ## § 6.1 Role of the Executive Board The Executive Board (EB) is the main decision-making body of the collaboration. It is responsible for setting scientific and technical objectives and priorities of the DUNE collaboration taking account of the financial aspects as well as other resources. The EB establishes procedures for making technical choices and will oversee progress and developments in various projects. The mode of operation of the Executive Board is described in the DUNE Management Plan. (See Attachment A.2.) ## § 6.2 Membership of the Executive Board The EB will consist of the leadership of the main collaboration activities, as defined in the DUNE Management Plan including: the Co-Spokespersons, the Physics, Technical and International Resource Coordinators and the IB Chair. The longest serving of the Co-Spokespersons serves as the EB Chair. The Co-Spokespersons, with the approval of the IB, may appoint up to three additional members to the EB. Such appointments will be for one year. Changes to the EB membership must be ratified by the IB. ## **_Article 7 Collaboration General Assembly_** The DUNE Collaboration General Assembly (CGA) is a forum of all DUNE collaboration members. All major decisions by the EB and IB as well as collaboration-wide issues should be reported and discussed at the CGA. This provides a forum where individual collaborators can express their opinions on particular issues. The shortest serving of the Co-Spokespersons serves as the CGA Chair. ## **_Article 8 Young DUNE_** The younger members of the collaboration constitute “Young DUNE” (YD). YD members are, in general, students or post-docs in an early stage of their career (e.g. first postdoc). The exact membership of the YD group can be defined by the group itself and the group will elect its own Chair based on rules it establishes. YD has the right to send an observer (non-voting) to all IB meetings and to send representatives (one each) to the Authorship and Publication Board and Speakers Committee. The group will organize its own activities and will have regular meetings with the Co-Spokespersons and/or the IB Chair. 8 ## **_Article 9_** ## **_Physics, Technical and Resource Coordinators_** The Co-Spokesperson will appoint one or two physics coordinators.
