Source: docdb Title: Photon Detector System Update for May 29, 2015 PD Status – May 29, 2015 Norm Buchanan Colorado State University ###### Colorado State University # Technical Review FD Design Independent Review -May 19-20th Close out report circulated via email - Executive Summary: "The purpose of the review was to evaluate the DUNE project's technical progress and readiness to proceed to CD-1 - Refresh. The Committee found that the DUNE project design is sufficiently advanced and that several promising alternative design options were actively being pursued. The Committee was very impressed with the progress made in the LBNE transition to DUNE and encourages a timely advance from prototypes to the industrial production needed to construct and mount the large and complex DuNE as to fully optimize the DUNE experiment. Three areas were considered; TPC and Installation,PhotonDetection and Electronicsand DAQ." ·Very successful -Thanks again to everyone involved Feb 6, 2015 2 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 1 The simulation does not yet allow for the effects of Ar39 decay, cross talk, dark counts or other SIPM effects. What is the plan to incorporate these issues? - 39 Ar Decay: - A radiological “generator” has been written by Tom Junk, we need to turn it on and study the output in the photon detectors. - The tools are ready, we just need (a person) to do the study. - Once we have an estimate of the rate, we can either turn on the simulation all the time, or just increase the effective dark rate to compensate. DUNE FD Technical Review – May 19-20, 2015 3 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 1 - Electronics response: - The following effects have already been implemented in the simulation: - Dark rate - Cross talk - Cable noise - The following are still in the works - Afterpulsing - Saturation - Performance studies with realistic electronics - Need reconstruction to evaluate performance with these effects. - Have prototypes, but not ready for performance studies yet - Have some ideas on how to get to “good enough” to get started - Have a Duke grad student working on these issues now - Hope to have working tools in a few weeks. - Then we just need manpower to do the studies it enables. DUNE FD Technical Review – May 19-20, 2015 4 ###### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 2 The SIPM spec cannot be fully determined (for example cross talk) without knowledge based on simulation. What is the plan for formalizing the SIPM spec? In terms of providing timing for the events – the primary purpose of the PD system – the effect of the SiPM specs are the following: Cross talk Only affects the measured energy of an event – in time with the initial signal After-pulsing More significant issue as it can provide false coincidences giving incorrect timing – but the rate is low (< 10Hz). This is covered by the dark rate spec. S Title of Review – Review Date 5 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 2 Dark Rate ~10 Hz at bias voltage of 24.5 V The simulation to confirm these requirements would be to generate a series of test event samples, scanning over possible values of the cross-talk, after pulsing, etc., and see how the reconstruction performance changes. Timing resolution, fake rate, and reco. efficiency are the obvious metrics. S Title of Review – Review Date 6 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 3 SIPMs have not been extensively used in cryogenic envirnments and may experience effects like premature aging or other issues. What is the plan to qualify the SIPMs for safe operation in this environment. What is an acceptable failure rate in the full detector? How will you know that the chosen SIPM will satisfy this rate? (The Dune electronics group has worried about electronics lifetimes at LAr temperature. Is any of this relevant.) The plan to qualify the SiPMs for cold operation is to both thermally cycle a population of the devices and subject another population to a long term test at cryo temperature. Both of these tests are happening now with small populations. We still need to understand what size of samples is needed to give confidence in device qualification and to project failure rates. Determining the failure rate of the devices to ensure it is within the tolerable failure rate coming from simulation is addressed in the first part of the answer. Title of Review – Review Date 9 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 4 What are the criteria for the optical detector down-select (in addition to the Tallbo cosmic ray test)? 1. The primary criteria is relative performance – coupled with cost. (We have other tests planned for the CSU 500 liter dewar – one just completed with the CSU and LSU alternatives). 2. We will have simulation and reconstruction at the level to allow us to compare relative simulated performance between designs. PDK kaons (200 MeV) as well as SN interactions of 5 MeV and 10 MeV would be good signals to use for the comparison. 3. Complexity of production and handling will also be considered for the down selection. Title of Review – Review Date 10 ##### Colorado State University Executive Summary for Photon Detection System The requirements and documentation of the conceptual design are in place and at the appropriate level for CD-1. However, the reference design has difficulties reaching the performance required to meet the physics goals, specifically the signal to noise. The ability to determine to is a desirable capability for both the proton decay and the supernova physics goals of Dune. Several alternatives were presented that should meet the specification. It would be useful to rapidly choose a reference design that meets the stated goals of Dune with some headroom. Prototype results will soon aid in choosing. In addition, better simulation is needed to evaluate the alternative designs. Extended experience of SiPM in a LAr environment would also help quantify the requirements. Proposal for Contributions to the Development of a photon detector system for the DUNE Liquid Argon TPC Detector for the Period February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016 Overview This statement of work provides details of funding for R&D and design tasks related to the development of a photon detector (PD) sub-detector for the DUNE far detector (FD). Members of the NIU team involved in this effort are: professors Gerald Blazey, Michael Eads and Vishnu Zutshi (PI), senior research scientist Alexander Dyshkant, senior technician Kurt Francis, students and electrical and mechanical machine shops. Funds are requested here to: Set up infrastructure for the evaluation, characterization and long-term performance of Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) in a cryogenic environment Study SiPM parameters and performance in warm and cold conditions Initiate the development of a quality assurance plan and procedure for SiPM qualification for LAr TPC prototypes under the following scheduled activities: 13122.05.290 Test passive ganging of 3 SiPMs 13122.05.300 Test passive ganging of 6 SiPMs 13122.05.310 Prepare final report on passive SiPM ganging The period of execution of these tasks is February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016. The tasks will be executed in coordination with existing members of the PD group especially CSU and Caltech. Statement of Work During FY2016, the NIU group will contribute in the following areas: Initiate SiPM characterization in warm (room temperature) conditions. The test stand will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, x-talk, after-pulsing etc.) using DUNE electronics. Of particular interest will be characterization of ganged sensors. Studies will initially look at performance of three ganged sensors and then explore the possibility of ganging six of them. This task will primarily involve Francis and a student with oversight by Zutshi and assistance from Gary Drake (ANL). Setup cryogenic test-stand for SiPM characterization and qualification. Once the test stand is setup it will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, x-talk, after-pulsing etc.) using DUNE electronics. Ganging studies will be extended to this realm. Failure modes, both electrical and mechanical will be explored. This task will primarily involve Dyshkant, Francis and NIU machine & electrical shops with oversight by Blazey and Zutshi. Detailed comparisons of sensor parameters in warm and cold environments to understand the performance correlations and dependencies. This will be used to demonstrate how well the determination of sensor parameters in the warm environment can be extrapolated to LAr temperatures. This task will primarily involve a student with oversight by Eads. Initiate development of a work plan and procedure for quality control and assurance of SiPMs for the LAr TPC prototypes under design or construction. This should be considered as the first step in the development of long-term (~30 years) qualification procedures for the SiPMs. This task will primarily involve Francis and a student with oversight by Eads and Zutshi. Cost Proposal for Brookhaven National Laboratory N.B. The NIU Division of Research and Innovation Partnerships has approved a cost share of up to $13K.

Muon-neutrino flux optimization at the LBNF/DUNE Far detector By Tyler Johnson, Supervised by Dr. Laura Fields at Fermilab introduction I am studying the different simulations of the 3-horn optimized design identified by Laura’s genetic algorithm, the one described in the BOTF Interim Report. There’s a significant drop in neutrino flux between the ideal, optimized design and the realistic design. My objective is to determine the reasons for this flux loss and understand which of the factors can be altered to optimize the flux. Factors considered in my studies: Obstructions in the Beamline (Target Assembly, Strip Lines, etc.) Horn Flare Starting Point Material Thickness Target Placement Scan 2 Reference vs. ideal/optimzed design Through running a genetic algorithm, Laura identified an optimized 3 horn design which surpassed the reference design in both neutrino flux and CP sensitivity. 3 Realistic design This design was created by Paul Lebrun and, as the name suggests, is a more realistic version of the optimized (ideal) design. The flares on both the upstream and downstream ends are rounded off. For Horn A, there is the problem of the target assembly. The target assembly holds the graphite target and has the issue of it being in the beamline so was suspected to cause a drop in the neutrino flux. 4 Initial problem Here is the difference in unoscillated, Muon-neutrino flux at the far detector due to changes in the horn A design (Ideal vs. Realistic) Note: This is the flux loss from horn A alone. to the new milestones for the remainder of the CD-3 scope, but there will not be any new control accounts (except for those WBS where there is no CD-3b or CD-3c scope). See Section 7 of this document to see how the CD-3c chargeable task codes are handled after the ESAAB approval of the entire project and the S=P=A reset. Table -: Control Accounts and Chargeable Task Codes for the CD-3c scope of the FDC subproject. Table -: List of Tier1 and Tier 2 milestones for the CD-3c scope with dates that must be met by the FDC subproject. When a milestone has been completed, the actual date is provided with a “A” appended to it. If the date of a milestone has not been met or is not being met the “F” flag is appended. Management of CD-3 scope CD-3 Chargeable Task codes and Milestones Once a date for the ESAAB approval is ready, the following steps will be taken by the project: A date for the S=P=A reset will be established, possibly matching the end of a fiscal year quarter (as explained below). New activities will be created in each of the existing control accounts to reflect all the actuals up to the transition dates. Activities that extend past the transition date will be split between an activity that will be completed on the transition date and an activity that will start after the transition date. Given the large number of LOE activities that are matched to fiscal year quarters this explains the motivation for matching the transition date to the end of a fiscal year quarter. Activities that are performed by international partners (identified as having the Funding Type code set to a non-DOE value) will not be split. All the activities that are completed before the transition date are left in their current WBS. The same applies for activities that are not started and are not part of the CD-3a, CD-3b, or CD-3c scope. These activities will get a new chargeable task code that is separate from those use prior to the S=P=A reset and that are also separate from the chargeable task codes used for the CD-3a, CD-3b, or CD-3c portions of the project. Activities that start after the transition date and that are part of the CD-3a, CD-3b, or CD-3c scope are moved from their current WBS into a new WBS using the mapping provided in Table 7-1 below. These activities will keep their current chargeable task code but use the new Control Account corresponding to the new WBS. This is done to satisfy the DOE requirement that we are able to provide an end date for the execution of the existing CD-3a, CD-3b, and CD-3c scope as well as a comparison between the budget established at the time of baselining each portion of the scope and the actual costs. At the same time this arrangement allows for sharing the contingency between the different portions of the overall FDC scope as well as simplifying the reporting in PARS where there will be a single report for the entire project. The mapping of chargeable task code for each control account for the activities that start after the transition date is given in Table 7-2. Table -: Map indicating how activities that are currently part of the CD-3a, CD-3b, or CD-3c scope and that are not complete at the time of the S=P=A reset are migrated from their current WBS to the WBS used for the execution of the entire scope of the FDC subproject. After the ESAAB approval the FDC Subproject will track the progress toward achieving 1 Tier 0 milestone, 10 Tier 1 milestones and 22 Tier 2 milestones over the course of the six years that are needed to complete the execution of the project. The list of these milestones together with the dates that must be met by the FDC subproject are listed in Table 7-3. Table -: Control Accounts and Chargeable Task Codes for the CD-3 Scope of the FDC Subproject after the S=P=A reset. Chargeable task codes associated to CD-3a, CD-3b, or CD-3c activities that are moved to a new WBS are identified by the (3a), (3b), or (3c) flag attached to the CTC. Additions to EVMS Reporting The Project Execution Plan (PEP) for the Far Detectors and Cryogenics Infrastructure (FDC) Subprojects states (Section 5.2 on Performance Measurement) that “The FDC subproject will provide EVMS reporting along with supplemental metrics for activities that may not be accurately tracked by earned value metrics alone. The FDC subproject will also take additional steps to ensure the forecast schedule and anticipated resource needs are accurate for areas where use of EV variances alone may not be able to correctly model the estimated time and resources to completion”. This section discusses the Supplemental Data that the FDC subproject will provide to the Federal Project Director to complement the PARS-II uploads that are done each month. Work performed by international partners and their contractors Work performed by international partners and their contractors is represented in the project Primavera P6 schedule by schedule visibility tasks (SVTs) without any resources and milestones. The progress for these activities is measured on a monthly basis with the percent complete metric by the Control Account Managers (CAMs) of the US project. Forecast and actual dates for milestones are also updated monthly in the same way. The information provided by the international partners is verified by the CAMs prior to the monthly P6 update. The downstream impact of changes to the timeline of these tasks and milestones is taken into account when performing the monthly update of the P6 schedule and included in the FDC subproject Estimate to Complete (ETC). Cost reports for the CD-3b and CD-3c scopes After the S=P=A reset the project will maintain separate chargeable task codes within control accounts in order to obtain the total cost of the CD-3b and CD-3c scopes. The total cost of the CD-3b and CD-3c scopes will be reported and compared to the corresponding TPCs established at the time of the respective ESAAB approvals (and including following BCPs). Performance Indices without LOE contributions The FDC subproject has a significant portion of oversight work and of work in support of international partners of the level of effort (LOE) type. The LOE work is segregated into dedicated WBS and Control Accounts, following Government Accountability Office rules. The FDC subproject will report the Cost and Schedule Performance Indices (CPI and SPI) for both the total project cost and for the cost in the WBS and Control Accounts that do not have significant contributions from LOE work (the WBS / Control Accounts excluded from the modified performance indices are indicated in Table 1 (this table is taken from the FDC subproject dollarized Responsibility Assignment Matrix). Table : List of WBS/Control Accounts for the FDC subproject with LOE fraction exceeding 85%. Corrections to the Estimate to Complete The FDC subproject will include each month in the ETC the following contributions: 1) pending baseline changes requests, and 2) corrections to total cost of LOE activities in the WBS / Control Accounts listed in Table 1 deriving from changes in the duration of the project. The second correction is meant to capture the need for additional LOE resources in case some of the construction/installation tasks take longer than planned, resulting in the need for extending the usage of those resources. The extension in the duration of the LOE tasks is measured by the following milestones that are already part of the report to the FPD: Items 1-3, 16-17: Objective KPP Demonstrated Items 4-9: HD Detector Manholes Closed and Final Warm Detector Tests Completed Items 10-14: Complete Turn-On of VD Detector Item 15: HD Cryogenics Ready for Operations When one of these milestones moves by more than three months, a baseline change request will be performed to add the corresponding resources to the FDC subproject baseline. Additional information for the FPD Additional information that can be provided to the FPD includes: Details on major subcontract efforts Lower-level schedules provided by subcontractors or vendors Review of near-critical path activities. Analysis at a work-package level. External Advisory Boards Neutrino Scope Group (NSG) The Neutrino Scope Group (NSG), described in the Project Management Plan, is part of the international governance and oversight structure for DUNE. Its purpose is to review the scope, schedule, and associated risks for the DUNE experiment, and to provide reports and recommendations to the Fermilab Director and the RRB. The NSG utilizes a common methodology to value international contributions to DUNE. Long-Baseline Neutrino Committee (LBNC) The LBNC, described in the Project Management Plan, provides external scientific peer review and monitors the technical progress of the International DUNE collaboration and those aspects of the facility construction that have direct impact on the DUNE experiment. It acts effectively as an adjunct to the Fermilab Physics Advisory Committee (PAC), meeting on a more frequent basis than the PAC. The LBNC may employ Scrutiny Groups for more detailed reports and evaluations. DUNE Program Committee (DPC) As of October 2025, the tasks of the NSG and of the LBNC have been taken over by the newly formed DUNE Program Committee (DPC), that essentially results from the merger of the two previous committees. The DUNE Program Committee (DPC) is charged by the Fermilab Director to review the scientific, technical, and managerial progress, plans and decisions associated with the Fermilab Long Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) and the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). The committee also considers some specific aspects of the Short Baseline Neutrino (SBN) Program. The DPC provides candid assessments for the Director and for the Resources Review Board (RRB) that are also available to the LBNF and DUNE leaderships and to the funding agencies that support these international projects. All estimates are made in base-year $ and include all labor and material required to complete the work scope. An overall contingency calculation is based on (1) estimate uncertainty related to design maturity, (2) the technical, cost, and schedule risks, and (3) an assessment by the Project leadership of unknown unknowns. Contingency is controlled by the DOE Federal Project Director, with a management reserve available to the Project up to the levels documented in the change control section of the Systems Engineering Management Plan. Escalation is based on the latest laboratory inflation estimates for labor and materials and services, with Conventional Facilities work being escalated in accordance with guidance developed from industry cost projections. This is detailed in Section 7.2.2. #### **7.2.1 Basis of Estimate** The cost estimates have been developed in accordance with various procedures, using US Project-wide contingency rules for the technical systems, and separate guidelines for conventional-facilities-type work [13]. The WBS and WBS dictionary are starting points for identifying the level within the project at which the Basis of Estimates (BOE) are developed. Estimates are developed at the Control Account level of the WBS or below, as appropriate. Each cost estimate package is filed as an electronic document that contains similar categories of information, such as the basis of estimate document, the supporting activity-based resource breakdown, and other supporting documents (quotes, drawings, specifications, etc.) that support estimated resource needs and applied pricing. BOE packages are completed by those assigned to manage the WBS elements or, when warranted, by outside consultants, with oversight from the responsible manager. This ensures that the Project work scope is well known and properly estimated. The cost estimate packages contain backup documentation that explains the basis on which the estimate is founded and effectively translates the technical design into detailed labor and procurement elements of cost. The development of the cost estimate packages Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) - US 7-32 Project Baseline for Cost and Schedule Project Management Plan (PMP) follows the definition of the work, with the estimator assembling basic information concerning the Project, including the Project background, the general description of the technical scope, the anticipated estimate classification with associated contingencies based on design maturity, and other related information. #### **_7.2.1.1 Cost Estimating Guidance Given to Estimators_** Control Account Managers (CAMs), WBS System managers and their designees are instructed to make honest estimates for each element of work. Material and Services (M&S) costs are to be supported by quotes or previous work and free of any hidden contingencies. Labor hours are to be supported by documented estimates, based on prior experience or quotes, without contingency. For the DOE-funded portion of the work, estimate uncertainty contingency is identified for each activity in each BOE founded on programmatic contingency rules established by EVMS, associated with the level or understanding and/or maturity of the design. Below is a list of steps the estimators follow when preparing the BOE: - Review the WBS Dictionary and technical scope - Assemble technical scope detail - Develop estimate by specific WBS elements - Identify estimate activities (level of detail as supported by the current level of design completion) - Identify resources, including labor, materials, services and other budget items required to complete the scope of work - Assign contingency % associated with existing estimate uncertainty rules (for DOE-funded portion of the work) - Provide for time-phasing of the work scope via a resource-loaded schedule Note: Contingency associated with risk events is handled outside of the estimating process. #### **_7.2.1.2 Labor – Costed to the DOE-funded Portion of Project_** Project labor estimates are created by loading the labor resources from the BOEs into the resource-loaded project schedule. The resources are loaded into the schedule with hour units estimated to complete specific activities/tasks. For the DOE-funded portion of the work, the next step is to apply standard wage, overhead and indirect rates from the various laboratories and universities in the Deltek Cobra Cost Management program (Cobra), the commercially available cost processing tool used by Fermilab projects. Labor resources are estimated based on hours to complete specific tasks to the level of detail available with the following basic cost estimating assumptions: - The project will use the Fermilab working calendar for scheduling the work. - For Level-of-Effort type activities, an 85% allocation rate of an employee’s time (or FTE = 1768 hrs./yr.) is assumed. Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) - US 7-33 Project Baseline for Cost and Schedule Project Management Plan (PMP) - For the DOE-funded portion of the work: - labor resources will have the escalation factors for salary from the various participating laboratories applied; - direct labor rates are used and applied to labor resources for each labor category (type) as provided by the performing organization; - direct labor rates are then fully burdened, with indirect factors/rates applied to all resources; the factors are based on the associated laboratory-posted burden rates as provided by the budget departments. #### **_7.2.1.3 Labor – Uncosted Scientists for the DOE-funded Portion of Project_** The Project uses scientific effort for planning, designing, and constructing the Project. All of the labor necessary to the DOE-funded portion of the Project is to be estimated and captured in the resourceloaded schedule. Some of the scientific labor resources are provided to the Project without cost through the DOE base science program funded outside of the Project. Uncosted scientific resources use $0 rate in the Resource Loaded Schedule (RLS) as outlined in the LBNF/DUNE Guidelines for Charging Scientists’ Effort [14]. #### **_7.2.1.4 Materials & Service Resources_** Project material and services estimates are created by loading M&S resources from the BOEs into the resource-loaded project schedule, then applying standard indirect rates from the various laboratories and universities in Cobra. The material resource units estimated are loaded into the schedule in dollar units ($1/ unit). M&S resources include materials and other labor resources secured from outside the DOE laboratories. M&S resources are estimated based on current year US$, as appropriate to the level of detail available with the following basic cost estimating assumptions: - The US Project will use the Fermilab working calendar for scheduling the work. - For the DOE-funded portion of the Project, M&S resources will use the official escalation factors as provided by the various funded laboratories; with conventional facilities work utilizing specially developed escalation factors. - For the DOE-funded portion of the work, indirect rates are applied to M&S resources as provided by the institution’s procurement practices. This includes limiting indirect charges once procurements exceed a specified threshold as defined by the funded institution. #### **7.2.2 Base Year Dollars and Escalation** The Project’s base year for cost-estimating purposes is updated at the beginning of each fiscal year to be the current fiscal year. This is done by adjusting all labor and indirect rates to the current year and applying escalation rates to work beyond the base year. The Project’s assumed escalation rates are maintained in Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) - US 7-34 Project Baseline for Cost and Schedule Project Management Plan (PMP) Cobra and come to the Project from the Fermilab Budget Office for the Fermilab and BNL resources; BNL has concurred with using FNAL Budget Office rates. #### **7.2.3 Labor Rates** Labor rates have been developed by the direct-funded DOE laboratories, using guidelines provided by the individual laboratory’s Budget Office as described below. Fully loaded rates are built-up in Cobra Cost, using direct rates, labor burdens, laboratory indirect charges, and escalation. #### **_7.2.3.1 Fermilab_** Fermilab uses a process to identify all employees according to a defined functional role. Each functional role correlates to one or more job titles, and functional roles aggregate up to functional categories, which roll up to functional disciplines. Part of the intent of associating individuals with a single functional role is to identify staffing needs for projects; another is to facilitate the long-term efficient use of employees at the laboratory. Fermilab resource rates determined in this way are based on a weighted average wage or salary of the employees within that functional role. To establish direct labor rates, the weighted average is occasionally adjusted to reflect the laboratory’s project experience. The direct labor rates are then multiplied by several overhead factors including vacation/other paid time off/fringe benefits, overhead, and shared site support to produce fully burdened or fully loaded rates. These overhead factors occasionally require adjustment. All resources will be charged to the LBNF/DUNE Project using Fermilab rates. The rates used by the Project reflect the Project base year and are entered into Cobra, which adjusts the Fermilab rates to account for escalation in labor costs. #### **_7.2.3.2 BNL_** DOE direct-funds work at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) to support detector activities. BNL resource rates are determined by BNL management and are based on a percentage of the average wages or salary of the employees within that functional role. This percentage is adjusted occasionally to reflect the laboratory’s project experience. The rates used reflect the Project base year and are entered into Cobra, which multiplies the direct labor rates (the gross pay of an individual) by a composite factor provided by the BNL Budget Office to produce fully burdened or fully loaded rates, which are charged to the Project or other effort to which the resource is assigned. #### **_7.2.3.3 Other Institutions_** LBNF/DUNE has several other institutions involved in R&D, design and construction of the DOE-funded portion of the Project. Rates for resources from these other institutions are handled by the Project as M&S resources, supported by purchase orders with each stakeholder institution. The unit measure loaded into the schedule is labor hours, whereas rates are loaded into the cost processor; the rates include all burdening from the home institution, with the associated overhead rate being added by Cobra. Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) - US 7-35 Project Baseline for Cost and Schedule Project Management Plan (PMP) #### **7.2.4 Indirect Costs** In the cases where the funding goes directly from DOE to another funded DOE laboratory, indirect costs from each of these labs are included within Cobra as percentages of the direct labor and M&S costs, using guidelines provided by the individual laboratory Budget Offices as described below. If the funding goes via Fermilab to the other labs, then their overheads are included as part of the “direct rate,” and the Fermilab indirect costs are added as percentages. #### **_7.2.4.1 Fermilab_** Fermilab allocates indirect expenses to all resource types. These indirect expenses are maintained as percentages in Cobra, and applied to the burdened direct labor and M&S costs. Indirect rates in Cobra reflect the current fiscal year laboratory indirect rates as prepared by Fermilab’s Budget Office. These rates are updated in Cobra annually through the change control process (if necessary). Fermilab labor costs incur indirect expenses when charged, in accordance with rates for common site support, program support (divisions only), general and administrative expenses, and laboratory-directed R&D. Fermilab M&S costs incur indirect expenses when invoiced in accordance with rates for material/services acquisition, general and administrative, and laboratory-directed R&D. Fermilab has developed reduced indirect rates for three areas of capital construction activities, defined as Project Engineering and Design (PED), Line-Item Construction (LIC), and Major Item of Equipment (MIE) costs. The rates automatically apply to these costs and are not applicable to Other Project Costs (OPC). The Project construction rate is calculated each year by analyzing the component activities/services of the lab-level indirect pools based on a determination of whether a self-fabricated capital asset in the construction phase would benefit from the activity or service. Complex procurement for identified major capital project purchase orders that meet the definition of a procurement supported by dedicated Procurement Administrator staffed by the project are subject to a reduced Materials/Services rate. Fermilab’s policy for the application of indirect expenses is available upon request. The Indirect Rates as provided for each Directorate/Division/Section can be found on the Fermilab Finance Section <u>Rates, Reports and Policies page under Current Burden

Final Designs are documented in Technical Design Reports, which describe the scope at the time of the Final Design Review. Project Baseline for Cost and Schedule Portions of the Projects proceed through Preliminary and Final Designs according to project priorities and available funding. At the appropriate time, but no earlier than the conclusion of Preliminary Design, a project scope and schedule baseline will be established for each subproject. For the DOE-funded portion of the project, this takes place at Critical Decision 2 (CD-2); the DOE cost and schedule will also be baselined at this milestone. Schedule The work plan for the LBNF/DUNE Project is developed through iterative planning by technical managers working with project controls specialists to create detailed cost and schedule plans. This work plan has resulted in an integrated project schedule with the LBNF/DUNE-US portions resource-loaded, and any in-kind contributions tracked through milestones. DOE Schedule Details For the DOE-funded Projects, the schedule is assembled by loading resource quantities from the Basis of Estimates (described in Section 7.2.1) into a multi-project scheduling tool, Primavera Project Planner (P6), at the activity level. Control Account Managers (CAMs) and WBS system managers are responsible to generate and maintain the schedules for their subsystems, in conjunction with their designated project controls specialists. The schedule is built from tasks and milestones: interdependencies are created between tasks of various durations and milestones that define the flow of the work. The labor effort required to complete each task is specified, with separate allocations made for various types of technical personnel, such as mechanical and electrical engineers, designers/drafters, technicians, and physicists, by institution where known. Thus, profiles in time of various work groups are readily obtained to aid in the establishment of labor effort requirements and the allocation of personnel as the Project evolves. By importing the scheduled resources into Deltek Cobra Cost Management program (Cobra), rates for each type of labor resource are applied (for the DOE-funded portion of the work) and labor hour and cost profiles are built. The Materials and Services (M&S) work necessary to complete each task is extracted from the Basis of Estimates (BOEs) and assigned to the corresponding tasks in the schedule. M&S work is allocated in base-year $ units (with escalation for the DOE-funded portion of the Project), allowing for expenditure plans to be developed for each subproject and for the full Project. Using this information, a work plan is established by making appropriate adjustments to the schedule to yield an overall budgeting plan that matches the profile of funds available from the DOE. In addition to a budget plan, a labor plan is produced to align with the funding profile. This plan is shared with the U.S.-funded institutions for labor resource management coordination and validation. The scheduling program identifies the critical path (or paths). This is accomplished at the subproject level, with inter-project links made to ensure that all WBS elements are coordinated. The critical path calls attention to those tasks that have no ‘float’ or slack and that must therefore be carefully monitored to prevent delay in Project completion. Knowledge of the critical path facilitates changes to optimize the work and to hasten completion. As noted above, the schedule has been optimized based on an assumed funding profile for the Project; therefore changes to the funding profile will impact the critical path. Resource Loading A list of the resources required to complete the scope of work, as included in the BOE, is used to load the activities into a resource-loaded schedule. Resources loaded into the schedule conform to the laboratories’ functional roles and standard M&S resource types. Each resource in the schedule will have an associated unit cost included in Cobra. Types and quantities of resources as assigned to each activity are spread across each activity’s duration. To create the cost profile, the spread matches the expected accrual of effort across the activities. An obligation profile is created based on resource spreads shifted to earlier dates, to align with the timing of the release of contracts and purchase orders. The obligation profile is leveled to match the projected time-phased funding. Standard Calendar The standard Project calendar is based on the Fermilab work calendar which assumes a 40-hour, 5-day work week with common non-work periods associated with laboratory holidays. Other calendars may be used to accommodate non-standard work periods, such as work impacted by inclement weather, work requiring extended or multiple shifts, work associated with shutdowns of laboratory equipment, etc., and this work is assigned at the activity level. Milestones Milestones are established at these specific tiers: T0 = DOE Project Management Executive T1 = DOE Associate Director HEP T2 = DOE Federal Project Director T3 = LBNF/DUNE-US Project Director T4 = Deputy Project Director T5 = Subproject Manager T6 = CAM Inter-project milestones between key interface points of the LBNF/DUNE-US subprojects are utilized to ensure integration of schedule across the Project. In addition, key inter-project milestones between the DUNE International Project schedule and the US Project schedule provide links for monitoring interfaces between all aspects of the Project. A milestone dictionary has been developed that captures milestones at these tiers, including the completion of design and construction of various major subsystems. Milestones are updated as part of the reporting cycle, described above. The milestone dictionary is maintained within P6. Project Scope Provided by Non-DOE Partners The US Project schedule carries some scope identified as “non-DOE” without specific commitments in place until baselining. As agreements are reached and commitments are made by non-DOE partners to execute facilities work, activities are replaced by monitoring milestones to allow adequate tracking of progress on these deliverables. DOE Cost Estimate The cost estimate for the DOE-funded portion of the project encompasses all work contained within the WBS and develops into the budget for the DOE project. The cost estimate evolves towards greater levels of detail as the Project definition and the available information increases. When less mature, cost estimates rely predominantly on expert opinion, leveraging the cost estimator’s experience on similar, past projects and parametric modeling methods. However, for portions of the project in which the work is routine or based on commercially available systems, cost is estimated in greater detail and with greater confidence. As the Project design advances past the conceptual level, it becomes further refined and coordinated, more details are developed, the cost estimates become more specific, and estimate uncertainty contingency percentages are reduced. The budget/actual cost begins with the first year of funding in FY10 (CD-0) and continues through project completion CD-4. The development of the cost estimates is consistent with the requirements set forth in DOE Order 413.3-21, Cost Estimating Guide. Cost estimates are prepared by the Control Account Managers (CAMs), or other WBS Managers under the CAMs’ oversight, using the WBS to align the scope of work with the estimated costs. All estimates are made in base-year $ and include all labor and material required to complete the work scope. An overall contingency calculation is based on (1) estimate uncertainty related to design maturity, (2) the technical, cost, and schedule risks, and (3) an assessment by the Project leadership of unknown unknowns. Contingency is controlled by the DOE Federal Project Director, with a management reserve available to the Project up to the levels documented in the change control section of the Systems Engineering Management Plan. Escalation is based on the latest laboratory inflation estimates for labor and materials and services, with Conventional Facilities work being escalated in accordance with guidance developed from industry cost projections. This is detailed in Section 7.2.2. Basis of Estimate The cost estimates have been developed in accordance with various procedures, using US Project-wide contingency rules for the technical systems, and separate guidelines for conventional-facilities-type work . The WBS and WBS dictionary are starting points for identifying the level within the project at which the Basis of Estimates (BOE) are developed. Estimates are developed at the Control Account level of the WBS or below, as appropriate. Each cost estimate package is filed as an electronic document that contains similar categories of information, such as the basis of estimate document, the supporting activity-based resource breakdown, and other supporting documents (quotes, drawings, specifications, etc.) that support estimated resource needs and applied pricing. BOE packages are completed by those assigned to manage the WBS elements or, when warranted, by outside consultants, with oversight from the responsible manager. This ensures that the Project work scope is well known and properly estimated. The cost estimate packages contain backup documentation that explains the basis on which the estimate is founded and effectively translates the technical design into detailed labor and procurement elements of cost. The development of the cost estimate packages follows the definition of the work, with the estimator assembling basic information concerning the Project, including the Project background, the general description of the technical scope, the anticipated estimate classification with associated contingencies based on design maturity, and other related information. Cost Estimating Guidance Given to Estimators Control Account Managers (CAMs), WBS System managers and their designees are instructed to make honest estimates for each element of work. Material and Services (M&S) costs are to be supported by quotes or previous work and free of any hidden contingencies. Labor hours are to be supported by documented estimates, based on prior experience or quotes, without contingency. For the DOE-funded portion of the work, estimate uncertainty contingency is identified for each activity in each BOE founded on programmatic contingency rules established by EVMS, associated with the level or understanding and/or maturity of the design. Below is a list of steps the estimators follow when preparing the BOE: Review the WBS Dictionary and technical scope Assemble technical scope detail Develop estimate by specific WBS elements Identify estimate activities (level of detail as supported by the current level of design completion) Identify resources, including labor, materials, services and other budget items required to complete the scope of work Assign contingency % associated with existing estimate uncertainty rules (for DOE-funded portion of the work) Provide for time-phasing of the work scope via a resource-loaded schedule Note: Contingency associated with risk events is handled outside of the estimating process. Labor – Costed to the DOE-funded Portion of Project Project labor estimates are created by loading the labor resources from the BOEs into the resource-loaded project schedule. The resources are loaded into the schedule with hour units estimated to complete specific activities/tasks. For the DOE-funded portion of the work, the next step is to apply standard wage, overhead and indirect rates from the various laboratories and universities in the Deltek Cobra Cost Management program (Cobra), the commercially available cost processing tool used by Fermilab projects. Labor resources are estimated based on hours to complete specific tasks to the level of detail available with the following basic cost estimating assumptions: The project will use the Fermilab working calendar for scheduling the work. For Level-of-Effort type activities, an 85% allocation rate of an employee’s time (or FTE = 1768 hrs./yr.) is assumed. For the DOE-funded portion of the work: labor resources will have the escalation factors for salary from the various participating laboratories applied; direct labor rates are used and applied to labor resources for each labor category (type) as provided by the performing organization; direct labor rates are then fully burdened, with indirect factors/rates applied to all resources; the factors are based on the associated laboratory-posted burden rates as provided by the budget departments. Labor – Uncosted Scientists for the DOE-funded Portion of Project The Project uses scientific effort for planning, designing, and constructing the Project. All of the labor necessary to the DOE-funded portion of the Project is to be estimated and captured in the resource-loaded schedule. Some of the scientific labor resources are provided to the Project without cost through the DOE base science program funded outside of the Project. Uncosted scientific resources use $0 rate in the Resource Loaded Schedule (RLS) as outlined in the LBNF/DUNE Guidelines for Charging Scientists’ Effort . question: According to the Interface Control Document (Doc‑69) titled “OBSOLETE Interface Control Document Far Site CF Surface to Nitrogen System Design,” what condition must cryogenic system design materials meet to avoid re‑packaging for transport through the Yates and Ross headframes?
reference_answer: They must be configured (size and weight) so that they do not need to be re‑packaged to fit within the cage or be slung.
evidence_quote: Cryogenic systems design materials/components that are configured (size and weight) such that they do not need to be re-packaged to fit within the cage or slung
generated_answer: The cryogenic‑system design must specify materials and components that are **sized and weighed so they can be loaded directly into the Yates or Ross cage (or slung) without needing any re‑packaging**.

Title: LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan

Improvement process may be to request change(s) to the design requirements. QA reporting formality escalates as the significance of the inspection, test, or review nonconformance increases. Higher levels of management must be aware of and participate in the correction of the most significant nonconformance. Section 4, Quality Improvement, identifies the required course of action when nonconformance is encountered. ### **8.3 Design Reviews** The _LBNF/DUNE Review Plan_ [7] describes the design reviews recommended for its subprojects. #### **8.3.1 Design Review** Technical design reviews are an essential feature of the quality management process. Design reviews are internal to the project and are conducted for the system, subsystem, and critical components at major milestones in the development and production processes. Design reviews are attended by representatives of all concerned with the design including the project ES&H and quality assurance managers. For technically critical components outside experts may be appropriate. Recommendations and actions items are recorded and tracked for follow up and for subsequent reviews. While design reviews are primarily technical in nature and independent of management, cost and schedule reviews, effective value engineering practices are in integral part of the design review process. #### **_8.3.1.1 Conceptual Design Review (CDR)_** Before design activity begins, the requirements are reviewed for consistency with the scientific and technical objectives of the project as well as for completeness, accuracy and compliant with engineering and safety standards. The review is based on the Design Requirements Document. The successful completion of the DRR imitates the preliminary design phase. #### **_8.3.1.2 Preliminary Design Review (PDR)_** When the initial design concept has been defined, engineering studies between alternative approaches have been completed and a Preliminary Design Report has been prepared, a PDR is held to affirm the design approach. In addition to the Preliminary Design Report, inputs to the review are the design requirements, preliminary design drawings, parts lists and supporting documents. The successful completion of the PDR allows the detailed design to begin. Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) 8-25 LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan Design #### **_8.3.1.3 Final Design Review (FDR)_** When the design is complete but before fabrication begins, the FDR is held to ensure that the design is complete, correct, and satisfies requirements. In addition, the design is reviewed for manufacturability. The inputs to the FDR are the design documents (drawings, specifications, manufacturing plans, test plans, test procedures, etc.) in a form ready for formal sign-off for release for fabrication. Successful completion of the FDR and any related actions initiates production. #### **_8.3.1.4 Production Readiness Review (PRR)_** When the design is complete and delivered to the fabricator and before serial production has begun, a PRR is held, ideally at the fabrication site. The PRR is preceded by a pre-production run. The objective of the PRR is to assure that the component or subsystem is ready for production. - Pre-production units meet all requirements and specifications. - Adequate material, components and labor are available. - The QA/QC plan for production is place and training complete. - Inspection and test equipment and associated software are production ready. - Production tooling is complete and adequate both for product quality and production External Review Team The PM also has the option to request assistance from the Fermilab ESH Committee for equipment reviews involving resources outside of the Project. Examples of this would be wire targets, flammable gas systems, mechanical apparatus, etc. #### **_8.3.1.5 Operational Readiness Clearance (ORC)_** Prior to the initial operation of a critical system or subsystem, a production readiness review is held. The objective of the ORC is to validate the performance of the system, assure that safety requirements are met and that all drawings, manuals, operating and maintenance procedures readily available. Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) 8-26 LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan Procurement ## **9 Procurement** ### **9.1 Procurement Controls** Procurement controls will be implemented to ensure that purchased (Supplier) items and services meet LBNF/DUNE requirements and comply with this Quality Assurance Plan. The various managers, coordinators and technical leads requesting procurement of items and services are responsible for providing all documentation that adequately describes the item or service being procured so that the Supplier can understand what is required for the Projects’ acceptance. Development of this documentation may be achieved through the involvement of Sub-Project Managers and Consortia Leaders and established review and approval systems. The following factors will be considered for review and approval of this documentation: - Inclusion of technical performance requirements - Identification of required codes and standards, laws, and regulations - Inclusion of acceptance criteria, including requirements for receiving inspection and/or source inspection - LBNF/DUNE requirements for vendor qualifications and certifications - LBNF/DUNE intention to perform acceptance sampling in lieu of full inspection and test item acceptance NOTE: For Vendor Qualification and acceptance of purchased items or material by Project Partners this may be performed under their own institution requirements. Previously accepted Suppliers shall be monitored to ensure that they continue supplying acceptable items and services. Source surveillance is the recommended method to ensure that items are free of damage and that specified requirements are met. Supplier deliveries will be verified against previously established acceptance criteria. Unacceptable Supplier items or services shall be documented. Records of Supplier performance, Inspection Test Records (ITR) and contract-required submittals, are kept for future procurement consideration. Receipt Inspections shall be conducted to ensure the equipment or material meets the purchase order and technical requirements and also to detect counterfeit and/or suspect parts. For work funded by DOE, when counterfeit/suspect parts are found, they will be identified, segregated, and disposed of in accordance with the Fermilab Quality Assurance Manual Chapter 12020 Suspect/Counterfeit Items (S/CI) Program. DUNE Consortia may use their own institution’s procedure for counterfeit/suspect parts. Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) 9-27 LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan Inspection and Acceptance Testing ## **10 Inspection and Acceptance Testing** There are two inspection types in LBNF/DUNE: 1) inspections associated with Architecture/Engineer (A/E) design and construction (Conventional Facilities); and 2) inspections associated with electrical, mechanical, and structural component manufacture and installation. Acceptance testing generally applies only to item 2 and to computer code. Inspections of A/E construction activities are established by the A/E responsible for the design and certification of the completed work. Once the work is designed, the A/E will identify the applicable codes, standards, and specific testing requirements to apply from a set of established criteria. At the completion of specified stages of construction, the A/E signs off that the completed work is in compliance. LBNF will use a third-party inspection firm for sampling inspections of subcontractors work along with a commissioning agent for the Conventional Facilities procurements. Inspections and tests are performed in order to verify that the physical and functional aspects of items, services, and processes meet requirements and are fit for use. The performance expectations, inspections, and tests are considered during the design phase and, where appropriate, are specified in the design output and/or procurement documents. The various managers, coordinators and technical leads including in kind contributors are responsible for specifying when/what type of inspection is required and for ensuring that adequate inspections are performed and documented. ### **10.1 Inspection & Testing Process** Inspection and acceptance testing plans identify item characteristics and processes to be inspected/acceptance tested, inspection techniques, acceptance criteria, hold points, and the individuals or organization responsible for performing the inspection. Appropriate corrective actions shall be taken where deficiencies are identified accompanied by the appropriate follow-up to ensure effectiveness. When appropriate, inspections and tests are performed by personnel who are independent of the activities being inspected. ### **10.2 Control of Nonconforming Items** Items that do not conform to specified requirements are subject to controls to prevent their inadvertent installation or use. The various managers, coordinators and technical leads including in kind contributors are responsible for control of nonconforming items. Controls include identification, documentation, evaluation, segregation (when practical), item disposition (reject, repair, rework, use-as-is), and notification to affected organizations. Item disposition of use-as-is or repair shall be approved by the appropriate design authority since the item does not meet the technical requirements but meet its functionality. Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) 10-28 LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan Inspection and Acceptance Testing ### **10.3 Inspection & Test Records** Inspection and test results are documented and preserved. The inspection and test status of items or processes requiring examination are clearly identified to ensure that only those with acceptable results are used. At a minimum, inspection/test records identify the following: item(s) inspected, the inspection/test procedure used, who performed the inspection/test, the identification number(s) of the measuring & test equipment (M&TE) used to perform the inspection or test, the inspection/test data, the inspection/test criteria, and the inspection/test results. The management assessment process shall periodically include an evaluation of the organization's products and processes to determine whether the Project's missions are being fulfilled. The results of management assessments that focus on means of improving the quality of work performed shall be reported to the appropriate responsible line or Project management level. When performance does not meet established standards, management shall, with the assistance of others with appropriate expertise, determine the cause and initiate corrective action. QA representatives may assist, lead, or facilitate cause investigations. For research activities, management assessments shall include the review and evaluation of research results by managers or peer groups (e.g., standing or ad hoc panels and committees) directed by management. ### **11.2 Independent Assessments** The LBNF/DUNE QAM will plan reviews as independent assessments to assist LBNF Project Management and the DUNE Technical Coordinator in identifying opportunities for quality/performance-based improvement and to ensure compliance with specified requirements. Independent assessments of the LBNF/DUNE Project can be requested by LBNF/DUNE-US Project Manager, Deputy Project Directors, SubProject Managers, DUNE Technical Coordinators. Independent assessments typically focus on quality or ESH&Q management systems, self- assessment programs, or other organizational functions identified by management. The LBNF/DUNE Project use a formal process for assigning responsibility in response to recommendations from independent assessments. These recommendations are tracked to closure. Personnel conducting independent assessments shall be technically qualified and knowledgeable in the areas assessed. A qualified lead assessor (auditor), who is a Subject Matter Expert (SME) in the technical area of assessment, is required. The team may include other SMEs to evaluate the adequacy and effectiveness of activities only if they are not responsible for the work being assessed. The Fermilab Directorate appoints an independent Long Baseline Neutrino Committee (LBNC) to advise it and LBNF and DUNE Management. The role of this standing committee is described in the _LBNF/DUNE PMP_ . The DOE and other funding agencies perform external assessments that provide an objective view of performance and thus contribute to the independent assessment process. Since such assessments are not under the control of LBNF/DUNE, they are not necessarily considered a part of the independent Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) 11-30 LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan Assessments assessment criterion. However, LBNF/DUNE management considers external assessment results in determining the scope and schedule of independent assessments. For contracted work, such as that by A/E and or construction contractors, they will receive independent assessments in accordance with the requirements of their contracts. The subprojects are organized according to the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) [5]. The LBNF/DUNE Systems Engineering teams maintain a _LBNF/DUNE Systems Engineering Management Plan (SEMP)_ [6], which identifies the Projects’ Interface Control matrices that provide the tier structure for the flow down of QA Plans, with this QA Plan as the top tier. Specific QA plans shall be developed by Project Partners with the assistance of the LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Manager (QAM) for particular component or system quality assurance. Due to the limited scope of work of some of the Partners on the projects, they may elect to work under the LBNF/DUNE QA Plan for their scope of work. For contracted activities, such as that for conventional facilities and cryogenic infrastructures, additional QA plans developed by Architect/Engineer (A/E) firms, Construction Managers (CM), and other contractors will govern work in their areas of responsibility. For both Near Site and Far Site Conventional Facilities (CF) and well as contractors for other subprojects, each construction contractor will work within its own QA plan and procedure system, which must comply with the requirements in this Plan and with its own QA program. In case of conflict between sets of QA requirements, LBNF/DUNE-US Project Management will provide resolution. With many institutions carrying responsibility for various aspects of the Projects, institutional QA Plans will be reviewed by the LBNF/DUNE-US Project to ensure compliance with this QAP. Using a graded approach, supplements to institutions’ existing plans will be implemented for their LBNF/DUNE-US scope of work, if necessary. Overall QA supervision, including all activities described above, is the responsibility of the LBNF/DUNE-US Sub-Project Managers, and DUNE Technical Coordinators. ### **3.1 Responsibility for Project Management** The various managers, coordinators and technical leads including in kind contributors manage their Projects and are responsible for achieving performance goals. The LBNF/DUNE QAM is responsible for ensuring that a quality system is established, implemented, and maintained in accordance with requirements. The LBNF/DUNE-US QAM reports to the LBNF/DUNE-US Project Manager and LBNF/DUNEUS Deputy Project Directors for quality related issues and provides oversight and support to the Project Partners to ensure a consistent quality program. The LBNF and DUNE Projects are composed of five subprojects described above. See the LBNF/ DUNE-US Organization Charts in the _LBNF/DUNE-US Project Management Plan_ and the _DUNE Management Plan_ . The various managers, coordinators and technical leads including in kind contributors are responsible for quality within their Project scope and report their Quality Assurance issues to the appropriate Deputy Project Director and LBNF/DUNE QAM. They shall retain overall responsibility for these activities even though they have designated a QAR. ### **3.2 Levels of Authority and Interface** The _DUNE Management Plan_ , the _LBNF/DUNE-US PMP_ , and this _LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan_ (QAP) define the responsibility, authority, and interrelation of personnel who manage, perform, and verify work that affects quality. This QAP defines the QA roles and responsibilities of these management and working levels of the LBNF/DUNE Project. All LBNF/DUNE team members, Collaborators, In-Kind Contributors, Contractors, and Subcontractors are responsible for the quality of the work that they do and for using guidance and assistance that is available. Each has the authority to stop work and report adverse conditions that affect quality of LBNF/DUNE products to their Manager, Technical Lead or Coordinator and the LBNF/DUNE QAM. The various managers, coordinators and technical leads including in kind contributors responsible for LBNF/DUNE components or systems are required to determine and document their acceptance criteria. LBNF/DUNE personnel at each level are responsible for evaluation of quality through self-assessments; however, independent quality assessments may also be requested by Project management. The LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Manager (QAM) is responsible for development, implementation, assessment, and improvement of the QA program. The LBNF/DUNE QAM is also responsible for periodically reporting on the performance of the quality system to the LBNF/DUNE US Project Manager, Deputy Project Directors and DUNE Technical Coordinators for their review and as a basis for improvement of the quality system. The LBNF/DUNE-US Project Manager, Deputy Project Directors, and DUNE Technical Coordinators or higher authority may call for Quality Assurance Program readiness assessments as the Project nears major milestones. The various managers, coordinators and technical leads including in kind contributors and the LBNF/DUNE QAM are all responsible for providing the resources needed to conduct the Project successfully, including those required to manage, perform, and verify work that affects quality. ### **3.3 Quality Assurance Organization** The LBNF/DUNE QAM may request personnel from across the five sub-Project Teams to act on behalf of the LBNF/DUNE QAM to perform quality assurance functions, based on need, in accordance with the Graded Approach described above. The requested personnel shall possess qualifications or receive the appropriate training required to perform these functions. The various managers, coordinators and technical leads including in kind contributors are required to ensure personnel possess the experience, knowledge, skills, and abilities necessary to fulfill their responsibilities. This includes: - Identifying and providing required project/task-specific training. - Identifying and providing required On-The-Job (OJT) training. OJT can be mentor based where an expert is assigned by line management to train personnel. It is line management’s responsibility to ensure mentors assigned to conduct OJT are qualified. - Maintaining appropriate records of training. - Utilizing position descriptions, hazard analyses, new personnel requisitions, to identify the functional requirements and any physical limitations. This ensures that a continuous match exists between the capabilities of the personnel and the physical requirements and/or mental demands of the current assignment. **1 Overview** The global neutrino physics community is developing a multi-decade physics program to measure unknown parameters of the Standard Model of particle physics and search for new phenomena. The program will be carried out as an international, leading-edge, and dual-site experiment for neutrino science and proton decay studies, which is known as the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). The detectors for this experiment will be designed, fabricated, commissioned, and operated by the international DUNE Collaboration and installed by the Far Detectors + Cryogenics Subproject team. The facility required to support this experiment, the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF), is hosted by Fermilab. The LBNF/DUNE-US Project is organized as a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) project incorporating international partners. Together LBNF and DUNE will comprise the world's highest-intensity neutrino beam at Fermilab, in Batavia, IL, a high-precision near detector on the Fermilab site, massive liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) far detectors installed deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) 1,300 km away in Lead, SD, and all of the conventional and technical facilities necessary to support the beamline and detector systems. The management of the LBNF/DUNE Project elements are described in the _LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan_ [1] (PMP) and the _DUNE Management Plan_ [2]. ### **1.1 Purpose** The primary objective of the LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance (QA) program described in this document is to implement quality in the construction of the LBNF facility and DUNE experiment while providing protection of LBNF/DUNE personnel, the public, and the environment. This QA Plan aligns the LBNF/DUNE QA activities, which are spread around the world, with the Fermilab Quality Assurance Manual [3]. The Manual identifies the Fermilab Integrated Quality Assurance Program features that serve as the basis for this QA Plan. These include: - Personnel training and qualification - Quality improvement programs - Document, records, and configuration management - Work process control - Engineering design quality standards - Procurement quality processes - Inspection and acceptance testing - Management assessments - Independent assessments - Suspect/Counterfeit items prevention Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) 1-9 LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan Overview This QA Plan outlines the QA requirements for LBNF/DUNE project team members, collaborators, and subcontractors, henceforth referred to as Project Partners, and describes how the requirements shall be met. QA criteria can be satisfied using a graded approach. This Plan is implemented by the development of quality plans, procedures, and guides to accommodate those specific quality requirements. ### **1.2 Scope** This plan provides Quality Assurance requirements applicable to all Project Partners, encompassing all activities performed by or for the LBNF/DUNE Project, from research and development (R&D) through fabrication, shipping, receipt, installation, facility acceptance and component commissioning. The Quality Assurance requirements applicable to the A/E, Construction Manager/General Contractor (CM/GC), other subcontractors and In-Kind Contributors will be incorporated into the applicable contracts/agreements and will meet the requirements provided in this plan. The LBNF/DUNE – US Project is divided into five sub-projects: - FSCF EXC SP (Far Site Conventional Facilities Sub-Project) - FSCF BSI SP (Far Site Conventional Facilities Infrastructure Sub-Project) - NSCF+B SP (Near Site Conventional Facilities Plus Beam Line Subproject) - FD+C SP (Far Detectors Plus Cryogenics Sub-Project) - ND SP (Near Detector Sub-Project) Contracted A/E firms will be responsible for elements of the design, and contracted Construction Management firms will be responsible for supplying design-phase pre-construction services of the Conventional Facilities. Construction Management during the Conventional Facilities construction phase of the Project will be performed by a sub-contracted Construction Manager/General Contractor (CM/GC) at the Far Site and a CM/GC at the Near Site. Subcontractors and Project Partners will be responsible for providing their deliverables, whether subsystems, components, or services in accordance with applicable contracts and agreements. All parties will be responsible for implementing a quality plan that meet the requirements of this quality plan. Oversight of the work of these parties will be the responsibility of the LBNF/DUNE-US Project Manager, DUNE Technical Coordinators, Sub-Project Managers, and LBNF/DUNE QA Manager. Additional quality requirements for conventional facilities construction activities will be invoked through the application of the Construction Quality Management Program which is an addendum to this quality plan. This Construction Quality Management program will define the QC responsibilities of the Subcontractors and the QA oversight activities of the FSCF EXC, FSCF BSI and NSCF+B sub-projects. ### **1.3 Definitions** Below is a set of definitions as they are used in this plan: Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) 1-10 LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan Overview - **Inspection Test Record (ITR)** – a document listing the criteria that will be checked prior to making an item or service acceptable. - **Quality** – Fitness of an item, service, process, or design for its intended use. - Quality Assurance Representative – A person or persons designated by the LBNF Project Manager and DUNE Consortia Technical Lead to perform Quality Assurance functions. - **Quality Assurance (QA)** – The set of actions taken to provide confidence that quality requirements are fulfilled, and to detect and correct poor results. - **Quality Assurance Plan** - The plan establishes principles, requirements, practices, and methods for integrating quality into the project. - **Quality Control Plan** - Written description of the measures for controlling the variations in a process within the acceptable limits. - **Quality-assuring actions** – Planning, analyses, documentation, and other actions necessary to comply with requirements and ensure that goals are achieved. - **Safety** – Environment, Safety, and Health (ES&H) as defined in _LBNF/DUNE Integrated ESH&Q Plan_ [4]. ### **1.4 Graded Approach** This LBNF/DUNE QA Plan utilizes a graded approach to tailor the types and extent of controls applied to implement quality in fulfilling applicable requirements. The graded approach is applied based on prudent management, planning, and cost. This methodology follows the _Fermilab Quality Assurance Manual, Chapter 12070: Graded Approach Procedure_ . Application of the graded approach entails: - Identifying activities which present significant quality risk - Defining the activity - Evaluating risk and control choice - Documenting and approving the application of the graded approach. This process supports the project’s responsibility to prioritize resource usage in areas where the activities have been identified as requiring the most control and oversight. All Project Partners shall ensure that a graded approach to quality requirements is applied in accordance with this section for products and services under their control and is used when establishing levels of control. Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) 1-11 LBNF/DUNE Quality Assurance Plan Responsibilities ## **2 Responsibilities** - **2.1 LBNF/DUNE-US Project Director, Deputy Project Directors, LBNF/DUNEUS Project Manager** - Aligns with, supports, and promotes the LBNF/DUNE QA Program; has ultimate accountability for all aspects of Quality for all work done under the scope of the project. - Holds project management accountable for the implementation of and compliance with this QA plan as well as for its effectiveness - **2.2 LBNF/DUNE-US Subproject Managers, DUNE Technical Coordinators** - Ensure compliance with this quality plan

Proposal for Contributions to the Development of a photon detector system for the DUNE Liquid Argon TPC Detector for the Period February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016 Overview This statement of work provides details of funding for R&D and design tasks related to the development of a photon detector (PD) sub-detector for the DUNE far detector (FD). Members of the NIU team involved in this effort are: professors Gerald Blazey, Michael Eads and Vishnu Zutshi (PI), senior research scientist Alexander Dyshkant, senior technician Kurt Francis, students and electrical and mechanical machine shops. Funds are requested here to: Set up infrastructure for the evaluation, characterization and long-term performance of Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) in a cryogenic environment Study SiPM parameters and performance in warm and cold conditions Initiate the development of a quality assurance plan and procedure for SiPM qualification for LAr TPC prototypes under the following scheduled activities: 13122.05.290 Test passive ganging of 3 SiPMs 13122.05.300 Test passive ganging of 6 SiPMs 13122.05.310 Prepare final report on passive SiPM ganging The period of execution of these tasks is February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016. The tasks will be executed in coordination with existing members of the PD group especially CSU and Caltech. Statement of Work During FY2016, the NIU group will contribute in the following areas: Initiate SiPM characterization in warm (room temperature) conditions. The test stand will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, x-talk, after-pulsing etc.) using DUNE electronics. Of particular interest will be characterization of ganged sensors. Studies will initially look at performance of three ganged sensors and then explore the possibility of ganging six of them. This task will primarily involve Francis and a student with oversight by Zutshi and assistance from Gary Drake (ANL). Setup cryogenic test-stand for SiPM characterization and qualification. Once the test stand is setup it will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, x-talk, after-pulsing etc.) using DUNE electronics. Ganging studies will be extended to this realm. Failure modes, both electrical and mechanical will be explored. This task will primarily involve Dyshkant, Francis and NIU machine & electrical shops with oversight by Blazey and Zutshi. Detailed comparisons of sensor parameters in warm and cold environments to understand the performance correlations and dependencies. This will be used to demonstrate how well the determination of sensor parameters in the warm environment can be extrapolated to LAr temperatures. This task will primarily involve a student with oversight by Eads. Initiate development of a work plan and procedure for quality control and assurance of SiPMs for the LAr TPC prototypes under design or construction. This should be considered as the first step in the development of long-term (~30 years) qualification procedures for the SiPMs. This task will primarily involve Francis and a student with oversight by Eads and Zutshi. Cost Proposal for Brookhaven National Laboratory N.B. The NIU Division of Research and Innovation Partnerships has approved a cost share of up to $13K.

Coordinate efforts with NIU for development of tests in order to ensure reproducibility and reliability of the testing procedures by repeating measurements and measuring independently with a DC characterization program.
