The _LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan_ (PMP) [1] describes the project management, high-level governance, and oversight structures; responsibilities, systems, project management documents, and processes used for managing the LBNF/DUNE enterprise to achieve its scientific, technical, cost, and schedule objectives for the construction project. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) project that supports this is the LBNF/DUNE-US Project (“Project”). The U.S. Project is divided into six subprojects, each is described in separate appendices to the PMP: ● Far Site Conventional Facilities Excavation (FSCF-EXC) ● Far Site Conventional Facilities Buildings and Site Infrastructure (FSCF-BSI) ● Near Site Conventional Facilities (NSCF) ● Beamline ● First two Far Detector modules and Cryogenics (FDC) ● Near Detector (ND) U.S. scope as part of the LBNF/DUNE-US Near Detector (ND) Subproject covers the liquid argon TPC near detector (ND-LAr), ND-LAr Cryostat, the muon spectrometer (TMS) accompanying ND-LAr, the off-axis movement system (PRISM), integration/installation, and all liquid argon (LAr) cryogenics infrastructure to support ND-LAr, to be installed at the Near Site (Fermilab). This document describes the management of the ND Subproject. Section 2 lists the partners that interact with the ND Subproject. Section 3 describes host lab support for the ND Subproject. Section 4 describes the roles and responsibilities of the ND Subproject team. The scope of the ND Subproject is represented by the WBS structure discussed in Section 5. Section 6 describes the ND Integration and Installation roles and responsibilities for execution of work at the Near Site, following receipt of the facility from the Near Site Conventional Facilities (NSCF) Subproject. Section 7 describes external boards that the ND Subproject interacts with in managing the U.S. deliverables to the DUNE Near Detector. ND Key Performance Parameters (KPPs) are found in the LBNF/DUNE Project Execution Plan (PEP) and must be approved by the Federal Project Director. The ND Subproject is responsible for coordinating with the DUNE Collaboration to design, fabricate, construct, and install ND-LAr (including its Cryostat and liquid argon Cryogenics), TMS, and PRISM. Note that the on-axis neutrino detector (SAND) and its associated liquid Helium Cryogenics system, while part of the DUNE Near Detector, are not part of ND Subproject scope and will be handled via a separate agreement between INFN and Fermilab according to the MOU between DOE and the Italian Ministry of Universities and Research. Title: LBNF/DUNE Overview - Logistics Workshop Aug 2015

LBNF/DUNE Project Overview Elaine McCluskey, LBNF Project Manager LBNF/DUNE Logistics Planning Workshop 11 Aug 2015 International Particle Physics Community Steps toward LBNF/DUNE 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 2 2013: European Strategy for Particle Physics updated Endorsed high priority of neutrino physics Bottom line: CERN should help the European neutrino community participate in a long-baseline program outside of Europe 2014: P5 Plan A strategic plan for U.S. particle physics maximizing opportunities for breakthrough science Explicit prioritization, hard choices made within realistic budget scenarios Particle physics community unified behind the plan: 2,331 signatures on letter sent to DOE Secretary Moniz P5 Mandate: a new international collaboration 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 3 P5 recommendation 13: “Form a new international collaboration to design and execute a highly capable Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) hosted by the U.S. To proceed, a project plan and identified resources must exist to meet the minimum requirements in the text [of the report]. LBNF is the highest-priority large project in its timeframe” Basically asks Fermilab to do for neutrinos what CERN did for the Higgs, involving the worldwide community The science from DUNE will be game changing for particle and astro-particle physics and will be in all the textbooks. P5 Mandate: Scope of LBNF/DUNE based on science requirements 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 4 “For a long-baseline oscillation experiment, based on the science drivers and what is practically achievable in a major step forward, we set as the goal a mean sensitivity to CP violation of better than 3σ over more than 75% of the range of possible values of the unknown CP-violating phase δCP.” “With a wideband neutrino beam produced by a proton beam with power of 1.2 MW, this … implies a far detector with fiducial mass of more than 40 kilotons of liquid argon and a suitable near detector.” This is the scope of the LBNF/DUNE project. DUNE is a discovery science program….science requirements drive the scope and design 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 5 Determine if neutrinos violate leptonic CP and by how much Extract multiple detailed properties of neutrinos in a single experiment to test the current 3-flavor paradigm Look for surprises Search for nucleon decay Detect thousands of neutrinos from galactic supernova explosions And more Facility and Experiment as separate major subprojects 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 6 The facility, LBNF, is treated as a separate project from the experiment, “DUNE”, but with a single Federal Project Director....this facilitates CERN as facility partner DUNE Collaboration comprises 776 members from 26 countries and 144 institutions (~ half international) DUNE has brought together the world liquid argon TPC neutrino community, as well as an underground neutrino particle astrophysics community Collaboration has come together faster than even the optimistic schedule considered by P5….an indication of intense interest in this science and the perception that the DOE is prepared to host an ambitious world class neutrino facility LBNF/DUNE Partners 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 7 Strong domestic and international scientific and funding partners are key to LBNF/DUNE success. CERN is a major partner in facility infrastructure at both Fermilab and SURF (such as cryostats) who will also facilitate European engagement. UK, Switzerland, Italy, India are showing strong leadership and support Groups from France, Poland, Spain, Brazil, Netherlands… campaign soon to begin to engage all 26 countries involved Agreements with individual countries will take 3-4 years, once DOE commits to the project. And of course, South Dakota, where more than $100M has been invested in the facility to date. P5 “Minimum to Proceed” 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 8 It will take considerable time to secure the international agreements needed for full scope of LBNF/DUNE Recognizing this, P5 defined a “minimum to proceed”: “The minimum requirements to proceed are the identified capability to reach an exposure of at least 120 kt*MW*yr by the 2035 timeframe, the far detector situated underground with cavern space for expansion to at least 40 kt LAr fiducial volume, and 1.2 MW beam power upgradable to multi-megawatt power.” Non-DOE contributions to the LBNF/DUNE project can thus be divided into those needed for the minimum to proceed, and those additional contributions needed to reach the full scope LBNF/DUNE Scope 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 9 LBNF will provide facilities at Fermilab and at SURF to enable the scientific program of DUNE. Title: DUNE Governance Document

Governance of the DUNE Collaboration The DUNE Collaboration DUNE-docdb-1 Version 10, approved on 25-July-2026 Table of Contents Preamble Preparation, Approval and Amendments of the Agreement Collaboration membership Institutional Board Co-Spokespersons Deputy Spokesperson Executive Board Collaboration General Assembly Young DUNE Physics, Technical and Resource Coordinators Other Management Structures Dissenting opinions and Procedure to Appeal Attachments Records of drafts and amendments Preamble The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a multi-purpose neutrino and nucleon decay experiment that will use the Fermilab accelerator complex, a neutrino beam line, a near detector complex, and a far detector composed of a set of large liquid argon TPC’s situated deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, Lead, South Dakota, U.S.A. The DUNE experiment will be designed and constructed by the collaborating institutions (The DUNE Collaboration). This document, “Governance of the DUNE Collaboration” (GDC) provides a formal framework of the governance of the DUNE Collaboration. The participating institutions and collaborators recognize that the DUNE experiment is an exciting and important experiment that must be designed, constructed, operated and completed successfully. The DUNE Collaboration recognizes the core values of international scientific collaboration across borders as a driver for peace. We work together in the spirit of peaceful collaboration, and we are unified in support of fundamental human rights. Thus, all participants agree that they will do their best to collaborate in a congenial and constructive manner beyond the language of this document for the ultimate success of the experiment. The relationship between the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) and the DUNE collaboration as well as their respective roles are described in the DUNE/LBNF Project Management Plan (See Attachment A.1). Article 1 Amendments of the Agreement Amendments to this document can be made as needed by a 2/3 majority vote by the DUNE Institutional Board (IB), which is defined in Article 3. The proposed amendments must be announced at least two weeks ahead of an IB meeting and the outcome will be determined by a vote. Article 2 Collaboration Membership § 2.1 Membership of the DUNE Collaboration Members of the DUNE collaboration must be affiliated with collaborating institutions. The IB representative for an institution has the following responsibilities: determination of the list of DUNE members at the institution; notifying the IB Chair of any changes to institutional membership; ensuring that members of the institution fulfill agreed commitments to DUNE. (The different types of members and their responsibilities are defined in attachment A.6.) Through their membership of the DUNE collaboration, collaborators agree to abide by the DUNE Community Agreement (see attachment A.5). Membership in the DUNE collaboration may be restricted, suspended or revoked for serious violations of the DUNE Community Agreement or the general principles stated in this document, as determined by the procedures provided in that document. Restrictions may include qualifications or limits to the privileges of membership. Collaborators whose membership has been revoked may not reapply for membership. The DUNE Collaboration recognizes that collaborating institutions or their funding agencies may sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with relevant parties that defines in whole or in part their contribution to the experiment. § 2.2 Admission of New Institutions and New Senior Members to DUNE A prospective new institution, after conferring with the Co-Spokespersons, will submit a written application to the IB Chair and to the Co-Spokespersons at least two weeks prior to the meeting of the IB at a scheduled IB meeting. The application will include a proposal stating the intended contributions that the prospective institution is proposing to make to the experiment and a well thought out plan for the group’s effective participation in the experiment, and include CV’s and past research experience of the proposed senior members (faculty or equivalent) from the institution. For a successful application, there must be at least one senior member in the institution who proposes to join. The IB Chair will circulate the application materials to the IB members prior to the meeting and put consideration of the application on the agenda of the IB meeting, which may include a presentation by the prospective institution. The IB may ask for verbal or written clarifications of items in the application. The IB may: (1) approve the proposal and formally admit the institution to the Collaboration, (2) request written clarifications to be considered at the next IB meeting, or (3) reject the proposal. IB approval should be sought if new persons of rank equivalent to faculty at a member institution wish to join the collaboration. The IB will attempt to make decisions on admission of new institutions or new members by consensus. If consensus is not possible, an open vote will be taken on admission. Admission will require a 2/3 majority vote, in favor of the application, of those representatives with the right to vote present and voting (an abstention is not a vote for this purpose). Existing senior members of the collaboration who move to a different collaborating institution should notify the IB Chair and Co-Spokespersons but do not require IB approval to change their DUNE institutional affiliation. § 2.3 Associate Membership The collaboration may decide to admit associate institutions. The type of membership must be specified during the application process. Associate Institutions will join the collaboration for an initial period of 2 years, which can be extended by application to the IB. The purpose of this limited membership is either to prepare an intuition for full membership or for it to make time- or subject-limited contributions to the experiment, which do not justify full membership. IB representatives of associate institutions can attend IB meetings but not vote (see § 3.3). § 2.4 Secession from DUNE An institution may leave the collaboration by notification to the IB chair. However, the items contributed to the experiment by the out-going institution that are not covered by any relevant MOUs may not be removed without an approval by the IB. § 2.5 Removal of Institutions from DUNE Removal of an institution from DUNE can be proposed by any IB or Executive Board member for actions by the institution that are judged to be gravely detrimental to the experiment, against the spirit of peaceful collaboration laid out in this document, or for no activity in the experiment by the institution for more than one year. An open vote will be taken on removal. Removal will require a 2/3 majority vote, in favor of the removal, of those representatives with the right to vote present and voting (an abstention is not a vote for this purpose). Details of the procedure are specified in attachment A.7 and A.8. Article 3 Institutional Board § 3.1 Role of the Institutional Board In general, the Institutional Board (IB) is responsible for establishing governance rules of the DUNE collaboration and regulating the governance related issues. The responsibilities of the IB include but are not limited to: admission of new collaborating institutions and members; oversight of Co-Spokesperson election process; approval of common funds assessments; establishment and governance of detector operations shifts; and establishment of procedures for publication of scientific results and authorship rules. The IB can request presentations on and discussion of specific issues relating to the collaboration or the experiment. The results of such discussions may be recorded and passed to the Co-Spokespersons as formal advice. § 3.2 Membership of the Institutional Board All collaborating institutions except the host lab will be given one seat in the IB regardless of their varying sizes. Fermilab will be given two seats to reflect the lab’s large DUNE membership as well as its role as the host lab of the DUNE experiment. Each institution designates its IB representative. § 3.3 IB Voting In general, the IB will attempt to make decisions by consensus. If consensus is not reachable, the IB can have open or secret votes on various issues. Normally, IB votes will be open votes and each IB member’s vote will be counted as one vote regardless of the number of collaboration members they represent. On issues deemed to be sensitive the IB can decide to have a secret vote, which can be triggered by a motion by any IB member. The IB will then decide whether to have a secret vote or not on the issue by an open vote. Even for secret votes, the “one IB representative, one vote” principle will normally apply. For exceptional cases, the IB can decide to have a secret vote that is weighted by the number of collaboration members (eligible voters for general election) each IB member represents, following the procedure described above. Any IB representative that attends an IB meeting physically or virtually will be considered present for that meeting. For votes conducted during a scheduled IB meeting, representatives of the IB must be present at the time of the vote to vote and, when required, to count toward quorum; if unable to attend, a member may designate another collaboration member from their institution to attend by notifying the IB chair prior to the start of the meeting. In general, votes may be conducted electronically, unless otherwise specified in this document. Requirements for an ordinary (more than 1/2) or extraordinary (2/3 or more) majority will be taken with respect to all votes cast. Abstentions count for purposes of quorum but are not counted as votes cast. For votes requiring quorum, the quorum will be calculated with respect to voting members of the IB at the time the preliminary agenda or electronic ballot is distributed; any fractional quorum requirement will be rounded up to the nearest whole number. Routine IB decisions do not require quorum. These include approval of minutes; admission of new collaborating institutions and members; selection of collaboration meeting locations and dates; routine administrative decisions; requests for presentations or discussions; and establishment of IB committees. Committees proposing changes of the governance structure of the collaboration do require a vote. Major collaboration-wide policy decisions require a quorum of 40% of voting members of the IB. These include approval or material revision of common funds assessments or policy; detector operations shifts; service work requirements; publication or authorship rules; collaboration-wide data access or data sharing policy; and other policies or regulations that materially affect the collaboration as a whole. Governance decisions require a quorum of 50% of voting members of the IB and an extraordinary majority of votes cast. These include changes to this governance document, and major changes to the structure of the collaboration. The quorum requirement for removal of the IB Chair and the Co-spokespeople is specified in § 3.4 and § 4.3, respectively. If quorum is not present for a quorum-requiring vote at an IB meeting, the IB shall not take final action on that item at that meeting. The IB may discuss the matter and take a non-binding straw vote. Unless the motion is withdrawn, the IB Chair shall then submit the item to an electronic vote within 4 weeks, with the final motion, decision category, quorum and majority requirements, supporting materials, and a summary of the discussion circulated to the IB. The voting period will remain open for at least ten business days. If the electronic vote also fails to reach quorum and the motion is not withdrawn, the item shall be placed on the agenda of a subsequent IB meeting held at a collaboration meeting; at that meeting the item may be decided without quorum requirement or discussion, subject to the applicable majority requirement. This paragraph does not apply to removal of the IB Chair or Co-spokesperson under § 3.4 and § 4.3 respectively. Any motion made at an IB meeting requires the motion be seconded by another IB member in order to go forward. When timely action is necessary to avoid significant harm to DUNE operations, collaboration obligations, or commitments of the experiment, the IB may approve interim action without satisfying the quorum requirements above, by ordinary majority of votes cast at an IB meeting. Such interim action may not modify this governance document; change authorship rights; impose new common funds assessments; or establish continuing institutional obligations. Interim action expires after 90

The experiment and far site facility are assumed to operate for twenty years starting after a fully complete far detector in 2027, after which time the far detector decommissioning is initiated in 2047. The DOE LBNF/DUNE TPC has a CD-1 point estimate of $1,457M, and a total life cycle cost of $2,026M. All costs in the analysis include escalation. The operations at each site are assumed to be incremental to the existing operations of facilities or experiments. The overall increase in operations costs at both FNAL and SURF would be $494M for twenty years of running. The detector and facilities at SURF would cost $173M to operate for twenty years, however the international DUNE collaboration will support the detector operations cost. This is expected to be funded through a common fund supported by all of the international partners that contributed to detector construction. DUNE detector maintenance and operations cost estimates will be refined as design matures and individual partner contributions will be defined as the international and common fund agreements are established. The LBNF beamline is not assumed to be decommissioned or demolished upon conclusion of the experiment; other experiments are assumed to use this facility at that time. Far detector decommissioning and demolition at SURF would occur in FY47 to FY48, and include removal of detector components and restoring the surface. This is estimated to cost $75M. 13 ###### **4 ACQUISITION APPROACH** Acquisition of the LBNF/DUNE will be conducted through Fermi Research Alliance (FRA), the FNAL M&O contractor, which will have the ultimate responsibility to successfully execute the LBNF/DUNE project for DOE. The LBNF/DUNE project is separated into two parts: the facilities project, LBNF and the detector project, DUNE. LBNF will be built by FNAL as a host laboratory, with international contributions. DUNE near and far detectors will be built by the international DUNE collaboration through many contributors including DOE. FRA/FNAL, in coordination with DOE-OHEP and DUNE collaboration has established a set of structures to provide coordination among participating funding agencies, oversight of LBNF/DUNE project, and coordination between LBNF and DUNE parts of the project. These are in place and are described further in Section 7. DOE will cooperate and coordinate with interested international and domestic partners to plan and execute the overall LBNF/DUNE project. International contributions to the design and construction of LBNF/DUNE will be defined in the context of bi‐lateral agreements between the U.S. and other participating countries. Mechanisms are in place to facilitate joint consultation between the partner funding agencies, such that coordinated oversight and actions will be taken to ensure the success of the overall program. The LBNF/DUNE project makes use of existing FNAL staff and facilities to support design and construction and provide project management and oversight for both LBNF and DUNE parts of the project. FNAL is the location for the near site facility delivering the neutrino beam. The design, construction, and installation of the LBNF/DUNE components will be carefully coordinated with other research activities at FNAL. At the far site, LBNF Project will coordinate with the South Dakota Science & Technology Authority (SDSTA), owner of the former Homestake Mine property and operator of SURF. The LBNF project will contract directly with SDSTA to provide pre-construction services and design of LBNF Conventional Facilities (CF) at SURF. Construction contracting for the CF will be directly from FNAL as described further in the Acquisition Strategy and supporting acquisition planning documents. DOE is presently funding SDSTA ongoing operations through Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) and its SURF Operations Office through FY16; this is expected to change to funding through FNAL starting in FY17. Coordination between SDSTA, FNAL and the LBNF Project will ensure efficient operations at SURF while meeting LBNF requirements. This will be facilitated with an agreement being developed between SDSTA and FNAL regarding the LBNF Project that defines responsibilities and methods of working together during the LBNF Project design and construction. 35 Ton Run 2 Hardware and Operational experiences Alan Hahn 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 1 Organization Overall Run Cryo Detector “Hardware” Categories TPC Including HV Cold Electronics Photon Detectors DAQ Systems 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 2 Run: 35T Cooldown and Filling 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 3 Run: e- Lifetime 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting PrM2 & 3, both long PrMs midway heights in Cryostat(these lifetimes may drop a bit (~10%) using PrM0 as a constraint) Sitewide Power Outage LN2 Cooling Loss Tubing Break Pump Start 4 3 ms Bad News Period Run: Purity Stratification near start of Purification 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting PrM 1 (near Cryostat bottom) PrM 4 (near surface) O2 Gas Analyzer, ~(~80 cm from bottom) 5 Geometry of 35 Ton Cryostat (from E.Voirin recent 35 Ton FEA calculations Dune DocDb 1156) 4/14/16 6 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 4 purity monitors in this corner (Geometry Not in CFD model) PrM1 Pump intake Pump outflow Discussion of Results / Lessons Learned Phase separator cools inlet flow to approach saturation temperature, which is below the “bulk temperature” of the argon. This cooler, more dense layer of argon tends to stay at the bottom, and not mix well with the rest of the argon. Back pressure control at the phase separator could allow us to flow in warmer argon, which would then mix well with the bulk. 4/14/16 7 Dune Friday Phone Meeting Pump Suction Pump Discharge Pipe with Phase Separator on Top, LAr flows down, and impinges on cryostat floor. New constraint RTD measurements previous slide verifies this temperature stratification Run: Stratification Explanation PrM1&4 with 3 Precision RTDs Opportunity provided by Power Outage 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 8 Pump is off PrM 1&4 show same lifetime 3 RTD offsets made to match Barometric Pressure Pump is on Uppermost RTD Lowest RTD PrM 1&4 lifetimes diverge 12 hrs after Outage Run: Beware the Ides of March Three consecutive “events” ~one week apart and all on weekends Site-wide power outage stopped our recirculation and dropped the LAr Purity (3/4—Friday Night) See the loss of purity due to outage on previous slides. Loss of LN2 Cooling (broken valve) caused a loss of LAr (~1/2 ton through boil off) (3/12--Saturday) Amount of loss because Autodialer Alarm had not been reset since the previous week’s Power Outage—Doh! Only noticed on Sunday and fixed in afternoon Dropped LAr level below desired HV-precaution level Unrecoverable Contamination of LAr (3/17-Saturday 2 AM) Small tube attached to GAr Bellows Pump that was being used to transfer GAr between LAPD and 35Ton broke- pulling in air and injecting it into the LAr stream. Estimate it would take ~20 weeks of filtering/filter regeneration to remove just the O2, N2 would not be removed. Went from 100 ppt to 30 ppm O2 in about 3/4 hr. 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 9 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting This broken tubing is on the suction side of pump that was pulling GAr out of LAPD, compressing it and injecting it into the LAr coming from 35T just before the purification filters. This was how we were raising the LAr level in the Cryostat 10 Bellows Pump Cryo Issues Pumping Had problems establishing the 35Ton Internal LAr Pumping Pumps had been rebuilt after Phase 1, but had never been run in. Finally putting 3 phase 208 AC on pump motor broke it free. Then normal AC Drive worked fine. Lesson learned—nothing goes into cryostat without a functionality test Even if it worked fine last time (e.g. Phase 1). Need a better interface into Controls and Alarms Autodialer not working cost us LAr level when LN2 valve stopped functioning. Did it help lead us a bit quicker into the Tubing break?? (Speculative) Painful to use the Cryo Interface at time incredible slow downs. Discourages one from looking at trends if it takes forever to get up and run. Massive Contamination of LAr I believe there will be a review of exactly what happened and that will suggest several lessons to be learned from How did we get into this situation in the first place? Recognition of how fast you can completely contaminate a sizeable amount of LAr How to identify other similar modes that might cause same problem. Perhaps a way to quickly and automatically respond to an event since there is almost no time for people to recognize what is going on. 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 11 TPC Detector Installation in Cryostat was a well planned and effectively carried out enterprise Thanks Jack Fowler, Dan Wenman, Bo Yu, Lee Scott, Bob Kubinski Demonstrates that careful planning actually works! Field Cage, Cathode, HV 60 kV (@Cathode) in “clean” LAr Wanted to get track measurements made at this lower field before “risking” raising the HV higher and potentially breaking something. Did see small spikes, and did have two apparent breakdowns (one while ramping back up after first breakdown). These breakdowns happened just ~12 hrs before the LAr contamination Large disappointment with LAr contamination is that we weren’t able to test Cathode HV at 120 kV in pure LAr However we did continue the tests in what we had Held 120 kV for 1 week without breakdown Held 135 kV for 1 day with breakdown. A summary of the HV studies will be made. Most info is in elog 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 12 HV History over Run 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 13 Cold Electronics As is well known, the FEMBs + the APAs have been plagued by relatively high noise levels These swamp the original specs that were based on thermal noise figures, as measured with capacitive loads Clearly see noise influences that correlate to the individual wire planes 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 14 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 15 Recent data from Cold Run17366 3/16) Test done by Bo Y. and Matt W. at BNL with 3 Bd APA. DocDB 9439, 7/2014 Data from 4 Bd taken at DAB (7/15) Our “low noise” state includes this correlated noise. In addition, we are occasionally/often triggered into an extremely high noise state that makes it impossible to use the data for anything. Much work is being done now by Marvin Johnson, Brian Kirby, Linda Bagby, Steve Chappa… in trying to characterize this noise Hope that understanding can be fed into the electronics/APA design/??? for ProtoDune 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 16 Noise (Continued) Online Event Display -Collection Plane Top view of APA 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 17 “Normal” Noise State Very High Noise State APA Long drift Short drift Photon Detectors Detectors One Detector left unplugged during cabling Observed Low noise level for those channels wasn’t recognized as the serious problem it was. PD Signals seem to be impacted by noise—not positive if this is noise being generated by the APAs SSPs After fixing an issue with the NOvA timing chain (back at DAB), these have been reliable We have had very good response from ANL when we have had any problems Calibration Module Working fine, able to calibrate the PDs 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 18 DAQ Flange Board All signals/electrical services to APA/PD pass through this Board. Had serious issues with initial version Second version much better Issue with Bias lines—leakage currents quite high, and very non-linear with voltage Eventually we bypassed the FB and went directly to SHV bulkhead connectors on own flanges. PennTrigger Board Slow start, but eventually it wsa providing our triggers Cosmic Ray Counters Allowed us to trigger on tracks that are useful for looking at the APA features. Fiber Links Very problematic at DAB and early at PC4. Often had to “reseat” the optical transceivers, or reset the links. Settled down at some point and were less of a problem for rest of run. RCE systems Once things calmed down, they appear to be working fine. Spares were an issue, since a failure would take down ½ the TPC APAs 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 19 DAQ (continued) NEMA 12 Rack Turned out to be one of the highest risk items for the 35 T run (until Tubing at least). Contains DAQ Servers, RCE Systems, Network Switches in a closed Air Condition Rack The power for the Air Conditioning was put on an interlock that was tied into the Rack Smoke Detection Module and was not plugged into the rack power. Also an internal power switch for Air Conditioning could be switched off. Three“near miss” incidents Two were early in the DAQ installation at PC4 where the air conditioner could or actually was disabled, with the rack doors closed. However these were caught before anything happened. 3rd event was much more advanced when it was caught—rack temperatures were in > 60C range as reported by Network switch in rack Fortunately M. Convery came by PC4 from ROC-W (@7PM because he noticed the RCE readout wasn’t working at ROC-W. He opened the doors, things cooled off. After this last episode, we established a management control signage to be used whenever rack was opened to be worked on. Added an external light that was lit as long as power was available to the AC. Recently a 50C klixon (thermal switch) was added that will drop rack power in case the Air Conditioning fails. Recommendation that one needs to do a careful risk analysis on a system like this. Operation For better or worse, the DAQ servers were not setup as Fermi Standard, so we had several cases where we were halted because the experts were not available to get the systems running. DAQ Running. Due to event size we were typically limited to event rates ~1 Hz Reliability had vastly improved near the end of the run. 4/14/16 Dune Friday Phone Meeting 20 Systems—or how things play together Grounding The 35 T cryostat was never designed with grounding in mind. There is no way that the internal membrane could be kept isolated from contact with the concrete structure that encased the Cryostat. LBNF Neutrino Beam Jim Strait, Fermilab For the LBNF/DUNE Team NuFact 2015 Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 14 August 2015 14 Aug 2015 Jim Strait | LBNF Neutrino Beam 2 Outline Overview of LBNF/DUNE Current and expected capabilities of the Main Injector complex Reference design of the LBNF Neutrino Beam Optimizing the focusing system for greater physics reach Summary 14 Aug 2015 Jim Strait | LBNF Neutrino Beam 3 Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility A facility to enable a world-leading experimental program in neutrino physics, nucleon decay, and astroparticle physics. LBNF comprises: Underground and surface facilities at the Sanford Underground Research Facility capable of hosting a modular LAr TPC of fiducial mass ≥ 40 kt (~70 kt liquid mass) Cryostats, refrigeration and purification systems to operate the detectors A high-power, wide-band, tunable, n beam at Fermilab Underground and surface facilities to host a highly-capable near detector at Fermilab … and potentially other non-oscillation neutrino experiments 14 Aug 2015 Jim Strait | LBNF Neutrino Beam 4 LBNF/DUNE LBNF is a DOE/Fermilab hosted project with international participation. Major partners include CERN and SURF. Title: Dune Speaker's Committee (SC) rules

## **Version 1.5, 14 August 2015, changes compared to 1.4 indicated in red.** # **DUNE Speakers Committee Guidelines** ## (1) Purpose and Responsibilities The primary functions of the Speakers Committee (SC) are to ensure that the DUNE Collaboration is well represented at international conferences and to manage the assignment of DUNE speakers for all presentations (talks, posters) given on behalf of the DUNE Collaboration at international conferences and workshops. It will promote the science and technology of DUNE to the scientific community through conference presentations, seminars, and colloquia with the goal to encourage and attract new collaborators. The SC provides a single point of contact for conference and workshop organizers. ~~The scope of the SC also includes physics presentations from LBNF, but does not cover its engineering and accelerator aspects.~~ The SC solicits and promotes DUNE presentations and will support conference organizers in the planning of DUNE presentations. It assigns speakers for all DUNE presentations at international conferences and workshops, as specified by the guidelines given below. The SC maintains a record of presentations given and ensures that the material presented remains accessible to the DUNE Collaboration. Personal invitations for DUNE overview talks at international conferences and workshops may not be accepted by members of the DUNE Collaboration without the approval of the Speakers Committee. The SC assigns speakers for seminars at ~~national and~~ major international physics laboratories (e.g., Fermilab, CERN). Unless there is a new major result or discovery to present, the SC does not assign speakers to seminars or colloquia at universities and for regional meetings. On request, it can advise organizers of such events. Regional meetings are usually meetings of national physics societies without international participation, but not meetings organized by the APS and EPS. The SC submits abstracts to international conferences. If individual collaborators want to submit a DUNE abstract to a conference, prior approval by the SC is required. ## (2) Membership The SC is composed of at least six members, including the SC Chair and SC Deputy Chair, all appointed by the Spokespeople. Members serve for renewable one-year terms. To ensure continuity, not more than half of the members should be replaced each year. In addition, the Spokespeople, the Physics Coordinator, and the Technical Coordinator are ex-officio members. ## (3) Speaker Selection The SC in choosing speakers for DUNE presentations will follow the following general guidelines. - Speakers must have the expertise and background to represent the Collaboration well in their particular presentation. - Preference will be given to collaborators who have not given talks recently. - Preference will be given to collaborators making important contributions to the DUNE experiment. - Preference should be given to collaborators at an early or critical stage of their career. Other criteria can be developed and applied by the SC. The SC can exempt certain talks or speakers from these guidelines if it lies within the general interest of the Collaboration. The SC Chair will regularly ask for recommendations and input by Working Group conveners and Institutional Board representatives. The SC will also seek regional balance in assigning speakers proportional to the number of DUNE authors from that region. ## (4) Presentations All talks and posters at international workshops and conferences, as well as plenary talks at regional meetings, must be made available to the Collaboration and the SC for comments at least one week prior to the presentation. A rehearsal talk should be scheduled prior to the presentation, which at least one member of the SC can attend. This rehearsal is open to the entire Collaboration and the connection information must be announced to the Collaboration. Talks and posters shown at conferences, seminars, and colloquia can only include material that has been approved for public presentation following the publications policy of the DUNE Collaboration. The authorship of presentations should include “for the DUNE Collaboration.” The final version of presentations (ppt and pdf format) and proceedings must be stored in the public DUNE DocDB. The approval process for proceedings will be defined in the publications policy. ## (5) Other Procedures The SC meets regularly, at least twice a year. In between regular meetings, business is conducted by email. The SC Chair reports regularly to the Institutional Board and the Executive Committee.

Title: Minutes of the DUNE Institutional Board, 5 June 2015

Minutes of the DUNE institutional board meeting by telephone of 5 June 2015, 9:00 am U.S. Central Time Approved 14 August 2015 Present: The meeting was called to order by IB chair Maury Goodman 1. Minutes The minutes of the first official DUNE institutional board meeting of 18 April 2015 were approved. DUNE-docdb-14. Minutes were also included for the ELBNF institutional board meetings of 22 January 2015, 20 February 2015, 6 March 2015 and 13 March 2015, in which many of the DUNE structures were established. They are all included in docdb-14. 2. Discussion of Election Procedures During the spokesperson elections and the executive committee elections, there were a couple of complaints that the ballots were made by email and weren't strictly secret ballots. The committee(s) running the elections investigated numerous voting systems and did not (yet) find one that prevented the person from running the election from finding out how people voted if he/she chose to do so. We only want valid voters to vote but we aren't together in person. For both the spokesperson and executive committee elections there was one instance of an ineligible voter submitting a vote (just due to misunderstanding - nothing nefarious). Maury plans to investigate a "token" system. Alternative suggestions are welcomed. In the meantime, such as for the approval of appointed EC nominees, votes will be done by email with the counting done by a secretary who doesn't know or care who votes for whom. 3. Need for a governance amendment - IB vice chair The IB chair was thinking of appointing Lisa Whitehead from Houston as a deputy, to run meetings in his absence, and to distribute applications for membership in DUNE when we get them. Alfons Weber, who had helped to draft the governance rules, pointed out that this wasn't covered under those rules and an amendment to the rules would be needed. A governance amendment will be considered at a later date. 4. Approval of DUNE logo The result of the logo contest was a preference for a design that had been made by Louisa Castomonte, the wife of Cesar Castromonte from Goias. The logo was tuned by the Fermilab Media Services Department and this process iterated a few times with communication between that department and the designer. The result is 6 versions of the logo, with two layouts (vertical and horizontal) and three color patterns (colored, black on white, and white on black). There was considerable discussion, particularly about the ability to distinguish the two neutrinos which make up the N in the black on white and white on black versions. Maury will ask Media Services if they can solve this problem with a thin line or a greyscale. The IB chair asked for the following motion which was made and seconded: The IB approves the logo as submitted by FNAL and authorizes the IB chair to thank: Louisa Castromonte (wife of Cesar Castromonte from Goias) for creating the winning design Diana Brandonisio (FNAL) for tweaking the design and for vectorizing it (not yet done) Dan Cherdack (Col State) for running the elections The motion passed on a voice vote. The logos are available in docdb-4 5. Appointment of member to the executive committee There are two slots on the executive committee to be filled by Spokesperson nomination and IB ratification (Section 6.3 of the governance document). At this time, the spokespersons were nominating Bonnie Fleming for one of the two positions. A vote was taken by email to dune-election@fnal.gov, and the nomination was accepted unanimously. 6. September collaboration meeting It was previously decided that the September collaboration meeting would be in Fermilab or South Dakota. Attempts were made to plan the meeting in Deadwood, but they did not work out, in part because of the 75th Sturgiss motorcycle rally a month earlier was keeping all of the hotels filled. We also investigated holding the meeting in Rapid City SD, and that possibility existed, but we were told that good hotel prices and availability would be limited for the same reason. So the decision was made to go to Fermilab, with Deadwood and Rapid City meetings in the future. A doodle poll was taken between 2-5 September and 9-12 September and the clear preferences was 2-5 September. 7. Future collaboration meetings The January 2016 meeting should be held in a warm U.S. location. Initial conversations have been held with collaborators from University of Texas at Arlington, and Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge. Maury was asked to conduct a doodle poll of these two locations with possible dates. A possible future meeting schedule of May 2016 in Deadwood, September 2016 at Fermilab, and January 2017 in CERN was mentioned. Chris Mauger pointed out that we had skipped July this year due to the CD1-refresh, and that would be a good month for a meeting. The EC will be asked to consider a March-July-November schedule along with a January-May-September rotation. 8. Establishment of a committee to establish procedures for a DUNE speaker's committee When a new chair is appointed for the DUNE speaker's committee, a set of SC procedures will be drafted to be discussed by the executive committee and approved by the IB. Respectively Submitted Maury Goodman

execution processes that are used to ensure that DOE funded Long Baseline Neutrino Facility/ Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (LBNF/DUNE) Project scope is completed on time and within budget and effectively coordinated with the international contributions. The preliminary PEP defines the preliminary project scope; describes the organizational framework and overall management systems for the project; and identifies roles and responsibilities of the project participants. It also describes the formal change control process by which the DOE project scope, cost, and schedule may be revised. This preliminary PEP is an update of the prior PPEP approved at CD-1 and supports the Critical Decision (CD)-1 Refresh approval package. It will be updated as part of the CD-2 approval package, or to support any long-lead procurement Critical Decision approvals as needed. ###### **1.1 Project Background** The U.S. today enjoys a leadership role in exploration of neutrino properties. Neutrino experiments currently operating are designed to observe neutrino oscillations using small detectors located at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (FNAL), with much larger detectors located at distances of 700-800 km away from the FNAL neutrino source. This distance is referred to as the “baseline” of the experiment. These experiments provide important initial information on neutrino parameters relating to “mixing angles” governing neutrino oscillations, and matter-antimatter asymmetries. Current scientific results and knowledge indicates that a larger, longer-baseline neutrino detector illuminated by a high intensity neutrino source will be an important and unmatched facility for advancing neutrino physics research. On January 8, 2010, the Department of Energy Deputy Secretary approved CD-0, Mission Need [1], for a new long-baseline neutrino experiment that would enable a world-class program and firmly establish the U.S. as a leader in neutrino science. A facility to carry out this science requires a specialized detector of unprecedented size with sensitivity surpassing that of current experiments, and that can be located 1000-1500 km from the neutrino beam source. The LBNF/DUNE project is designed to meet these requirements and fulfill this mission need, by providing a U.S.-hosted facility that supports a world-class, international long-baseline neutrino research program. The earlier Long-Baseline Neutrino Experiment (LBNE) project was proposed to meet mission need, formulated primarily as a domestically funded experiment and having a minimal CD-1 configuration of a 10 kiloton far detector on the surface, with an experiment baseline of 1300 km. LBNE’s CD-1, approved December 2012, was tailored to allow for enhancement of scientific capabilities and additional scope opportunities (such as a near neutrino detector, and far detector sited underground with additional mass), should the opportunity attract the support of other domestic and international agencies. This opportunity has now attracted increasing international support following a May 2014 report issued by the High Energy Physics Advisory Panel (HEPAP) Particle Physics Project Prioritization Panel (P5), _Building for Discovery, Strategic Plan for U.S. Particle Physics in a Global Context._ [2] This report noted that a more 1 ambitious long-baseline neutrino facility has been called for by the Snowmass particle physics community study and in expressions of interest from physicists in other regions. Minimum requirements to meet scientific goals of this more ambitious program are not met by the prior LBNE project’s CD-1 minimum scope, requiring a change in approach. P5 recommended that a new international collaboration be formed to design and execute a highly capable Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) hosted by the U.S, to meet the minimum specified requirements in beam power, detector mass and exposure. These requirements are intended to achieve desired sensitivity to Charge-Parity (CP) violation, along with capability to search for phenomena such as supernova bursts and proton decay in support of meeting the mission need. An international collaboration has recently formed, called the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), bringing together a global neutrino community to pursue an acceleratorbased long-baseline neutrino experiment, as well as neutrino astrophysics and nucleon decay, with a large liquid-argon detector located deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) and a high-resolution near detector located at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (FNAL). The name LBNF/DUNE refers to this new vision of the project developed to support this program. In the DOE system, LBNF/DUNE is defined as a single project, with two main parts: LBNF, a DOE project with international contributions; and DOE contributions to the international DUNE project, which is managed by the DUNE collaboration and primarily supported by multiple international partners. For clarity, DOE only contributions to the international DUNE project will be referred to as DUNE-US. ###### **1.2 Justification of Mission Need** The physics program enabled by a large, long-baseline, detector and neutrino beam facility is fully consistent with the Secretarial Strategic Priority of Science, Discovery, and Innovation. The program would demonstrably "Advance fundamental knowledge in high energy physics and nuclear physics that will result in a deeper understanding of matter, energy, space and time." There is a capability gap in the U.S. HEP program and world-wide particle physics program for neutrino physics. Further progress in the investigation of neutrino oscillation, mass ordering and matter-antimatter asymmetry requires a combination of large detectors and more powerful beams capable of observing neutrino interactions where the beam and detector(s) are separated by 1000-1500 km. The large detector located underground and shielded from cosmic backgrounds can also be sensitive to proton decay and serve as an observatory of supernovae generated neutrinos, yielding a broader program in support of mission need. Other than the LBNF/DUNE Project, no existing or planned facility in the U.S. or internationally fills this capability gap. The LBNF/DUNE Project will provide the U.S. an opportunity to host a world-leading program in neutrino physics and support DOE HEP's strategic plan to mount a balanced and vital U.S. program in particle physics in the next decade. Without the research capabilities implemented in this project, crucial information fully characterizing the neutrino sector such as the degree of Charge-Parity (CP) violation and the ordering of the neutrino mass states, would not be 2 obtained. This would compromise the ability to understand such fundamental physical phenomena as the matter-antimatter asymmetry that results in dominance of matter in the universe, as well as nucleon decay and atmospheric and astrophysical neutrino physics, which provide insight into grand unified theories and collapse mechanisms of stars. ###### **2 PROJECT BASELINE** This section documents the project preliminary Performance Baseline (PB) that consists of the preliminary scope, total project cost (TPC), schedule (CD-4 date), funding profile, and other information related to developing the PB for DOE contributions to LBNF/DUNE. Source: docdb Title: An Experimental Program in Neutrinos, Nucleon Decay and Astroparticle Physics Enabled by the Fermilab Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility **An Experimental Program in Neutrinos, Nucleon Decay and Astroparticle Physics Enabled by the Fermilab Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility** **Alec Habig**_∗_† _University of Minnesota Duluth E-mail:_ ahabig@umn.edu A new International Team (DUNE - Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment) has been formed to pursue an accelerator-based long-baseline neutrino experiment, as well as neutrino astrophysics and nucleon decay, with an approximately 40 kt (fiducial) modular liquid argon TPC (LAr-TPC) detector located deep underground and a high-resolution near detector. Several independent worldwide efforts, developed through years of detailed studies, are converging around the opportunity provided by the megawatt neutrino beam facility planned at Fermilab and by the new significant expansion with improved access at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, 1,300 km from Fermilab. The principle goals of this experiment are: a comprehensive investigation of neutrino oscillations to test CP violation in the lepton sector, determine the ordering of the neutrino masses, and test the three-neutrino paradigm; to perform a broad set of neutrino scattering measurements with the near detector; and to exploit the large, high-resolution, underground far detector for non-accelerator physics topics including atmospheric neutrino measurements, searches for nucleon decay, and measurement of astrophysical neutrinos especially those from a core-collapse supernova. _The European Physical Society Conference on High Energy Physics 22–29 July 2015 Vienna, Austria_ > _∗_ Speaker. †for the DUNE collaboration > _⃝_ c Copyright owned by the author(s) under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). http://pos.sissa.it/ _The DUNE Experiment_ Alec Habig # **1. Organization** The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is the new name for the combined efforts of the collaborations formerly known as LBNE and LBNO with some new participants. It has new leadership: Mark Thomsen of Cambridge and André Rubbia of ETH Zurich are the spokesmen; a new Conceptual Design Report [1]; and has passed the US Department of Energy’s “CD1” milestone in July 2015. DUNE covers the detector and science goals of the project: the beam and infrastructure part of the project is now called the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF). The DUNE collaboration includes 750 scientists from 150 institutions in 23 countries. The goals this collaboration is working towards are described in this talk, with details of all sorts available online in the CDR [1]. # **2. Experimental Overview** DUNE aims to study neutrino oscillations using a new more intense beam of _νµ_ from Fermilab to an underground 40 kt liquid argon Time Projection Chamber (TPC) on the 4850 level of the Sanford Underground Lab. The 1,300 km baseline will be longer and cross more mass than current beams do, allowing for a better probe of matter effects in _νµ → νe_ appearance and thus mass hierarchy and _δCP_ . The new beam will be 1.2 MW, increasing the statistics by creating more neutrino interactions in the far detector; and tunable in energy, allowing more parameter space to be mapped out. A liquid argon TPC has fine spatial resolution, making the most out of each individual neutrino interaction and decreasing systematic error bars. The LArTPC modules will be staged as four separate 10 kt modules, the first of which will be a single phase detector in the mold of ICARUS, with the possibility of later modules to be dual-phase designs to catch ionization in the gas above the liquid. Both methods are the subject of intense R&D, with LARIAT, MicroBoone, CAPTAIN, and SBND exploring single-phase issues at Fermilab; and WA105 prototyping the dual-phase methods at CERN. To best evaluate the neutrino signal seen at the “far detector” at Homestake, a “near detector” near the beam source at Fermilab is needed to precisely measure the pre-oscillation neutrino beam and thus establish a precise “before and after” measurement. The reference design for this instrument is a fine-grained straw tube tracker with calorimeters and a 0.6 T magnet. The near detector will also be able to study the neutrino interactions themselves, expanding our knowledge of how neutrinos interact. # **3. Beam Neutrino Physics Goals** The parameters of the beam and detectors being designed are set by the desire to be sensitive to as many possible different values of the currently unknown parameter _δCP_ (the charge-parity violating phase of a neutrino) and learn what the neutrino mass hierarchy might be for any given value of _δCP_ . Figure 1 shows the reach of DUNE for these parameters vs. exposure: 5 _σ_ sensitivity to the neutrino mass hierarchy for all possible values of _δCP_ after 400 kt-MW-years, and 3 _σ_ sensitivity to _δCP_ itself for 75% of possible values of _δCP_ after 850-1300 kt-MW-years. Those are large exposures, but as seen in the figure, the simple act of designing a tunable energy beam (part of the “optimized design”) substantially accelerates the physics reach. 2 _The DUNE Experiment_ Alec Habig CP Violation Sensitivity MH Sensitivity

While the overall probability of _νe_ appearing from a beam of pure _νµ_ is governed by the recently discovered _θ_ 13 parameter, the presence of MSW-style matter effects on the oscillation as the beam passes through the earth impose a different structure on the spectrum of appearing _νe_ compared to that of _ν_ ¯ _e_ in an anti-neutrino beam: more matter in the baseline creates a larger effect, driving the location of the DUNE far detector. A “Normal Hierarchy” where the solar doublet of mass eigenstates is larger than the third state would experience an enhancement of the _νµ → νe_ appearance caused by coherent forward scattering of _ν −e_ on electrons in the earth: the “Inverted Hierarchy” would likewise experience a reduction in the appearance oscillations. This experiment’s goal is to be able to tell apart the patterns shown in Fig. 2: hence the need for a LArTPC’s fine energy resolution and sensitivity to the resulting electromagnetic shower, and the need for long exposures to both neutrino and anti-neutrino beams. One such topic is the search for proton decay, particularly modes involving kaons, predicted by many super-symmetric models. LArTPC’s spatial resolution and low thresholds are ideal for identifying the outgoing kaon, and 40 kt of mass operating for years would push limits far past what current detectors could do. Neutrinos make up 99% of the energy released when a large star reaches the end of its life and undergoes core collapse, creating a supernova. While this basic scheme was confirmed by observations of neutrinos from SN1987A, a supernova somewhere in our galaxy as observed by the DUNE detector would generate an order of magnitude more interactions. Liquid Argon is sensitive to electron neutrinos and neutral current interactions: other water-based or scintillatorbased neutrino experiments are primary sensitive to anti-electron neutrinos. Observing the time evolution of the neutrino “light curves” will be an unprecedented window into one of the most extreme places in the astrophysical universe, and seeing what those high densities of neutrinos and matter do to the neutrinos themselves via extreme matter effects and neutrino collective interactions that are not possible to probe in a lab. As well as providing a “before” picture to the “after” oscillations spectra seen in the far detector, the intense beam as seen in the DUNE near detector will provide high statistics insights into the way neutrinos interact with matter. Additionally, current neutrino experiments have taught us that it is possible to use the detectors for many other analyses. For example the atmospheric neutrinos can also be used for astrophysical neutrino observations and indirect dark matter searches. Many models of Lorentz or CPT violation, non-standard interactions, and sterile neutrinos would impose variations on the beam neutrinos which could be seen. The cosmic ray backgrounds to these neutrino searches are themselves of interest to cosmic ray physicists. Finally, if backgrounds can be controlled well enough to push down energy thresholds, DUNE might also be able to study solar neutrinos or the diffuse supernova neutrino background. 4 _The DUNE Experiment_ Alec Habig # **5. Schedule and Conclusion** The task of building this large experiment is daunting and expensive, and then it must run in the beam for many years to reach the science goals outlined above. Thus, work is happening now on design and prototyping, with civil construction and excavating planned for FY18 and a start on the far detector at Homestake planned for FY20. The first LArTPC module will be commissioned in FY25 with the beamline completed in FY26. The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment is a large experiment with large goals, and will take a lot of work over many years to come to fruition. However, that process is well under way, has many collaborators and a solid funding plan, and is off to a good start. # **References** - [1] ”LBNF/DUNE Conceptual Design Report”, https://web.fnal.gov/project/LBNF/ ReviewsAndAssessments/LBNF_DUNE%20DOE%20CD-1%20Refresh%20Review/ SitePages/Conceptual%20Design%20Report.aspx, and references therein, 2015. _Headed to an arXiv listing soon for easier reference_ 5

It is a merger of previous efforts and other interested parties to build, operate and exploit a staged 40-kt liquid argon detector and a high precision near detector exposed to a high-power, broad-band neutrino beam. The goals of the experiment are precision oscillation measurements, including CP violation and neutrino mass hierarchy determination, search for nucleon decay, and neutrino astrophysics, as well as precision neutrino physics at the near site. ## **INTRODUCTION** The DUNE Collaboration[1] plans to address a number of the fundamental open questions in particle physics and astroparticle physics utilizing a massive liquid argon time-projection chamber (LAr TPC) located at a depth of 4,300 meters water equivalent at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, South Dakota; a high-power, broad band, sign-selected _νµ_ beam at Fermilab with a baseline distance from source to detector of 1,300 km; and a precision neutrino detector located on the Fermilab site[2]. The primary science objectives[3] include: neutrino oscillation physics to search for CP is violation in the leptonic sector, determine the ordering of the neutrino mass eigenstates, make precision measurements of oscillation parameters, test the three-neutrino paradigm; searches for baryon number violating processes (nucleon decay); and neutrino astrophysics, most notably precision measurements of neutrinos from a core-collapse supernova within the Galaxy, should one occur during the multi-decade lifetime of the experiment. DUNE is a newly formed international collaboration, with strong representation from the previous LBNE, LBNO and other collaborations. As of the time of _NuFact15_ , DUNE had 776 collaborators from 144 institutions located in 26 different countries on five continents. The DUNE Collaboration will design, build, commission and operate the near and far detectors[4] and is responsible for carrying out the scientific program utilizing them. Facilities necessary to mount this experiment[5], including the neutrino beam[6], the cryostats and cryogenics systems to house the LAr TPC far detector, and conventional facilities at both Fermilab and SURF will be designed, built and commissioned by the Long- _NuFact15 - Rio de Janeiro, Brazil - August 2015_ 3 Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) Project. A new, broad-band and tunable neutrino beam is being designed, optimized for the Fermilab-SURF baseline. It will be driven by a 1.2 MW proton beam provided by the PIP-II upgrade[7], and is designed to accommodate future beam power upgrades to 2.4 MW. The design of the beam is still being optimized, and physics results are presented below for different options currently under study. LBNF is a U.S. Project based at Fermilab with contributions from a number of international partners. ## **THE DUNE DETECTORS** The far detector[4] is a 40 kt fiducial mass ( _∼_ 70 kt total mass) LAr TPC, located deep underground at SURF. The detector is divided into four independent 10 kt modules, each housed in its own cavern, as shown in Fig. 1. The detectors are placed in cryostats each of inner dimension 15 m wide _×_ 14 m high _×_ 62 m long. This arrangement allows for a staged construction and gives flexibility for evolution of the LAr TPC technology. While the cryostats will be identical, the LAr TPC detectors may not be, allowing lessons learned from the construction of the first module or information gleaned from the DUNE or other R&D programs to be incorporated in subsequent modules. The reference design is a single-phase LAr TPC, which is an evolution of the successful ICARUS design[8] and in which alternating anode and cathode planes divide the liquid volume into four 3.6 m drift regions. DRAFT last modified 25 Feb 2015 Minutes of the ELBNF proto-institutional board phone meeting held 20 Feb 2015 Attendance: There were about 45 on the phone and 26 on the web, with some overlap. 1. interim chair Sergio Bertolucci proposed the membership of the by-laws committee: Chang Kee Jung (chair), Bonnie Fleming, Brajesh Choudhary, Alfons Weber, Yannis Karyotakis, Joe Lykken (ex officio) This was approved unanimously 2. Governance Committee Report (Jung) The rules will be brought forward to the IB for discussion as they are being worked on. It was agreed there would be a monthly IB meeting 3. Dario reported the status of the co-spokesperson election. There were 14 nominees and 7 chose to stand as candidates. The election will be 27 February to 6 March, with one vote per institution. 4. Maury reported on the status of the Naming contest, Over 100 names were suggested so far and the top 5-10 would be put to the collaboration in a second round soon. 5. Maury reported that the creation of a collaboration email list was proceeding slowly, and IB members should respond quickly when asked who is in the collaboratoin. 6. Mike Lindgren who chaired the last iEFIG meeting had been invited to report to the group, but did not answer the invitation. Jim Strait reported on a meeting earlier in the week; some members were working on cryogenic issues and cavern layouts. There were two strategies being considered for civil work: 1) dig a hole for 10kT and then one for 30 kT; 2) Dig 4 10kT holes each sequentially. The conversation drifted between crogenic issues, costs, decision process, and other issues. It was pointed out that the iEFIG needs a charge. It was requested that slides from the iEFIG be presented at a future meeting. The 27 February collaboration phone call had already been devoted to iEFIG issues. 7. Future meetings, the next IB meeting will be in 2 weeks. Maury Goodman

Title: Minutes of the DUNE Institutional Board, 5 June 2015

Minutes of the DUNE institutional board meeting by telephone of 5 June 2015, 9:00 am U.S. Central Time Approved 14 August 2015 Present: The meeting was called to order by IB chair Maury Goodman 1. Minutes The minutes of the first official DUNE institutional board meeting of 18 April 2015 were approved. DUNE-docdb-14. Minutes were also included for the ELBNF institutional board meetings of 22 January 2015, 20 February 2015, 6 March 2015 and 13 March 2015, in which many of the DUNE structures were established. They are all included in docdb-14. 2. Discussion of Election Procedures During the spokesperson elections and the executive committee elections, there were a couple of complaints that the ballots were made by email and weren't strictly secret ballots. The committee(s) running the elections investigated numerous voting systems and did not (yet) find one that prevented the person from running the election from finding out how people voted if he/she chose to do so. We only want valid voters to vote but we aren't together in person. For both the spokesperson and executive committee elections there was one instance of an ineligible voter submitting a vote (just due to misunderstanding - nothing nefarious). Maury plans to investigate a "token" system. Alternative suggestions are welcomed. In the meantime, such as for the approval of appointed EC nominees, votes will be done by email with the counting done by a secretary who doesn't know or care who votes for whom. 3. Need for a governance amendment - IB vice chair The IB chair was thinking of appointing Lisa Whitehead from Houston as a deputy, to run meetings in his absence, and to distribute applications for membership in DUNE when we get them. Alfons Weber, who had helped to draft the governance rules, pointed out that this wasn't covered under those rules and an amendment to the rules would be needed. A governance amendment will be considered at a later date. 4. Approval of DUNE logo The result of the logo contest was a preference for a design that had been made by Louisa Castomonte, the wife of Cesar Castromonte from Goias. The logo was tuned by the Fermilab Media Services Department and this process iterated a few times with communication between that department and the designer. The result is 6 versions of the logo, with two layouts (vertical and horizontal) and three color patterns (colored, black on white, and white on black). There was considerable discussion, particularly about the ability to distinguish the two neutrinos which make up the N in the black on white and white on black versions. Maury will ask Media Services if they can solve this problem with a thin line or a greyscale. The IB chair asked for the following motion which was made and seconded: The IB approves the logo as submitted by FNAL and authorizes the IB chair to thank: Louisa Castromonte (wife of Cesar Castromonte from Goias) for creating the winning design Diana Brandonisio (FNAL) for tweaking the design and for vectorizing it (not yet done) Dan Cherdack (Col State) for running the elections The motion passed on a voice vote. The logos are available in docdb-4 5. Appointment of member to the executive committee There are two slots on the executive committee to be filled by Spokesperson nomination and IB ratification (Section 6.3 of the governance document). At this time, the spokespersons were nominating Bonnie Fleming for one of the two positions. A vote was taken by email to dune-election@fnal.gov, and the nomination was accepted unanimously. 6. September collaboration meeting It was previously decided that the September collaboration meeting would be in Fermilab or South Dakota. Attempts were made to plan the meeting in Deadwood, but they did not work out, in part because of the 75th Sturgiss motorcycle rally a month earlier was keeping all of the hotels filled. We also investigated holding the meeting in Rapid City SD, and that possibility existed, but we were told that good hotel prices and availability would be limited for the same reason. So the decision was made to go to Fermilab, with Deadwood and Rapid City meetings in the future. A doodle poll was taken between 2-5 September and 9-12 September and the clear preferences was 2-5 September. 7. According to the **OBSOLETE: LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan**, the four key elements of Configuration Management (CM) are:

1. **Configuration Identification** – defining system components through CAD models, drawings, interface and requirements documents.  
2. **Change Control** – a formal process for proposing, reviewing, approving, implementing and tracking changes to the baseline.  
3. **Configuration Status Accounting** – tracking and reporting the current status of all controlled items and changes.  
4. **Configuration Verification** – confirming that the as‑built configuration matches the approved design, including periodic audits and reviews.
