Configuration Management Plan** **Page viii** **Overview** ## **1 OVERVIEW** This Configuration Management Plan (CMP) describes the configuration management (CM) responsibilities and processes that support the design and implementation of the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF), Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), and Integration project elements. The purpose of this CMP is to identify the organization providing the configuration control, describe the change control process, and identify the plan for configuration status accounting and verification. It is a living document that is developed and maintained by the combined efforts of the Projects. LBNF, DUNE, and Integration are separate organizational entities with correlated objectives. Management of these entities is defined in the _LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan_ (PMP) and its Appendices [1] and the _DUNE Management Plan_ (DMP) [2]. Roles and responsibilities of management groups and individuals are defined in these management documents. This CMP does not attempt to duplicate information in the PMP or DMP; rather, it defines roles and responsibilities of groups and individuals for Configuration Management and refers to those defined in the PMP and DMP by title only. Due to the differences in the management structures of LBNF and DUNE, it is necessary to distinguish the Projects clearly in this document: - _LBNF/DUNE_ is used in reference to the combined and coordinated efforts of the project elements, including Integration - _LBNF/DUNE-US_ is used in reference to practices that are applicable to the LBNF, DUNE, & Integration scope funded by DOE - _LBNF and DUNE_ is used in reference to efforts undertaken independently by each project toward a common goal (e.g., CM processes unique to each Project that result in the combined LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management) - Either _LBNF_ or _DUNE_ or _Integration_ is used in reference to efforts unique to project elements, particularly when the DUNE Collaboration structure dictates a separate process. ## **1.1 Purpose** This CMP is designed to ensure that: - LBNF/DUNE configuration documentation is identified, released and controlled - The LBNF/DUNE Configuration Control Manager (CCM) position is established, including definition of roles and responsibilities - Processes are established in LBNF and DUNE, and within the LBNF/DUNE global enterprise, by which Configuration Changes are proposed, controlled, managed, approved, implemented and tracked - Change Control Boards (CCB) are established and function according to the CMP guidelines - Configuration status accounting is implemented This Configuration Management Plan provides for implementation of a system of management and engineering controls that are necessary for effective execution of the Projects. **LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan** **Page 9** **Overview** ## **1.2 Plan Overview** A CMP is employed to identify and control relationships during design and construction at both the Near Site and the Far Site. It is important to maintain clear, concise, and accurate records to remain within cost & schedule boundaries and minimize interface issues. This CMP has been established to ensure that the Projects’ organizations are aware of their roles and responsibilities during the design, construction, and testing phases of the Projects. The main goal of the LBNF/DUNE CMP is to prevent unauthorized or uncontrolled changes to engineering design or analysis, hardware, controlled documents, and controlled software. The plan integrates the various Configuration Management (CM) control systems. It is also meant to focus on the control of active documents and not on longer-term records management, retention, or archiving. The key elements of CM are Configuration Identification, Change Control, Configuration Status Accounting, and Configuration Verification. Configuration Identification defines the system through Computer-Aided Design (CAD) models, drawings, interface and requirements documents that specify the system components in terms of functional and physical characteristics, as well as how they are to be manufactured and tested. All Project elements utilize a single Change Control process as the vehicle by which proposed changes are reviewed and approved. It ensures that the science, technical scope, cost and schedule impacts of each major change are considered before approval is granted. Configuration control is the means to track configuration information and relay it to key personnel in order to support management decisions and ensure that all work is performed according to the current approved design. The Configuration Verification process ensures that the current engineering, facilities, hardware, software and requirements configurations match the intended design by verifying the implementation of each approved change and by conducting periodic configuration audits. ## **1.3 Definitions** **Approval Thresholds –** All proposed changes to Project documentation are assigned approval thresholds as per Table 5-1 and Table 5-2 in this CMP and per the draft _DOE Project Execution Plan_ (draft PEP) . **Baseline –** The point at which requirements and design are formally recorded as a starting point for change control, and after which all changes must be tracked and approved. **Change Classification -** All proposed Project changes submitted to the Change Control Board for consideration are assigned a “type” and “category” in the Fermilab Baseline Change Request Tool. Configuration changes may affect multiple project WBS elements and may be a combination of cost, schedule or technical change. **Change Control Board (CCB) –** A board composed of technical and administrative representatives who recommend approval or disapproval of proposed changes to the Projects approved configuration. These are currently considered to be the LBNF Project Management Boards (PMB) and the DUNE Technical Board/Executive Board (TB/EB). **Change Request –** A proposal to change the preliminary baseline or configuration baseline (defined in Section 3) of the LBNF or DUNE Project. **Configuration Management (CM) –** The systematic control and evaluation of all changes to the configuration that affect deliverables that have been baselined. **LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan** **Page 10** **Overview** **Documentation -** The controlled data that define the current configuration and controlled changes (both proposed and approved). **Interface Control Document –** A document that records technical and programmatic interfaces between at least two systems or project elements. An ICD can exist in many different formats such as documents or drawings. **Pending Changes -** Pending changes are those for which conceptual design has been approved, those that have been approved for implementation, or those that are approved and unincorporated and that have been implemented in the field, but for which the document revision has not been completed. **Requirements** – A statement of what a sub-system component needs to do in order to meet the science goal of the project **Technical Design Report (TDR)–** Defines the technical specifications, physical characteristics, and functional operating parameters of the various technical systems and facilities of the LBNF and DUNE projects. **LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan** **Page 11** **Scope and Applicability** ## **2 SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY** ## **2.1 Scope** The scope of the LBNF/DUNE Project encompasses the fabrication and construction of components, systems and facilities for LBNF/DUNE. ## **2.2 Applicability** This CMP is applicable to all work performed as part of LBNF/DUNE, which includes the design, testing, integration, and assembly of non-facilities components, as well as the design and construction of technical and conventional facilities. It provides guidance for all personnel on CM activities in support of the Projects, i.e., for all subsystem teams, scientific collaborators. The scope of this CMP encompasses the lifecycle of the LBNF/DUNE Projects, but not the lifecycle of the experiment itself. The CMP governs control of the following items: - Mechanical, civil, and electrical CAD models, design drawings and text documents showing the specifications and procedures for the facility, equipment and subcomponents - Requirements, interfaces schedule and cost **LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan** **Page 12** **Baseline Definition and Review Process** ## **3 BASELINE DEFINITION AND REVIEW PROCESS** The technical configuration baseline of the Projects is defined as the technical scope at CD-2 for LBNF/DUNE-US and the completion of the TDR for DUNE. A technical configuration baseline is established for the purpose of implementing Change Control. The configuration baseline is defined by the design output documents, which include requirements, procurement and construction specifications, ICD (Interface Control Document), drawings, test procedures, operating and maintenance information. The configuration is developed, baselined, maintained and evaluated via peer review processes, which are detailed in docdb 1069 for LBNF and in EDMS 2216079 for

The subproject’s engineers, in conjunction with the associated project manager, is responsible for reviewing and approving all such subproject requirements, parameters, and specifications in consultation with the SE. ## **5.2 Requirements Definition** The goals of the requirements definition process are to understand how a lower-level requirement relates to higher-level ones, and to establish clear linkages between the derivation of requirements and the analyses that go into the derivation process. This helps to link individual requirements both to parent and child requirements, allowing verification that requirements are suitably parsed into lower level ones, make sure that lower level requirements have viable parents, and understand the impact of changes flowing from above or pushing back from below. Requirements at each control level define the minimum performance and functional capabilities of the corresponding system. Thus, requirements must be defined such that they are clear and unambiguous, and that they can be used in the design process. Requirements should have the following characteristics to ensure clarity: - Achievable—the requirement or specification must be technically achievable within the allowed schedule and budget constraints - Verifiable—the requirement or specification must be defined in a way that can be verified by an objective measurement, test or analysis. - Clear—the requirement or specification must be unambiguous with only one meaning and must be capable of being met solely by the system being defined. - Complete—the set of requirements and specifications must define all information necessary to successfully meet the objectives of the system being defined, including operational and maintenance concepts. - Consistent—individual requirements must not conflict with each other. There are five aspects in the process of defining a requirement. Each is a separate action that needs to be completed to fully define a requirement. These are not exactly steps of the definition process, since they do not need to be strictly performed in sequence, but all must be accomplished to produce a wellunderstood requirement. These aspects are: - Identify: describe the requirement and check that it is separable, achievable, clear, complete, and consistent. - Flow down: determine where in the hierarchy a requirement belongs (science-projectsubproject-subsystem). - Establish verification: establish the method by which the requirement will be checked as met. This verification process may include measurement, testing, or analysis, or some combination of these. - Trace: identify the “parent” of the requirement at the next higher level. This process may unearth missing requirements at one or more levels if the trace process cannot identify a viable “parent” requirement. - Validate: check that the requirement has been correctly derived from its parent and that nothing is missing. **LBNF/DUNE Systems Engineering Management Plan** **Page 17 of 40** Baseline Definition and Review Process The results of this definition process are a well-formed requirement that is clearly defined, and whose flow-down path is understood. ## **5.3 Requirements Management Process** All requirements are captured in a requirements software database tool. Figure 5-1 displays these roles within the Change Control process. ## **7.1 DUNE Technical Coordinator** The DUNE TC, or designee, is responsible for the following tasks: - Participate in the Project Change Control Board - Chair the DUNE Change Control Board. - Advise the DUNE CCB of pending changes that must be approved by higher levels of management. - Advise the Experiment Facilities Interface Group (EFIG) of proposed changes that affect LBNF and Integration. - Oversee and coordinate Project CM activities. - Notify the CCB of any need to change documentation or a system as soon as that need is identified and determined to be valid. - Ensure that all project elements are identified and controlled. - Ensure that any changes to controlled documents are appropriately recorded, tracked, and incorporated into existing CAD models, drawings and/or documents in a timely manner. - Ensure that any additional testing or certification required as a result of changes is explicitly identified and included in the appropriate places. - Maintain a list that identifies controlled documents, their owners and the locations of these documents for the Project. - Periodically audit the CMP to determine the effectiveness of this Plan. This may include reviewing controlled copies of documents to ensure their accuracy and their consistency with the master copies, the electronic master, or CAD models. ## **7.2 DUNE Consortia Leaders** Consortia leaders are responsible for the following tasks: - Serve on the DUNE Change Control Board. - Determine if proposed changes have potential impacts upon LBNF, and if so, identify them as such. - Maintain CM control over their area of responsibility, including work by subcontractors and collaborators. - Notify the DUNE TC of any need to change documentation or a system as soon as that need is identified and determined to be valid. - Ensure that the TC is informed of as-built changes and revisions to controlled documents. **LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan** **Page 23** **DUNE Responsibilities in Change Control** - Assess impacts of proposed changes on cost, schedule, resources, risk, technical performance, and scientific objectives. - Submit Change Requests and implement approved changes to technical, cost and schedule baselines. ## **7.3 DUNE Consortia Technical Leads** Consortium technical leads are responsible for the following tasks: - Serve on the DUNE Change Control Board - Compile all technical, cost and schedule data associated with Change Requests to their baseline configurations. - Keep track of progress on work activities under their area of work, including work by subcontractors and collaborators. - Notify the consortium leader of any need to change a CI as soon as that need is identified and determined to be valid. - Ensure that people under their authority use the latest versions of documentation available. - Submit changes made as a result of fieldwork for processing in an orderly and timely manner. - May also be designated as the DUNE-US control account manager. ## **7.4 DUNE Change Control Board** The DUNE Technical Board (TB), see DMP [1], functions as the DUNE Change Control Board (DUNE CCB). The DUNE CCB makes recommendations to the DUNE Executive Board regarding proposed changes that affect the Project baseline cost, schedule, and technical specifications at Change Control threshold identified in Table 5-2. The DUNE CCB is chaired by the DUNE TC or designee. The Board meets at regular intervals, and as necessary to process pending actions. Notices of approval or denial of all Change Requests are distributed to the relevant consortia leaders by the Technical Coordinator. The DUNE CCB is responsible for evaluating the impact of a proposed CR on LBNF and whether the CR needs to be reviewed by higher levels of management. ## **7.5 DUNE Consortia** DUNE Consortia are the collaboration bodies responsible for the design, construction, installation, and commissioning of the detector elements. Each Consortia has a Consortia Leader and Technical Lead charged with leading the activities of the consortia. DUNE Consortia are responsible for reviewing Change Requests that impact their areas of responsibility. Recommendations on Change Requests that require higher level management approval are forwarded by the Consortium leader to the DUNE Technical Coordinator. **LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan** **Page 24** **DUNE Responsibilities in Change Control** ## **7.6 DUNE Document Control Managers** The DUNE Project encompasses multiple international institutions. Therefore, the DUNE Technical Coordinator or designee can evaluate and establish satellite sites to maintain different DUNE Configuration Items. Each site must have a Document Control Manager (DCM) whose responsibilities include transmission of the site's documentation to the DUNE DCM. Each site’s DCM and the DUNE DCM are both responsible for ensuring that the latest versions are disseminated and available, and that they clearly replace any older versions. If outdated documentation is requested for any reason, it shall be labeled as outdated or obsolete in a clear and distinctive manner. Document Control Managers are responsible for data management systems used for storage of any configuration items under their responsibility. ## **7.7 DUNE Executive Board (EB)** The DUNE EB, defined within the DUNE Management Plan [2] is tasked with participating in the decision-making process for Change Requests. The EB considers CRs that affect the Project baseline cost, schedule, and technical specifications at levels above the Change Control thresholds identified in Table 5-2. Change Requests approved by the EB that have impacts on multiple funding agencies are passed to the RRB through the DUNE RC. If the EB, which is consensus-driven decision-making body, is unable to reach a consensus on a particular CR, decision-making authority is transferred to the Fermilab Director. **LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan** **Page 25** <u>Groups in the Change Control Process for both LBNF and DUNE</u> ## **8 GROUPS IN THE CHANGE CONTROL PROCESS FOR BOTH LBNF AND DUNE** ## **8.1 LBNF/DUNE Experiment - Facility Interface Group (EFIG)** The EFIG is an oversight group defined within the LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan that considers the broad ramifications of CRs submitted within the LBNF/DUNE Change Control process according to Figure 5-1. If the EFIG, endorses the change, the CR is referred to each of the Projects for full consideration and implementation through their respective change management procedures. ## **8.2 DUNE Resource Review Board (RRB)** The DUNE Resources Review Board (RRB) is part of the international project governance structure for DUNE and is described in the _Project Management Plan_ . The RRB receives periodic reports and recommendations from both the Long-Baseline Neutrino Committee (LBNC) and the Neutrino Cost Group (NCG), which are review committees for DUNE charged by and reporting to the Fermilab Directorate. The LBNC reviews DUNE from a technical perspective, and the NCG reviews DUNE from a cost and schedule perspective. The RRB is informed of changes affecting multiple funding agencies. **LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management Plan** **Page 26** **<u>Data Management Systems and Tools</u>** ## **9 DATA MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS AND TOOLS** There are several systems and tools utilized to perform Configuration Management. Many have been mentioned and described in this document. Management documents and reports that are under Configuration Management control are managed using EDMS (Engineering Data Management Service), the DUNE document database (DUNE docdb) and DOORS . EDMS is the preferred repository and docdb is being phased out for storage of configuration managed and most technical documents. When a document is migrated from docdb to EDMS, the old document is obsoleted in docdb and there is a link in EDMS to docdb so that earlier versions can be viewed. Configuration Management for LBNF and DUNE engineering documentation (including CAD models, drawings, technical notes, and specifications) created by participating organizations are also controlled and versioned in EDMS. CAD models are being produced by multiple sources throughout LBNF and DUNE. It is not realistic to think that all these models will be produced using the same CAD platform. Systems Engineering works with all sources of CAD models to determine what format is the least disruptive path for the conversion needed to insert these models into the global controlled model. Once these formats are determined and agreed upon, each model is then uploaded and release in EDMS. The Systems Engineering group works with the subproject integration engineers to develop models for each subsystem. These are then inserted into the global model. Due to the size of the project, the subsystem and global models are difficult to navigate without very specialized computers. In order to make these models available to the stakeholders, Systems Engineering is converting the CAD models into formats that can be used and viewed in AutoDesk Navisworks as a compliment to the 3D models. Navisworks allows the stakeholders to navigate the models, combine subsystem models, take measurements, check for interference and make realistic renderings. As previously mentioned, DOORS is being used for the input and traceback of requirements. It is a management tool that provides a way to define, trace, analyze and manage requirements. Access is somewhat limited to DOORS because of the number of seats owned and the need for FNAL credentials. To address LBNF/DUNE’s larger audience, the approved versions of the requirements are being stored in EDMS for easier and more broadly accessibility. The LBNF/DUNE-US Project Master Schedule information (resources, schedule, and cost) is documented in the Primavera P6 scheduling and Cobra cost processing software tools. Change requests are submitted via the Baseline Change Request

The primary science objectives[3] include: neutrino oscillation physics to search for CP is violation in the leptonic sector, determine the ordering of the neutrino mass eigenstates, make precision measurements of oscillation parameters, test the three-neutrino paradigm; searches for baryon number violating processes (nucleon decay); and neutrino astrophysics, most notably precision measurements of neutrinos from a core-collapse supernova within the Galaxy, should one occur during the multi-decade lifetime of the experiment. DUNE is a newly formed international collaboration, with strong representation from the previous LBNE, LBNO and other collaborations. As of the time of _NuFact15_ , DUNE had 776 collaborators from 144 institutions located in 26 different countries on five continents. Title: Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report

The DUNE Far Detector will be constructed at the SURF, see Figure 3-3. The reference design Far Detector is a modular liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC); four 10-kt modules to be constructed at the 4850L. The mass of fluid quoted is the fiducial portion of the detector – the mass of vital importance for physics measurements. The basic components of each detector module include a cryostat to contain the LAr, a TPC detection mechanism immersed in the LAr, a photon-detection system, readout electronics and a cryogenic system to keep the LAr temperature at 87 K and maintain the required purity. Excavated space will need to accommodate detector modules that hold a total LAr volume larger than the fiducial 10 kt. Refer to DUNE CDR Volume 4 for additional information on the Far Detector design. Fermilab & SURF Utilities and Services Facility Components LBNF at Fermilab will be utilizing accelerator-type enclosures which are thick-walled, reinforced concrete structures. The actual near-site area where the LBNF/DUNE facilities are to be located consists of a combination of previously disturbed and undisturbed natural areas. The LBNF/DUNE Project at SURF will be utilizing presently active surface spaces along with new underground facilities at the 4850L including four neutrino detector caverns at 4850L and a cryogenic equipment cavern. Electrical Systems Electrical systems throughout the facilities include high voltages, high currents, and high levels of stored energy. Much of the equipment in use has been designed and built for a specific purpose and is not commonly found in other industrial facilities. Although workplace experience with this equipment has been very good from both safety and operational perspectives, a program has been established to review all equipment that is not labeled by a Nationally Recognized Testing Lab (NRTL). The primary AC distribution to both LBNF/DUNE sites is at 13.8 kV. For most systems, transformers convert the 13.8 kV to 480 volts AC for subsequent distribution. Because of the very high potential hazards, the substations are fenced, and access is limited to qualified high-voltage electricians. Most secondary distribution is 480 V, 3-phase, 60 Hz, ungrounded delta. This is used directly in many motors, pumps, power supplies, and other equipment. It is further transformed to 208/120 V, 3-phase for lights, utility outlets, and other general needs. The 480/277 V neutral is grounded. The facilities will have both emergency and standby power systems. The emergency power system will include support of fire detection/alarm systems, exit signage, emergency lights, and elevator car lighting, and two-way Fire department communication systems. The standby power systems will support critical systems including elevators, air handling systems, sump pumps, and shaft cranes. The design will follow the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 110 Standard for Emergency and Standby Power Systems. Heating, Ventilation and Cooling Systems Heating and air conditioning will be forced air systems. All buildings will be equipped with electric exhaust fans to meet the temperature stability and ventilation loads. Grills, diffusers, and ductwork will be provided for proper and complete air distribution system. Gas and Cryogenic Gas Distribution Systems LBNF/DUNE detectors and support systems will be designed in conformance with applicable cryogenic design standards and the Fermilab and SURF ESH Manuals. All cryogenic systems will be installed as per Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) requirements. Fire Protection, Suppression Fire & life safety requirements for LBNF/DUNE areas were analyzed as described in the LBNF/DUNE Near and Far Site Preliminary Fire Protection/Life Safety Assessments . The conclusions developed through this assessment process will be reflected in the final facility design. Fermilab maintains an on-site fire station which is fully equipped and provides 24/7 coverage. There are nineteen (19) personnel employed by the department, of which eighteen (18) are on three (3) shifts of six (6) each, and the other is the Chief. In order to provide the best service possible, the Laboratory is a member of M.A.B.A.S. Division 12 & 13, comprised of fire departments in DuPage and Kane Counties, which provides additional equipment and personnel through a systematic call-up procedure in times when our resources are not able to handle an emergency. The department also participates in Auto-Aid Response with Batavia & Warrenville Fire Departments. SURF’s primary responder in the case of a fire or emergency for the surface facilities is the Lead Volunteer Fire Department. The Lead Fire Department maintains 24/7 coverage on a volunteer basis and there are twenty-eight (28) personnel employed by the Department. In order to provide the best service possible, the SURF is a member of a Lawrence County wide mutual aid agreement with all departments in the county (Deadwood, Spearfish, etc.), which provides additional equipment and personnel through a systematic call-up procedure in times when our resources are not able to handle an emergency. SURF is also a member of a state wide mutual aid agreement. SURF maintains a site Emergency Rescue Team (EMT) that provides underground emergency response with supplemental support from the Lead Fire Department. The twenty-seven (27) member Emergency Rescue Team is trained to Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) mine-rescue standards. The facility also maintains a life flight landing area. Fire Protection is supplied by Fermilab’s industrial cooling water (ICW) system. The piping distribution network is well gridded to reduce the impact to any one building from a single water main break. The primary water supply feed into the building from the site’s ICW supply will be via a fire protection connection. Due to the high value of the facility, the reliability of water supplies will be improved by looping the supply from the existing main (also a loop). Each leg of the loop will be hydraulically sized to accommodate required flows. Fire sprinkler protection provided at SURF throughout the buildings will meet the requirements of NFPA 13 “Standard for Installation of Sprinklers.” Due to the facility’s size, multiple fire sprinkler riser stations will be installed throughout the facility. A water mist system will be installed to protect the Far Site Detector Halls. A fire standpipe system will be provided at SURF throughout the occupiable portions of the facility, meeting the requirements of NFPA 14 “Standard for the Installation of Standpipe and Hose Systems.” The system will be a “Class 1 System” as defined by this standard. Fire hydrants are sited within 300 ft. of each facility at Fermilab. Fermilab and the local Fire Departments use National Standard Thread couplings. The Fermilab Facilities Engineering Services Section Operations Group inspects the valves on the distribution system to ensure reliability of firefighting water supplies. Manual fire alarm stations (see Fire Alarm System Reference Manual) are located throughout the Fermilab facilities and are connected to the site-wide fire alarm system. Additionally, portable CO2 fire extinguishers are provided in designated areas the in compliance with NFPA 10 spacing requirements. The probability of a fire in the LBNF/DUNE areas is similar to that in other Fermilab underground facilities. Accelerator components are fabricated primarily from non-flammable materials, and combustible materials are kept to a minimum. The most likely fire with substantial consequences will be in the insulating material of the electrical cable plant caused by an overload condition. Cables installed for the LBNF/DUNE and other new projects are being chosen to be consistent with current Fermilab standards for cable insulation and comply with National Electrical Code (NEC) standards concerning cable fire resistance reducing the probability of a fire starting and the deleterious health effects of combustion products of cable insulation materials. The use of tray-rated, low-smoke zero halogen cable and of fire breaks in the cable trays mitigate fire spread potential. Support buildings at Fermilab for power supplies and electronic equipment are protected by automatic wet-pipe sprinkler systems. Fire extinguishers are located in all buildings and accelerator housings. The combination of smoke detection systems (type to be determined), sprinklers and the on-site fire department ensures a rapid response to any fire or smoke related incident. The building occupancy classifications for all LBNF/DUNE spaces are based on NFPA 101, Life Safety Code. An updated Fire & Life Safety Assessment will be conducted for LBNF during the design phase. The classification of the buildings, their subparts, and underground spaces were carefully selected to assure an adequate level of functionality, protection of occupants, code compliance, as well as an affordable design. The initial occupancy of the overall building was classified as Business, based on investigating the anticipated amount of hazardous materials and chemicals to be used. The potential fire hazards at both sites associated with LBNF/DUNE are as follows: Electrical cable insulation LAr Detector Polymer liner and Teflon jacketed cable installations at Far Site Detector Hall. Overheating or electrical breakdown in power supplies or other electronic components. (These devices are constructed in noncombustible steel cabinets which limit the extent and speed with which a fire could spread.) Overheating of magnets, causing smoking of the epoxy insulation (Because magnets are of primarily noncombustible construction, they pose minimal danger.) Existing oil-filled transformers located in power supply rooms located both in service building and underground spaces. Transient combustible materials. Fire Alarms and Detection Fire alarm systems will be installed at Fermilab and at SURF, meeting the requirements of NFPA 72 “National Fire Alarm Code”. The facility’s fire alarm control panel (FACP) will be placed inside the receiving area to allow easy access for the Fire Department. The fire alarm system will monitor water flow in the sprinkler system and modulate the sprinkler valves and the installed fire detection systems. Audible/visual alarm-notification devices will be put in place to alert the building’s occupants. At all the buildings’ exits there will be manual fire alarm pull stations. Area smoke detection systems types to be decided will be provided in high-value and underground areas. For spaces in which area smoke detection is not provided, photoelectric area smoke detectors will be set up in the air-handling systems and monitored, as required by building code and NFPA Standards. A combination of audible/visual alarm and/or visual only annunciation devices to alert the occupants will be provided throughout the facility. Fire alarm and supervisory signals will be transmitted to the Fermilab Fire Department via the Site Fire Alarm System. At Fermilab, Security Dispatch will monitor all fire alarms and system supervisory signals. They initiate the primary response. Typically, the Fermilab Fire Department responds to the scene at a Fermilab facility within five minutes of an alarm annunciation. SURF will monitor all fire alarms and system supervisory signals as described in their emergency management plan. The Site Emergency Rescue Team will respond, with additional support from the Lead-Deadwood Fire Department to follow. LBNF/DUNE will be supplied with fire extinguishers in compliance with applicable NFPA Standards. Instrumentation and Control Systems The environmental conditions in the LBNF/DUNE facilities at both sites must be precisely controlled to assure the optimal performance of the beamline and the research instruments. Standard commercial Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) controls, typically utilized for office environments, will be inadequate to meet these requirements. It is anticipated that the LBNF/DUNE underground and experimental spaces will be monitored and controlled by a combination of commercial HVAC controls and industrial grade process controls linked to a direct digital control system specially programmed to serve the precise requirements. Communications The communications systems provide for distributing data and telephone communications. Generally, these provisions encompass the installation of cabling, equipment, and tie-in terminations by Telecomm, Physical Plant, and LBNF/DUNE technicians. A public address and emergency notification system will be provided at both sites for communication to staff in the various buildings and work areas. Facility Access Control LBNF will be equipped with access control systems at both sites, most likely in the form of card readers, to allow entry to authorized personnel only. The card readers will be located at each exterior entrance to the building, along with access-restricted areas within the LBNF/DUNE facility. Additional restriction on card-reader access will be utilized as necessary. Conventional Facilities Near Site Facility The LBNF/DUNE Near Site Facilities consist of the following eight (8) functional areas: • Primary Beamline Enclosure (below grade) • Beamline Service

LBNF/DUNE Project Overview Elaine McCluskey, LBNF Project Manager LBNF/DUNE Logistics Planning Workshop 11 Aug 2015 International Particle Physics Community Steps toward LBNF/DUNE 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 2 2013: European Strategy for Particle Physics updated Endorsed high priority of neutrino physics Bottom line: CERN should help the European neutrino community participate in a long-baseline program outside of Europe 2014: P5 Plan A strategic plan for U.S. particle physics maximizing opportunities for breakthrough science Explicit prioritization, hard choices made within realistic budget scenarios Particle physics community unified behind the plan: 2,331 signatures on letter sent to DOE Secretary Moniz P5 Mandate: a new international collaboration 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 3 P5 recommendation 13: “Form a new international collaboration to design and execute a highly capable Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) hosted by the U.S. To proceed, a project plan and identified resources must exist to meet the minimum requirements in the text [of the report]. LBNF is the highest-priority large project in its timeframe” Basically asks Fermilab to do for neutrinos what CERN did for the Higgs, involving the worldwide community The science from DUNE will be game changing for particle and astro-particle physics and will be in all the textbooks. P5 Mandate: Scope of LBNF/DUNE based on science requirements 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 4 “For a long-baseline oscillation experiment, based on the science drivers and what is practically achievable in a major step forward, we set as the goal a mean sensitivity to CP violation of better than 3σ over more than 75% of the range of possible values of the unknown CP-violating phase δCP.” “With a wideband neutrino beam produced by a proton beam with power of 1.2 MW, this … implies a far detector with fiducial mass of more than 40 kilotons of liquid argon and a suitable near detector.” This is the scope of the LBNF/DUNE project. DUNE is a discovery science program….science requirements drive the scope and design 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 5 Determine if neutrinos violate leptonic CP and by how much Extract multiple detailed properties of neutrinos in a single experiment to test the current 3-flavor paradigm Look for surprises Search for nucleon decay Detect thousands of neutrinos from galactic supernova explosions And more Facility and Experiment as separate major subprojects 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 6 The facility, LBNF, is treated as a separate project from the experiment, “DUNE”, but with a single Federal Project Director....this facilitates CERN as facility partner DUNE Collaboration comprises 776 members from 26 countries and 144 institutions (~ half international) DUNE has brought together the world liquid argon TPC neutrino community, as well as an underground neutrino particle astrophysics community Collaboration has come together faster than even the optimistic schedule considered by P5….an indication of intense interest in this science and the perception that the DOE is prepared to host an ambitious world class neutrino facility LBNF/DUNE Partners 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 7 Strong domestic and international scientific and funding partners are key to LBNF/DUNE success. CERN is a major partner in facility infrastructure at both Fermilab and SURF (such as cryostats) who will also facilitate European engagement. UK, Switzerland, Italy, India are showing strong leadership and support Groups from France, Poland, Spain, Brazil, Netherlands… campaign soon to begin to engage all 26 countries involved Agreements with individual countries will take 3-4 years, once DOE commits to the project. And of course, South Dakota, where more than $100M has been invested in the facility to date. P5 “Minimum to Proceed” 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 8 It will take considerable time to secure the international agreements needed for full scope of LBNF/DUNE Recognizing this, P5 defined a “minimum to proceed”: “The minimum requirements to proceed are the identified capability to reach an exposure of at least 120 kt*MW*yr by the 2035 timeframe, the far detector situated underground with cavern space for expansion to at least 40 kt LAr fiducial volume, and 1.2 MW beam power upgradable to multi-megawatt power.” Non-DOE contributions to the LBNF/DUNE project can thus be divided into those needed for the minimum to proceed, and those additional contributions needed to reach the full scope LBNF/DUNE Scope 08.11.15 E McCluskey | LBNF/DUNE Project Overview 9 LBNF will provide facilities at Fermilab and at SURF to enable the scientific program of DUNE. These facilities are geographically separated into Near Site Facilities, those to be constructed at Fermilab Far Site Facilities, those to be constructed at SURF. question: According to the analysis procedures in the document 'First Look at Passively Ganged SiPMs', how is the estimated cross talk defined?
reference_answer: It is defined as the ratio of the integral of the integrated spectrum from 1.5 PE onward to the integral from 0.5 PE onward.
evidence_quote: Estimated Cross Talk: Ratio of integral of integrated spectrum from 1.5 PE on to that from 0.5 PE on
generated_answer: **Estimated cross‑talk** is calculated as the **ratio of the integral of the integrated spectrum above 1.5 photo‑electrons (PE) to the integral of the same spectrum starting at 0.5 PE**. In other words, it is the fraction of events that exceed the 1.5 PE threshold relative to all events above the 0.5 PE threshold.

Proposal for Contributions to the Development of a photon detector system for the DUNE Liquid Argon TPC Detector for the Period February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016 Overview This statement of work provides details of funding for R&D and design tasks related to the development of a photon detector (PD) sub-detector for the DUNE far detector (FD). Members of the NIU team involved in this effort are: professors Gerald Blazey, Michael Eads and Vishnu Zutshi (PI), senior research scientist Alexander Dyshkant, senior technician Kurt Francis, students and electrical and mechanical machine shops. Funds are requested here to: Set up infrastructure for the evaluation, characterization and long-term performance of Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) in a cryogenic environment Study SiPM parameters and performance in warm and cold conditions Initiate the development of a quality assurance plan and procedure for SiPM qualification for LAr TPC prototypes under the following scheduled activities: 13122.05.290 Test passive ganging of 3 SiPMs 13122.05.300 Test passive ganging of 6 SiPMs 13122.05.310 Prepare final report on passive SiPM ganging The period of execution of these tasks is February 1, 2016 – September 30, 2016. The tasks will be executed in coordination with existing members of the PD group especially CSU and Caltech. Statement of Work During FY2016, the NIU group will contribute in the following areas: Initiate SiPM characterization in warm (room temperature) conditions. The test stand will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, x-talk, after-pulsing etc.) using DUNE electronics. Of particular interest will be characterization of ganged sensors. Studies will initially look at performance of three ganged sensors and then explore the possibility of ganging six of them. This task will primarily involve Francis and a student with oversight by Zutshi and assistance from Gary Drake (ANL). Setup cryogenic test-stand for SiPM characterization and qualification. Once the test stand is setup it will be used to study relevant sensor parameters (breakdown, gain, dark rate, x-talk, after-pulsing etc.) using DUNE electronics. Ganging studies will be extended to this realm. Failure modes, both electrical and mechanical will be explored. This task will primarily involve Dyshkant, Francis and NIU machine & electrical shops with oversight by Blazey and Zutshi. Detailed comparisons of sensor parameters in warm and cold environments to understand the performance correlations and dependencies. This will be used to demonstrate how well the determination of sensor parameters in the warm environment can be extrapolated to LAr temperatures. This task will primarily involve a student with oversight by Eads. Initiate development of a work plan and procedure for quality control and assurance of SiPMs for the LAr TPC prototypes under design or construction. This should be considered as the first step in the development of long-term (~30 years) qualification procedures for the SiPMs. This task will primarily involve Francis and a student with oversight by Eads and Zutshi. This question should be addressed with a preliminary assessment of the impact on the overall sensitivity.** Existing long-baseline oscillation experiments have relied largely on the Near Detector to limit the impact of large flux uncertainties. In this flux times cross section paradigm, detailed knowledge of the neutrino beam and neutrino scattering cross-sections are not required, as oscillation parameters are estimated by comparing event rates in the far detector to predictions extrapolated from the Near Detector before the beam has oscillated. While this has been sufficient for statistically limited experiments, it may lead to serious mistakes as neutrino oscillation measurements push to higher precision. One reason for this is that the composition of the neutrino flux depends on the geometry of the beam and detectors. The Near Detector sees a broad cross section of the beam, while the far detector sees only a very narrow solid angle. Finally, we not that the measurements discussed here are the first goals of a facility that is likely to run for decades. We do not currently know what the facility will be asked to do after DUNE’s initial goals are reached, but in essentially any scenario, a measurement of the neutrino fluxes via the spectrometer will be valuable. ## **If so, is it required to be installed inside the LBNF target station every time there is a change of target/horn configuration?** In case we do not have an ex situ facility, two distinct sets of circumstances will prompt us to re-install the spectrometer in the chase: - The replacement of any of the focusing system components (target or horns) may prompt us to measure again the flux. It will be a requirement for any change in the target design (such as a modification of the geometry of the target or a change in materials), or a change in the horns design (such as a modification of the shape/thickness of the inner 6 conductor, or a reconfiguration of the horn positions). - The observation of an unexpected and significant change of particle flux detected in the muon monitor system (and possibly in the hadron monitor), or a distortion of the neutrino interaction spectrum shape and/or normalization change in the near detector. Such changes may occur, for instance, if a horn goes out of alignment, or if the target degrades, e.g. its density changes. If we are equipped with an ex situ facility, we may still need some measurement in the target chase to address point 2, since the observations in the muon monitors or the near detector may not be enough to identify the problem. In this case, a simpler tracking plane downstream of the horns just to record the particle flux would be of great help to identify the problem. **For the two options of installing the spectrometer in situ either after Horn C or between Horn B and C, provide an estimate of the additional costs (spectrometer and CF) and the impact on the operational schedule how much time would be devoted to spectrometer operation and how often.** ### _Additional Costs_ In order to be able to operate the spectrometer in the LBNF target chase, slow extraction at MI10 is required, such that the instantaneous intensity be of the order of one proton per 53 MHz bucket. The presently installed septa in the Main Injector can provide the right phase advance for beam extraction in the LBNF beamline at MI10. Removable collimators will need to be installed in the LBNF beamline to further reduce the beam intensity by a factor 104 _−_ 105 . Additional removable instrumentation (BPMs, SWICS), sensitive to the low intensity slow extracted beam, will need to be installed in the LBNF beamline. The cost of these modifications to the LBNF beamline has been estimated to be about $xxM. The spectrometer has not been fully designed yet. For the in situ option, it will be approximately 4 m long, with an aperture of 5x5 cm2 . Tracking will be provided by planes of silicon 7 strip detectors. The

8 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 3 We will of course continue to learn from the work of other experiments using SiPMs in cold environments. As to the number of failures we can tolerate, determining this value will require the ability to reconstruct photon system events. This capability will be available within a month and studies will be undertaken then. Determining the failure rate of the devices to ensure it is within the tolerable failure rate coming from simulation is addressed in the first part of the answer. More work is needed to ensure we understand the anticipated failure rate – or the limit on this rate. Title of Review – Review Date 9 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 4 What are the criteria for the optical detector down-select (in addition to the Tallbo cosmic ray test)? 1. The primary criteria is relative performance – coupled with cost. (We have other tests planned for the CSU 500 liter dewar – one just completed with the CSU and LSU alternatives). 2. We will have simulation and reconstruction at the level to allow us to compare relative simulated performance between designs. PDK kaons (200 MeV) as well as SN interactions of 5 MeV and 10 MeV would be good signals to use for the comparison. 3. Complexity of production and handling will also be considered for the down selection. Title of Review – Review Date 10 ##### Colorado State University Executive Summary for Photon Detection System The requirements and documentation of the conceptual design are in place and at the appropriate level for CD-1. However, the reference design has difficulties reaching the performance required to meet the physics goals, specifically the signal to noise. The ability to determine to is a desirable capability for both the proton decay and the supernova physics goals of Dune. Several alternatives were presented that should meet the specification. It would be useful to rapidly choose a reference design that meets the stated goals of Dune with some headroom. Prototype results will soon aid in choosing. In addition, better simulation is needed to evaluate the alternative designs. Extended experience of SiPM in a LAr environment would also help quantify the requirements. Develop a requirement for SiPM reliability and develop a plan for verifying that SiPMs can achieve this reliability while operating in LAr. 2. Complete the simulation and reconstruction development and use these tools to better define the requirements on the PD. 3. Continue on the path to make a down-select in the fall. The team should consider the feasibility of continuing low level R&D on a backup as well. 4. Complete a test of the electronics with baseline configuration of 3 SiPMs ganged on a 40m cable. Title: Minutes of the DUNE Institutional Board, 5 June 2015

Minutes of the DUNE institutional board meeting by telephone of 5 June 2015, 9:00 am U.S. Central Time Approved 14 August 2015 Present: The meeting was called to order by IB chair Maury Goodman 1. Minutes The minutes of the first official DUNE institutional board meeting of 18 April 2015 were approved. DUNE-docdb-14. Minutes were also included for the ELBNF institutional board meetings of 22 January 2015, 20 February 2015, 6 March 2015 and 13 March 2015, in which many of the DUNE structures were established. They are all included in docdb-14. 2. Discussion of Election Procedures During the spokesperson elections and the executive committee elections, there were a couple of complaints that the ballots were made by email and weren't strictly secret ballots. The committee(s) running the elections investigated numerous voting systems and did not (yet) find one that prevented the person from running the election from finding out how people voted if he/she chose to do so. We only want valid voters to vote but we aren't together in person. For both the spokesperson and executive committee elections there was one instance of an ineligible voter submitting a vote (just due to misunderstanding - nothing nefarious). Maury plans to investigate a "token" system. Alternative suggestions are welcomed. In the meantime, such as for the approval of appointed EC nominees, votes will be done by email with the counting done by a secretary who doesn't know or care who votes for whom. 3. Need for a governance amendment - IB vice chair The IB chair was thinking of appointing Lisa Whitehead from Houston as a deputy, to run meetings in his absence, and to distribute applications for membership in DUNE when we get them. Alfons Weber, who had helped to draft the governance rules, pointed out that this wasn't covered under those rules and an amendment to the rules would be needed. A governance amendment will be considered at a later date. 4. Approval of DUNE logo The result of the logo contest was a preference for a design that had been made by Louisa Castomonte, the wife of Cesar Castromonte from Goias. The logo was tuned by the Fermilab Media Services Department and this process iterated a few times with communication between that department and the designer. The result is 6 versions of the logo, with two layouts (vertical and horizontal) and three color patterns (colored, black on white, and white on black). There was considerable discussion, particularly about the ability to distinguish the two neutrinos which make up the N in the black on white and white on black versions. Maury will ask Media Services if they can solve this problem with a thin line or a greyscale. The IB chair asked for the following motion which was made and seconded: The IB approves the logo as submitted by FNAL and authorizes the IB chair to thank: Louisa Castromonte (wife of Cesar Castromonte from Goias) for creating the winning design Diana Brandonisio (FNAL) for tweaking the design and for vectorizing it (not yet done) Dan Cherdack (Col State) for running the elections The motion passed on a voice vote. The logos are available in docdb-4 5. Appointment of member to the executive committee There are two slots on the executive committee to be filled by Spokesperson nomination and IB ratification (Section 6.3 of the governance document). At this time, the spokespersons were nominating Bonnie Fleming for one of the two positions. A vote was taken by email to dune-election@fnal.gov, and the nomination was accepted unanimously. 6. September collaboration meeting It was previously decided that the September collaboration meeting would be in Fermilab or South Dakota. Attempts were made to plan the meeting in Deadwood, but they did not work out, in part because of the 75th Sturgiss motorcycle rally a month earlier was keeping all of the hotels filled. We also investigated holding the meeting in Rapid City SD, and that possibility existed, but we were told that good hotel prices and availability would be limited for the same reason. So the decision was made to go to Fermilab, with Deadwood and Rapid City meetings in the future. A doodle poll was taken between 2-5 September and 9-12 September and the clear preferences was 2-5 September. 7. Future collaboration meetings The January 2016 meeting should be held in a warm U.S. location. Initial conversations have been held with collaborators from University of Texas at Arlington, and Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge. Maury was asked to conduct a doodle poll of these two locations with possible dates. A possible future meeting schedule of May 2016 in Deadwood, September 2016 at Fermilab, and January 2017 in CERN was mentioned. Chris Mauger pointed out that we had skipped July this year due to the CD1-refresh, and that would be a good month for a meeting. The EC will be asked to consider a March-July-November schedule along with a January-May-September rotation. 8. Establishment of a committee to establish procedures for a DUNE speaker's committee When a new chair is appointed for the DUNE speaker's committee, a set of SC procedures will be drafted to be discussed by the executive committee and approved by the IB. Respectively Submitted Maury Goodman

question: According to the TallBo Update, what optical components are used in the CSU paddle?
evidence_quote: ➢ CSU WLS fibers + WLS radiator
generated_answer:
**CSU paddle optical layout (as reported in the TallBo Update):**  

- **Wavelength‑shifting (WLS) fibers** that collect the blue‑shifted photons and transport them by total‑internal‑reflection.  
- **A separate WLS radiator plate** (coated with a UV‑to‑blue shifter such as TPB) that converts the 128 nm LAr scintillation light into visible light which is then absorbed by the fibers.

Thus the CSU paddle uses *WLS fibers plus a WLS radiator* as its optical components.

Source: docdb Title: Photon Detector System Update for May 29, 2015 PD Status – May 29, 2015 Norm Buchanan Colorado State University ###### Colorado State University # Technical Review FD Design Independent Review -May 19-20th Close out report circulated via email - Executive Summary: "The purpose of the review was to evaluate the DUNE project's technical progress and readiness to proceed to CD-1 - Refresh. The Committee found that the DUNE project design is sufficiently advanced and that several promising alternative design options were actively being pursued. The Committee was very impressed with the progress made in the LBNE transition to DUNE and encourages a timely advance from prototypes to the industrial production needed to construct and mount the large and complex DuNE as to fully optimize the DUNE experiment. Three areas were considered; TPC and Installation,PhotonDetection and Electronicsand DAQ." ·Very successful -Thanks again to everyone involved Feb 6, 2015 2 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 1 The simulation does not yet allow for the effects of Ar39 decay, cross talk, dark counts or other SIPM effects. What is the plan to incorporate these issues? - 39 Ar Decay: - A radiological “generator” has been written by Tom Junk, we need to turn it on and study the output in the photon detectors. - The tools are ready, we just need (a person) to do the study. - Once we have an estimate of the rate, we can either turn on the simulation all the time, or just increase the effective dark rate to compensate. DUNE FD Technical Review – May 19-20, 2015 3 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 1 - Electronics response: - The following effects have already been implemented in the simulation: - Dark rate - Cross talk - Cable noise - The following are still in the works - Afterpulsing - Saturation - Performance studies with realistic electronics - Need reconstruction to evaluate performance with these effects. - Have prototypes, but not ready for performance studies yet - Have some ideas on how to get to “good enough” to get started - Have a Duke grad student working on these issues now - Hope to have working tools in a few weeks. - Then we just need manpower to do the studies it enables. DUNE FD Technical Review – May 19-20, 2015 4 ###### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 2 The SIPM spec cannot be fully determined (for example cross talk) without knowledge based on simulation. What is the plan for formalizing the SIPM spec? In terms of providing timing for the events – the primary purpose of the PD system – the effect of the SiPM specs are the following: Cross talk Only affects the measured energy of an event – in time with the initial signal After-pulsing More significant issue as it can provide false coincidences giving incorrect timing – but the rate is low (< 10Hz). This is covered by the dark rate spec. S Title of Review – Review Date 5 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 2 Dark Rate ~10 Hz at bias voltage of 24.5 V The simulation to confirm these requirements would be to generate a series of test event samples, scanning over possible values of the cross-talk, after pulsing, etc., and see how the reconstruction performance changes. Timing resolution, fake rate, and reco. efficiency are the obvious metrics. S Title of Review – Review Date 6 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 3 SIPMs have not been extensively used in cryogenic envirnments and may experience effects like premature aging or other issues. What is the plan to qualify the SIPMs for safe operation in this environment. What is an acceptable failure rate in the full detector? How will you know that the chosen SIPM will satisfy this rate? (The Dune electronics group has worried about electronics lifetimes at LAr temperature. Is any of this relevant.) The plan to qualify the SiPMs for cold operation is to both thermally cycle a population of the devices and subject another population to a long term test at cryo temperature. Both of these tests are happening now with small populations. We still need to understand what size of samples is needed to give confidence in device qualification and to project failure rates. Title of Review – Review Date 7 ### Photon Detector Question 3 An example of a study to look at longevity is being carried out at IU. Six devices are being operated (biased) in LN2 for an extended period. Three of the devices are being operated with an increased bias voltage to stress them. Gain Slope @ 24.5 V, SiPMs 4-6

As to the number of failures we can tolerate, determining this value will require the ability to reconstruct photon system events. This capability will be available within a month and studies will be undertaken then. Determining the failure rate of the devices to ensure it is within the tolerable failure rate coming from simulation is addressed in the first part of the answer. More work is needed to ensure we understand the anticipated failure rate – or the limit on this rate. Title of Review – Review Date 9 ##### Colorado State University ### Photon Detector Question 4 What are the criteria for the optical detector down-select (in addition to the Tallbo cosmic ray test)? 1. The primary criteria is relative performance – coupled with cost. (We have other tests planned for the CSU 500 liter dewar – one just completed with the CSU and LSU alternatives). 2. We will have simulation and reconstruction at the level to allow us to compare relative simulated performance between designs. PDK kaons (200 MeV) as well as SN interactions of 5 MeV and 10 MeV would be good signals to use for the comparison. 3. Complexity of production and handling will also be considered for the down selection. Title of Review – Review Date 10 ##### Colorado State University Executive Summary for Photon Detection System The requirements and documentation of the conceptual design are in place and at the appropriate level for CD-1. However, the reference design has difficulties reaching the performance required to meet the physics goals, specifically the signal to noise. The ability to determine to is a desirable capability for both the proton decay and the supernova physics goals of Dune. Several alternatives were presented that should meet the specification. It would be useful to rapidly choose a reference design that meets the stated goals of Dune with some headroom. Prototype results will soon aid in choosing. In addition, better simulation is needed to evaluate the alternative designs. Extended experience of SiPM in a LAr environment would also help quantify the requirements. Feb 6, 2015 11 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University #### Recommendations for Photon Detection System 1. Develop a requirement for SiPM reliability and develop a plan for verifying that SiPMs can achieve this reliability while operating in LAr. 2. Complete the simulation and reconstruction development and use these tools to better define the requirements on the PD. 3. Continue on the path to make a down-select in the fall. The team should consider the feasibility of continuing low level R&D on a backup as well. 4. Complete a test of the electronics with baseline configuration of 3 SiPMs ganged on a 40m cable. Feb 6, 2015 12 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University ## Summary Overall the review was very successful and when I talked to two of the reviewers after the review they re-iterated that they were very impressed with what the group has accomplished and fully believe that we will be able to deliver a system that will meet the DUNE requirements (which do still need to be optimized with collaboration). The recommendations will figure into prioritization of PD tasks going forward. Director’s review is next week. Feb 6, 2015 13 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University Looking forward Short term priorities (next 3 months) • Down-selection § Tallbo and CDDF tests § Simulation/Reconstruction • Simulation § Inclusion of39 Ar background § Model effect of SiPM failure rates § PD reconstruction Feb 6, 2015 14 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University - Medium term priorities (next 6-12 months) • SiPM Qualification/Testing § Development of qualification plan § Undertake cryogenic testing - Light-guide optimization § Optimize material choice § Optimize design § Develop QA - Electronics testing/modeling § Basic ganging and long cable tests - § Model/test effect on physics given reduced electronics performance – part of value engineering plan - Continued simulation/reconstruction development Feb 6, 2015 15 Photon Detector Meeting ##### Colorado State University ### What to expect There will be some reorganization for FY16. It depends on a number of things: - Off-project involvement (esp. with international partners) - • Funding levels (expected to be reduced) - Ensuring medium term priorities are met I will keep people informed as I become informed to avoid last minute surprises. staffing of the cryogenics supporting the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility / Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment – United States (LBNF/DUNE-US) Far Detector & Cryogenics (FDC) subproject. It also describes a plan to augment resources in case of planned or unplanned needs exceeding the current staffing. ## **2 Introduction** LBNF (http:/lbnf-dune.fnal.gov/) will provide the infrastructure necessary to support the massive neutrino detectors located deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, SD. DUNE will employ four (4) such detectors, housed in cryostats requiring almost 70,000 tons of liquid argon (LAr), about 17,500 tons for each cryostat. DUNE (http://www.dunescience.org/) is expected to achieve transformative discoveries, making definitive determinations of neutrino properties, examining the dynamics of supernovae that produced the heavy elements necessary for life, and probing the possibility of proton decay. The LBNF/DUNE program is hosted by Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab). Construction of LBNF along with the US scope of the detector project are managed as a single DOE O 413.3b project. Partner contributions to the project are managed with the LBNF/DUNE-US project. The FDC scope includes equipment delivered by the US project and partners as In-Kind Contributions (IKCs). IKCs from partners are installed as part of the US project. Together LBNF and DUNE will comprise the world's highest-­‐intensity neutrino beam at Fermilab, in Batavia, IL, a high-­‐precision near detector on the Fermilab site, a massive liquid argon time-­‐projection chamber (LArTPC) far detector installed deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) 1,300 km away in Lead, SD, and all of the conventional and technical facilities necessary to support the beamline and detector systems. The strategy for executing the experimental program presented in this Conceptual Design Report (CDR) has been developed to meet the requirements set out in the P5 report and takes into account the recommendations of the European Strategy for Particle Physics. It adopts a model where U.S. and international funding agencies share costs on the DUNE detectors, and various international participants provide in-­‐kind contributions to the supporting infrastructure of LBNF. LBNF and DUNE **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 2-­‐13** **Introduction** will be tightly coordinated as DUNE collaborators design the detectors and infrastructure that will carry out the scientific program. The scope of the LBNF covers the following components: - An intense neutrino beam aimed at the far site. - Conventional facilities at both the near and far site. - Cryogenics infrastructure to support the DUNE liquid argon time-­‐projection chamber (LArTPC) detectors at SURF. The DUNE detectors include - a fine-­‐grained neutrino detector and beamline monitoring system located a few hundred meters downstream of the neutrino source - a massive LArTPC neutrino detector located deep underground at the far site With the facilities provided by LBNF and the detectors provided by DUNE, the DUNE Collaboration proposes to mount a focused attack on the puzzle of neutrinos with broad sensitivity to neutrino oscillation parameters in a single experiment. The focus of the scientific program is the determination of the neutrino mass hierarchy and the explicit demonstration of leptonic CP violation, if it exists, by precisely measuring differences between the oscillations of muon-­‐type neutrinos and antineutrinos into respectively electron-­‐type neutrinos and antineutrinos. Siting the far detector deep underground will provide exciting additional research opportunities in nucleon decay, studies utilizing atmospheric neutrinos, and neutrino astrophysics, including measurements of neutrinos from a core-­‐collapse supernova should such an event occur in our galaxy during the experiment’s lifetime. **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 2-­‐14** **Description of the Site, Facility and Operations** ### **3 DESCRIPTION OF THE SITE, FACILITY AND OPERATIONS** ### **3.1 Characterization of the LBNF/DUNE Site Locations** SERVICE BUILDING
