Baseline Definition and Review Process The technical configuration baseline of the Projects is defined as the technical scope at CD-2 and is defined in LBNF/DUNE-US Design Plan . A technical configuration baseline is established for the purpose of implementing Change Control. The configuration baseline is defined by the design output documents, which include requirements, procurement and construction specifications, ICD (Interface Control Document), drawings, test procedures, operating and maintenance information. The configuration is developed, baselined, maintained and evaluated via peer review processes. Interface Control The LBNF/DUNE Systems Engineering group is responsible for implementing a configuration management system, including interface control. A deliverable generally has multiple physical and programmatic interfaces with other deliverables of one or both Projects as illustrated in Figure 6. Figure 6: Example Interface Control Matrix for Far Site, with EDMS numbers Interface control occurs both within and among LBNF/DUNE subprojects. Management of interfaces between subprojects occurs under the leadership of the LBNF/DUNE SE in coordination with the subproject engineers. Interface control documents (ICD) are used to identify and document interface boundaries and responsibilities around the boundaries between two entities. These are summarized in an ICD matrix (sample Figure 6). ICDs require approval of the managers/engineers in each entity. Future changes to these interfaces require review and re-approval, to ensure that all impacts are understood and mutually agreed. As ICDs are updated, they are uploaded and approved in EDMS so that approved versions are available and referenced. Interface Definition The goal of the interface definition and control process is to clarify subsystem boundaries, ensure clean definitions of work scope on both sides of the interface, and document dependencies of one subsystem on another. For systems with many complex interfaces and interactions, managing internal interfaces is essential to reduce the risk of design incompatibilities arising at interfaces or scope gaps. Furthermore, documenting and managing interfaces ensures that subsystems on both sides of the interface clearly understand their scope of work and deliverables. Interfaces are located in EDMS (https://edms.cern.ch/project/CERN-0000198206). The diagram defines all interfaces between subsystem entities for the area identified the nature of the interface. These interfaces are developed under the leadership of the SE and project engineers, in coordination with and concurrence by the subsystem managers involved. Internal ICD’s are defined as subproject-level items, since they signify agreements between subproject subsystems (such as within the Far Detector or Beamline). Upon approval, ICD’s are brought under configuration control. ICDs form the core of the interface definition and agreements. These are text documents that describe the interface features in writing. Supporting documents may be needed to fully define the interface, but these must be referenced from the ICD and not developed as stand-alone documents. Supporting documents may include drawings, schematics, drawings showing interface details, or separate documents describing generic protocols. The intent is that the ICD forms the single definition of the interface and calls on supporting documents as needed. Interface control documents are agreements between the two interfacing entities and are not to be construed as one imposing requirements on the other. Interface agreements arise out of the design implementation plans. Thus, they are largely dependent on design choices made and are not flowed down from higher level performance or functional requirements. However, interface development involves designing interfaces to minimize the overall system-level cost and risk to the system and subsystems involved. Thus, interface issues may well be driven more by needs of one side than the other. In any case, once an ICD is approved by both sides, the agreed-to interface details become design requirements for the involved subsystems. These must be verified prior to delivery and should be treated as seriously as any other subsystem requirement. Toward that end, the ICD’s should be clear about the nature of all interface details. This includes: Defining requirements and constraints: describing agreed-to constraints for the interface, or requirements imposed on one side by the other because of the interface. Identifying the supplier: listing who provides what to complete the interface, so there is no ambiguity. Agreeing on subsystem deliverables: listing and describing items required of one subsystem from another before the completion of the interface. These could be beneficial occupancies for CF, specific hardware or software to qualify or verify functionality across the interface. This includes the requirements of the delivered units and any differences between them and the final implementation. Phasing of Interface Development Interface development follows a phased approach to match the design development process and completion of subsystem design and operations details. This phasing process is intended to reduce the risk to the design associated with incomplete interfaces, while ensuring that ultimately all interfaces are fully specified and agreed to. Interface topics are grouped into three phases, depending on their relative importance in driving the design at that phase. Phases are defined as follows: Phase I: basic interface connectivity and design envelopes; list of deliverable items and interface hardware definitions; these interfaces define the basic interconnectivity and scope of the subprojects and often drive the conceptual and preliminary design. Phase II: engineering details of all aspects of the interface; full definition of physical connections, loads, flows, and communication protocols across the interface; these details drive subsystem preliminary design decisions. Phase III: component-level interface details, such as feedthroughs in the cryostat roof; this information is needed to finalize part design details, integration resolution, and installation planning. This Plan includes: Organizational responsibilities—including relationships with the rest of the LBNF/DUNE-US management team and the DUNE collaboration. Processes—including requirements and interface management, and operations concept development, as well as integration and verification test planning; also involves design value management and risk management, as well as configuration control plans. Methodology—plans for communication within the system engineering team and with the rest of the LBNF/DUNE teams; description of system engineering involvement and planning for programmatic and other external reviews, as well as the internal technical review process for the detectors. The SEMP supports and is subordinate to the LBNF/DUNE Project Management Plan (PMP), and the DUNE Management Plan. The SEMP defines the technical management across the LBNF/DUNE teams to provide the specific processes required to manage the systems engineering effort, while the other documents describe other project management systems for the DOE Project, LBNF/DUNE-US and DUNE. Systems Engineering Management Organization The LBNF/DUNE Project team includes members from the LBNF/DUNE-US DOE Project and the DUNE Collaboration. Systems Engineering serves all project entities as part of the Joint Project Office. The organizational interaction is represented in Figure 1. The various Subproject Managers, Technical Coordinators & Deputy Directors have responsibility for day-to-day execution of the Projects. DUNE retains responsibility for design and operation of the detectors. Figure 1: LBNF/DUNE Organization Roles and Responsibilities Recognizing the importance of working across subprojects, Systems Engineering, project engineers, LBNF/DUNE subproject managers, and DUNE-Technical Coordinators provide technical leadership and direct the work of the subproject teams through the development and tracking of requirements, interface control documents, design and computer-aided drafting (CAD) integration, requirement verification efforts and adherence to change control processes. This group is responsible for assuring that the subprojects are integrated and meet their overall objectives. The members work closely together through a variety of communication methods outlined later in this document, section 11.1. The specific roles/responsibilities of the SE team are shown in Figure 2 below with “L” designated for those taking the lead in a specific area and “S” indicating a supporting role. Figure 2: LBNF/DUNE Systems Engineering Responsibilities The system engineering organization has responsibilities for the design development process in three ways. First, it supports project-wide and subproject trade studies and value engineering analyses. Second, it supports integrated technical analyses of the facilities and detectors. Third, system engineering maintains the design baselines by handling configuration management for project and subproject-level configuration items, and the mechanisms whereby technical baselines are modified, and designs implemented. Other responsibilities of the Systems Engineering Manager include: Ensure that all project elements are identified and controlled. Ensure that any changes to controlled documents are appropriately recorded, tracked, and incorporated into existing CAD models, drawings and/or documents in a timely manner. Ensure that any additional testing or certification required as a result of changes is explicitly identified and included in the appropriate places. Maintain a list that identifies controlled documents, their owners and the locations of these documents for the Project. Periodically audit the SEMP to determine the effectiveness of this Plan. This may include reviewing controlled copies of documents to ensure their accuracy and their consistency with the master copies, the electronic master, or CAD models. The processes by which these responsibilities are executed are described in the following sections. Systems Engineering Process within the Project Timeline LBNF/DUNE proceeds with design development and construction, fabrication, installation, and start of operations through a series of technical design and readiness reviews to ensure project success. This process is shown in Figure 3 along with necessary completion of key subproject and subsystem documents and reviews. A detailed discussion of the LBNF/DUNE-US design status is in the LBNF/DUNE-US Design Plan. Figure 3: Design Timeline Figure 4 below is one of the draft flow sequences that depicts the interactions between various JPO elements, Technical Coordination, and the FDC Project Management team to address design development from the physics requirements through operational readiness. The process is detailed in the LBNF/DUNE Far Detector subproject approval process document. This document describes the final design review (FDR), production readiness review and installation readiness review processes. Scope and Applicability Scope The scope of the LBNF/DUNE Project encompasses the fabrication and construction of components, systems, and facilities for LBNF/DUNE/Integration. Applicability CM is applicable to all work performed as part of LBNF/DUNE/Integration, which includes the design, testing, integration, and assembly of non-facilities components, as well as the design and construction of technical and conventional facilities. It provides guidance for all personnel on CM activities in support of the Projects, i.e., for all subsystem teams, scientific collaborators. The scope of CM encompasses the lifecycle of the LBNF/DUNE Subprojects, but not the lifecycle of the experiment itself. The CM process governs control of the following items: Mechanical, civil, and electrical CAD models, design drawings and text documents showing the specifications and procedures for the facility, equipment, and subcomponents Requirements, interfaces schedule and cost Configuration management This section describes the CM responsibilities and processes that support the design and implementation of the LBNF, DUNE, and Integration project elements. The purpose is to identify the organization providing the configuration control, describe the change control process, and identify the plan for configuration status accounting and verification. It is a living document that is developed and maintained by the combined efforts of the Projects. Each LBNF/DUNE-US subproject is a separate organizational entity with correlated objectives, overseen by the LBNF/DUNE-US Project Directorate. Management of these entities is defined in the PMP and its Appendices and the DUNE Management Plan (DMP) . Roles and responsibilities of management groups and individuals are defined in these management documents. This document does not attempt to duplicate information in the PMP or DMP; rather, it defines roles and responsibilities of groups and individuals for Configuration Management and refers to those defined in the PMP and DMP by title only. Due to the differences in the management structures of LBNF and DUNE, it is necessary to distinguish the Projects clearly in this document: LBNF/DUNE is used in reference to the combined and coordinated efforts of the project elements, including Integration LBNF/DUNE-US is used in reference to practices that are applicable to the LBNF, DUNE, & Integration scope funded by DOE LBNF and DUNE is used in reference to efforts undertaken independently by each project toward a common goal (e.g., CM processes unique to each Project that result in the combined LBNF/DUNE Configuration Management) Purpose The CM process is designed to ensure that: LBNF/DUNE/Integration configuration documentation is identified, released and controlled The LBNF/DUNE Configuration Control Manager (CCM) position is established, including definition of roles and responsibilities Processes are established in LBNF/DUNE, and within the LBNF/DUNE global enterprise, by which Configuration Changes are proposed, controlled, managed, approved, implemented and tracked Change Control Boards (CCB) are established and function according to the Change Control section of this document Configuration status accounting is implemented Configuration Management provides for implementation of a system of management and engineering controls that are necessary for effective execution of the Projects. Configuration Management Overview Configuration Management (CM) is employed to identify and control relationships during design and construction at both the Near Site and the Far Site. It is important to maintain clear, concise, and accurate records to remain within cost & schedule boundaries and minimize interface issues. This document has been established to ensure that the Projects’ organizations are aware of their roles and responsibilities during the design, construction, and testing phases of the Projects. One of the main goals of LBNF/DUNE CM is to prevent unauthorized or uncontrolled changes to engineering design or analysis, hardware, controlled documents, and controlled software. The plan integrates the various CM control systems. It is also meant to focus on the control of active documents and not on longer-term records management, retention, or archiving. The key elements of CM are Configuration Identification, Change Control, Configuration Status Accounting, and Configuration Verification. Configuration Identification defines the system through Computer-Aided Design (CAD) models, drawings, interface, and requirements documents that specify the system components in terms of functional and physical characteristics, as well as how they are to be manufactured and tested. The DOE-funded Project encompasses multiple international institutions. Each institution is responsible for separate Configuration Items. Each institution/site must have a Document Control Manager whose responsibilities include transmission of the site's documentation to document management systems as described in Section 9. Each site’s Document Control Manager (DCM) and the LBNF/DUNE Document Control Manager are responsible to ensure that the latest versions are disseminated and available, and that they clearly replace any older versions. If outdated documentation is requested for any reason, it shall be labeled as outdated or obsolete in a clear and distinctive manner. DCMs are responsible for the data management system in their organization. All Project elements utilize a single Change Control process as the vehicle by which proposed changes are reviewed and approved. It ensures that the science, technical scope, cost, and schedule impacts of each major change are considered before approval is granted. Configuration control is the means to track configuration information and relay it to key personnel to support management decisions and ensure that all work is performed according to the current approved design. The Configuration Verification process ensures that the current engineering, facilities, hardware, software, and requirements configurations match the intended design by verifying the implementation of each approved change and by conducting periodic configuration audits. Definitions Approval Thresholds – All proposed changes to Project documentation are assigned approval thresholds as outlined in Figure 7 and Figure 8 in this SEMP and the draft DOE Project Execution Plan (draft PEP). Baseline – The point at which requirements and design are formally recorded as a starting point for change control, and after which all changes must be tracked and approved. Change Classification – All proposed Project changes submitted to the Change Control Board for consideration are assigned a “type” and “category” in the Fermilab Baseline Change Request Tool. Configuration changes may affect multiple project WBS elements and may be a combination of cost, schedule or technical change. Change Control Board (CCB) – A board composed of technical and administrative representatives who recommend approval or disapproval of proposed changes to the Projects approved configuration. Membership is defined in section 8.3.4 Change Request – A proposal to change the preliminary baseline or configuration baseline (defined in Section 6) of the LBNF/DUNE Project. Configuration Management (CM) – The systematic control and evaluation of all changes to the configuration that affect deliverables that have been baselined. Documentation – The controlled data that define the current configuration and controlled changes (both proposed and approved). Interface Control Document – A document that records technical and programmatic interfaces between at least two systems or project elements. LBNE Risk Form (Rev. 2) 9/11/14 Analysis: Concrete is used in Civil Construction extensively, and the production and placement costs are generally well understood for typical structures and pavements. The LBNE Decay Pipe, however, is a unique structure, and the volume, mass, and detailing of the shielding concrete introduces some uncertainty in the unit cost when estimated using normal methods and assumptions. The original decay pipe shielding concrete concept was an unreinforced monolithic concrete placement. The engineer’s estimate included 64,252.47 CY at $173.36/CY for a total FY2010 Construction Cost of $11.1M. The engineer’s unit cost was developed using RS Means and is based on the unit cost of foundation mats > 20 CY, pumped, and was adjusted for high formwork. Although the engineer’s estimate selected costs based on large quantities, it is difficult to state what economic benefit (if any) will exist due to the scale of the decay pipe. The evolution of the concept has suggested that the concrete will need to be reinforced, would benefit the project by having multiple construction joints, and that the mix design will incorporate admixtures to reduce its permeability. Additionally, measures will need to be taken to manage the heat of hydration. To reflect this additional complexity, CF has adjusted the unit cost upward by 12.5% to $195.03/CY in CR0096 with no change in quantity for a total FY2010 Construction Cost of $12.5M, or an increase of $1.4M. If, however, the additional complexity represents an increase of 50%, rather than 12.5%, the unit cost would become $260.04/CY for a total FY2010 Construction Cost of $16.7M, or $4.2M more than the current value. Note: All costs in FY2010 Construction $ Escalated to FY2019, $4.2M FY2010 Construction becomes $7.1M BCWS. The NSCF budget includes a cost contingency of 25% for most items, including for the Decay Pipe shielding concrete. For the decay pipe shielding, the value of the contingency is $3.7M. Assuming that 50% of the $3.7M contingency value applies to this risk and the other 50% applies to other potential changes / uncertainties associated with the shielding concrete, the contingency available to offset the impact of this risk is $1.9M. Therefore the true cost impact of this risk is a BCWS of $7.1M – 0.5 x $3.7M = $5.3M BCWS.

Adding the additional muon hill shielding ($238,341) and fencing ($20,930) yields a construction cost of $FY12 = $590,843 which is a BCWS cost impact of $958,318 ($823,869/$507,950 = 62.2% increase). June 16, 2016 Updated Analysis LBNE Change Request 0058 was for a 10cm (0.1m) increase in the thickness of the decay pipe concrete shielding from 550 cm to 560 cm. Documentation for this change, including a detaiked cost estimate, is found in the LBNE document database https://docs.dunescience.org:440/cgi-bin/ShowDocument?docid=7969 . The executive summary of that change shows that cost of this increase was a BCWS of $539,576 plus EDIA of $48,562 = $588,138. These calculations were based on a mid-point of decay pipe construction of approximately April 2020. The updated risk is based on an assumed additional increase in thickness of 0.3m (1-ft) that the current schedule shows a construction mid-point of 2023. Thrre eyears of additional escalation is 10.53%. Therefore, the cost impact of this risk is 3 x $588,138 x 1.1053 = $1,950,207, say $2M.

LBNF/DUNE Risk Supplement (Rev. 4 AEH 9/9/15) This form is intended to document risk-related analyses in more detail than the LBNF/DUNE risk register at https://fermipoint.fnal.gov/collaboration/PM-Tools/Pages/Risk-Register.aspx accommodates. Risk Title: Cryogenics or FD changes impact layout/design of Far Site facilities Risk Long Description: Included in Risk Register Chronological Update History: Date of Update: Initial (10 Jun 2015) Analysis Type: Risk impact Analysis Details: Initial and mitigated scope and ES&H impacts re-assessed. Date of Update: 16 Apr 2015 Analysis Type: Risk impact Analysis Details: It is not unusual that technical system designs continue to change as conventional facilities to house them are being designed and constructed. The question will become whether or not management of the project allows changes to be made to conventional facilities as technical system subproject groups request changes. Analysis Type: Exposure Analysis Details: Depending upon each specific change requested and when changes occur, costs can be greater than $5M and perhaps as great as $10M. (Risk register says $10.5M) Analysis Type: Mitigation Analysis Details: Management control of changes requested through a formal change control, or configuration control, board is the only way to mitigate impacts of changes that will be requested. Date of Update: 15 September 2015 Analysis Type: (risk impact, mitigation, response) Risk Impact Analysis Details: The following information was included in an email to T. Lundin from D. Vardiman dated 9/10/15 at 11:54am CT. A budgetary (Direct Cost plus Indirect Cost, no contingency) estimate for a three meter extension to each cavern for all four caverns is $1.9M. There are no cost included for additional changes in design due to addition to cavern length. Total unit cost per meter3 is based upon Arup’s highest unit cost for Cavern #1 direct cost of $191/ meter3 with an average of 54% Indirect Cost added. Therefore the upper limit of the cost impact is $1.9M plus $0.6M in contingency for a total of $2.5M. The schedule impact is estimated to be 2 months to 6 months.

Introduction** This amendment to the Statement of Work describes the collaboration by members of Indiana University and Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) in the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). The purpose of this collaboration is design, fabrication, operation and scientific exploitation of the Liquid Argon Detector (LAr) sub-project of the DUNE. The initial detector concept is described in Conceptual Design Report, prepared for the DUNE CD-1 review, July, 2015. Two of the most important goals of the project during the CD-1 to CD-2 phase are the development of the DUNE Preliminary Design Report and a baseline schedule for the project. The Scope of Work to reach CD-2 for the DUNE is the basis for meeting this requirement and is accepted as part of this Statement of Work. The LAr Project Management infrastructure, (LAr Project Office), resides at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and the responsibility for LAr Project Management resides in the LAr Project Manager, serving as BNL’s technical representative and reporting to the BNL Associate Director for High Energy and Nuclear Physics and to the DUNE project office at Fermilab. This Memorandum of Understanding describes the anticipated funding from the DOE, together with the contributions of Indiana to the LAr Far Detector as part of the DUNE Project. It is 1 understood that the anticipated contributions of Indiana may later be modified or that additional responsibilities may be added to those described here. An annual amendment to this SOW will include funding for the contributions of Indiana as the DUNE Project proceeds. The normal period of performance will be the U.S. fiscal year (October 1-September 30). It is understood that shortfalls in funding will result in reduced deliverables. This SOW is made between Indiana and the LAr Project Manager. It does not constitute a legal contractual obligation on the part of either of the parties. It reflects an arrangement that is currently satisfactory to the parties involved. The parties agree to negotiate amendments to this SOW as required to meet the evolving requirements of the LAr sub-project. This particular SOW is made to provide funding for the work agreed to between the parties covering the specific period of performance from October 1, 2015 through September 30, 2016. It is subject to all the points of agreement and conditions in the current version of the parent Memorandum of Understanding and the current version of the Conceptual Design Report. Indiana University is expected to submit monthly financial reports to BNL, by the fifteenth day of each month, and should include all costs incurred during the preceding month and outstanding commitments to the end of the month. LBNF/DUNE’s scope is to build an intense neutrino beam originating at FNAL aimed at a large neutrino detector located at the far detector site. Scope is described below for each of the two parts: LBNF, a DOE project with international contributions, and the international DUNE project, managed by the DUNE collaboration and primarily supported by multiple international partners, including a DOE contribution. For LBNF the main scope elements on the FNAL site, called the “near site”, include: - Conventional facilities and excavation to support the technical components of the primary proton beam, the neutrino beam and the near neutrino detector - Magnets and support equipment to transport the primary proton beam to the neutrino Target Hall _(this element may include international contribution)_ - Target and magnetic focusing horns to direct pions and kaons into a decay tunnel _(this element includes international contribution)_ - A decay tunnel where the pions and kaons will decay into neutrinos - A beam absorber at the end of the decay tunnel - Muon detectors and the main LBNF scope elements at the SURF site, called the “far site”, include: - Conventional facilities and excavation at SURF to house and support the technical components of the far detector - Cryogenic infrastructure required for underground installation and operation of the far detector _(this element includes international contribution)_ For the international DUNE project the main scope elements at the near site include: 3 - The near neutrino detector to monitor the beam downstream of the absorber _(this element includes a DOE contribution)_ and the main DUNE scope element at the far site includes: - The Far Detector (Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber), implemented as four separate ten fiducial kiloton modules _(this element includes a DOE contribution)_ Preliminary key performance parameters (KPPs) of the project are presented below in Table 1. LIFE CYCLE COST The DOE LBNF/DUNE TPC has a CD-1 point estimate of $1,457M including escalation. A detailed analysis of the DOE life cycle costs has been done. The experiment and far site facility are assumed to operate for twenty years starting assuming a fully complete far detector in 2027, after which time the far detector is decommissioned. The operations at each site are assumed to be incremental to the existing operations of facilities or experiments. The overall increase in operations costs at both FNAL and SURF would be $494M for twenty years of running. The detector and facilities at SURF would cost $173M to operate for twenty years, however the international DUNE collaboration will support the detector operations cost. This is expected to be funded through a common fund supported by all of the international partners that contributed to detector construction. DUNE detector maintenance and operations cost estimates will be refined as design matures and individual partner contributions will be defined as the international and common fund agreements are established. The LBNF beamline is not assumed to be decommissioned or demolished upon conclusion of the experiment; other experiments are assumed to use this facility at that time. Far detector decommissioning and demolition at SURF would occur in FY47 to FY48, and include removal of detector components and restoring the surface. This is estimated to cost $75M. ACQUISITION APPROACH Acquisition of the LBNF/DUNE will be conducted through Fermi Research Alliance (FRA), the FNAL M&O contractor, which will have the ultimate responsibility to successfully execute the LBNF/DUNE project for DOE. The LBNF/DUNE project is separated into two parts: the facilities project, LBNF and the detector project, DUNE. LBNF will be built by FNAL as a host laboratory, with international contributions. DUNE near and far detectors will be built by the international DUNE collaboration through many contributors including DOE. FRA/FNAL, in coordination with DOE-OHEP and DUNE collaboration has established a set of structures to provide coordination among participating funding agencies, oversight of LBNF/DUNE project, and coordination between LBNF and DUNE parts of the project. These are in place and are described further in Section 7. DOE will cooperate and coordinate with interested international and domestic partners to plan and execute the overall LBNF/DUNE project. International contributions to the design and construction of LBNF/DUNE will be defined in the context of bi‐lateral agreements between the U.S. and other participating countries. Mechanisms are in place to facilitate joint consultation between the partner funding agencies, such that coordinated oversight and actions will be taken to ensure the success of the overall program. The LBNF/DUNE project makes use of existing FNAL staff and facilities to support design and construction and provide project management and oversight for both LBNF and DUNE parts of the project. FNAL is the location for the near site facility delivering the neutrino beam. The design, construction, and installation of the LBNF/DUNE components will be carefully coordinated with other research activities at FNAL. At the far site, LBNF Project will coordinate with the South Dakota Science & Technology Authority (SDSTA), owner of the former Homestake Mine property and operator of SURF. The LBNF project will contract directly with SDSTA to provide pre-construction services and design of LBNF Conventional Facilities (CF) at SURF. Construction contracting for the CF will be directly from FNAL as described further in the Acquisition Strategy and supporting acquisition planning documents. DOE is presently funding SDSTA ongoing operations through Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) and its SURF Operations Office through FY16; this is expected to change to funding through FNAL starting in FY17. Coordination between SDSTA, FNAL and the LBNF Project will ensure efficient operations at SURF while meeting LBNF requirements. This will be facilitated with an agreement being developed between SDSTA and FNAL regarding the LBNF Project that defines responsibilities and methods of working together during the LBNF Project design and construction. A separate agreement will be written for LBNF Operations. FNAL would serve as the single point of contact for the DUNE collaboration on all matters pertaining to the far site. Additional information can be found in the Acquisition Strategy (AS) for the LBNF/DUNE Project , and in the Tailoring and Management sections of this document. The AS describes the approaches taken for design, fabrication and installation of beamline conventional construction at the near and far sites and near and far detector systems. The AS also discusses major procurements critical to the project because of their overall cost or because of limited commercial vendors and for which the project has prepared acquisition plans. TAILORING STRATEGY This tailoring strategy is intended to support approval of the CD-1 Refresh for LBNF/DUNE and will be updated to support approval of future Critical Decisions as needed. Tailoring principles will be considered or applied in the following areas: Critical Decision 1 Refresh: The CD-1 Refresh will support the updated plan for the internationalization of the long baseline neutrino facility and experiment, called LBNF/DUNE. The prior CD-1 Tailoring Strategy allowed the project scope and plan to be refined after CD-1 and prior to CD-2 to include enhancement of scientific capabilities, such as a more massive detector to be sited underground and a near detector as enabled by international partners. The CD-1 refresh will evaluate the updated conceptual design, provide a cost range for the DOE contribution, identify scope assignments and costs associated with other parties, and present how FNAL and the project will manage and integrate the facility and detector projects comprising LBNF/DUNE. Critical Decision 3a, Approve Initial Far Site Construction: The project will request a CD-3a decision to approve start of DOE-funded far site facilities construction procurement for the LBNF. This scope will include excavation of caverns (pits) for the DUNE detector and conventional infrastructure as needed. This project has several discrete steps that must be done in series. The first is the excavation of caverns to house the liquid argon detectors. The next is the installation of cryogenic infrastructure to support the cryostats. The third is the completion and commissioning of the of the detectors in the cryostats. The time needed to complete the design work for each of these steps is different with the cavern design being the most advanced, the design of the cryostat and cryogenic infrastructure being the next most advanced, and the detector requiring the most design work. Starting the cavern excavation as soon as the cavern design is ready reduces the total cost of the project by eliminating multiple years of project management costs and avoiding cost escalation on a major cost driver of the project. It speeds the completion of the overall project while also advancing the date when data from a detector will be available for the international scientific collaboration. This strategy reduces the cost and schedule risk to the project and will ensure optimum use of resources, while awaiting CD-2 and CD-3 authority. The decision will be based on an evaluation of cost estimate and design maturity, with a plan for completing design that incorporates adequate risk assessment and mitigation, and includes sufficient contingency to provide confidence the work can be successfully completed. This plan will also demonstrate that proceeding with far site facilities construction poses only low and manageable project risk, relative to completion of the far detector design. The full cost of this long lead procurement action is expected to be in the $250-400M range, with the conventional facilities construction contract structured with options for sequential construction of 10 fiducial kiloton detector-size excavations. Site preparation, site characterization, or related minor early activities may be pursued prior to CD-3, with necessary approval and funding in place. The project will track and report performance associated with these activities to the FPD utilizing Fermilab’s certified EVMS. Critical Decision 3b, Approve Near Site Preparation and Far Site Long Lead Procurement: The project will request a CD-3b decision to approve long lead LBNF activities at the near site and far site. This scope will include advanced site preparation at the near site and far site cryogenics infrastructure. The advanced site preparation will build an embankment that will support the beamline, and allow for the required settlement period before beamline conventional facilities work proceeds. The near site conventional facilities define a parallel critical path for meeting the needs of the collaboration to have a completed beamline as soon as possible following completion of the far detector. This work will reduce cost, schedule and technical risk associated with constructing the beamline facility. The cost of this long lead procurement action is ~$20M. Long lead scope for far site cryogenic infrastructure is needed to allow outfitting of caverns while excavation continues. These parallel work activities support the planned schedule for cryostat delivery and installation (by non-DOE partners). The cryogenic infrastructure cost could be up to ~$100M. The project will track and report performance associated with these activities to the FPD utilizing Fermilab’s certified EVMS. This is a configurable GEANT4-based [5] simulation of all elements of the DUNE/LBNF neutrino beam from primary protons to hadron absorber. The basic output of G4LBNE is a list of all particle decays to neutrinos that occur anywhere along the beamline. Weights (commonly referred to as “importance weights”) are used to reduce the size of the output files by throwing out relatively common and unimpor- tant low energy neutrinos while preserving more relevant neutrinos. To produce neutrino flux distributions at a particular location, all of the neutrinos in the G4LBNE output file are forced to point toward the specified location and weighted according to the relative probability that the decay in question would produce a neutrino in that direction. The default simulation models the 2015 CD1 CDR beam design [1], which includes horns identical to those used in the NuMI beam and a target similar to the NuMI low-energy target, modified to accommodate a 1.2 MW proton beam. The decay pipe is a 204 meter long, 2 meter radius cylinder. To perform the optimization, we replace the first horn with a configurable horn with 12 variable shape parameters, shown in Figure 3. The second horn retains the ba- sic NuMI shape in the optimization, with the location of all components modified by radial and longitudinal scale factors as well as a radial shift. The position of the second horn was also allowed to vary, and in cases where it overlapped with the decay pipe, the start of the decay pipe was shifted downstream (with the end of the decay pipe unmoved). The decay pipe snout was removed from the beamline geometry for the optimization. The proton target used in the optimization was same as in the default simulation, with the total length of the target and the fin width allowed to vary. When the size of the target is varied from the default value of 10 mm, the beam spot (which has a standard deviation of 1.7 mm in both the x and y direction in the default simulation) is scaled by the same amount to ensure that 99% of the beam protons collide with the target. Finally, the primary proton energy and current in the horns was allowed to vary in the optimization. When considering lower proton momentum during the optimization, we assume the powers and corresponding proton-on-target adjust- ments given in table 3. For momenta between 60 and 120 GeV/c, we interpolate between the expected POT/year given in Table 3. Below 60 GeV/C, we assume the Main Injector cycle 12 time is constant at 0.7 s, which causes the expected power to fall quickly below 60 GeV/c. Above 120 GeV, we assume constant power of 1.2 MW. All parameters were varied separately for neutrino mode and antineutrino mode, result- ing in a total of forty optimization parameters. roc r4 r1 r2 r3 L1 L2 L6 L3 Figure 16: Side view of the Horn 1 shape considered in the optimization. To start, 100 beam configura- tions with randomly chosen parameters were simulated in neutrino mode and antineutrino mode using 500,000 protons per mode per configuration. The resulting fluxes were then used to calculate a “fitness” – the CP estimator described in 2 for each configuration. Two configu- rations were then randomly chosen from this sample, with the probably of each configuration being chosen proportional to its fitness. The parameters of these two configurations were then mated into a new child configuration using a two-point-crossover method. This process was 13 repeated 100 times to produce a new 100-beam generation. The parameters of the children were then “mutated” with the probability of mutation being 10%. During a mutation, the original child parameter was shifted by an amount drawn from a Gaussian with width 10% of the total allowed range of the parameter in question. The new generation was then simu- lated, the fitnesses of each configuration computed, and the entire process repeated to create a new generation. The optimization converged after approximately 100 generation (corre- sponding to 100,000 simulated beams). Each generation takes approximately four hours in the absence of significant grid congestion. 5 Results of Optimization The fitness of each configuration generated during the optimization is shown in figure 5, compared with the fitness of the default beam. The randomly chosen beam designs of the first generation are generally poorer than the default beam, but as the optimzation evolves, it rapidly finds beams significantly better than the default beam. The beam with the best fitness is configuration 9556, whose fitness is 1.94, an improvement of 32% over the fitness of the default configuration. Update: Modifications to the LBNF DK Region Concentration Model Chris Greer March 25, 2026 As discussed over the last week, variables for DK initial concentration (C0) are being adjusted to align between MARS, FLUKA, diffusion and the Concentration Model K (atom/star), Star rate averaging, compacted backfill soil density, starting POT and Tirr application Some adjustments decrease C0 while others increase C0. The focus here is on Reduction factors. Analytical migration calculations (Reduction factors) in the Concentration Model are dependent on individual dewatering cones of depression (CODs), but do not include regional flow direction (3D numerical modeling is needed) CODs overlap, introducing analytical uncertainty Calculations submitted for review (due next week) Caveats Assumed to start concurrently (per email with Tom Hamernik). The higher DK-AC withdrawal rate (1,000-1,500 gpm for first few months then 400-500 gpm) over 2 years will develop a larger dewatered area in the center of its cone of depression in the upper bedrock Joliet Fm compared to ND ND (total of 400 gpm during construction then 150 gpm max during operation)… How much water will be from upper bedrock Joliet Fm versus from deeper Kankakee-Elwood Fm? And when will it capture DK-AC area water (i.e., how much activated water might escape ND capture)? In rock, the permeable flow is not limited to the edge of the outer box so the average should be taken over the volume between the edge of the outer box out to the 99% extent. Title: Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report

drainage, a standard sump pump room for the support rooms, and utilities, a 30-­‐ton bridge crane, air handling equipment, and emergency systems. An exit stairway and an elevator to the surface will be provided within the shaft connecting the hall to the Absorber Service Building. A 770 sq.ft. Muon Alcove is centered on the beamline and adjacent to, and down beam of, the Absorber Hall. There is no connection between the Absorber Hall and the Near Detector Hall, or the Absorber Hall and the Target Complex. During installation and maintenance, this facility will be occupied by a maximum of 49 persons below grade. The hadron absorber structure (the absorber) is located directly downstream of the 204-­‐m long decay pipe. It is a pile of aluminum, steel, and concrete blocks (some of which are water-­‐cooled) that must absorb the energy of the particles that exit the decay pipe. #### **_3.3.1.6 Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30)_** The Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30) will be an above grade building with a near sub-­‐surface floor to accommodate the support equipment needed for assembly and operation of the equipment and technical components for the Absorber. The Absorber Service Building will be located above the Absorber Hall. The Absorber Service Building will be a 3,285 sq.ft., steel-­‐framed, metal-­‐sided building with a cast-­‐in-­‐ place concrete foundation. This building will have a 35-­‐ft. clear height and will house a 30 ton bridge crane and mechanical equipment, including a 600-­‐ton chiller, chilled water pumps, air handlers, and desiccant dryers for absorber complex for the absorber facility. Appropriate fire protection systems will be provided. A truck bay will be provided so that equipment can be unloaded by the overhead crane and lowered down the shaft to the Absorber Hall. #### **_3.3.1.7 Near Site Detector Service Building (LBNF 40)_** The Near Detector Service Building (LBNF 40), is a 45-­‐ft wide by 136-­‐ft long by 42-­‐ft high grade-­‐level building. It will be used to house the support equipment and truck bay/lay-­‐down area needed for the assembly and operation of the equipment and technical components for the Near Detector Hall and support rooms. The truck bay/staging area port ion of the building has a 35-­‐ft interior clear ceiling height. **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 3-­‐22** **Description of the Site, Facility and Operations** Also included in this building are the mechanical/electrical rooms, fire/life safety room, domestic water/meter room, and restroom. The mechanical room will house the shaft mechanicals, chilled water pumps, heat exchangers, exterior air cooled chillers, natural gas boilers, hot water pumps, CHW/HW air handlers, ventilation/exhaust fans for the surface building and desiccant dryers (dehumidifiers) for the Near Detector Hall and support rooms. The truck bay will be provided for equipment to be unloaded using the 15-­‐ton overhead bridge crane. Equipment and detector components will be lowered down the 22-­‐ft diameter shaft to the Near Detector Hall approximately 210 ft below grade. This equipment can then be moved, using carts or portable hoists, where required. Because the initial detector installation and possible future removal are isolated events, the building crane capacity is not designed for these infrequent loads. Instead, a removable service building roof hatch cover over the 22-­‐ft diameter shaft will be required for initial installation and future removal or replacement of Near Detector Hall components by use of a rented 200 -­‐ton crawler crane. #### **_3.3.1.8 Near Detector Hall_** The Near Detector Hall and support rooms will house the DUNE Near Detector and related components, and is located a minimum of 689-­‐ft (210-­‐m) downstream of the Absorber Hall approximately 185 ft below grade. The Near Detector Hall has been sized to accommodate either of two detector technologies that were considered during Conceptual Design; the reference design is a Straw Tube Tracker and alternative design is similar to the MicroBooNE (LAr) detector. At Conceptual Design, the Conventional Facilities design as presented is generic enough to accommodate either detector technology. The LAr detector will require special Oxygen Deficiency Hazard (ODH) emergency ventilation, and egress design criteria, which has been included in the reference design. The Near Detector Hall and support rooms will include access to a 22-­‐ft diameter shaft which will be used for equipment handling and primary egress that includes utilities and has a 4,000-­‐lb capacity elevator. This shaft serves as the major equipment access corridor from LBNF-­‐40 above to the surface. Near Detector Hall and support rooms are approximately 200 ft below grade. The Near Detector Hall will have a 15-­‐ton bridge crane running the length of the hall that will be used for installing detector components and related equipment lowered down from the surface building to the Near Detector Hall. A secondary egress shaft 17 feet in diameter will allow for personnel to egress the hall via a stairway to the surface. The Near Detector Hall and support rooms will also be outfitted with air handling equipment, power/control systems, and emergency systems. The 12-­‐ft wide by 21-­‐ft long control room is beam-­‐right of the shaft and the Sump and Pump Room is beam-­‐left of the shaft. To accommodate the LAr detector, a recessed sump design below the floor of the hall is included to capture any leak or spill of LAr from the alternate detector. A ventilation system is designed to ventilate the boil-­‐off of the LAr gas. Rock bolts or rock dowels will be used to provide both short-­‐and long-­‐term rock stability. The rock surface will be treated with shotcrete. The roof/ceiling of the Near Detector Hall and support rooms will be lined with an internal metal roof drip ceiling system (drip pans) to collect and route groundwater infiltration to protect the hall and support room contents from water and loose material. The groundwater will be channeled to the main sump via trench floor drains. **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 3-­‐23** **Description of the Site, Facility and Operations** The Conventional Facilities fit-­‐out work includes the bridge crane and its supports, internal CMU walls, fire walls, miscellaneous poured concrete walls and abutments, doors, fire protection, the sump pump system, fire detection, and mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) systems. #### **3.3.2 Far Site: Detector Facility** The LBNF Far Site will be generally located at the 4850L of SURF. These facilities include caverns and drifts to support four 10kT detectors and a Central Utility Cavern located underground at the 4850L. The Far Detector facilities will include the following: Detector Hall Caverns (below grade) - Central Utility Cavern (below grade) - Access/Egress Drifts (below grade) - Cryogenic Compressor Building (above grade) - Ross Dry Building (above grade) #### **_3.3.2.1 Detector Halls Caverns_** The DUNE experiment will be housed in four detector pits within two main caverns at the 4850L. Siting deep underground is required to shield from cosmic rays, as detailed in Report on the Depth requirements for a Massive Detector at Homestake. The 4850L is deeper than what is absolutely required, but is used because of existing access at this level (Figure 3-­‐5). The limits on size for the detector are determined by rock strength and the limits on the ability to produce large dimension anode and cathode plane arrays. Current assessment of rock quality indicates that a cavity of this size is reasonable with the rock quality assumed for this formation. Preliminary modeling of the proposed excavations included 2D and 3D numerical modeling. The intact-­‐rock strength and joint strength had the greatest impact according to the 2D modeling, and 3D modeling confirmed that the complex geometry is possible. The LBNF caverns will be excavated using modern drill and blast techniques, in phases from the top down. Excavation accesses to the crown of the cavity and to the base of the excavation will be via ramps. The upper ramp will begin at the access, while the lower ramp will begin further toward the Ross shaft. This lower ramp is necessary for outfitting the experiment as well as removal of waste rock. A raise bore will be pulled to the crown from the lower ramp. The cavity will then be excavated in lifts, with ground support installed as excavation progresses as seen in Figure 3-­‐4. Given the size of the FD cavity excavation, the presence of structural features, potential for overstress zones and critical requirements for long –term stability, special attention will be paid to controlled drilling and precision blasting techniques. This will minimize overbreak and create smooth, stable walls as much as possible. The far detector caverns and drifts will be supported using galvanized rock bolts/cables, wire mesh, and shotcrete for a life of 30 years. The floor of the cavern is not anticipated to require support. A groundwater drainage system will be placed behind the shotcrete in the arch and walls of the far detector cavern rock excavation. This drain system will collect groundwater (native) seepage and eliminate the potential for hydrostatic pressure build-­‐up behind the shotcrete. Channels will be placed in the concrete invert to drain groundwater to the sump system. #### **_3.3.2.2 Central Utility Corridor_** LBNF requires spaces for cryogenic equipment outside of the detector caverns. These requirements have been combined with that for the conventional facilities utilities in an independent central utility cavern. This area will house the experiment’s cryogen system, electrical equipment to supply power for **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 3-­‐24** **Description of the Site, Facility and Operations** facility and experiment needs, sump pump access and controls, fire sprinkler room, air handling units (AHUs), chilled water system, and exhaust ducting. The centralized location minimizes overall utility distribution costs. Isolating the utilities from the experiment simplifies electrical ground isolation to avoid interference with sensitive detector electronics, and also provides the opportunity to optimize ventilation to control heat emanating from the equipment in the central utility caverns. #### **_3.3.2.3 Access/Egress Drifts_** All primary access and egress for LBNF is through the Ross Shaft. The drift connections from the Ross Shaft to new excavations required for LBNF will be optimized to accommodate the maximum load size possible through the shaft plus the utilities required to service the facility. At the writing of this document, an assumed size of 5m wide by 6m tall is used for all access and egress drifts. The DOE Mission Need for the LBNF/DUNE Project proposes the following major elements: - A neutrino beamline, produced from a primary proton beam, aimed at a far detector site - A neutrino detector located at the Far Detector site The LBNF/DUNE Project scope includes construction of experimental systems and facilities at two separate geographical locations. The reference design is planned to achieve the Project's mission in which a proton beam extracted from the Fermilab Main Injector (MI) is used to produce a neutrino beam. The neutrino beam travels through the Earth's mantle to a Far Detector located 1,300 km away in the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF), the site of the former Homestake Mine in Lead, South Dakota. The 1,300-­‐km separation between the sites presents an optimal baseline for LBNF's neutrino-­‐oscillation physics goals. The main scope elements on the Fermilab site, also referred to as the Near Site, include: - Magnets and support equipment to transport the extracted protons to the target, where they interact, producing pions and kaons - A target and target hall - Magnetic focusing horns to direct the pions and kaons into a decay tunnel - A decay tunnel where these particles decay into neutrinos - A beam absorber at the end of the decay tunnel to absorb the residual secondary hadronic particles - Conventional Facilities at Fermilab to support the technical components of the primary proton beam, the neutrino beam and the near detectors. The main scope elements at the Far Site include: - The Far Detector Caverns - Central Utility Cavern - Access/Egress Drifts - Cryogenic Compressor Building - Ross Dry Building - Infrastructure required for the Far Detector ## **1.1 Purpose** The purpose of this Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report (PSVAR) is to identify the security requirements and integrate these requirements into the LBNF/DUNE Project at the early design phase of the Project’s life cycle. In addition the implementation of those requirements is assessed throughout the Project. ## **1.2 Scope** The PSVAR evaluates the potential security risk to employees, the public, and the environment at Fermilab during the design, construction, and operational phases of the LBNF/DUNE Project. The PSVAR **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report** **Page 6** **Overview** also develops the effective protection strategies that will be implemented during the Project’s different phases. The successful protection of security interests requires that effective protection strategies and procedures are developed and implemented. The Protection strategy for an asset will include consideration of the threat to the asset as a fundamental part of the design process. Establishing and integrating security requirements early in the projects lifecycle is necessary for project planning, cost estimating, facilities requirements, and to prevent project impacts that can arise when safeguards and security requirements are identified late into the design process, construction, or as part of the operational readiness review. Additionally, due to potential conflicts in meeting site security requirements and the requirements of other critical disciplines such as, safety, the integration of all requirements is critical to developing the best overall cost effective solution for the Project. ## **1.3 Objectives** The objectives of the PSVAR are as follows: - 1) To provide site security advice to Federal Project Directors (FPD) and Federal program/site office managers (contractors and subcontractors as applicable) in identifying and implementing key safeguards and security components of their projects and integrating site security consideration into each acquisition management phase (initiation, definition, execution and transition/closeout). - 2) To define security features and functions as developed or required by the security program or security policy, which minimizes impact on operations. - 3) To identify the function of the federal site security program representative who serves as security design point of contact for security features and is a member of the Integrated Project Team (IPT) as appropriate during the entire Project cycle. - 4) To facilitate communication and interaction between the site security professionals, other integrated project teams and the members of the Project design team. **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report** **Page 7** **Target Identification and Description** ## **2 TARGET IDENTIFICATION AND DESCRIPTION** The PSVAR for the LBNF/DUNE Project is developed to evaluate the potential risk to employees, the public, and the environment at Fermilab during Project design, construction and operation phases. The Project will not change the site security requirements at Fermilab. The site is designated as a Class PP (Property Protection) facility with nuclear materials graded Category IV, Attractiveness Level E. No sensitive or classified research is conducted by Fermilab. Currently the entry gates provide perimeter access control and basic visitor services and traffic management. The Sanford Underground Research Facility presently has no DOE security classification, as the facility is managed outside of the DOE complex. This classification for the LBNF/DUNE leased space at SURF is presently being studied. ## **2.1 Project Facilities** The Conventional Facilities scope includes the construction of new structures and modifications to existing structures and laboratory “system-­‐wide” services. Modifications include demolition of structures to clear the way for new construction. The LBNF/DUNE is a particle physics research project. Fermilab researchers have proposed to send a neutrino beam generated by Fermilab to SURF. The LBNF/DUNE Near Site Facilities will be constructed at the Fermilab site located in an area west of Kautz Road and south of Giese Road. In general terms, a proton beam will be extracted from the existing Main Injector, directed north and west towards new below grade enclosures housing the LBNF Target Hall, Absorber Hall, and Near Detector Hall. The proposed Far Detector (FD) and associated Conventional Facilities will be constructed at the SURF. The LAr far detector has a total fiducial mass of 40 kilotons of high purity LAr and will be located underground at the 4850 level in close proximity to the Ross shaft. ## **2.2 Near Site Facility Descriptions** The LBNF Near Site Facilities consist of the following eight (8) functional areas: - Beamline Extraction Enclosure and Primary Beam Enclosure (below grade) - Primary Beam Service Building (LBNF 5) (above grade) - Target Hall Complex (LBNF 20) (above grade, in fill) - Decay Pipe (below grade, in soil and bedrock) - Absorber Hall, Muon Alcove and support rooms (below grade, in soil and bedrock) - Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30) (above grade) - Near Detector Service Building (LBNF 40) (above grade) - Near Detector Hall (below grade) This section provides a description of each functional area. **Note** : All dimensions indicated here are based upon planning that existed at a single point in the conceptual design. Title: Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report

LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report (PSVAR) [lbne-doc-10768] 23 June 2015 Approvals and Signatures Change Log This version of the document may not be the current or approved revision. The current revision is maintained in the former LBNF/DUNE’s document Management system (DocDB) where all internal Project document approvals are also managed. DocDB can be accessed through the web by authorized users (http://lbne2-DocDB-.fnal.gov/) and this document can be identified by the document and version number as indicated in the Version Control Table below. Note: The version number in the table below and DocDB may not match. The current approved version is always available in DocDB. Abbreviations and Acronyms Overview The LBNF/DUNE Project is designed to support the Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science (SC) mission as described in the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF)/ Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) Mission Need Statements. The DOE Mission Need for the LBNF/DUNE Project proposes the following major elements: A neutrino beamline, produced from a primary proton beam, aimed at a far detector site A neutrino detector located at the Far Detector site The LBNF/DUNE Project scope includes construction of experimental systems and facilities at two separate geographical locations. The reference design is planned to achieve the Project's mission in which a proton beam extracted from the Fermilab Main Injector (MI) is used to produce a neutrino beam. The neutrino beam travels through the Earth's mantle to a Far Detector located 1,300 km away in the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF), the site of the former Homestake Mine in Lead, South Dakota. The 1,300-km separation between the sites presents an optimal baseline for LBNF's neutrino-oscillation physics goals. The main scope elements on the Fermilab site, also referred to as the Near Site, include: Magnets and support equipment to transport the extracted protons to the target, where they interact, producing pions and kaons A target and target hall Magnetic focusing horns to direct the pions and kaons into a decay tunnel A decay tunnel where these particles decay into neutrinos A beam absorber at the end of the decay tunnel to absorb the residual secondary hadronic particles Conventional Facilities at Fermilab to support the technical components of the primary proton beam, the neutrino beam and the near detectors. The main scope elements at the Far Site include: The Far Detector Caverns Central Utility Cavern Access/Egress Drifts Cryogenic Compressor Building Ross Dry Building Infrastructure required for the Far Detector Purpose The purpose of this Preliminary Security Vulnerability Assessment Report (PSVAR) is to identify the security requirements and integrate these requirements into the LBNF/DUNE Project at the early design phase of the Project’s life cycle. In addition the implementation of those requirements is assessed throughout the Project. Scope The PSVAR evaluates the potential security risk to employees, the public, and the environment at Fermilab during the design, construction, and operational phases of the LBNF/DUNE Project. The PSVAR also develops the effective protection strategies that will be implemented during the Project’s different phases. The successful protection of security interests requires that effective protection strategies and procedures are developed and implemented. The Protection strategy for an asset will include consideration of the threat to the asset as a fundamental part of the design process. Establishing and integrating security requirements early in the projects lifecycle is necessary for project planning, cost estimating, facilities requirements, and to prevent project impacts that can arise when safeguards and security requirements are identified late into the design process, construction, or as part of the operational readiness review. Additionally, due to potential conflicts in meeting site security requirements and the requirements of other critical disciplines such as, safety, the integration of all requirements is critical to developing the best overall cost effective solution for the Project. Objectives The objectives of the PSVAR are as follows: To provide site security advice to Federal Project Directors (FPD) and Federal program/site office managers (contractors and subcontractors as applicable) in identifying and implementing key safeguards and security components of their projects and integrating site security consideration into each acquisition management phase (initiation, definition, execution and transition/closeout). To define security features and functions as developed or required by the security program or security policy, which minimizes impact on operations. To identify the function of the federal site security program representative who serves as security design point of contact for security features and is a member of the Integrated Project Team (IPT) as appropriate during the entire Project cycle. To facilitate communication and interaction between the site security professionals, other integrated project teams and the members of the Project design team. Target Identification and Description The PSVAR for the LBNF/DUNE Project is developed to evaluate the potential risk to employees, the public, and the environment at Fermilab during Project design, construction and operation phases. The Project will not change the site security requirements at Fermilab. The site is designated as a Class PP (Property Protection) facility with nuclear materials graded Category IV, Attractiveness Level E. No sensitive or classified research is conducted by Fermilab. Currently the entry gates provide perimeter access control and basic visitor services and traffic management. The Sanford Underground Research Facility presently has no DOE security classification, as the facility is managed outside of the DOE complex. This classification for the LBNF/DUNE leased space at SURF is presently being studied. Project Facilities The Conventional Facilities scope includes the construction of new structures and modifications to existing structures and laboratory “system-wide” services. Modifications include demolition of structures to clear the way for new construction. The LBNF/DUNE is a particle physics research project. Fermilab researchers have proposed to send a neutrino beam generated by Fermilab to SURF. The LBNF/DUNE Near Site Facilities will be constructed at the Fermilab site located in an area west of Kautz Road and south of Giese Road. In general terms, a proton beam will be extracted from the existing Main Injector, directed north and west towards new below grade enclosures housing the LBNF Target Hall, Absorber Hall, and Near Detector Hall. The proposed Far Detector (FD) and associated Conventional Facilities will be constructed at the SURF. The LAr far detector has a total fiducial mass of 40 kilotons of high purity LAr and will be located underground at the 4850 level in close proximity to the Ross shaft. Near Site Facility Descriptions The LBNF Near Site Facilities consist of the following eight (8) functional areas: Beamline Extraction Enclosure and Primary Beam Enclosure (below grade) Primary Beam Service Building (LBNF 5) (above grade) Target Hall Complex (LBNF 20) (above grade, in fill) Decay Pipe (below grade, in soil and bedrock) Absorber Hall, Muon Alcove and support rooms (below grade, in soil and bedrock) Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30) (above grade) Near Detector Service Building (LBNF 40) (above grade) Near Detector Hall (below grade) This section provides a description of each functional area. Note: All dimensions indicated here are based upon planning that existed at a single point in the conceptual design. These dimensions and other units of measure may change as the Project design continues to evolve. Beamline Extraction Enclosure and Primary Beam Enclosure The first underground functional area is the Beamline Extraction Enclosure and Primary Beam Enclosure. This area, consisting of the upstream Beamline Extraction Enclosure and the downstream Primary Beam Enclosure are required to allow the beam to be extracted from the Main Injector and transported 328 m (1,078 ft) to the LBNF Target Complex. The construction of the upstream portion of this area will consist of a cut-and-cover below-grade section. The downstream portion of this area includes a transition from the below-grade section to an above-grade section located within an embankment. Some of these areas will be constructed using cast-in-place concrete sections and other areas will be pre-cast concrete enclosure sections. The 778-ft long Primary Beam Enclosure will start at the end of the extraction enclosure and continue along a 15% incline into and through the above-grade embankment, and then at a 10% decline to and through the Target Hall. The depth of the enclosure will be 36.5 ft from the top of the soil shielding fill to the invert/floor. This will provide a minimum of 25 ft of soil and concrete shielding (measured from the center of the beamline) for both the 1.2-MW and 2.3-MW beam power levels. The apex of the embankment over the Primary Beam Enclosure will be approximately 70 ft above existing grade. With the required minimum 25 ft of soil and concrete shielding, the apex of the beamline will be 45 ft above existing grade. The Primary Beam Enclosure has interior dimensions measuring 10 ft wide and 8 ft high. Primary Beam Service Building (LBNF 5) One of four at-grade service buildings is the Primary Beam Service Building (LBNF 5). The function of LBNF 5 is to provide housing for primary beam support equipment and utilities, and access for personnel and light equipment to the Primary Beam Enclosure below. This single-story, steel-framed, metal-sided service building will have approximately 3,600 ft2 of floor space (60 ft by 60 ft), with a minimum 12-ft interior clear height. The building will be positioned off center and right of the beamline and will have a corridor (conduits, Gerardi Coffin, and penetrations) for technical and conventional utilities routing to the Primary Beam Enclosure. Target Hall Complex (LBNF 20) The Target Complex (LBNF 20) will be a 22,200 ft2 near-surface facility constructed in the engineered fill embankment, that combines the Target Hall, corresponding beam-on and beam-off support rooms (power supply, remote crane controls, piped system carrying radioactive water (RAW), and air handling rooms), and the Target Hall service rooms (two truck bays with lay down/staging areas, morgue area, maintenance cell, mechanical/utilities rooms, and rest room). Beam-on spaces are accessible by personnel while the beam is energized, and beam-off spaces are only accessible when the beam is not energized. These support and service rooms accommodate the support equipment and utilities and provide access needed to assemble and operate the equipment and conventional and programmatic/technical components for the Target Hall. Decay Pipe The LBNF Decay Pipe begins at the downstream end of the target chase in the Target Hall and continues 668 ft (204 m) at a decline of approximately 10% to the Absorber Hall, which is approximately 94 ft below grade. The Decay Pipe consists of two concentric pipes; the inner pipe is a 13-ft 2-in (4-m) diameter pipe and the outer pipe is a 14-ft 5-in (4.4-m) diameter pipe. Both pipes are ½-inch thick steel pipes surrounded by the required 18-ft 0.5-in (5.5m) cast-in-place concrete shielding. The direction of supply airflow for Decay Pipe cooling is down through the 20-cm annulus between the two concentric decay pipes and returns through the inner decay pipe for the air-cooling of the beam heat load deposited in the steel and concrete shielding surrounding the decay pipe. Absorber Hall The Absorber Hall will be approximately 94 ft below existing grade. The Absorber Hall will house the concrete-shielded hadron absorber and monitor, the Muon Alcove, and the absorber support rooms, all constructed in an open cut soil excavation to bedrock and then a drill-and-blast rock excavation to the base of the underground facility. A water barrier system will be included between the soil and rock excavation and the internal concrete structure to seal the facility from groundwater infiltration. This underground facility will be a two-level cast in place concrete structure. The lower level of the Absorber Hall will house the Absorber, Muon Alcove, sump and pump systems, and will provide the base of the egress shaft. The middle level of this underground facility will house the top of the absorber, and the RAW room the upper level will house the instrumentation room. The roof/ceiling of the underground portion of the facility will serve as the floor of the above ground Absorber Service Building (LBNF 30). In coming up with answers, we gratefully acknowledge very informative and useful inputs from Phil Adamson, Sam Childress, Cory Crowley, Jim Hylen, Vaia Papadimitriou, Matt Quinn, Diane Reitzner and Salman Tariq. ## **Introduction** The LBNF/DUNE Flux spectrometer concept is a proposal to measure the muon and hadron flux after the LBNF focusing horns and before the decay pipe. A strawman design for the spectrometer is shown in Figure 1. There are two possible locations for the apparatus – inside the LBNF target chase in a very low-intensity configuration of LBNF (in situ), or in an external beamline at Fermilab (ex situ). The goal is for spectrometer to measure the absolute neutrino parent flux after the focusing horns to an accuracy of 1 to 2%. SpectrometerMagnetized CalorimeterSi-W

This question should be addressed with a preliminary assessment of the impact on the overall sensitivity.** Existing long-baseline oscillation experiments have relied largely on the Near Detector to limit the impact of large flux uncertainties. In this flux times cross section paradigm, detailed knowledge of the neutrino beam and neutrino scattering cross-sections are not required, as oscillation parameters are estimated by comparing event rates in the far detector to predictions extrapolated from the Near Detector before the beam has oscillated. While this has been sufficient for statistically limited experiments, it may lead to serious mistakes as neutrino oscillation measurements push to higher precision. One reason for this is that the composition of the neutrino flux depends on the geometry of the beam and detectors. The Near Detector sees a broad cross section of the beam, while the far detector sees only a very narrow solid angle. Thus, the neutrino flux for a given flavor is different at the Near and Far Detectors, as shown in Figure 2. X103

Although this is the most advanced procedure available for estimating flux uncertainties, it relies on guesses to how wrong models of unmeasured differential hadro production and elastic scattering cross sections may be. It also does not take into account the possibility of substantial mistakes in the beam simulation which could cause inaccuracies at the level of tens of percent. Issues such as overly simplified horn shape models, ommisions of cooling water, and unsimulated shifts in the horn positions have been recently discovered in the NuMI beam simulation. DUNE should be prepared for the possibility of similar problems. The 1-2% precision of the flux spectromter concept would be a substantial improvement over the current uncertainty estimate of 8%. Moreover, it would correct many of the potential simulation inaccuracies that are not accounted for in this estimate. The impact of the spectrometer measurement on the overall DUNE sensitivities is difficult to determine at this time, as it requires a complete and detailed simulation of the analysis.
