It will be a requirement for any change in the target design (such as a modification of the geometry of the target or a change in materials), or a change in the horns design (such as a modification of the shape/thickness of the inner 6 conductor, or a reconfiguration of the horn positions). - The observation of an unexpected and significant change of particle flux detected in the muon monitor system (and possibly in the hadron monitor), or a distortion of the neutrino interaction spectrum shape and/or normalization change in the near detector. Such changes may occur, for instance, if a horn goes out of alignment, or if the target degrades, e.g. its density changes. If we are equipped with an ex situ facility, we may still need some measurement in the target chase to address point 2, since the observations in the muon monitors or the near detector may not be enough to identify the problem. In this case, a simpler tracking plane downstream of the horns just to record the particle flux would be of great help to identify the problem. **For the two options of installing the spectrometer in situ either after Horn C or between Horn B and C, provide an estimate of the additional costs (spectrometer and CF) and the impact on the operational schedule how much time would be devoted to spectrometer operation and how often.** ### _Additional Costs_ In order to be able to operate the spectrometer in the LBNF target chase, slow extraction at MI10 is required, such that the instantaneous intensity be of the order of one proton per 53 MHz bucket. The presently installed septa in the Main Injector can provide the right phase advance for beam extraction in the LBNF beamline at MI10. Removable collimators will need to be installed in the LBNF beamline to further reduce the beam intensity by a factor 104 _−_ 105 . Additional removable instrumentation (BPMs, SWICS), sensitive to the low intensity slow extracted beam, will need to be installed in the LBNF beamline. Engineering Input on the 3-Horn Optimized Design Laura Fields Cory Crowley 21 January 2016 1 Introduction Cory Crowley (engineer at Fermilab) has provided some preliminary input on engineering considerations for the three-horn optimized design. The rest of this talk is copied verbatim from his email to me. 2 Input from Cory Crowley 1. All horn lengths are acceptable. I can think of few to no limitations regarding fabrication or remote handling so I would say they do not need to change. Horn A Horn B Horn C 3 Input from Cory Crowley 2. I agree that Horn A will require a neck wall thicker than 2mm. 2.5mm is plausible, but I believe 3mm is what has been used on older designs due to the joule heating from the current pulse. The hot spot will likely be right before the transition to the D.S. cone/parabola, and analysis will be needed to specifically determine what the wall thickness should be. I would suggest using 3mm going Horn A forward to be conservative, as we are facing increased pressure for longer horn lifetimes as well. The rest of the I.C. (last 40” or so) should be OK with the 2mm wall. Horn A will likely require 2 welds and 2 spider supports. That’s not bad and Horn B shouldn’t add much material. Horn C 4 Input from Cory Crowley 3. Horn B is fine and likely requires 2 welds and only one spider support. Wall thickness should be a minimum of 3mm based on previous input for entire I.C., however I would step the neck (Section F3B) up to 4mm for fabrication concerns (it’s not Horn A joule or beam heating related). Horn B Horn C 5 Input from Cory Crowley 4. Horn C is fine and also likely requires 2 welds and only one spider support. I.C. Wall thickness would need to be around 4mm if any sort of circularity tolerance is to be held, but not sure how loose we can go. It would be good to know what type of circularity and concentricity requirements these horns will require: i.e.… NuMI like (tight), or BNB like (loose). The neck could probably stay at Horn A the 4mm thickness. (Note from Laura: 4 mm is actually what I used in the simulation for Horn C conductor thicknesses — Horn B everything else was 2 mm) Horn C 6 Input from Cory Crowley 5. Overall there are no showstoppers to fabrication of what is shown here. The only limitation I can see is the issue of nickel plating. We have heard from our vendor that the largest they can do is on object 3657mm long and 914mm in diameter. Nickel plating would add a several hundred thousand dollar expense to find a vendor Horn A and build new tanks to fit these horns, although that’s likely only a one time charge. None of the larger horns should cost much more than 100K each to plate after that. The push for nickel plating will always be there, so I think if there’s a way to get the largest diameter down to 914mm, we should do it, Horn B but only if there’s negligible effect on the physics. I can’t imagine you wanting to do that, so we might just have to eat the nickel plating cost. LBNF Optimized Horn & Module Design Update Cory Crowley / Nicola Solieri 24 August 2016 Current Optimization Studies & Status 8/24/2016 2 Cory F. Crowley | LBNF Mechanical Horn Models Update Optimization team has pushed forward a 3 horn design with an integrated NuMI like target inside of Horn A. Mechanical models have been generated. Preliminary analysis is underway. Schedule allows for second design iteration with detailed follow-up analysis. Incorporating input from numerous EE support personnel, physicists, & mechanical engineers. New revision underway & planning to be ready by fall. Target Integration with Horn 1 – Current Optimization Status 3 Cory F. Crowley | LBNF Mechanical Horn Models Update One piece, NuMI style target, cantilevered design + D.S. centering support. Mounted to U.S. face of Horn A with attachment plate fastened to inner conductor. Cantilevered design becomes a simply supported design once inserted into inner conductor. Follows MiniBooNE & T2K like target mounting scheme directly to horn. Z=0 occurs once the Horn A inner conductor neck reaches the nominal diameter (68mm). ZXF-5Q graphite fins start at Z=0 in the horn neck. Optimized target length of 2m. 8/24/2016 Target Integration with Horn 1 – Current Optimization Status 4 Cory F. Crowley | LBNF Mechanical Horn Models Update Not a final design; further iterations will follow. Analysis underway, target support tube and hardware are likely quite hot due to lack of cooling. Possible alternatives are simplified horn A with extended target to reach downstream end. Separate analysis by Laura Fields using a beryllium target supports this design philosophy. Should also work well for graphite target if Horn B can be extended. 8/24/2016 Revised Optimization Study 5 Cory F. Crowley | LBNF Mechanical Horn Models Update Horn B. Additional length added to make up for missing section of Horn A. Horn B becomes slightly more expensive. Should have net savings in operational costs from Horn A & Target replacements. Horn C. Changes shape, but not scale. Will not be cause of significant redesign due to new optimized Horn A & B geometry. Horn A. Horn A becomes a shorter cylindrical horn. Much cheaper and quicker to build, as no D.S. cone is present on inner conductor geometry. 8/24/2016 Simplified Horn A Mechanical Model & Target Interface 6 Cory F. Crowley | LBNF Mechanical Horn Models Update One piece, NuMI style target, simply supported design with D.S. helium cooled support tubes. Mounted to U.S. face of Horn A with attachment plate fastened to inner conductor & isolation bellows. Target fins are primarily cooled by twin water tubes. Target length is slightly increased to ~2.2 meters to reach D.S. support tube location. Inner conductor still cooled by water spray & air flow. 8/24/2016 Simplified Horn A Mechanical Model & Target Interface 7 Cory F. Crowley | LBNF Mechanical Horn Models Update Downstream Target Mounting Details. Target body & cooling lines are held by support rings inside grade 5 titanium tube. Helium flows through support tube from upstream end for heat removal. Target window is 3D printed with helium exhaust lines & swirl vanes to cool window. Design exists as a “single pass” helium loop; does not flow back towards upstream end like T2K. Helium exhaust tubes act as support for D.S. end of target. No longer a cantilevered design. 8/24/2016 Work Going Forward 8 Cory F. Source: indico Title: Update on the LBNF Flux Spectrometer LBNF Spectrometer: Architecture & DutyFactor Paul Lebrun (for the LBNF Spectrometer group.) ND/Fermilab July 6 2017 Spectrometer Architecture & Duty Factor 1 ### Outline - My list of task, very broad overview - - Architecture & DAQ rate, counting strategy: relations, trade-of, etc - - Progress on Duty Factor estimate, status of T1315. Status, start of discussion on what's next. July 6 2017 Spectrometer Architecture & Duty Factor 2 ### Task list, one perspective. - LBNF Spectrometer primary Beam line. - We don't have one. This is a problem. - Silver lining: we have a chance of building the way we want: Optics, beam spot size range, intensity range, instrumentation.. What are the specs? - - Architecture & DAQ rate, counting strategy: relations, trade-of, etc - - The spectrometer itself : aperture, components, technology - - Progress on Duty Factor estimate, status of T1315. Status, start of discussion on what's next. July 6 2017 Spectrometer Architecture & Duty Factor 3 ### Introduction: Motivation A direct measurement of the neutrino's progenitors, with the entire target and focusing system turned “on” implies a stringent limit of the maximum duty factor one can expect, 6x5e-5 /60 ~ 5e-6 . The first terms is the number of pulses per seconds the LBNF horn power supply can deliver during the M.I 4 seconds long spill, the 2nd term is the pulse duration where we have a useful focusing field, the last term is the M.I. fixed target repetition rate. If a statistical precision of ~ 1% for a cell which is 1% of the entire 5D phase space, we need 1e6 pions. Running at 20 MHz, it will take less than a day to the take the data, assuming that (I) we take one proton per 50 ns long “time bin” (ii) assume a factor of ~1/3 inefficiency due to empty time bins or more than one proton per time bin. Not bad, but.. July 6 2017 Spectrometer Architecture & Duty Factor 4 ### Introduction: Are we there yet? We need to repeat these measurements many time, to study the effect of horn & target misalignment, different targets, cooling water flow rate in the horn, proton beam parameters, etc, etc… There will be pressure to do these measurements quickly: we will be using spare equipment!. 20 MHz is achievable for the tracking system. (But costly, if large aperture). Is it for the RICH, muon/pion calorimeter? Is the Poisson counting efficiency fair? (T1315 studies) We could accumulate data over all the 100 cells of phase space at once, large aperture spectrometer We could relax the requirement of one proton per DAQ “time bin”, and accept overlapping events in the spectrometer. July 6 2017 Spectrometer Architecture & Duty Factor 5 ### Why one proton at a time? Because it simplifies the analysis, and thereby improves the estimate of our systematic uncertainty. Title: Spectrometer Discussion

# Run Duration? DAQ rates in the spectrometer a. Detector Aperture: Horn B downstream Outer Conductor radius is about 0.634 m. Thus, to get the spatial distribution of the flux, we need to cover ~ 1.26 m^2. Assuming the entrance aperture of the small aperture LBNF spectrometer (LBNFS) is 9 by 3 inches, at any relevant position, LBNFS will then cover only 1.07 % of the area where the flux needs to be measured. b. Pion rate out of the Horn, per incident proton on target (PoT): We assume one, for round number. We can quibble by a factor of a few here. (We need more G4LBNF/Spectrometer simulation, I'll try to get this done by end of calendar year...) c. Required Statistical precision: Let us take 1% relative yield measurement, so 10,000 pions. => 10,000 PoT per Horn setting, and spectrometer position. Or, one millions PoT to cover the entire 1.26 m^2 area. d. Duty factor to get one and only PoT per unit time: Assuming the primary proton intensity per 53 MHz rf bucket can be dial to the required value, with an avrage probability of 50% (the so-called MI slow spill duty factor). Poisson statistics (1 and only 1), gives us an factor of 0.36 => duty factor is ~1/6. e. Assume the spectrometer DAQ can run at 53 MHz. Assume that only 50 microseconds of the horn pulse duration can be used, to get the nominal field. (Again here we can quibble a bit, as the data at lower current would be of some use.) This means that we will have 2600 buckets per horn pulse. Using the above duty factor, we get down to 430 buckets per horn pulse. f. We now compute a run duration, where a run covers the entire area. We need one million/430 = 2325 horn pulses. Assuming that we have slow extraction at MI-10, we can get a spill, one horn pulse per spill, every two seconds. The run duration is then 4650 seconds, or about 2 hours, of beam time, assuming a ~ 80 % operational efficiency (including moving the spectrometer, every few hundred spill. However, if we run ex-situ, where we can get (at most) one slow spill every minute, but ~ 3 horn pulse per spill, one such run would last ~ 20 hours. We think these rates are acceptable, we will be able to take multiple such runs, modifying the alignment of the horns, target position, etc, if need be.

cost of spectrometer itself is expected to be dominated by the engineering and technical man power. A rough estimate of the cost is about $5M. The spectrometer will need its own support module, with a precision alignment mechanism. In addition, a precise positioning table will be required, to move the spectrometer across the full cross section of the horn. The cost has been roughly estimated to be $3.5 M. This takes the $2.34 M cost of the current Horn 1 module, adds $0.2 M for a precision positioning table, and assumes a 30% contingency. Should the spectrometer be installed downstream of Horn C, the ideal location for it, then we will have to extend the chase by approximately 4.5 m., and to commensurately reduce the length of the decay pipe. Since we do need crane coverage for the spectrometer module and the beam decay pipe window, this means we have to extend the building hosting the chase as well. Note also that a small increase ( 10%) of the radius of the beam window is probably warranted, to maintain the same physical aperture for the neutrino progenitors beam. Thus, the design of this beam window would have to revisited. The cost for installation downstream of Horn C has been roughly estimated to be $12.35 M. Should the spectrometer be installed between Horn B and Horn C, only very basic modifications to the target shield pile would be necessary; a basic cost estimate for those modifications, including a new carriage support system for the spectrometer module, is $0.5 M. Finally, careful studies of the radiological background coming from the target, the horns, and probably more importantly, the wall of the chase will have to be estimated for an installation in situ. Based on a gamma survey of NuMI Horn1 and MARS/Geant4 simulations, this background was found to be not negligible. While we anticipate using a fine grained tracking detector, more studies of the existing NuMI chase will need to be done to assess the feasibility of a measurement in situ. A high precision germanium detector is required for such studies; the cost of such instrumentation is of the order of tens of thousands of dollar, up to 90k, depending on the ease of use, portability, and DAQ interface capabilities. _Impact on the operational schedule._ For the in situ option, we anticipate to be able to install the spectrometer, after a week cooling down period, in a few days, including alignment. We anticipate a running time of 1 week to characterize the flux, followed by a few days for removal of the spectrometer and the installa- 8 ||In Situ(After Horn C)|In Situ(After Horn B)|Ex Situ| |---|---|---|---| |Spectrometer|5M|5M|5 M| |Spectrometer Module|3.5 M|3.5 M|-| |Removable Colimators|XXX|XXX|-| |Low Intensity Instrumentation|XXX|XXX|-| |Chase Modifications|12.4 M|0.5 M|-| |HpGe Detector|0.1 M|0.1 M|-| |Horn Power Supply|-|-|4.5 M| Table 1: Summary of costs of the three location options tion of the top of the chase shielding. During this time neutrino running at LBNF will not be possible. Assuming the the measurement is performed once per year at the end of the yearly maintenance shutdown, it will impact data taking by 6%.<sup>1</sup> ## **For the in situ option, the collaboration would like to understand any the potential impact on the overall LBNF schedule.** We do not expect any impact on the LBNF construction schedule, except for a very modest cost increase for the design of the spectrometer support module and positioning table. ## **Can the ex situ option provide the necessary constraints? What are the estimated additional systematic uncertainties in transferring the results to the actual beam configuration?** Flux uncertainties arise from two broad categories of sources: models of hadron production off the target and modeling of focusing parameters such as horn positions and currents. The ex situ option would measure the dominant of these two sources, hadroproduction models, while the in situ option would measure both. Uncertainties on the ex situ measurement would therefore be added in quadrature to the focusing uncertainties. Current estimates of focusing uncertainties are 2-5% depending on neutrino energy, and are largest at the falling edge of the focusing peak. Several of the focusing uncertainties, such as the 2% uncertainty > 1This estimate assumes 276 days of LBNF running per year, 10 days of spectometer installation and extraction, and 7 days of spectrometer running. 9 on proton counting, can likely be reduced with further study. Moreover, with an ex situ setup, the effect of misalignments could be directly studied, by e.g. shifting horns by small amounts and remeasuring the hadron flux. Since these uncertainties that are accessible only to the in situ option are not large, the major advantage of the in situ option is that we would measure the flux in the real beamline, and would be sensitive to large shifts in focusing parameters not covered by the focusing uncertainties, such as the 3 mm horn tilt recently discovered in the NuMI beamline, or degradation in target material (also seen in NuMI). Two additional difficulties with the in situ option have emerged through preliminary Monte Carlo simulations, and subsequent discussions: - The radiological background coming from the horns, particularly if the spectrometer is placed in between Horn B and and Horn C, is not negligible compared to the charged pion flux we are trying to measure. While still small - of the order of 1 count per 53 r.f. bucket, in a fine grained silicon strip detector, this background can not be ignored, as we still do not have a quantitative understanding of what will come out of the downstream end of the target support and from the wall of the chase. Any attempts at shielding the spectrometer from the walls of the chase is tricky, as it would require thick ( one foot) piece of clean steel be inserted in chase just downstream of the Horn B or C. - Shielding steel, completely unnecessary and unwanted in the normal intensity mode, could also become the source of secondaries. More importantly, the material in the yoke and pole tips of the small ( 10 cm by 20 cm) aperture permanent magnet inside the spectrometer will create very significant background in the downstream section of the silicon tracker. In the ex situ case, we would use a much larger, conventional magnet, such the old Jolly Green Giant or Rosie magnet installed at the Meson West beam line. This background would be present at the edge of the 60 cm aperture radius, where the particle flux from the target/horn is much reduced. For the ex situ option, numerous beamlines (Old KTev Hall, MIPP beam line, old NMCenter..) exist at Fermilab and could be refurbished to host the target, horns, and spectrometer. However, the cost of duplicating the horn power supply must be be factored in. Again, 10 there would be no design costs, as this would a replica of the horn power supply for the LBNF beam. The cost of the capacitors, transformers, etc, has been estimated to be 4.5 $M, including a 30% contingency. The impact on the operational schedule is quite different for the ex situ and in situ options. For the in situ option, we estimate spectrometer running would require roughly 6% of LBNF running time. The ex situ case would have a negligible impact on LBNF protons on target. ## **Conclusion** Given the difficulties of the in situ option, and the fact that the primary purpose of the in situ option would be to indentify catastrophic problems with the focusing system, the proponents of the spectrometer currently believe the best option to be installation of the full spectrometer in a ex situ configuration, provided it is accompanied by a program of work to ensure that focusing uncertainties are as small as possible and very well quantified. Ideally this would include a simplified detector, such as a sheet of silicon sensors in situ. Such a detector would mitigate many of the disadvantages of the in situ option, such as the need for low intensity running and a complex support module for the spectrometer, but would be able to identify and help diagnose signficant alignment issues. An identical detector could be installed in the ex situ replica, providing a quantitative validation that the ex situ measurement is valid for the the actual beam. ## **References** - [1] R. # Response to Collaboration Questions on LBNF Muon Monitoring Jeremy P. Lopez January 2017 ## **1 What are the physics requirements of the muon monitors on top of what the DUNE ND will provide?** The principal goal of the beam monitoring systems is to quickly provide feedback on the beam quality. Some expected pieces of the monitoring system include - primary beam monitors, which measure the proton beam position, direction, intensity, and width - muon monitors, which measure the intensity, spatial profile, and spectrum of muons downstream of the hadron absorber - the near neutrino detector, which can monitor the properties of the neutrino beam over time, such as the beam direction, intensity, and spectrum The most important advantage of muon monitors over the near detector is the speed at which feedback is given to the beam group. Typical muon systems in other beamlines use arrays of very simple detectors, and this simplicity allows for information to be extracted on a spill-by-spill basis on timescale of seconds. With muon fluxes of order 10<sup>7</sup> to 10<sup>8</sup> per square cm per spill, measurements in the muon alcove are limited only by detector systematics and the difficulty of interpreting how anomalous results in the muon alcove may affect the neutrino fluxes at the main detectors. Any feasible near detector design will require the detector to build statistics over some period of time and to process through a fairly involved processing chain, so feedback will be much slower. While the Near Detector is expected to have sensitivity to changes in the overall event rate, changes in the muon spectrum from charged current events, and changes in the beam direction, these measurements are likely to take quite some time and some, such as the beam direction, may be quite difficult. Muon monitoring provides a way to have sensitivity to beam changes on a spill-by-spill basis. Furthermore, because of the simplicity of typical muon systems in other beamlines, information may be obtained on a timescale of seconds, much faster than is likely feasible at a near detector. 1 Furthermore, in the event that a problem in the beam is found, it will be necessary to diagnose the origin of the problem in order to repair or realign the system. The different monitoring systems provide complementary information that will be invaluable in diagnosing problems. For example, a tilt of horn A of several millimeters will lead to an approximately 3% decrease in the ND neutrino spectrum at 5 GeV. Effective monitoring at the near detector will likely only use muon information, so it will take a great deal of time to measure the effect of this on the energy distribution of charged current _νµ_ events. Primary beam monitors will not be sensitive to problems in the horn systems, but there will be an approximately 2% decrease in the flux of 4 GeV muons found in the muon alcove. In order to determine the feasibility of making measurements with the muon monitor, we have conducted a number of Monte Carlo studies of realistic nonoptimal beam conditions such as horn misalignments, beam misalignments, and target density changes. In order to be sensitive to these realistic beam problems, we have determined that we will want to achieve: - 1 to 2 cm sensitivity to changes in the peak position of the muon position just downstream of the hadron absorber. - Approximately 1 to 2% sensitivity to the total signal in a 2 m by 2 m region centered at the nominal beam center - Approximately 2% sensitivity to changes in the muon spectrum at several muon energies (likely around 0, 5, and 8 GeV kinetic energy in the muon alcove - after losing approximately 6 GeV in the absorber). These numbers may be slightly different for threshold detectors. Given the large signal sizes and significant radiation damage expected to detectors, it will be challenging to achieve these goals. ## **2 Are the muon systems required to be able to provide information on the neutrino flux spectrum?** In order to achieve our monitoring goals, measurements that are sensitive to the muon flux will be necessary.Many of the beam conditions that we have simulated generate significant changes to the muon spectrum found downstream of the absorber. In some cases, this will be the most effective observation that we have. In the case of the target density showing an effective reduction of 5% due to aging effects or damage, we find that for a 90 GeV proton beam, the total signal of charged particles in an array of ionization detectors will have a negligible change, but the muon spectrum shows a large increase of higher energy muons and a small decrease in low energy muons. Spectral measurements will be particularly important if the final hadron absorber design resembles the current one, with a mask in the upstream part 2 and sculpted aluminum layers in the core. Such a design makes measurements of position of the muon peak intensity very difficult. ## **3 Are all the types of muon systems needed?** There is already agreement that an array of ionization detectors is necessary in nearly any scenario. Additionally arrays of ionization detectors can be used as threshold detectors to gain spectral information if there are several detector stations with different amounts of shielding. However, our simulations show that some beam conditions are best measured by considering a narrow range of muon energies rather than everything above some set energy threshold. This is not possible with ionization detectors but will be possible with Cherenkov detectors and with stopped muon counters. These two technologies make very different measurements. A Cherenkov detector has a threshold set by the gas pressure in its volume. The current design is a long tube with a mirror directing light to a PMT set far from beam center. The detector response will be quite complicated, as the particle momentum, position, and incident angle all affect the efficiency. However, a Cherenkov detector is very flexible. It can be used to scan over Cherenkov thresholds to build a spectrum and has an easily replaceable target mass. The signals are also very fast, making it useful for timing and studying the beam structure. Stopped muon counters, however, measure signals from muons stopped in the detector inner volume. In order to count these, the detector must look at delayed signals occurring well after the beam pulse is finished. This has the advantage that it will be insensitive to delta rays associated with the beam, but a stopped muon counter will not be capable of precise measurements of timing or beam substructure. The detector stops only low energy muons, so the detector response will be much simpler than for a Cherenkov detector. There is ongoing work studying both Cherenkov counters and stopped muon counters, and it is possible that there are other useful detector types that have not been considered. Because we do not have a good comparison of the performance of the different detector types, it is too early to determine exactly which technology or technologies will be used. In order to ensure that the measurements can be made, we recommend that several alcoves or detector stations be available. ## **4 How do the muon system requirements impact the hadron absorber design?** The current design of the hadron absorber includes several features not included in existing beamlines that will impact the muon signal. The spoiler, mask, and sculpting of the core aluminum pieces creates targets and decay volumes for hadrons impacting the absorber. This can generate muons that will reach the muon monitors that do not originate in the decay pipe. The mask and sculpting 3 also shape the signal. There is significantly less material near the beam center, increasing the muon flux at nominal beam center. Finally, the size of the core also limits how far from beam center useful measurements can be made, since aluminum is less dense than the iron used outside the core. To test how these features affect the signals, we have run simulations with both the standard absorber and with a highly simplified geometry, where (1) the mask and spoiler are replaced with air, (2) the sculpted regions are filled in with aluminum, and (3) the core is expanded. The possible problems with the current design are most evident in beam conditions where the muons are shifted away from the nominal beam center. What we see is that the features of the current design suppress the effects of the beam being directed slightly away from nominal beam center. If the beam is shifted laterally in _x_ on the target by 1 mm, the muon signal shifts by several cm in the _−x_ direction. For the simplified absorber, we see that a Gaussian fit to the muon profile in _x_ with _|y| <_ 7 _._ 5 cm yields a mean position of -1.6 cm for a fit to _x ∈_ [ _−_ 1 _m,_ 1 _m_ ] and -3.8 cm for a fit to _x ∈_ [ _−_ 0 _._ 5 _m,_ 0 _._ 5 _m_ ]. Looking at the same for the current absorber design, the mean positions are -0.47 cm and -0.89 cm, respectively. If we define a left-right asymmetry as ( _R − L_ ) _/total_ , the asymmetry for the simple absorber is _−_ 2 _._ 5% for _x ∈_ [-1 m, 1 m] and _−_ 1 _._ 9% for _x ∈_ [-1 m, 1 m]. For the standard absorber, these two asymmetries are -0.84% and -1.3%. Furthermore, we find that the peak signal position seen in the muon monitor remains at the nominal center for the current absorber even when the mean muon position is well away from the center. A direct measurement of the beam position will be very unreliable, so information will need to be extrapolated from parameters such as the asymmetry or skewness. Without the ability to reliably measure the beam position, the muon systems will then need to rely on the overall signal size and the flux shape to identify problems with the position. This will make it much more difficult to interpret the results. It will be much more important for the near detector to provide this measurement, which may impact the ND design requirements. In order to measure the spatial distribution, we would want the hadron absorber to be as uniform as possible near the beam center. As we are focusing on sensitivity to shifts in the beam position of several cm, we do not expect to need to make measurements much beyond approximately 1 m from nominal beam center. In our simulations, we see that some parameters such as asymmetries are enhanced within 1 m of beam center compared to 0.5 m from beam center, so we would ideally have an approximately constant amount of material in the hadron absorber within 1 m or so from beam center. This would allow us to clearly see the effects of the beam shifting from nominal beam center by small amounts. 4 ## **5 How often do we think a near detector could provide monitoring feedback?** While the near detector group has not done extensive work yet on the topic of monitoring, there are some preliminary thoughts on how this might be done. For the purposes of monitoring the beam, charged-current _νµ_ events will give the highest statistics. The analysis would use events in the fiducial volume, but could be on any material. In the fine grained tracker (FGT) design, there are approximately 3 _×_ 10<sup>4</sup> CC events per day at a beam power of 1 MW. During normal running, this should be sufficient to achieve a 1% uncertainty on the POT-normalized signal (assuming negligible POT counting systematics) for each day.The time needed to gather sufficient statistics for a spectrum measurement will depend on the desired binning. Around the peak (around 1 to 5 GeV, there should be sufficient statistics to achieve a 1% uncertainty roughly every week with 0.5 GeV bins (assuming high efficiency & purity) At higher and lower energies,

# Response to Collaboration Questions on LBNF Muon Monitoring Jeremy P. Lopez January 2017 ## **1 What are the physics requirements of the muon monitors on top of what the DUNE ND will provide?** The principal goal of the beam monitoring systems is to quickly provide feedback on the beam quality. Some expected pieces of the monitoring system include - primary beam monitors, which measure the proton beam position, direction, intensity, and width - muon monitors, which measure the intensity, spatial profile, and spectrum of muons downstream of the hadron absorber - the near neutrino detector, which can monitor the properties of the neutrino beam over time, such as the beam direction, intensity, and spectrum The most important advantage of muon monitors over the near detector is the speed at which feedback is given to the beam group. Typical muon systems in other beamlines use arrays of very simple detectors, and this simplicity allows for information to be extracted on a spill-by-spill basis on timescale of seconds. With muon fluxes of order 10<sup>7</sup> to 10<sup>8</sup> per square cm per spill, measurements in the muon alcove are limited only by detector systematics and the difficulty of interpreting how anomalous results in the muon alcove may affect the neutrino fluxes at the main detectors. Any feasible near detector design will require the detector to build statistics over some period of time and to process through a fairly involved processing chain, so feedback will be much slower. While the Near Detector is expected to have sensitivity to changes in the overall event rate, changes in the muon spectrum from charged current events, and changes in the beam direction, these measurements are likely to take quite some time and some, such as the beam direction, may be quite difficult. Muon monitoring provides a way to have sensitivity to beam changes on a spill-by-spill basis. Furthermore, because of the simplicity of typical muon systems in other beamlines, information may be obtained on a timescale of seconds, much faster than is likely feasible at a near detector. 1 Furthermore, in the event that a problem in the beam is found, it will be necessary to diagnose the origin of the problem in order to repair or realign the system. The different monitoring systems provide complementary information that will be invaluable in diagnosing problems. For example, a tilt of horn A of several millimeters will lead to an approximately 3% decrease in the ND neutrino spectrum at 5 GeV. Effective monitoring at the near detector will likely only use muon information, so it will take a great deal of time to measure the effect of this on the energy distribution of charged current _νµ_ events. Primary beam monitors will not be sensitive to problems in the horn systems, but there will be an approximately 2% decrease in the flux of 4 GeV muons found in the muon alcove. In order to determine the feasibility of making measurements with the muon monitor, we have conducted a number of Monte Carlo studies of realistic nonoptimal beam conditions such as horn misalignments, beam misalignments, and target density changes. In order to be sensitive to these realistic beam problems, we have determined that we will want to achieve: - 1 to 2 cm sensitivity to changes in the peak position of the muon position just downstream of the hadron absorber. - Approximately 1 to 2% sensitivity to the total signal in a 2 m by 2 m region centered at the nominal beam center - Approximately 2% sensitivity to changes in the muon spectrum at several muon energies (likely around 0, 5, and 8 GeV kinetic energy in the muon alcove - after losing approximately 6 GeV in the absorber). These numbers may be slightly different for threshold detectors. Given the large signal sizes and significant radiation damage expected to detectors, it will be challenging to achieve these goals. ## **2 Are the muon systems required to be able to provide information on the neutrino flux spectrum?** In order to achieve our monitoring goals, measurements that are sensitive to the muon flux will be necessary.Many of the beam conditions that we have simulated generate significant changes to the muon spectrum found downstream of the absorber. In some cases, this will be the most effective observation that we have. In the case of the target density showing an effective reduction of 5% due to aging effects or damage, we find that for a 90 GeV proton beam, the total signal of charged particles in an array of ionization detectors will have a negligible change, but the muon spectrum shows a large increase of higher energy muons and a small decrease in low energy muons. Spectral measurements will be particularly important if the final hadron absorber design resembles the current one, with a mask in the upstream part 2 and sculpted aluminum layers in the core. Such a design makes measurements of position of the muon peak intensity very difficult. ## **3 Are all the types of muon systems needed?** There is already agreement that an array of ionization detectors is necessary in nearly any scenario. Additionally arrays of ionization detectors can be used as threshold detectors to gain spectral information if there are several detector stations with different amounts of shielding. However, our simulations show that some beam conditions are best measured by considering a narrow range of muon energies rather than everything above some set energy threshold. This is not possible with ionization detectors but will be possible with Cherenkov detectors and with stopped muon counters. These two technologies make very different measurements. A Cherenkov detector has a threshold set by the gas pressure in its volume. The current design is a long tube with a mirror directing light to a PMT set far from beam center. The detector response will be quite complicated, as the particle momentum, position, and incident angle all affect the efficiency. However, a Cherenkov detector is very flexible. It can be used to scan over Cherenkov thresholds to build a spectrum and has an easily replaceable target mass. The signals are also very fast, making it useful for timing and studying the beam structure. Stopped muon counters, however, measure signals from muons stopped in the detector inner volume. In order to count these, the detector must look at delayed signals occurring well after the beam pulse is finished. This has the advantage that it will be insensitive to delta rays associated with the beam, but a stopped muon counter will not be capable of precise measurements of timing or beam substructure. The detector stops only low energy muons, so the detector response will be much simpler than for a Cherenkov detector. There is ongoing work studying both Cherenkov counters and stopped muon counters, and it is possible that there are other useful detector types that have not been considered. Because we do not have a good comparison of the performance of the different detector types, it is too early to determine exactly which technology or technologies will be used. In order to ensure that the measurements can be made, we recommend that several alcoves or detector stations be available. ## **4 How do the muon system requirements impact the hadron absorber design?** The current design of the hadron absorber includes several features not included in existing beamlines that will impact the muon signal. The spoiler, mask, and sculpting of the core aluminum pieces creates targets and decay volumes for hadrons impacting the absorber. This can generate muons that will reach the muon monitors that do not originate in the decay pipe. The mask and sculpting 3 also shape the signal. There is significantly less material near the beam center, increasing the muon flux at nominal beam center. Finally, the size of the core also limits how far from beam center useful measurements can be made, since aluminum is less dense than the iron used outside the core. To test how these features affect the signals, we have run simulations with both the standard absorber and with a highly simplified geometry, where (1) the mask and spoiler are replaced with air, (2) the sculpted regions are filled in with aluminum, and (3) the core is expanded. The possible problems with the current design are most evident in beam conditions where the muons are shifted away from the nominal beam center. What we see is that the features of the current design suppress the effects of the beam being directed slightly away from nominal beam center. If the beam is shifted laterally in _x_ on the target by 1 mm, the muon signal shifts by several cm in the _−x_ direction. For the simplified absorber, we see that a Gaussian fit to the muon profile in _x_ with _|y| <_ 7 _._ 5 cm yields a mean position of -1.6 cm for a fit to _x ∈_ [ _−_ 1 _m,_ 1 _m_ ] and -3.8 cm for a fit to _x ∈_ [ _−_ 0 _._ 5 _m,_ 0 _._ 5 _m_ ]. Looking at the same for the current absorber design, the mean positions are -0.47 cm and -0.89 cm, respectively. If we define a left-right asymmetry as ( _R − L_ ) _/total_ , the asymmetry for the simple absorber is _−_ 2 _._ 5% for _x ∈_ [-1 m, 1 m] and _−_ 1 _._ 9% for _x ∈_ [-1 m, 1 m]. For the standard absorber, these two asymmetries are -0.84% and -1.3%. Furthermore, we find that the peak signal position seen in the muon monitor remains at the nominal center for the current absorber even when the mean muon position is well away from the center. A direct measurement of the beam position will be very unreliable, so information will need to be extrapolated from parameters such as the asymmetry or skewness. Without the ability to reliably measure the beam position, the muon systems will then need to rely on the overall signal size and the flux shape to identify problems with the position. This will make it much more difficult to interpret the results. It will be much more important for the near detector to provide this measurement, which may impact the ND design requirements. In order to measure the spatial distribution, we would want the hadron absorber to be as uniform as possible near the beam center. As we are focusing on sensitivity to shifts in the beam position of several cm, we do not expect to need to make measurements much beyond approximately 1 m from nominal beam center. In our simulations, we see that some parameters such as asymmetries are enhanced within 1 m of beam center compared to 0.5 m from beam center, so we would ideally have an approximately constant amount of material in the hadron absorber within 1 m or so from beam center. This would allow us to clearly see the effects of the beam shifting from nominal beam center by small amounts. 4 ## **5 How often do we think a near detector could provide monitoring feedback?** While the near detector group has not done extensive work yet on the topic of monitoring, there are some preliminary thoughts on how this might be done. For the purposes of monitoring the beam, charged-current _νµ_ events will give the highest statistics. The analysis would use events in the fiducial volume, but could be on any material. In the fine grained tracker (FGT) design, there are approximately 3 _×_ 10<sup>4</sup> CC events per day at a beam power of 1 MW. During normal running, this should be sufficient to achieve a 1% uncertainty on the POT-normalized signal (assuming negligible POT counting systematics) for each day.The time needed to gather sufficient statistics for a spectrum measurement will depend on the desired binning. Around the peak (around 1 to 5 GeV, there should be sufficient statistics to achieve a 1% uncertainty roughly every week with 0.5 GeV bins (assuming high efficiency & purity) At higher and lower energies,

In addition, look at the primary proton halo missing the target, or part of the target. - ✔ Status : Preliminary results. - ✔ Next: ? To be discussed.. Needs more realistic beam profile characteristics and target witdth, options and so forth. August 11 2016 Annular Beam for LBNF, first glance 2 ## Beam Profile function. - ✔ E­mail from Bob Zwaska, 07/14/2016 Hi Paul, The equation for the annular gaussian is: - f(r; R, sigma) = d^2N/drdTheta - = 1/(2*pi*sigma^2) * exp[(­r^2­R^2)/(2*sigma^2)] * I0(rR/sigma^2) Here you take an incident gaussian beam with rms sigma, and average it over a raster radius of R. So, for a beam configuration R and sigma are constant, r is the radial coordinate. There is no angular dependence, though this is an areal density. I0 is the modified Bessel function of the first kind. Source: indico Title: DUNE Hadron Production Flux Uncertainties ## PPFX FOR DUNE Amit Bashyal Oregon State University 1 ### INTRODUCTION - My Goals: - Improve DUNE flux prediction using external hadron production data - Obtain first estimate of DUNE’s hadron production flux uncertainties - Obtain an overall interaction map of all particles and sort out the interaction covered and not covered by current Thin Target Experiment - Method: - Use PPFX, a package developed by Leo Aliaga for MINERvA with successful results (see Leo’s Thesis Talk : **_Neutrino Flux Prediction for the NuMI Beamline_** ) 2 ### Overview of PPFX - Uses Dk2nu and dkmeta objects made by g4lbnf for each neutrino event as inputs - Identifies events covered by current thin target experiments with appropriate scaling of energy - Varies cross sections randomly within errors to propagate hadron production uncertainties to neutrino flux - Also can apply weight to correct simulation to match HP data - We are not doing this yet (it will require running a bunch of thin target simulations) Run Mode

Title: DPF Discussion

PPFX for DUNE PPFX for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment(DUNE) is a project that aims to improve the prediction of DUNE's flux and the estimation of hadron production uncertainties using hadron production data. Currently, the DUNE flux relies on GEANT4 based physics model which large uncertainties from hadronic interactions in the beamline. We used PPFX, a package developed by the MINERvA experiment at Fermilab to add improved hadronic interaction data to the GEANT4 based flux prediction. We use PPFX to study the predicted flux uncertainties for several candidate beamline designs. In this talk, I will discuss the process of applying the PPFX package to DUNE's flux and the resulting flux uncertainties.

However, it is likely that ND monitoring will require a fast processing chain that does not use full calibration information, so only the muon kinematics may be available. The monitoring process may not be able to use a reconstructed neutrino energy, so exact numbers will depend on the details of the analysis. One strategy to measure the direction of the beam would be to measure the spatial profile of CC events. In the FGT, the neutrino flux decreases only by approximately 4% from the center to the edge of fiducial volume. Measuring this will require a large data sample, so we might expect to have sufficient statistics on roughly the same time scale as an energy distribution measurement. If we wish to speed up this process, a detector similar to T2K’s INGRID could be used. Such a detector would require modules with layers of scintillator bars with heavy target layers mixed in. This would give a large fiducial mass and a very stable detector for monitoring, but the transverse size would need to be substantially larger than the DUNE ND. Thus, depending on the measurement, monitoring feedback may require collecting statistics on the timescale of approximately one day to several weeks. The processing chain will add additional time to this. If it is possible to use rock muons, or calorimeter and magnet interactions, these timescales could be reduced significantly. ## **6 Additional Thoughts** The LBNF beamline is expected to provide a neutrino beam for many years. Because beamline needs may change from what is planned at the moment, it is important for the design to be flexible. For example, at some point, it may be desired to run at a higher energy mode or with a power higher than currently expected. Monitoring needs may change, and we do not want beam monitoring to limit future analyses or even other experiments. The multiple muon alcoves at NuMI have proven to be extremely useful, as there is sufficient space to 5 test new detectors for other experiments (such as LBNF). If at some point it turns out that the flux becomes too high, it will be important to have space in LBNF to run with a reduced flux or to test new prototypes. The facilities and infrastructure for LBNF muon monitoring needs to consider possible future needs both at LBNF and even for the community beyond LBNF and DUNE. ## **7 Conclusions** Using simulations based on the 3-horn optimized beamline described in the BOTF report, and using a 90 GeV proton beam, a 10 mm wide ( _x_ ) and 2-m long NuMI-like target composed of rectangular fins, we have been able to define a number of high level physics requirements on the muon monitoring systems. From this work, we can answer the questions from the greater collaboration on muon monitors: - What can muon monitoring provide in addition to the near detector? The muon monitors can provide spill-by-spill monitoring of beam conditions and particularly of any problems with the target, horn A, and possibly horn B. Muon monitors are systematics limited rather than statistics limited. Monitors will likely be insensitive to realistic misalignments of horn C. These measurements are also complementary. Near detector and muon alcove monitoring will provide more information to diagnose any problems. However, in order to make use of these detectors, we need to ensure that there are sufficient personnel to operate the monitor and analyze its data. - Is information about the neutrino spectrum necessary? - For monitoring, setting constraints on the neutrino spectrum is not necessary. However, measurements of the muon spectrum in the muon alcove(s) will be very important. Large changes in the muon spectrum are expected for some adverse beam conditions, such as for target degredation. - Are all 3 systems (ionization detectors, Cherenkov detectors, and stopped muon counters) necessary? Ionization counters are very important and are used in existing beamlines. Simulations show that measurements at specific energies (particularly around 4-5 GeV) have a great deal of sensitivity to many beamline problems. This would require at least one other type of detector. Detector R&D is ongoing, so we do not have a good idea yet if Cherenkov detectors, stopped muon counters, or some combination of both is best. However, we need to ensure that the infrastructure is available to perform these measurements. - How do muon systems impact the hadron absorber design? The current hadron absorber design heavily biases muon signals toward the nominal beam center. This makes one of the standard muon monitoring 6 measurements, the beam position, very difficult to measure at LBNF. The near detector may be able to measure this on the timescale of a week or so, but fast monitoring will be impossible there. Spectral information can help mitigate this, but has not typically been done at existing beamlines. For optimal muon monitoring, we would want the absorber to be as uniform as possible withing approximately 1 m from nominal beam center. - On what time scale do we expect the near detector to be able to provide useful monitoring feedback? Ideally, the ND could monitor the total flux at the 1% level roughly every day, and the flux shape around the peak roughly every week (and several weeks for higher energies). This will depend on the final ND design and on how fast a monitoring processing chain might take to complete. The beam position/direction may be more complicated but could potentially be measured every week or so. These timescales might be reduced if calorimeter, magnet, and/or rock muons can be considered. An INGRIDlike modular neutrino monitor (in addition to the ND) could likely perform many of these measurements much faster and more reliably. 7

Source: indico Title: Muon Monitor & Absorber Practice Talks Physics Goals of DUNE/LBNF Muon Monitoring Systems Jeremy Lopez January 16, 2017 ### **Abstract** This tech note details simulation studies using G4LBNF to determine the physics potential of an idealized array of ionization detectors placed just downstream of the hadron absorber. This note will focus on the physics goals of the muon systems for monitoring the beam. We conclude that we will want to be sensitive to changes in the muon signals including: (1) the beam position moving by 1-2 cm, (2) the total muon signal within a 2 m x 2 m square around beam center changing by 1-2%, (3) the flux around 5 GeV changing by 2%, and (4) the flux around 7 or more GeV changing by 4% or so. We also conclude that measuring beam position changes reliably will be difficult with the reference absorber due to shaping of the signal due to the absorber design. # **Contents** |**1**|**Introduction**|**2**| |---|---|---| |**2**|**Simulations**|**3**| |**3**|**Nominal Beam Conditions**|**4**| |**4**|**Beam Shift in X**|**10**| |**5**|**Beam Shift in Y**|**17**| |**6**|**Reduction in Beam Width**|**24**| |**7**|**Horn Current Reduction**|**31**| |**8**|**Target Density Reduction**|**38**| |**9**|**Horn A Shift in X**|**45**| |**10**|**Horn A Shift in Y**|**52**| 1 |**11 Horn A Tilt in X**|**59**| |---|---| |**12 Horn A Tilt in Y**|**66**| |**13 Horn B Shift in X**|**73**| |**14 Horn B Shift in Y**|**79**| |**15 Summary and Conclusions**|**85**| |15.1 Summary of Observables to Monitor Different Beam Conditions .|85| |15.2 Physics Recommendations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .|86| |15.3 Conclusions . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .|87| # **1 Introduction** In several existing neutrino beamlines, detectors placed just downstream of the hadron absorber are able to monitor beam conditions by measuring muons with enough energy to pass through the entire absorber. In the beamline, most muons will be created by pion decay in the decay pipe, π + → µ + + νµ (1)
and some are also created by kaon decay, K + → µ + + νµ. (2)
The muons found in an alcove downstream of the absorber are, therefore, produced in the same decays that produce the neutrinos comprising most of the flux at the neutrino detectors. Furthermore, muon decays can also produce electron neutrinos that act as backgrounds in the oscillation analysis. By measuring the muons in the alcove, one can obtain information about things such as the beam intensity, direction, and width. To monitor muons, several types of measurements may be possible. The standard method for muon monitoring is to place a two-dimensional array of ionization detectors (typically gas ion chambers, but solid state devices may be used as well) just downstream of the absorber. The detectors in this array sample the distribution of charged particles at known positions with respect to the nominal beam center. The ionization detector array is simple and measures the beam profile, allowing us to extract the signal intensity and shape. Ionization detectors are unable to distinguish between different types of charged particles and are unable to distinguish between minimum ionizing particles (for muons, _Ekin >_ 100 MeV). As a result, ionization detectors cannot distinguish between muons and other particles such as electrons, complicating any attempts at determining the absolute muon flux, and also cannot typically monitor changes in the spectrum if the overall rate stays roughly constant. The muon spectrum, however, does potentially contain a great deal of useful information, and 2 detectors that are sensitive to the muon energy can also be used for monitoring. Dedicated spectral measurements have not generally been done at previous beamlines, although the NuMI beamline has several muon alcoves, which use ionization detectors to measure the flux for several different energy distributions of muons from the same beam. Current plans for muon monitoring systems at LBNF envision using both ionization detectors and detectors sensitive to the energy distribution (such as threshold Cherenkov detectors and stopped muon counters). This note details a number of simulations done to estimate the requirements needed in order to set useful physics constraints on the LBNF neutrino flux. These requirements can then be used to evaluate different possible detector technologies and to determine the practical requirements on detector performance needed to reach our goals. Muon monitoring may also play an important role in monitoring the safety of the facility. This will be much less strict than monitoring for setting physics requirements, so we will not address that in detail here. # **2 Simulations** This note makes use of simulations using G4LBNF. Each data set generates 109 protons on target at an energy of 90 GeV with a beam width of 1.62 mm. The simulations use the 3-horn optimized beamline recommendations from the Beam Optimization Task Force report. The simulations use a NuMI-style target composed of rectangular fins of graphite. The target is 2 m long and the fins are set to be 10 cm in width along the shorter ( _x_ ) dimension. Upstream of the target is a 1.5 m baffle with an inner diameter of 17 mm. The reference LBNF beamline uses a large “sculpted” absorber with many different features. The absorber consists largely of an aluminum core with an outer colume of iron and approximately 1 m of concrete downstream of the aluminum and iron layers. The considerable amount of energy that might be dumped into the absorber, particularly in the CDR reference design, requires that the energy be spread out over as large a volume as feasible. As a result, there are several important features in the absorber, including, 1. An aluminum spoiler at the upstream end of the absorber to help spread out the beam 2. A mask made of aluminum layers with pieces cut out to give particles room to spread out after interacting with the spoiler 3. “Sculpting” of the aluminum core layers, where some material is cut out of the center of each layer to prevent too much energy loss in any one solid volume. 4. Fairly small size of the aluminum core layers, substantially smaller than the decay pipe radius. 3 These features are expected to shape the muon profile in various ways, so that muon profile measured in the alcove does not perfectly represent the muon profile entering the absorber. In order to test the effects of this, the simulations are also done with a greatly simplified absorber. Downstream of the hadron absorber is a large air volume representing the muon alcove. We place a tracking volume in the alcove, tilted at the same angle as the decay pipe so that the tracking volume is perpendicular to the nominal beam direction. When a particle enters the volume, it is recorded into a file, along with relevant tracking information such as the position, energy, particle type, direction, and other things. To estimate the energy loss, the energy loss due to ionization and the step length are save for all steps where at least one end is located in the tracking volume. These are then used to estimate the track _dE/dx_ . The energy deposition for each track is then taken to be: ∆ E = dE dx L cos θ (3)
where _L_ is the width of the tracking volume and cos _θ_ is the angle with respect to the nominal beam direction. If ∆ _E_ is greater than the total track kinetic energy _Ekin_ then ∆ _E_ = _Ekin_ . Furthermore, all the energy deposition from a single track is added at the same position. # **3 Nominal Beam Conditions** In normal beam conditions, we will generally expect a muon signal that is peaked at nominal beam center and symmetric in both _x_ and _y_ . The signals will not in general show rotational symmetry. Figure 1 shows the two-dimensional distribution that we might expect to see in an array of ionization detectors just downstream of the absorber. A realistic array will sample this distribution at intervals of approximately 25 cm or so. Figure 2 shows “slices” of the twodimensional distributions. These slices look at the contributions from particles with _|x| <_ 7 _._ 5 cm for the _y_ slice and _|y| <_ 7 _._ 5 cm for the _x_ slice. These slices are much more useful in visualizing the differences between the nominal beam and the different beam alterations we will discuss later in this note. Figure 3 shows the two-dimensional distribution for the “simplified” absorber and 4 shows the _x_ and _y_ slices for that absorber model. Comparing the two absorber models, we clearly see the effects of shaping from the absorber design. While the simplified design shows a wide distribution that is approximately Gaussian within approximately 60 cm of beam center, the nominal design is a much narrower distribution with a much sharper peak. We will use some basic test statistics to numerically consider the kinds of measurements that might be useful. These include: the integral for the twodimensional distribution looking at a square with 5-cm bins and bin centers between -1 m and +1 m from beam center, the mean and RMS of the profiles between -1 m and +1m from beam center, the mean and standard deviation 4 for Gaussian fits of the profiles between -1 m and +1m, and the mean and standard deviation for Gaussian fits of the profiles between -50 cm and +50 cm. Overview and Update on Muon Monitors Jeremy Lopez University of Colorado 15 October 2015 C Muon Monitors Working Group • Conveners: Geoff Mills, Jeremy Lopez • Goals: 1) Evaluate requirements for neutrino beam monitoring and potential for neutrino flux, determine any limitations from the absorber design 2) Document the current design and ongoing work in detector development and tests 3) Simulate the response in the LBNF beamline and evaluate the muon monitoring system’s performance Personnel Include: Jan Boissevain, Charles Lane, Zachary Liptak, Jeremy Lopez, Alysia Marino, Geoff Mills, Eric Zimmerman, CU Undergrads: Branton Demoss, Kerrie Dochen, Andrew Loeliger, Peter Madigan 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 2 Primary Goals of Muon Monitors 1) Determine absolute muon flux > 6 GeV (nu energy > 1.6 GeV) to 5% accuracy 2) Measure beam direction to within 0.2 mrad (i.e. beam position downstream of absorber to within 5 cm) *DUNE CDR Vol. 4 Sec. 7.5 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 3 Overview of Muon Monitors Three Detector Types:Absorber 1) Ionization Counters Stopped Muon • Measure Beam Position Cherenkov Counters Counters • Get total flux of charged particles exiting the absorber 2) Cherenkov Counters • Scan over different pressures/detector angles to build muon flux from threshold Vbeam center measurements lonization Counters 3) Stopped Muon Counters • Select flux at different positions/energies 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 4 Ionization Counters Likely Three Main Options: Diamonds, Silicon, Gas Ionization Counters Diamond Silicon Gas Pros: Fast signals, Cheap, easy to use Proven technology, more rad hard than Si rad hard (can replace gas), likely cheap Cons: $$$, not much Not very rad hard: Sensitive to ambient of a track record so may degrade quickly, pressure, slow signal far, less signal (high cost of replacement development band gap), lifetime could add up if they unknown need to be replaced often 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 5 Current Ionization Counter Testing Hardware D2, D3 • Have borrowed 3 pCVD diamond detectors previously used in CNGS beamline, installed in NuMI muon alcove 2 • Have purchased some bare diamonds & a silicon photodiode at CU for testing and evaluation D1 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 6 Some NuMI Results Horn On Horn Off Average of Many Pulses 1 Point = Integral of One RF Bucket Best Fits Hypothesis: Muon signal follows: 1) RWM (proton signal) 2) Muon decay in vacuum 3) Muon decay/capture in iron Works surprisingly well, but not perfect 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 7 Cherenkov Detector Prototype Prototype installed in NuMI muon alcove 2 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 8 Qualitative Data/MC Comparison NuMI Data, G. Mills Simulation, P. Madigan Scan over different pressures and yaws Get same qualitative features Need to see how well we really understand the detector response in the NuMI beam 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 9 More NuMI Data Otherwise, signal very stable Signal Drops by ~1% over ~10 days. Why? 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 10 Stopped Muon Counters Liquid scintillator outer veto Inner detector measures Cherenkov radiation in non-scintillating mineral oil Commissioning an initial prototype at CU. Will look at cosmics before moving detector to FNAL Gated base being designed at Drexel (needed to use in the NuMI beamline) 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 11 Simulation Work • Using G4LBNE to determine gating requirements for stopped muon detectors and getting muon energy spectrum • Simulating Cherenkov detector response to try to understand scans over detector parameters • Starting to work on simulating NuMI flux in alcove 2 to better understand diamond detectors 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 12 There’s Still More • Muon flux originating in absorber not necessarily trivially small (see talk by P. Lebrun during the Sept. meeting) • Could complicate extrapolation of muon flux to neutrino flux • Maybe would also affect the beam direction measurement • Need full simulation of flux seen by the muon detectors to see how the beamline design affects this • Could also probably use simulated estimate of lifetime of solid state detectors (although an actual measurement is better) 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 13 Conclusions and Outlook • Muon monitoring detector development is making steady progress • One Cherenkov detector prototype and 3 diamond detectors installed in NuMI muon alcove 2 • One stopped muon counter prototype built, will start testing in Boulder soon before moving to the NuMI beamline • Biggest questions with hardware are how long the detectors will last without repairs/replacement and how stable they are in an actual beam • Also working on various simulations both to support the tests in the NuMI beamline and to estimate what is expected in LBNF • Big question here is probably how the absorber design affects the muon measurements 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 14

Source: indico Title: MARS15 Studies of Impact of Target/Horn Optimization on the Hadron Absorber and Particle Spectra - Update **_Fermilab_** ###### **_Accelerator Physics Center_** **MARS15 Studies of Impact of Target/Horn Optimization on the Hadron Absorber and Particle Spectra - Update** S. Striganov DUNE Accelerator and Beam Interface Meeting Fermilab May 5, 2016 ##### Introduction Target collimator has been designed to minimize interaction with proton beam: baffle radius ~ 5 sigma beam. Target horizontal size is ~ 3 sigma beam. About 0.3% of primary beam come through baffle, does not interact with target and creates large density of energy deposition in absorber. We need to consider complicated absorber. Long target with same transverse dimensions reduces total energy deposition in absorber, but does not decrease maximal energy deposition, because same number of primary protons misses target. It is possible radically reduce maximal energy deposition with small wings added to long target. Last upgrades - bug in calculation of nominal case was fixed and neutrino spectra calculation algorithm was improved to get better statistical accuracy. Wings reduce muon neutrino flux less than few percent in region of interest (<5 GeV) 25 # Conclusions Using optimized (long) target with 12-48 cm wings reduces maximal energy deposition in LBNF absorber 6-20 times. It is possible to consider simple absorber without spoiler and sculpted blocks for optimized setup. Such simple absorber can survive even for significantly increased beam power beyond 2.4 MW. Muon neutrino flux decreases a few percent for target with 48 cm wings and less than one percent with 24 cm wings for neutrino energies important for LBNF/DUNE experiment. High energy muon flux after fourth alcove is reduced by factor of 2-3 for long target setup. It significantly decreases ground water activation in rock after absorber. 26 26 Backup

Title: Thoughts and questions about the Absorber

Thoughts and questions on the Absorber Alberto Marchionni Fermilab The reference design quite a lot of work has gone into the design of an Al absorber that could work with a NuMI-like target and focusing system in addition to normal operation, accidents conditions have been considered where the full intensity proton beam could directly hit the absorber. beam is misdirected through the space between the target and the baffle the target “disappers” (it may bend or crack and rest over the horn inner conductor) The engineering analysis has shown that a maximum of 2 full beam pulses would be acceptable Already at the time of the absorber review Jim Hylen introduced the idea of a target with wings to mitigate the consequences of an accident condition Questions on the Absorber reference design Sam Childress is questioning that we would be able to safely stop the beam in just 2 pulses. One of the criteria to stop the beam is to use the muon monitor signal; when the beam hits directly the absorber, the muon production is strongly reduced, and this is something that we observe and measure in NuMI. But LBNF is not the same as NuMI. For LBNF we need to simulate the accident condition and the "absence" of muons including the spoiler, the sculpted absorber (NUMI has a compact absorber) and the wings to the target. The spoiler and wings would act like a target, and generate some pions decaying to muons. We cannot rely on NuMI, we need a realistic simulation of the accident condition for LBNF. The optimized focusing configuration would definitely help here. How to make a protection system based on the muon signal fail-safe, and without excessive fake trips? Impact of optimized focusing design on Absorber (I) The hadron flux can be reduced by an order of magnitude or more in all regions of the hadron absorber except the very center, where flux is dominated by beam halo that does not impinge on the target. This halo can be substantially reduced by adding ”wings” to the upstream end of the target Beam Task Force Optimization Interim Report S. Striganov Impact of optimized focusing design on Absorber (II) S. Striganov The combination of increased target length and wings would allow considerable simplification of the current hadron absorber design. This is very desirable from a physics point of view, as the sculpting of the current absorber design introduces significant backgrounds to the muon detectors that will both monitor the neutrino beam and constrain models of the neutrino flux. Possibility to reduce the cost of the absorber and of the 30 m long muon shielding (steel) downstream of the absorber The Muon Monitor group is still working on the evaluation of the Muon Monitors system requirements for neutrino beam monitoring and for its potential use for neutrino flux prediction Removal of the spoiler and the sculpting will not satisfy the requirements for the accident conditions Addition of a graphite section? Sam Childress has been advocating an initial section of graphite to help in case of accident conditions Graphite dumps have been safely used as accelerator dumps since a long time. Nikolai Mokhov designed a graphite dump for the Tevatron, the Main Injector has a graphite dump, the LHC has a graphite dump. On the neutrino side, CNGS and T2K have been/are using graphite dumps. One of the reason a graphite dump has not been considered for LBNF is a possible radiation damage of the graphite. Every single pulse, in the NuMI-like reference design, about 15% of the protons are dumped in the dump (about 350 kW deposited just by the protons when running at 2.4 MW). This is clearly a different operation from dumps used as aborts in accelerator machines. The optimized design, with longer targets and wings, would reduce the power in the dump by the residual protons by at least a factor ~3, and the maximum energy density by a factor ~10. This would open the possibility of using an initial section of graphite in the dump. LHC vs LBNF Main characteristics of LHC absorber core: 1) designed for 540 MJ (4.8E14 protons at 7 TeV) dumped in 86 us, with the beam (0.95 mm σ) swept over a length of 120 cm 2) 7 m graphite followed by 1 m Al and 2 m Fe 3) max energy density in graphite 3.1 MJ/kg To be compared to the LBNF absorber in case of accident condition (full beam dumped in the absorber): 1) 1.5E14 protons at 120 GeV, corresponding to 2.9E6 J/pulse 2) max energy density in Al 2.1E4 J/kg A simple extrapolation of max energy densities would predict a limit of ~100 pulses of misdirected beam (~2minutes) in an absorber with a graphite section, instead of 2 pulses (2.4 s) for the LBNF reference design How long should the graphite block be? I try..., a logarithmic extrapolation from 7 TeV to 120 GeV would indicate a graphite block of ~ 2 m length. I am sure Nikolai and others could come up with a much better estimate.
