The importance of the complex cement hydration properties relative to the effects on tritium leaching behavior was pointed out by Matsuzuru [7]. The authors noted that water that is not chemically bound as hydrated water is physically retained as capillary and gel water in hardened cement. This gel and capillary water in the pore https://www.osti.gov/elink/ostiview?mfid=8881736 3/17 4/23/24, 8:46 AM WSRC-TR-99-00081 structure of the cement is free to exchange with external water which may quickly penetrate into the capillaries and then slowly diffuse into the gel pores of the matrix. The chemistry involved in the hydration of cement and its subsequent leaching is further clarified in Zamorani [8] and Eichholz, et al. [9]. While these papers are specifically concerned with the leaching of various radioactive species including tritium from buried waste in a cement matrix due to water permeation, the chemistry and migration mechanisms discussed are useful in understanding the behavior of tritium in cement materials in general. Zamorani [8] describes the leaching process, primarily for Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions, from the calcium silicates in hardened cement by excess water. Initial hydration of cement produces Ca(OH)2 and calcium silicate hydrates, which form a gel. The gel is maintained as long as Ca(OH)2 is present, and the gel acts as barrier to slow the influx of water and outflow of Ca(OH)2 around the solid central clinker (constituent particle of cement). Although Ca(OH)2 is slightly soluble in water, it cannot be removed from the solid bulk without a flow of water through the cement pores. When the pores of the cement are saturated with static water, the solubility product of the hydroxide is reached stopping further dissolution and a equilibrium is maintained. Under such an equilibrium, hydrogen exchange between the pore water and gel is not stopped, but merely slowed by diffusion of tritium and by the limited solubilities of the cement hydration products involved. As a result, tritium initially present only in the pore or gel water will exchange with the other solid-phase species, albeit relatively slowly. These effects and the possible mechanisms for the mobility of tritium in concrete are broadly explained by Eichholz, et al. [9]. This laboratory study was started by briefly exposing dried concrete cylinders to a top layer of HTO, with the intent to measure the time for the pulse to reach the other side. This proved to be impossible because the pulse was immediately absorbed and retained at the top of the cylinder. Further study of absorption of standing water by dry concrete confirmed that a 3.75-cm tall cylinder reached 85% saturation in just over 10 hours of exposure, and a 15.5-cm one took about 130 hours. They conclude that in the absence of any surface coating, dry-cured cement will absorb much standing water and retain it over long periods, in the filled pores. Two recent papers tend to explain this rapid sorption of water. Martys and Ferraris [10] looked at the rates of water absorption of oven and bench-dried mortar and concrete specimens. They found that although oven-dried samples absorbed nearly three times the water of air-dried ones, both were characterized by a very rapid initial uptake followed by a much slower one later on. They suggest the observed sorption is caused by pores of two different size scales. The larger ones exist mostly at the air-surface interface and contribute to a rapid capillary suction. These are particularly susceptible to enlargement by leaching and drying from weathering effects. Much smaller pores exist within the bulk material and are responsible for the much slower sorption by diffusion. This difference in the water sorption between the near surface and deeper bulk material was confirmed by Beyea et. al. [11] using magnetic resonance imaging. This technique was able to show the depth profile of evaporable water with sub-millimeter resolution. Profiles of prepared concrete samples with varying water-to-cement ratios and curing times all showed large amounts of capillary flow at early air-drying times and diffusive drying fronts which dominated at longer times. Most of the capillary action occurred in the first few millimeters from the surface after one-day drying with significant water loss down to twenty millimeters for longer times (7 and 90 days of air-drying) for samples with increasing porosity. Presumably, resorption of liquid water would be largely the reverse of desorption seen during evaporative air-drying. Most of the literature cited thus far deals with experiments designed to explain the uptake or release of tritium from contaminated cement paste or concrete from a diffusion view point. While these are useful for material comparisons and estimating tritium gain or loss under certain conditions, they address little of the chemical mechanisms involved. Much insight to the chemical state of concrete is discussed in Lea [12]. Neville [13] has more information relevant to states of water and mechanisms of its migration in concrete. Neville's discussion on the structure of hydrated cement is excellent [13]: "Fresh cement paste is a plastic network of particles of cement and water, but once the paste has set its apparent gross volume remains approximately constant. At any stage of hydration the hardened paste consists of hydrates of the various compounds, referred to collectively as gel, of crystals of Ca(OH)2, some minor components, https://www.osti.gov/elink/ostiview?mfid=8881736 4/17 4/23/24, 8:46 AM WSRC-TR-99-00081 unhydrated cement, and residue of the water-filled spaces in the fresh paste. These voids are called capillary pores, but within the gel itself there exist interstitial voids, called gel pores." "Since most of the products of hydration are colloidal, during hydration the surface area of the solid phase increases enormously, and a large amount of free water becomes adsorbed on this surface. If no water movement to or from the cement paste is permitted the reactions of hydration use up the water until too little is left to saturate the solid surfaces, and the relative humidity within the paste decreases. This is known as selfdesiccation. Since gel can form only in water-filled space, self-desiccation leads to a lower hydration compared with moist-cured paste." ## **Expected Tritium Behavior in Cement and Concrete** From the above discussion, it is now possible to hypothesize about the behavior of tritium in cements and concrete. Most cements never fully hydrate unless more water is introduced after setting. Self-desiccation dries the capillaries, and further hydration virtually stops, leaving some dry cement that will react only if more water enters. Neville shows that at typical water/cement ratios of about 0.5, as much as 25-30% of the cement remains unhydrated unless more water is absorbed. As a result, most hardened cements can take up condensed water contacting the exterior of the concrete very rapidly. If enough additional water is absorbed, however, hydration products start to fill the capillaries and they become segmented rather than continuous. This condition effectively ends the hydration process. In general case, both tritiated water and elemental tritium can migrate in cement and concrete. Five potential pathways for the migration of tritium in cement are [9]: 1. Movement of pore water through cracks and pores in the concrete, 2. tritium exchange with hydrogen in the hydrated cement components, 3. vapor movement as HT through open pores or cracks, 4. diffusion of dissociated H<sup>+</sup> ions and HT molecules through the concrete crystal structure, and 5. a combination of pore movement and diffusion of HTO through pore-boundary materials under barometric or hydrostatic pressures. (Thought not stated by the authors, with tritiated water, species HT in pathways 3 and 4 is primarily HTO, and H<sup>+</sup> should include T<sup>+</sup> and OT<sup>-</sup> ions as well.) If the absorbed condensed water from the environment contacting the concrete contains HTO or T2O, tritium is integrated into the new gel that forms at unhydrated sites in the old gel mass. The gel containing tritium is otherwise indistinguishable from that with protium. Neville further points out that below relative humidity of 45%, the capillaries are emptied of water. Under the same conditions, the gel pores are not emptied of water. The gel pores are only 15-20 Å across and water primarily adsorbs onto the surface of the gel. Surface forces in the small gel pores bind water with significantly more energy than in capillaries. Of the various types of water in hardened cement, only water in the capillaries is relatively free to move. But even this freedom depends on prevailing environmental conditions. In the presence of high humidity, capillary water will be stagnant unless there is hydraulic flow (flow due to external water pressure difference across the concrete structure), since the capillary pores are filled with water. In low humidity, capillary water is lost leaving the bulk much as a dry sponge, able to soak up water given the opportunity. The other non-capillary waters may be thought of as being fixed to varying degrees. Tritiated water introduced into the capillaries will, especially with the help of liquid water, percolate and exchange with other hydrogen species throughout the capillaries and eventually reach a fairly uniform concentration throughout the bulk. The case of an airborne exposure of concrete to tritium gas or tritiated water vapor is quite different from the exposure of concrete to condensed water discussed above. The amount of tritium contained in air, aside from extraordinary conditions, will be nearly a thousand times lower than that in a liquid from density considerations alone. Tritium concentration profiles in cement or concrete exposed in this manor invariably show a rapid decrease in concentration with distance from the exposed surface (discussed above [2, 3, 4, 5]). This type of https://www.osti.gov/elink/ostiview?mfid=8881736 5/17 4/23/24, 8:46 AM WSRC-TR-99-00081 profile is typical of diffusion controlled processes. Unhydrated cement can readily react with the oxide form as the tritiated vapor will diffuse very rapidly into the capillary pores of the cement. However for elemental forms, a different mechanism likely exists. Exchange with normal hydrogen in the water of the gel phase, aided by surface forces to help break bonds might be an explanation. But unmentioned in any of the reviewed literature are radiolysis and radiation effects. Although the beta decay energy released during tritium decay is very low (18 keV maximum, 5.7 keV average), it is still about 1000 times that needed to break chemical bonds. Broken bonds caused by radiation acting on moisture in air is a primary mechanism for the conversion of HT and T2 into HTO. This effect should be even more important in cement, because of the close proximity of matter inside the small capillaries and pores of hardened cement. In addition, the species T2 produces a reactive tritium atom or ion when the other tritium nucleus decays. These are all highly reactive species, which will quickly react with water and the other cement constituents. These five tritium migration pathways listed above involve both redistribution of tritium within the bulk material and releases to the surroundings. Both diffusion and mass flow of tritium are involved, and once at the surface boundary, physical and atmospheric conditions may further affect surface activity. Understanding all of these mechanisms from an atomistic viewpoint is beyond the scope of this work. Instead, we focus on the qualitative understanding outlined above, which leads to an empirical relationship relating the surface and bulk tritium activity. This relationship may allow surface activity measurements to be reliable estimators of bulk tritium burden, adequate for waste disposal characterization. ## **Surface Activity Measurement Methods** Probe surveys are used as a primary method of contamination detection of many isotopes in nuclear facilities, but not with tritium. The low energy of tritium betas requires a windowless detector be used to measure tritium surface activity. Such devices are available but they often encounter operational problems with in-situ measurements. Equipment size, need for counting gas, and effects of changes in ambient conditions, which invariably will occur, have all limited the usefulness of past instrumental approaches. Instead, the main method of detecting tritium contamination has been by smears of the surface in question followed by liquid scintillation counting (LSC) of the smear. The detection of

_Images from: Vladimir Sidorov_ Fermilab Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 9 ###### **State of design** - The core is the most challenging part of absorber design, and is where our effort has been concentrated. Its advanced conceptual design is the focus of this review. We believe that the analysis that will be presented shows this to be a very viable design, and is _ready to proceed to detailed mechanical design_ . - Some effort has also been directed at civil construction requirements, to allow cost estimates, and radiological issues that drive the civil construction have been seriously investigated. Some of that will be presented, although not the focus of this review. - The designs of the outer part of the absorber, the water systems, and the monitoring systems are at a conceptual level; real work on those systems will not start until after the core design passes review. They will then be subject to their own reviews after design and optimization efforts occur. - However, the concepts for the absorber protection monitoring follow fairly straightforwardly from NuMI experience, and will be shown in this talk. Fermilab 10 Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 ###### **Conditions used as input to FEA** LBNE will have two phases, 1.2 MW beam, then upgrade to 2.4 MW beam; but because of difficulty to upgrade absorber, design absorber from start for 2.4 MW There will be different configurations of targets and horns in LBNE over its lifetime, in particular: - The current baseline target/horn (using NuMI target/horn design) is financially driven; we know we can improve the beam by re-optimizing components - The current target/horn will only take 1.2 MW; we know we will re-design these components for 2.4 MW Want to leave **_flexibility_** to accommodate those future configurations. Thus we have designed to meet “worst case” scenarios: - Have assumed shortest reasonable target (two interaction lengths) - Giving worst non-interacting proton spot at absorber for normal operation - Have assumed beam can totally miss target, hitting absorber directly - Giving worst accident condition at absorber, although current baffle/target design does not allow such a severe condition - Have assumed tightest focus of beam at absorber (optics + beam-spot-attarget) for accident condition Fermilab 11 Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 **Beam parameters (see LBNE Beamline Operating Parameters LBNE-doc-10095 on review web site for details on phases and energy dependence)** - If not noted, results presented for 120 GeV proton beam (worse than 60 GeV). Will also present results that show design is OK for 60 GeV proton beam. (In fact, absorber could take _MUCH_ higher beam power at 60 GeV). - Beam parameters for various studies were picked for worst case upgrades: – 2.4 MW beam is 1.5e14 POT/spill, 1.2 second repetition at 120 GeV - Beam spot size at target is 1.7 mm RMS for 1.2 MW design, may be up to 3 mm for 2.4 MW designs; used 2.4 mm for accident study since with our optics this gives smallest spot at absorber (7 mm RMS) for beam accident condition - Baffle hole diameter: 17 mm at 1.2 MW, but may be up to 30 mm for 2.4 MW, so have used 30 mm for range of possible beam accidents - Normal operation modeled with fin-type two-interaction-length target where: - 0.3% of beam misses target entirely, giving 9 mm central spot on absorber (7 kW) - 13% of beam protons multiple scatter through target, giving 5 cm central spot on absorber (~300 kW) - The 2.4 MW target will probably include spoiler feature (described later for 1.2 MW target) and be longer, so these beam assumptions are conservative Designing to above parameters leaves **_significant flexibility_** for future configurations Fermilab Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 12 ###### **Using experience with NuMI** - LBNE core (gun-drilled water lines in aluminum blocks) based on NuMI absorber, which has been operating for a decade without any problems. - NuMI upstream decay pipe window is same material (Al 6061-T6) as absorber core, has seen same integrated proton-flux-density as LBNE absorber spoiler will, and has no problems so far. - Remote handling of core blocks based on T-block hanging system used successfully for last decade in NuMI target hall to swap horns and targets. - • Beam Position Monitor (BPM) input to NuMI Beam Permit System, checking that beam is directed toward the target, has been used for last decade. - Thermocouples in absorber core watching for overheating have been an input to NuMI Beam Permit System for last decade. - Muon monitor has been used at NuMI, but not as input to Beam Permit System; some modifications/upgrades required to make this operate smoothly and reliably, and will be discussed. Concern was expressed that Aluminum can fatigue, creep, lose temper over time at high temperature, and a more conservative design was desired. ###### **LBNE absorber design features to keep temperature low:** - Spoiler layer initiates particle shower, then air space between it and the rest of the core blocks lets shower spread out, reducing energy density before further showering - Sculpted core blocks (thin at center, thicker at water line) - Provide increased heat transfer conductance to water lines per amount of material at the center - Give more air space for shower to spread out (Aluminum dT < 1 C per pulse) - Water lines are drilled near center of core blocks, reducing transport dT (major contribution) - • Multiple water lines are drilled in each block (also provides redundancy, could run 1 line off) - • Water flows at high enough velocity (2.5 m/s) to give good heat transfer coeff. (dT < 15 C) - • Water flows at high rate (80 gpm /block), gives low water dT in block ( dT max. = 2 C ) • Low temperature water supply (10 C) (will dehumidify air to keep dew point below this) The combination reduces aluminum maximum normal operating temperature to 88 C with the worst target configuration we imagine using. We believe this is a robust design. Title: Thoughts and questions about the Absorber

Thoughts and questions on the Absorber Alberto Marchionni Fermilab The reference design quite a lot of work has gone into the design of an Al absorber that could work with a NuMI-like target and focusing system in addition to normal operation, accidents conditions have been considered where the full intensity proton beam could directly hit the absorber. beam is misdirected through the space between the target and the baffle the target “disappers” (it may bend or crack and rest over the horn inner conductor) The engineering analysis has shown that a maximum of 2 full beam pulses would be acceptable Already at the time of the absorber review Jim Hylen introduced the idea of a target with wings to mitigate the consequences of an accident condition Questions on the Absorber reference design Sam Childress is questioning that we would be able to safely stop the beam in just 2 pulses. One of the criteria to stop the beam is to use the muon monitor signal; when the beam hits directly the absorber, the muon production is strongly reduced, and this is something that we observe and measure in NuMI. But LBNF is not the same as NuMI. For LBNF we need to simulate the accident condition and the "absence" of muons including the spoiler, the sculpted absorber (NUMI has a compact absorber) and the wings to the target. The spoiler and wings would act like a target, and generate some pions decaying to muons. We cannot rely on NuMI, we need a realistic simulation of the accident condition for LBNF. The optimized focusing configuration would definitely help here. How to make a protection system based on the muon signal fail-safe, and without excessive fake trips? Impact of optimized focusing design on Absorber (I) The hadron flux can be reduced by an order of magnitude or more in all regions of the hadron absorber except the very center, where flux is dominated by beam halo that does not impinge on the target. This halo can be substantially reduced by adding ”wings” to the upstream end of the target Beam Task Force Optimization Interim Report S. Striganov Impact of optimized focusing design on Absorber (II) S. Striganov The combination of increased target length and wings would allow considerable simplification of the current hadron absorber design. This is very desirable from a physics point of view, as the sculpting of the current absorber design introduces significant backgrounds to the muon detectors that will both monitor the neutrino beam and constrain models of the neutrino flux. Possibility to reduce the cost of the absorber and of the 30 m long muon shielding (steel) downstream of the absorber The Muon Monitor group is still working on the evaluation of the Muon Monitors system requirements for neutrino beam monitoring and for its potential use for neutrino flux prediction Removal of the spoiler and the sculpting will not satisfy the requirements for the accident conditions Addition of a graphite section? Sam Childress has been advocating an initial section of graphite to help in case of accident conditions Graphite dumps have been safely used as accelerator dumps since a long time. Nikolai Mokhov designed a graphite dump for the Tevatron, the Main Injector has a graphite dump, the LHC has a graphite dump. On the neutrino side, CNGS and T2K have been/are using graphite dumps. One of the reason a graphite dump has not been considered for LBNF is a possible radiation damage of the graphite. Every single pulse, in the NuMI-like reference design, about 15% of the protons are dumped in the dump (about 350 kW deposited just by the protons when running at 2.4 MW). This is clearly a different operation from dumps used as aborts in accelerator machines. The optimized design, with longer targets and wings, would reduce the power in the dump by the residual protons by at least a factor ~3, and the maximum energy density by a factor ~10. This would open the possibility of using an initial section of graphite in the dump. LHC vs LBNF Main characteristics of LHC absorber core: 1) designed for 540 MJ (4.8E14 protons at 7 TeV) dumped in 86 us, with the beam (0.95 mm σ) swept over a length of 120 cm 2) 7 m graphite followed by 1 m Al and 2 m Fe 3) max energy density in graphite 3.1 MJ/kg To be compared to the LBNF absorber in case of accident condition (full beam dumped in the absorber): 1) 1.5E14 protons at 120 GeV, corresponding to 2.9E6 J/pulse 2) max energy density in Al 2.1E4 J/kg A simple extrapolation of max energy densities would predict a limit of ~100 pulses of misdirected beam (~2minutes) in an absorber with a graphite section, instead of 2 pulses (2.4 s) for the LBNF reference design How long should the graphite block be? I try..., a logarithmic extrapolation from 7 TeV to 120 GeV would indicate a graphite block of ~ 2 m length. I am sure Nikolai and others could come up with a much better estimate. Source: indico Title: Muon Monitor & Absorber Practice Talks Physics Goals of DUNE/LBNF Muon Monitoring Systems Jeremy Lopez January 16, 2017 ### **Abstract** This tech note details simulation studies using G4LBNF to determine the physics potential of an idealized array of ionization detectors placed just downstream of the hadron absorber. This note will focus on the physics goals of the muon systems for monitoring the beam. We conclude that we will want to be sensitive to changes in the muon signals including: (1) the beam position moving by 1-2 cm, (2) the total muon signal within a 2 m x 2 m square around beam center changing by 1-2%, (3) the flux around 5 GeV changing by 2%, and (4) the flux around 7 or more GeV changing by 4% or so. We also conclude that measuring beam position changes reliably will be difficult with the reference absorber due to shaping of the signal due to the absorber design. # **Contents** |**1**|**Introduction**|**2**| |---|---|---| |**2**|**Simulations**|**3**| |**3**|**Nominal Beam Conditions**|**4**| |**4**|**Beam Shift in X**|**10**| |**5**|**Beam Shift in Y**|**17**| |**6**|**Reduction in Beam Width**|**24**| |**7**|**Horn Current Reduction**|**31**| |**8**|**Target Density Reduction**|**38**| |**9**|**Horn A Shift in X**|**45**| |**10**|**Horn A Shift in Y**|**52**| 1 |**11 Horn A Tilt in X**|**59**| |---|---| |**12 Horn A Tilt in Y**|**66**| |**13 Horn B Shift in X**|**73**| |**14 Horn B Shift in Y**|**79**| |**15 Summary and Conclusions**|**85**| |15.1 Summary of Observables to Monitor Different Beam Conditions .|85| |15.2 Physics Recommendations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .|86| |15.3 Conclusions . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .|87| # **1 Introduction** In several existing neutrino beamlines, detectors placed just downstream of the hadron absorber are able to monitor beam conditions by measuring muons with enough energy to pass through the entire absorber. In the beamline, most muons will be created by pion decay in the decay pipe, π + → µ + + νµ (1)
and some are also created by kaon decay, K + → µ + + νµ. (2)
The muons found in an alcove downstream of the absorber are, therefore, produced in the same decays that produce the neutrinos comprising most of the flux at the neutrino detectors. Furthermore, muon decays can also produce electron neutrinos that act as backgrounds in the oscillation analysis. By measuring the muons in the alcove, one can obtain information about things such as the beam intensity, direction, and width. To monitor muons, several types of measurements may be possible. The standard method for muon monitoring is to place a two-dimensional array of ionization detectors (typically gas ion chambers, but solid state devices may be used as well) just downstream of the absorber. The detectors in this array sample the distribution of charged particles at known positions with respect to the nominal beam center. The ionization detector array is simple and measures the beam profile, allowing us to extract the signal intensity and shape. Ionization detectors are unable to distinguish between different types of charged particles and are unable to distinguish between minimum ionizing particles (for muons, _Ekin >_ 100 MeV). As a result, ionization detectors cannot distinguish between muons and other particles such as electrons, complicating any attempts at determining the absolute muon flux, and also cannot typically monitor changes in the spectrum if the overall rate stays roughly constant. The muon spectrum, however, does potentially contain a great deal of useful information, and 2 detectors that are sensitive to the muon energy can also be used for monitoring. Dedicated spectral measurements have not generally been done at previous beamlines, although the NuMI beamline has several muon alcoves, which use ionization detectors to measure the flux for several different energy distributions of muons from the same beam. Current plans for muon monitoring systems at LBNF envision using both ionization detectors and detectors sensitive to the energy distribution (such as threshold Cherenkov detectors and stopped muon counters). This note details a number of simulations done to estimate the requirements needed in order to set useful physics constraints on the LBNF neutrino flux. These requirements can then be used to evaluate different possible detector technologies and to determine the practical requirements on detector performance needed to reach our goals. Muon monitoring may also play an important role in monitoring the safety of the facility. This will be much less strict than monitoring for setting physics requirements, so we will not address that in detail here. # **2 Simulations** This note makes use of simulations using G4LBNF. Each data set generates 109 protons on target at an energy of 90 GeV with a beam width of 1.62 mm. The simulations use the 3-horn optimized beamline recommendations from the Beam Optimization Task Force report. The simulations use a NuMI-style target composed of rectangular fins of graphite. The target is 2 m long and the fins are set to be 10 cm in width along the shorter ( _x_ ) dimension. Upstream of the target is a 1.5 m baffle with an inner diameter of 17 mm. The reference LBNF beamline uses a large “sculpted” absorber with many different features. The absorber consists largely of an aluminum core with an outer colume of iron and approximately 1 m of concrete downstream of the aluminum and iron layers. The considerable amount of energy that might be dumped into the absorber, particularly in the CDR reference design, requires that the energy be spread out over as large a volume as feasible. As a result, there are several important features in the absorber, including, 1. An aluminum spoiler at the upstream end of the absorber to help spread out the beam 2. A mask made of aluminum layers with pieces cut out to give particles room to spread out after interacting with the spoiler 3. “Sculpting” of the aluminum core layers, where some material is cut out of the center of each layer to prevent too much energy loss in any one solid volume. 4. Fairly small size of the aluminum core layers, substantially smaller than the decay pipe radius. 3 These features are expected to shape the muon profile in various ways, so that muon profile measured in the alcove does not perfectly represent the muon profile entering the absorber. In order to test the effects of this, the simulations are also done with a greatly simplified absorber. Downstream of the hadron absorber is a large air volume representing the muon alcove. We place a tracking volume in the alcove, tilted at the same angle as the decay pipe so that the tracking volume is perpendicular to the nominal beam direction. When a particle enters the volume, it is recorded into a file, along with relevant tracking information such as the position, energy, particle type, direction, and other things. To estimate the energy loss, the energy loss due to ionization and the step length are save for all steps where at least one end is located in the tracking volume. These are then used to estimate the track _dE/dx_ . The energy deposition for each track is then taken to be: ∆ E = dE dx L cos θ (3)
where _L_ is the width of the tracking volume and cos _θ_ is the angle with respect to the nominal beam direction. If ∆ _E_ is greater than the total track kinetic energy _Ekin_ then ∆ _E_ = _Ekin_ . Furthermore, all the energy deposition from a single track is added at the same position. # **3 Nominal Beam Conditions** In normal beam conditions, we will generally expect a muon signal that is peaked at nominal beam center and symmetric in both _x_ and _y_ . The signals will not in general show rotational symmetry. Figure 1 shows the two-dimensional distribution that we might expect to see in an array of ionization detectors just downstream of the absorber. A realistic array will sample this distribution at intervals of approximately 25 cm or so. Figure 2 shows “slices” of the twodimensional distributions. These slices look at the contributions from particles with _|x| <_ 7 _._ 5 cm for the _y_ slice and _|y| <_ 7 _._ 5 cm for the _x_ slice. These slices are much more useful in visualizing the differences between the nominal beam and the different beam alterations we will discuss later in this note. Figure 3 shows the two-dimensional distribution for the “simplified” absorber and 4 shows the _x_ and _y_ slices for that absorber model. Comparing the two absorber models, we clearly see the effects of shaping from the absorber design. While the simplified design shows a wide distribution that is approximately Gaussian within approximately 60 cm of beam center, the nominal design is a much narrower distribution with a much sharper peak. We will use some basic test statistics to numerically consider the kinds of measurements that might be useful. These include: the integral for the twodimensional distribution looking at a square with 5-cm bins and bin centers between -1 m and +1 m from beam center, the mean and RMS of the profiles between -1 m and +1m from beam center, the mean and standard deviation 4 for Gaussian fits of the profiles between -1 m and +1m, and the mean and standard deviation for Gaussian fits of the profiles between -50 cm and +50 cm. Title: Impact of Realistic Optimized Horns on Neutrino Flux

Muon-neutrino flux optimization at the LBNF/DUNE Far detector By Tyler Johnson, Supervised by Dr. Laura Fields at Fermilab introduction I am studying the different simulations of the 3-horn optimized design identified by Laura’s genetic algorithm, the one described in the BOTF Interim Report. There’s a significant drop in neutrino flux between the ideal, optimized design and the realistic design. My objective is to determine the reasons for this flux loss and understand which of the factors can be altered to optimize the flux. Factors considered in my studies: Obstructions in the Beamline (Target Assembly, Strip Lines, etc.) Horn Flare Starting Point Material Thickness Target Placement Scan 2 Reference vs. ideal/optimzed design Through running a genetic algorithm, Laura identified an optimized 3 horn design which surpassed the reference design in both neutrino flux and CP sensitivity. 3 Realistic design This design was created by Paul Lebrun and, as the name suggests, is a more realistic version of the optimized (ideal) design. The flares on both the upstream and downstream ends are rounded off. For Horn A, there is the problem of the target assembly. The target assembly holds the graphite target and has the issue of it being in the beamline so was suspected to cause a drop in the neutrino flux. 4 Initial problem Here is the difference in unoscillated, Muon-neutrino flux at the far detector due to changes in the horn A design (Ideal vs. Realistic) Note: This is the flux loss from horn A alone. Horn A 5 Ratio: Ideal vs realistic horn a (first design) Flux loss from the first design for the realistic horn A 6 Alteration #1: horn a flare starting point Parent Production Plot: indicates where the particle that decay into neutrino are created after collision Ideal Horn A Radial View 7 Old horn a radial view The starting point of the flare in the original, realistic design is further downstream 8 New horn a design radial view The new realistic design pulls the starting point of the flare upstream (but admittedly not quite as far as the ideal design) 9 New horn a muon neutrino flux The new design has a noticeably higher neutrino flux 10 New vs. old design Ratio Flux increase from old Horn A to new horn A This is the remainder of the flux loss due to the horn A design to make up for with further analysis 11 Focusing Horns b & c Now Horns B & C will be introduced. There was observed to be significantly less flux loss due to these horns but nonetheless need to be accounted. 12 Total loss between ideal and realistic horn abc With the new Horn A, here is the remaining flux loss contributed by all 3 horns 13 14 15 16 Flux loss from horn B The flux difference between the two designs in the histogram to the right is Horn B’s contribution to the flux loss. 17 Flux loss because of horn B 18 Flux loss due to horn C 19 It appears that the realistic Horn C causes a still increase in flux in the 2-5 GeV range 20 All 3 horns so far 21 Factor #2: obstructions in the beamline List of part removed: Target Assembly from Horn A Inconel Spring Outer Rings Support Ring Titanium Tube Struts Outer Conductor form Horn A Outer Conductor Flange from Horn A Equalizer from Horn A IO Transition from Horn A Insulator Ring from Horn A Strip Lines from Horn B 22 Target assembly Outer Rings Titanium Tube Support Ring Struts 23 All Target assembly removed 24 All target assembly removed 25 No inconel Spring 26 No inconel spring 27 No Outer rings 28 No outer rings 29 No struts 30 No struts 31 No support ring 32 No support ring 33 No titanium tube 34 No titanium tube 35 Remaining parts Strip Lines from Horn B Outer Conductor of Horn A Outer Conductor Flange of Horn A Equalizer of Horn A Insulator Ring of Horn A 36 Strip lines on Horn b 37 Strip lines ratio 38 No outer conductor 39 No outer conductor 40 No Outer conductor flange 41 19 No outer conductor flange 42 No insulator ring 43 No insulator ring 44 No io transition 45 No io transition 46 No equalizer 47 No equalizer 48 Factor #3: Inner conductor thickness Horn A: The thickness of the inner conductor neck (a significant portion of horn A) is reduced from 2.5 to 2 cm. Tritium modeling cross checks update Brendan Casey with inputs from Chris Greer, Mary Convery, and Nisarg Patel Fermilab April 15, 2026 Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 1 Get all the numbers in one place from protons on target to tritium readings at the nearest well to try and simplify Q&A and provide decent visualization tools Stacking effects Subtracting one effect at a time Internally consistent numbers that are easy to modify and update Do this in a way that’s a little more continuous than the spreadsheet calculations and a little easier to modify and adjust than a spreadsheet (i.e. a python script) Today: Report on where I am for stage 1 and give some brief thoughts on stage 2 Numbers are not yet internally consistent, but you can get a feel for what I’m trying to do. More at the level of a working group meeting. My Goals Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 2 Nominal: 7e13 protons per pulse sent to target 1.2 second MI cycle time Protons on target at 1.2 MW Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 3 Uptimes from the TDR (from Mary C) 0.85: Proton source x LINAC x Booster 0.93: MI including switchyard tax I believe 0.93: Horn/Target replacements Treating as average versus discrete every few years 0.98: Other LBNF beamline components 0.95: Extra overall Fermilab downtime Average uptime: 0.68 Downtime 1: overall averages Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 4 TDR: Historical average is 60 days Run time / year = 0.83 Total uptime = 0.83 x 0.68 = 0.57 Not sure where the 0.54 comes from. Will keep investigating. Just using 0.57 for now in the rest of this presentation. 1.12e21 protons per year Downtime 3: Shutdowns Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 5 Haven't traced back exactly where these numbers come from but these numbers are consistent with what Chris has been showing Y1 1e21 POT Y2 1.5e21 Y3 1.5e21 Y4 1.75e21 Y5 1.8e21 Recall, TDR design with uptime for 1.2 MW was 1.12 POT/year Will try and tie these in with the other numbers The numbers from Mary also now seem to indicate a 3-month shutdown so I’m going with that for now Ramp up Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 6 It would be helpful for me to have these in per proton instead of per second What was assumed for this plot? For now, I’m taking 3.5e13 p/sec I would also like to separate the numbers for what is produced at the concrete-soil interface and what is produced at the concrete-rock interface since the overall evolution of these will be very different Is there a table or a histogram where I can grab the values? In per proton units? From Nisarg’s presentation, my guess is S = 2 Stars/cm3/sec averaged over the outer box. Star Density per second Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 7 Integrated Star Density Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 8 Using k = 0.0407 from Nisarg’s talk Integrated Tritium in Rock in atoms, decay off Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 9 Using 9.6e6 atoms/pC for H3 Integrated Tritium in Rock in pC, decay off/on Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 10 Using 9.6e6 atoms/pC for H3 Integrated Tritium in Rock in pC, decay on Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 11 First try to get some internally consistent set of numbers based on the various inputs In no order yet Add in tritium produced in the soil and how it migrates to the rock along the concrete outer wall Add in time dependent diffusion numbers Add in time dependent mixing numbers Add in distance to wells and ND and predict H3 at those locations Extrapolate out to 50 years Next steps Casey | Tritium Modeling Cross Checks 12

Title: The DUNE Flux and LBNF Facility

LBNF Beam and the DUNE Flux Anne Norrick, NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Introduction Introduction to DUNE • Structure of the beamline • Modeling the DUNE Flux • Uncertainties • PRISM • Far to Near Flux Ratio • Into the Future • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 2 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Introduction to DUNE Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment Sanford Underground Fermi National North Dakota ResearchFacility AcceleratorLaboratory Lead,SouthDakota Batavia,Illinois Minnesota South Dakota SURF Wisconsin lowa Fermilab Nebraska Illinois 32km/20miles 1,300kilometers/800miles Anne Norrick, Fermilab 3 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Introduction to DUNE Map of the actual DUNE experiment Over 1400 collaborators, 35+ countries. Big group project! • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 4 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Introduction to DUNE Broad based physics • program! Not just targeting a specific neutrino oscillation parameter, instead looking to validate or reject the entire three flavor framework. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 5 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Role of the Beam Beam is a statistics creation machine. • Goal for the first phase of DUNE is to • hit 1.2 MW beam power. Made possible with the installation of • the PIP-II LINAC. Eventual goal of DUNE is to reach 2.4 • MW beam power. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 6 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Role of the Beam LBNF’s broad spectrum with 120 GeV • proton beam from the Fermilab Main Injector has critical advantages: We can cover both the first and • second oscillation maximum with substantial flux High energy tail allows for a nu tau • program! Independent of power, we get more • neutrinos per POT at 120 GeV than we would at a lower energy. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 7 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 LBNF Design For those of you that are familiar • with NuMI, this is going to look quite familiar. That’s not an accident! NuMI has • been a very stable, powerful beam over a 20 year period. Design decision was to re-use as • much of NuMI designs as possible to save costs on prototyping, as well as making sure we were building a stable and robust beamline for LBNF. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 8 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 LBNF Overview REPLACE THIS PICTURE WITH SOMETHING BETTER • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 9 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 LBNF Primary Beamline Primary Beam Window 6.4 m Vehicle Access Ground Level MI Penetration Lambertsons Kickers at Q100 Anne Norrick, Fermilab 10 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 LBNF Primary Beam Instrumentation Apart from the normal tracking of the • beam as it goes through the beamline to make sure we aren’t having losses, we have two important pieces of instrumentation that affects the flux/experiment. RWM — important for timing • information because it gives the most accurate idea of when the protons are actually passing through to hit the target. Final wire chambers — important for • making sure the incoming proton beam direction is stable and correct. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 11 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Target Complex Large building which holds the • target and the horns and all the shielding. Operating in a high intensity • environment Want to ensure consistent • operations through the life of the experiment Monitoring positions of the target • and horns is important for DUNE Design optimized for 3 horns • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 12 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Three Horn System Anne Norrick, Fermilab 13 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Target and Horn System Primary Beam A Window B C Decay Pipe NuMI horns 200kV -> LBNF horns at 300kV Challenges: • • Inner conductor is water cooled, outer Horn A — Target mounted to the front • • conductor is nitrogen cooled plate Horns B &C — Giant! Difficult to weld • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 14 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Target and Horn System Graphite rod cooled by helium gas • More precise cooling than NuMI water cooling line design • Reduces radiation damage (annealing) • Mounted to a support plate at the upstream face of horn A • Provided by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) • Also providing second target for hadron production experiments • Currently designed for 1.2 MW • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 15 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Absorber Complex 194 m long decay pipe — helium filled. Considerably shorter than NuMI. (NuMI is 675 m) • Shielded against maximum 2.4 MW intensity • Muon and hadron monitors to help constrain the flux and monitor the beam. • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 16 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Hadron Monitor Provides alignment of the LBNF primary • proton beam Sits at the end of the Decay pipe, • upstream of the absorber Can be moved into and out of the beam • line Horn A and target installed -> beam • scan and measure the results in HADeS Smaller pixels than the NuMI hadron • monitor Anne Norrick, Fermilab 17 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Muon Monitors Changes in the muon flux (rate, shape) tracks overall changes in the • beam. Critical to monitoring the beam and protecting from damage due to • mis-steering in the beam. Three detectors at three different positions • Designed to stay in the beam continuously • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 18 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 DUNE Flux Anne Norrick, Fermilab 19 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Sources of Uncertainty: Hadron Production Uncertainties Hadron Production Uncertainties Uncertainties that arise from • Outgoing Pion the interactions that occur between the protons entering the target material Includes secondary particle • 120 GeV Proton reinteractions. Largely constrained via hadron • production experiments. Stay tuned for Jon Paley’s talk • on Wednesday for more details on these experiments! Anne Norrick, Fermilab 20 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Sources of Uncertainty: Focusing Uncertainties Focusing Uncertainties Uncertainties that arise from the • focusing system. Horn Uncertainties: Horn • Position, tilt, construction tolerance, horn current etc. Beam Uncertainties: Proton beam • position, angle, and intensity Target Uncertainties: Target • position, angle, and density Decay Pipe Uncertainties: Decay • pipe length, position, angle, cross section and geomagnetic fields. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 21 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Package to Predict the Flux DUNE relies on the Package to Predict the Flux (PPFX) • software to predict the flux using available hadron production data. Incorporates multiple data sets, with the ability to expand • and include additional data when available. Stay tuned for the talk from Leo Aliaga on Wednesday! • Anne Norrick, Fermilab 22 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Geometry Geometry of the beamline modeled • using G4LBNF, a Geant4 based application Allows for the propagation of particles • through the materials of the beamline. Uses the QGSP_BERT physics list. • Output is a file type called dk2nu • which saves the details of every step of the chain for each neutrino back to the incident proton. Computing power is saved by only • saving neutrinos that are likely to go through the ND Anne Norrick, Fermilab 23 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Systematics Flux uncertainties are calculated using a multiuniverse technique • Hadron production uncertainties vary to produce 100 different universes. • Focusing uncertainties have a shifted up and a shifted down by 1 sigma • universe. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 24 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Correlations Anne Norrick, Fermilab 25 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Total Uncertainties Far Detector Near Detector Anne Norrick, Fermilab 26 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Importance of Uncertainties DUNE is a precision experiment • The goal is always to reduce the • uncertainties as much as possible. Adding additional hadron • production data will definitely help… Chances for improved in-situ flux • constraints from instrumentation like the muon monitors But what else could we do to try • and restrain the uncertainties? Anne Norrick, Fermilab 27 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Off Axis Fluxes DUNE’s LAr Near Detector will • be capable of moving to multiple off axis positions. Goal is to be able to use the • off axis data to construct oscillated fluxes at the Far Detector. Concept called DUNE- • PRISM. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 28 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Off Axis Fluxes DUNE’s LAr Near Detector will • be capable of moving to multiple off axis positions. Goal is to be able to use the • off axis data to construct oscillated fluxes at the Far Detector. Concept called DUNE- • PRISM. Anne Norrick, Fermilab 29 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Conclusions Completing design work on LBNF now • DUNE and PIP-II construction underway! • Ongoing work to better model the flux • and reduce flux uncertainties! Anne Norrick, Fermilab 30 NuFlux Workshop, March 2026 Thanks! Questions? Title: Request from LBNF

# **Request to DUNE Accelerator and Beam Interface WG** DUNE has received a request from LBNF for clarification on the physics arguments and technical implications of two systems that impact the optimization of the LBNF beam line design. These are the muon monitors and the idea of adding a spectrometer to measure _in situ_ the meson and muon flux after the LBNF target and horns. The information has been requested on the timescale of the January 2017 Collaboration meeting. DUNE management requests that the Accelerator and Beam Interface WG actively engages with the Muon Monitor team and the proponents of the Spectrometer concept to come up with answers to the questions below. These questions are based on the list sent to the collaboration by LBNF. It should be assumed that a capable near detector system will be operational at the time of the start of beam operations. ### **1) Questions from LBNF: Muon Systems** The following questions focus on the scope of the muon monitors. - a) What are the physics requirements of the muons monitors on top of what the DUNE Near Detector will provide? - b) Are the muon systems required to be able to provide information on the neutrino flux spectrum? If so, what physics benefit is delivered. - c) There are currently 3 types of muon monitors proposed: i) Array of Ionization detectors, ii) threshold gas Cherenkov detectors, iii) stopped muon counters. The Beamline Team needs the ionization detectors to help monitor beam stability and possibly beam alignment. Are the remaining muon systems required for the DUNE physics program? - d) What are the requirements that the muon systems impose on the Hadron Absorber core related to the DUNE physics goals mentioned above? - e) Based on the experience with MINOS and NOvA, with what frequency is the DUNE Near Detector expected to be able to provide sufficient statistics to monitor changes in the neutrino spectrum from, for example, degradation of the LBNF target? ### **2) Questions from LBNF: Spectrometer** The spectrometer concept has been presented by Paul LeBrun at the September 2016 collaboration meeting and in a collaboration bi-weekly call (October 2016). - a) Do the DUNE physics goals require the spectrometer? This question should addressed with a preliminary assessment of the impact on the overall sensitivity. - b) If so, is it required to be installed inside the LBNF target station every time there is a change of target/horn configuration? - c) For the two options of installing the spectrometer _in situ_ either after Horn C or between Horn B and C, provide an estimate of the additional costs (spectrometer and CF) and the impact on the operational schedule – how much time would be devoted to spectrometer operation and how often. - d) For the _in situ_ option, the collaboration would like to understand any the potential impact on the overall LBNF schedule. - e) Can the _ex situ_ option provide the necessary constraints? What are the estimated additional systematic uncertainties in transferring the results to the actual beam configuration? ## **Proposed Actions and Timeline** It is proposed that the Accelerator and Beam Interface WG follows a similar procedure to the NuPIL discussion, whereby the ideas and arguments are discussed and refined within the ABI WG meetings. The timeline is driven by the desire to give early feedback to LBNF: 1. November – December: presentations in the ABI WG with the aim of refining the arguments; 2. January collaboration meeting: presentations from the Muon Monitors and Spectrometer systems during the first-day plenary, presenting the progress. The focus should be on scientific arguments. 3. Collaboration input presented at the face-to-face EFIG meeting during the January collaboration meeting.

Together LBNF and DUNE will comprise the world's highest-­‐intensity neutrino beam at Fermilab, in Batavia, IL, a high-­‐precision near detector on the Fermilab site, a massive liquid argon time-­‐projection chamber (LArTPC) far detector installed deep underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) 1,300 km away in Lead, SD, and all of the conventional and technical facilities necessary to support the beamline and detector systems. The strategy for executing the experimental program presented in this Conceptual Design Report (CDR) has been developed to meet the requirements set out in the P5 report and takes into account the recommendations of the European Strategy for Particle Physics. It adopts a model where U.S. and international funding agencies share costs on the DUNE detectors, and various international participants provide in-­‐kind contributions to the supporting infrastructure of LBNF. LBNF and DUNE **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 2-­‐13** **Introduction** will be tightly coordinated as DUNE collaborators design the detectors and infrastructure that will carry out the scientific program. The scope of the LBNF covers the following components: - An intense neutrino beam aimed at the far site. - Conventional facilities at both the near and far site. - Cryogenics infrastructure to support the DUNE liquid argon time-­‐projection chamber (LArTPC) detectors at SURF. The DUNE detectors include - a fine-­‐grained neutrino detector and beamline monitoring system located a few hundred meters downstream of the neutrino source - a massive LArTPC neutrino detector located deep underground at the far site With the facilities provided by LBNF and the detectors provided by DUNE, the DUNE Collaboration proposes to mount a focused attack on the puzzle of neutrinos with broad sensitivity to neutrino oscillation parameters in a single experiment. The focus of the scientific program is the determination of the neutrino mass hierarchy and the explicit demonstration of leptonic CP violation, if it exists, by precisely measuring differences between the oscillations of muon-­‐type neutrinos and antineutrinos into respectively electron-­‐type neutrinos and antineutrinos. Siting the far detector deep underground will provide exciting additional research opportunities in nucleon decay, studies utilizing atmospheric neutrinos, and neutrino astrophysics, including measurements of neutrinos from a core-­‐collapse supernova should such an event occur in our galaxy during the experiment’s lifetime. **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 2-­‐14** **Description of the Site, Facility and Operations** ### **3 DESCRIPTION OF THE SITE, FACILITY AND OPERATIONS** ### **3.1 Characterization of the LBNF/DUNE Site Locations** SERVICE BUILDING

**Figure 3-­‐2: LBNF/DUNE Near Site at Fermilab** #### **3.1.2 Site Locations** The LBNF/DUNE is a high energy physics research project. Fermilab researchers have proposed to send a neutrino beam generated by Fermilab to the Sanford Underground Research Facility. The LBNF/DUNE Near Site Facilities will be constructed on the Fermilab site located in an area west of Kautz Road and south of Giese Road, see Figure 3-­‐1. In general terms, a proton beam will be extracted from the existing Main Injector, directed north and west towards new below grade enclosures housing the LBNF/DUNE Target Hall and Absorber Hall. The LBNF/DUNE Beamline complex at Fermilab will be designed to provide a neutrino beam of sufficient intensity and energy to meet the goals of the LBNF/DUNE experiment with respect to long baseline neutrino-­‐oscillation physics. The design is a conventional, horn-­‐focused neutrino beamline. The components of the beamline will be designed to extract a proton beam from the Fermilab Main Injector (MI) and transport it to a target area where the collisions generate a beam of charged particles. This secondary beam, aimed toward the far detector, is followed by a decay-­‐pipe where the particles of the secondary beam decay to generate the neutrino beam. At the end of the decay pipe, an absorber pile absorbs the residual energy from uninteracted protons and the secondary particles (hadrons) that do not decay. The facility is designed for initial operation at proton beam power of 1.2 MW, with the capability to support an upgrade to 2.4 MW. In the reference design, extraction of the proton beam occurs at MI-­‐10, a new installation. After extraction, this primary beam establishes a horizontally straight compass heading west-­‐northwest toward the far detector, but will be bent upward to an apex before being bent downward at the appropriate angle, 101 milliradians, as shown in Figure 3-­‐2 . The primary beam will be above grade for 500 feet; this design minimizes expensive underground construction and significantly enhances capability for ground water radiological protection. The design requires, however, construction of an earthen embankment, or hill, whose dimensions are commensurate with the bending strength of the dipole magnets required for the beamline. The embankment will need to be approximately 950 feet long and 58 feet high above grade at its peak. The Beam Loss Monitor will be located in the region of the Absorber Complex at the downstream end of the decay region to measure the muon fluxes from hadron decay. **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 3-­‐16** **Description of the Site, Facility and Operations** The Near Detector Hall is located near the west Fermilab site boundary east of Kirk Road, approximately 200 ft underground. The reference design is a straw-­‐tube tracker. Refer to DUNE CDR Volume 4 for additional information. The DUNE Far Detector will be constructed at the SURF, see Figure 3-­‐3. The reference design Far Detector is a modular liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC); four 10-­‐kt modules to be constructed at the 4850L. The mass of fluid quoted is the fiducial portion of the detector – the mass of vital importance for physics measurements. The basic components of each detector module include a cryostat to contain the LAr, a TPC detection mechanism immersed in the LAr, a photon-­‐detection system, readout electronics and a cryogenic system to keep the LAr temperature at 87 K and maintain the required purity. Excavated space will need to accommodate detector modules that hold a total LAr volume larger than the fiducial 10 kt. Refer to DUNE CDR Volume 4 for additional information on the Far Detector design. ### **3.2 Fermilab & SURF Utilities and Services** #### **3.2.1 Facility Components** LBNF at Fermilab will be utilizing accelerator-­‐type enclosures which are thick-­‐walled, reinforced concrete structures. The actual near-­‐site area where the LBNF/DUNE facilities are to be located consists of a combination of previously disturbed and undisturbed natural areas. The LBNF/DUNE Project at SURF will be utilizing presently active surface spaces along with new underground facilities at the 4850L including four neutrino detector caverns at 4850L and a cryogenic equipment cavern. #### **3.2.2 Electrical Systems** Electrical systems throughout the facilities include high voltages, high currents, and high levels of stored energy. Much of the equipment in use has been designed and built for a specific purpose and is not commonly found in other industrial facilities. Although workplace experience with this equipment has been very good from both safety and operational perspectives, a program has been established to review all equipment that is not labeled by a Nationally Recognized Testing Lab (NRTL). The primary AC distribution to both LBNF/DUNE sites is at 13.8 kV. For most systems, transformers convert the 13.8 kV to 480 volts AC for subsequent distribution. Because of the very high potential hazards, the substations are fenced, and access is limited to qualified high-­‐voltage electricians. Most secondary distribution is 480 V, 3-­‐phase, 60 Hz, ungrounded delta. This is used directly in many motors, pumps, power supplies, and other equipment. It is further transformed to 208/120 V, 3-­‐phase for lights, utility outlets, and other general needs. The 480/277 V neutral is grounded. The facilities will have both emergency and standby power systems. The emergency power system will include support of fire detection/alarm systems, exit signage, emergency lights, and elevator car lighting, and two-­‐way Fire department communication systems. The standby power systems will support critical systems including elevators, air handling systems, sump pumps, and shaft cranes. The design will follow the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 110 Standard for Emergency and Standby Power Systems. **LBNF/DUNE Preliminary Hazard Analysis Report** **Page 3-­‐17** **Description of the Site, Facility and Operations** #### **3.2.3 Heating, Ventilation and Cooling Systems** Heating and air conditioning will be forced air systems. All buildings will be equipped with electric exhaust fans to meet the temperature stability and ventilation loads. Grills, diffusers, and ductwork will be provided for proper and complete air distribution system. #### **3.2.4 Gas and Cryogenic Gas Distribution Systems** LBNF/DUNE detectors and support systems will be designed in conformance with applicable cryogenic design standards and the Fermilab and SURF ESH Manuals. All cryogenic systems will be installed as per Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) requirements. #### **3.2.5 Fire Protection, Suppression** Fire & life safety requirements for LBNF/DUNE areas were analyzed as described in the LBNF/DUNE Near and Far Site Preliminary Fire Protection/Life Safety Assessments [1]. The conclusions developed through this assessment process will be reflected in the final facility design. Fermilab maintains an on-­‐site fire station which is fully equipped and provides 24/7 coverage. There are nineteen (19) personnel employed by the department, of which eighteen (18) are on three (3) shifts of six (6) each, and the other is the Chief. In order to provide the best service possible, the Laboratory is a member of M.A.B.A.S. Division 12 & 13, comprised of fire departments in DuPage and Kane Counties, which provides additional equipment and personnel through a systematic call-­‐up procedure in times when our resources are not able to handle an emergency. The department also participates in Auto-­‐Aid Response with Batavia & Warrenville Fire Departments. SURF’s primary responder in the case of a fire or emergency for the surface facilities is the Lead Volunteer Fire Department. The Lead Fire Department maintains 24/7 coverage on a volunteer basis and there are twenty-­‐eight (28) personnel employed by the Department. In order to provide the best service possible, the SURF is a member of a Lawrence County wide mutual aid agreement with all departments in the county (Deadwood, Spearfish, etc.), which provides additional equipment and personnel through a systematic call-­‐up procedure in times when our resources are not able to handle an emergency. SURF is also a member of a state wide mutual aid agreement. SURF maintains a site Emergency Rescue Team (EMT) that provides underground emergency response with supplemental support from the Lead Fire Department. The twenty-­‐seven (27) member Emergency Rescue Team is trained to Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) mine-­‐rescue standards. The facility also maintains a life flight landing area.

Title: Dune Speaker's Committee (SC) rules

Version 1.5, 14 August 2015, changes compared to 1.4 indicated in red. DUNE Speakers Committee Guidelines (1) Purpose and Responsibilities The primary functions of the Speakers Committee (SC) are to ensure that the DUNE Collaboration is well represented at international conferences and to manage the assignment of DUNE speakers for all presentations (talks, posters) given on behalf of the DUNE Collaboration at international conferences and workshops. It will promote the science and technology of DUNE to the scientific community through conference presentations, seminars, and colloquia with the goal to encourage and attract new collaborators. The SC provides a single point of contact for conference and workshop organizers. The scope of the SC also includes physics presentations from LBNF, but does not cover its engineering and accelerator aspects. The SC solicits and promotes DUNE presentations and will support conference organizers in the planning of DUNE presentations. It assigns speakers for all DUNE presentations at international conferences and workshops, as specified by the guidelines given below. The SC maintains a record of presentations given and ensures that the material presented remains accessible to the DUNE Collaboration. Personal invitations for DUNE overview talks at international conferences and workshops may not be accepted by members of the DUNE Collaboration without the approval of the Speakers Committee. The SC assigns speakers for seminars at national and major international physics laboratories (e.g., Fermilab, CERN). Unless there is a new major result or discovery to present, the SC does not assign speakers to seminars or colloquia at universities and for regional meetings. On request, it can advise organizers of such events. Regional meetings are usually meetings of national physics societies without international participation, but not meetings organized by the APS and EPS. The SC submits abstracts to international conferences. If individual collaborators want to submit a DUNE abstract to a conference, prior approval by the SC is required. (2) Membership The SC is composed of at least six members, including the SC Chair and SC Deputy Chair, all appointed by the Spokespeople. Members serve for renewable one-year terms. To ensure continuity, not more than half of the members should be replaced each year. In addition, the Spokespeople, the Physics Coordinator, and the Technical Coordinator are ex-officio members. (3) Speaker Selection The SC in choosing speakers for DUNE presentations will follow the following general guidelines. Speakers must have the expertise and background to represent the Collaboration well in their particular presentation. Preference will be given to collaborators who have not given talks recently. Preference will be given to collaborators making important contributions to the DUNE experiment. Preference should be given to collaborators at an early or critical stage of their career. Other criteria can be developed and applied by the SC. The SC can exempt certain talks or speakers from these guidelines if it lies within the general interest of the Collaboration. The SC Chair will regularly ask for recommendations and input by Working Group conveners and Institutional Board representatives. The SC will also seek regional balance in assigning speakers proportional to the number of DUNE authors from that region. (4) Presentations All talks and posters at international workshops and conferences, as well as plenary talks at regional meetings, must be made available to the Collaboration and the SC for comments at least one week prior to the presentation. A rehearsal talk should be scheduled prior to the presentation, which at least one member of the SC can attend. This rehearsal is open to the entire Collaboration and the connection information must be announced to the Collaboration. Talks and posters shown at conferences, seminars, and colloquia can only include material that has been approved for public presentation following the publications policy of the DUNE Collaboration. The authorship of presentations should include “for the DUNE Collaboration.” The final version of presentations (ppt and pdf format) and proceedings must be stored in the public DUNE DocDB. The approval process for proceedings will be defined in the publications policy. (5) Other Procedures The SC meets regularly, at least twice a year. In between regular meetings, business is conducted by email. The SC Chair reports regularly to the Institutional Board and the Executive Committee.
