Source: indico Title: Summary of Geosyntec Report # **Technical Memorandum** |**Date:**|June 19, 2026| |---|---| |**To:**|Fermi Forward Discovery Group| |**Copies to:**|Ryan Hill, Longenecker & Associates, Inc.| |**From:**|Garry Stanley, PG and Chriso Petropoulou, PhD, PE, BCEE, Geosyntec
Consultants, Inc.| |**Subject:**|Evaluation of the Application of Non-Degradation Provisions to Tritium
in Class I Groundwater in Illinois| |**Project #**|26012478| ## **INTRODUCTION** Longenecker & Associates, Inc. retained Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. (Geosyntec) on behalf of Fermi Forward Discovery Group (FFDG) to provide environmental consulting services regarding the applicability of Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (IEPA) groundwater regulations pertaining to tritium, FFGDs application of Fermi’s National Accelerator Laboratory (FNAL) tritium monitoring plans, and Long Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF)/Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) near site construction plans related to tritium monitoring. This technical memorandum evaluates the consistency of FFDG’s proposed tritium monitoring and management approach with the Illinois non‑degradation framework, including consideration of how these provisions are implemented in practice at FNAL and for LBNF design. ## **Project Objectives** As discussed with the FFDG, the primary objective of Geosyntec’s scope of work is to evaluate whether FFDG’s proposed monitoring infrastructure and management approach provide a technically defensible basis for maintaining compliance with applicable IEPA groundwater regulations for tritium, including non-degradation provisions. The specific objectives of Geosyntec’s scope of work are summarized below. - Review of IEPA groundwater regulations pertaining to tritium with a special focus on nondegradation provisions - Review of FFDG’s application of lab-wide tritium management processes, including monitoring - Review of the LBNF/DUNE near site construction planning as it pertains to tritium monitoring - Prepare a report providing analysis of FNAL’s tritium management processes against applicable IEPA regulations Specific questions posed by FFDG and Geosyntec's responses are provided under Key Findings of Facts, below. Evaluation of the Application of Non-Degradation Provisions to Tritium in Class I Groundwater in Illinois June 19, 2026 Page 2 ## **Documents Reviewed** Our understanding of the environmental, geological, and monitoring conditions at FNAL included review of the applicable portions of the following documents provided by FFDG: - Fermilab (2024a): Annual Site Environmental Report - Fermilab (2024b): Comprehensive Tritium Management Plan, 2024 Update - Greer, Chris (2026), Slide deck provided to Geosyntec by FFDG during the project kick off call on May 20, 2026 - Kamran Vaziri, N. Mokhov, I. Rakhno, S. D. Reitzner, I. Tropin (2024): Long Baseline Neutrino Facility Preliminary Shielding Assessment (Draft-8). May 30, 2024 Additional documents obtained and reviewed by Geosyntec included the following: - Illinois Administrative Code (IAC), Title 35, Part 620 (35 IAC 620) Groundwater Quality, effective March 28, 2025 - Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (IEPA), 2013. Sample Collector’s Handbook – GW Quality Standards. Chapter 16, Groundwater Quality Standards (GQS). June. https://epa.illinois.gov/topics/compliance-enforcement/drinking-water/sample-collectorshandbook.html - United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), 2006. Liquid Radioactive Release, Lessons Learned Task Force, Final Report. September 1. - United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) 2025. Water Quality eXchange (WQX) User Guidance: Detection Limits. August 2025. These documents provide the technical and regulatory basis for understanding how tritium generation, transport, monitoring, and compliance are addressed in practice at FNAL and in the LBNF design. ## **SUMMARY OF KEY FINDINGS OF FACTS** FFDG questions and Geosyntec’s findings are provided below. ## **FFDG Question #1** _Provide an interpretation of applicable State of Illinois regulations and how the non-degradation clauses may apply to the LBNF beamline based on the geo-hydrological conditions at Fermilab, including clarification on the following points:_ - _Propriety of using 1 pCi/ml as the detection reporting level for tritium in Class I groundwater_ . Evaluation of the Application of Non-Degradation Provisions to Tritium in Class I Groundwater in Illinois June 19, 2026 Page 3 ## **Geosyntec Finding** Since the inception of the Illinois Environmental Protection Act (Act) (415 ILCS 5) in 1970, it has been the policy of the State of Illinois to restore, protect, and enhance the groundwater of the State as a natural and public resource. Groundwater resources should be utilized for beneficial and legitimate purposes; waste and degradation of the resource should be prevented; and the underground water resource should be managed to allow for maximum benefit of the State. Groundwater used as drinking water is one of the highest beneficial uses of the groundwater resource. The **Illinois Groundwater Protection Act (IGPA)** (415 ILCS 55) defines "Resource groundwater" as groundwater that is presently being or in the future capable of being put to beneficial use by reason of being of suitable quality (415 ILCS 55/3(j)) (IEPA 2013). The IGPA included Sections 11 and 12(a). Section 11 describes part of the purpose of Title III, as follows: “…assure that no contaminants are discharged into waters without being given the degree of treatment or control necessary to prevent pollution.” The Illinois Pollution Control Board’s (i.e., the Board) final order and opinion, for 35 Ill. Adm. Code: Subtitle C, indicated that (IEPA 2013): “…Standards are applicable to groundwaters that are a present or are a potential source of water for potable use or for food processing, except where deviation is due to natural causes. It is significant to note that these standards apply in situ; that is they are ambient water quality standards. They also apply irrespective of whether they are used by a public water supplier, a private water supplier, or have the potential for being so used.” “…Since general criteria apply to all waters designated for public water supply, the present regulation omits separate requirements for those parameters whose general standards are tight enough to protect public water supplies: boron, chromium, copper, fluoride, mercury, silver and zinc. The remaining standards are based largely upon Public Health Service (PHS) standards. While the PHS explicitly states that its standards are intended to prescribe the quality of finished rather than of raw water, it is clear from the evidence that many of the metals and other contaminants here listed are not substantially affected by ordinary water supply treatment, and therefore, the raw water must itself meet the standard to assure satisfactory finished water.” The phrase “ordinary treatment processes”, emphasized in the Board’s opinion above, is essential to understanding Illinois’ **nondegradation** requirements for groundwater. A private well owner typically only has to chlorinate his or her well to use the groundwater for potable uses. Thus, this defines the lowest common denominator of what ordinary treatment processes means to the protection of Class I potable resource groundwater. In other words, the Act and Board regulations prohibit a person for causing, threatening or allowing contamination of potable resource groundwater above what is not removed by “ordinary treatment processes” in a private drinking water system well. For example, **a plume of tritium** at a concentration above background or Evaluation of the Application of Non-Degradation Provisions to Tritium in Class I Groundwater in Illinois June 19, 2026 Page 4 naturally occurring levels, moving toward a private drinking water system well, is considered a threat to diminishing the existing Class I groundwater resource, since **tritium cannot be removed by advanced treatment processes let alone ordinary treatment processes** . This diminishment of resource groundwater (415 ILCS 55/3(j)) may lead to preclusion of the use of the well if the private well owner chooses not to use it (e.g., suitability) due to the contamination (IEPA 2013). States have adopted ground-water protection strategies that frequently include the concept of nondegradation. Although these rules have been adopted under the general authority delegated to the States by the EPA, there are no specific analogous Federal regulations, as is the case for the drinking water rules (NRC 2006). Non-degradation rules have no absolute quantity or concentration limit. Depending on the classification of the water, the water quality criteria can be based on site-specific existing conditions, regional background or even detection limits. **However, as a practical matter, at least for tritium, the common interpretation is that they are based on anything above the Lower Limit of Detection (LLD)** (NRC, 2006). NRC (2006) reports that in 2006, ambient tritium concentrations in the United States were below 50 picocuries per liter (pCi/L), whereas most common methods of detection yield LLDs in the range of 100 to 500 pCi/L. Variations in the LLD from one laboratory to another can lead to compliance disagreements if no guidance documents or prior agreements are negotiated. In Illinois, an LLD of 200 pCi/L was used by Exelon in evaluating ground water near the Braidwood and Byron nuclear plants. These non-numerical rules are usually designed to prevent the degradation of groundwater as a natural resource. **Under Illinois regulations, no person shall cause, threaten or allow the release of any contaminant to a resource groundwater such that an existing or potential use of such groundwater is precluded.** Therefore, it is Illinois’ view that if upon hearing about nearby tritium contamination a farmer declines to use his well for watering of livestock or for vegetable irrigation, a violation may result (NRC 2006). In general, there are different types of detection limits for any laboratory analysis. The variation stems from instrument noise, matrix complexity, analytical reagents and other factors. The LLD, also referred to as the detection limit, simply identifies the presence of a substance, but the concentration measurement is "too low” to be numerically accurate because of instrument noise. The method detection limit (MDL) is the statistically adjusted version of the LLD for a specific laboratory setup. Established primarily by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the MDL is a statistically calculated value that adapts the LLD for a specific laboratory's method and equipment. It represents the minimum concentration of a substance that can be measured and reported with 99% confidence that the concentration is greater than zero. The Reporting Limit (RL) is the lowest concentration that can be accurately and quantitatively measured. Also referred to as the Limit of Quantitation (LOQ), the RL is the lowest concentration of an analyte that a laboratory can confidently report with a specified, reproducible level of certainty, including both Evaluation of the Application of Non-Degradation Provisions to Tritium in Class I Groundwater in Illinois June 19, 2026 Page 5 precision and accuracy. Concentrations at or above this limit are dependable and precise, whereas values below the RL are reported as "Not Detected" or "Estimated" (EPA, 2025). 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), Chapter I—Environmental Protection Agency, Subchapter D‐Water Programs, Part 141, Subpart C specifies a **required detection limit** for tritium in drinking water of 1,000 pCi/L or 1 pCi/milliliter (ml), **meaning that drinking water supplies, where required, should be monitored for tritium at a sensitivity of 1 pCi/ml** (40 CFR 141.25(c)(2), Table C). This is consistent with EPA Method 906.0 for tritium water analysis (USEPA-600/4-80032/Section 10). ## **FFDG Question #2** _Appropriate application of the non-degradation clause regulatory level:_ - _at breakthrough into Class I groundwater (which aligns with past lab practice), or_ - _at nearby surveillance well(s), or_ - _at the property boundary._ ## **Geosyntec Finding** In general, FNAL is underlain by approximately 50 to 80 feet of unconsolidated glacial sediments on top of bedrock designated as a Class I potable resource groundwater aquifer. Based on information provided by FFDG, tritium is a byproduct of accelerator operation and formed when high energy protons impact or travel through materials. When tritium is exposed to air, the atoms of 3H combine with oxygen to form tritiated water. The generation of tritium presents a risk for tritium migration into the underlying Class I potable resource groundwater bedrock aquifer. As indicated in the 2024 Fermilab Annual Site Environmental Report (Fermilab 2024a), groundwater residing in or below the Silurian dolostone bedrock aquifer, the upper surface of which ranges from 50 to 80 feet below the ground surface in the Joliet Formation at FNAL, is classified as Class I potable resource groundwater. The Board has established groundwater quality standards found in 35 IAC 620 and defines Class I groundwater as a non-degradable resource that is to be highly protected. As such, the concentration of tritium is regulated through a Class I groundwater quality standard of 20 pCi/mL, with more conservative detection-level thresholds (e.g., 1 pCi/mL) often used in practice to demonstrate non-degradation of the resource.1 The groundwater quality standard of 20 pCi/mL is a human health risk

Title: Muon Monitor Update

Overview and Update on Muon Monitors Jeremy Lopez University of Colorado 15 October 2015 C Muon Monitors Working Group • Conveners: Geoff Mills, Jeremy Lopez • Goals: 1) Evaluate requirements for neutrino beam monitoring and potential for neutrino flux, determine any limitations from the absorber design 2) Document the current design and ongoing work in detector development and tests 3) Simulate the response in the LBNF beamline and evaluate the muon monitoring system’s performance Personnel Include: Jan Boissevain, Charles Lane, Zachary Liptak, Jeremy Lopez, Alysia Marino, Geoff Mills, Eric Zimmerman, CU Undergrads: Branton Demoss, Kerrie Dochen, Andrew Loeliger, Peter Madigan 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 2 Primary Goals of Muon Monitors 1) Determine absolute muon flux > 6 GeV (nu energy > 1.6 GeV) to 5% accuracy 2) Measure beam direction to within 0.2 mrad (i.e. beam position downstream of absorber to within 5 cm) *DUNE CDR Vol. 4 Sec. 7.5 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 3 Overview of Muon Monitors Three Detector Types:Absorber 1) Ionization Counters Stopped Muon • Measure Beam Position Cherenkov Counters Counters • Get total flux of charged particles exiting the absorber 2) Cherenkov Counters • Scan over different pressures/detector angles to build muon flux from threshold Vbeam center measurements lonization Counters 3) Stopped Muon Counters • Select flux at different positions/energies 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 4 Ionization Counters Likely Three Main Options: Diamonds, Silicon, Gas Ionization Counters Diamond Silicon Gas Pros: Fast signals, Cheap, easy to use Proven technology, more rad hard than Si rad hard (can replace gas), likely cheap Cons: $$$, not much Not very rad hard: Sensitive to ambient of a track record so may degrade quickly, pressure, slow signal far, less signal (high cost of replacement development band gap), lifetime could add up if they unknown need to be replaced often 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 5 Current Ionization Counter Testing Hardware D2, D3 • Have borrowed 3 pCVD diamond detectors previously used in CNGS beamline, installed in NuMI muon alcove 2 • Have purchased some bare diamonds & a silicon photodiode at CU for testing and evaluation D1 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 6 Some NuMI Results Horn On Horn Off Average of Many Pulses 1 Point = Integral of One RF Bucket Best Fits Hypothesis: Muon signal follows: 1) RWM (proton signal) 2) Muon decay in vacuum 3) Muon decay/capture in iron Works surprisingly well, but not perfect 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 7 Cherenkov Detector Prototype Prototype installed in NuMI muon alcove 2 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 8 Qualitative Data/MC Comparison NuMI Data, G. Mills Simulation, P. Madigan Scan over different pressures and yaws Get same qualitative features Need to see how well we really understand the detector response in the NuMI beam 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 9 More NuMI Data Otherwise, signal very stable Signal Drops by ~1% over ~10 days. Why? 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 10 Stopped Muon Counters Liquid scintillator outer veto Inner detector measures Cherenkov radiation in non-scintillating mineral oil Commissioning an initial prototype at CU. Will look at cosmics before moving detector to FNAL Gated base being designed at Drexel (needed to use in the NuMI beamline) 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 11 Simulation Work • Using G4LBNE to determine gating requirements for stopped muon detectors and getting muon energy spectrum • Simulating Cherenkov detector response to try to understand scans over detector parameters • Starting to work on simulating NuMI flux in alcove 2 to better understand diamond detectors 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 12 There’s Still More • Muon flux originating in absorber not necessarily trivially small (see talk by P. Lebrun during the Sept. meeting) • Could complicate extrapolation of muon flux to neutrino flux • Maybe would also affect the beam direction measurement • Need full simulation of flux seen by the muon detectors to see how the beamline design affects this • Could also probably use simulated estimate of lifetime of solid state detectors (although an actual measurement is better) 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 13 Conclusions and Outlook • Muon monitoring detector development is making steady progress • One Cherenkov detector prototype and 3 diamond detectors installed in NuMI muon alcove 2 • One stopped muon counter prototype built, will start testing in Boulder soon before moving to the NuMI beamline • Biggest questions with hardware are how long the detectors will last without repairs/replacement and how stable they are in an actual beam • Also working on various simulations both to support the tests in the NuMI beamline and to estimate what is expected in LBNF • Big question here is probably how the absorber design affects the muon measurements 10/15/2015 Muon Monitors 14

# Response to Collaboration Questions on LBNF Muon Monitoring Jeremy P. Lopez January 2017 ## **1 What are the physics requirements of the muon monitors on top of what the DUNE ND will provide?** The principal goal of the beam monitoring systems is to quickly provide feedback on the beam quality. Some expected pieces of the monitoring system include - primary beam monitors, which measure the proton beam position, direction, intensity, and width - muon monitors, which measure the intensity, spatial profile, and spectrum of muons downstream of the hadron absorber - the near neutrino detector, which can monitor the properties of the neutrino beam over time, such as the beam direction, intensity, and spectrum The most important advantage of muon monitors over the near detector is the speed at which feedback is given to the beam group. Typical muon systems in other beamlines use arrays of very simple detectors, and this simplicity allows for information to be extracted on a spill-by-spill basis on timescale of seconds. With muon fluxes of order 10<sup>7</sup> to 10<sup>8</sup> per square cm per spill, measurements in the muon alcove are limited only by detector systematics and the difficulty of interpreting how anomalous results in the muon alcove may affect the neutrino fluxes at the main detectors. Any feasible near detector design will require the detector to build statistics over some period of time and to process through a fairly involved processing chain, so feedback will be much slower. While the Near Detector is expected to have sensitivity to changes in the overall event rate, changes in the muon spectrum from charged current events, and changes in the beam direction, these measurements are likely to take quite some time and some, such as the beam direction, may be quite difficult. Muon monitoring provides a way to have sensitivity to beam changes on a spill-by-spill basis. Furthermore, because of the simplicity of typical muon systems in other beamlines, information may be obtained on a timescale of seconds, much faster than is likely feasible at a near detector. 1 Furthermore, in the event that a problem in the beam is found, it will be necessary to diagnose the origin of the problem in order to repair or realign the system. The different monitoring systems provide complementary information that will be invaluable in diagnosing problems. For example, a tilt of horn A of several millimeters will lead to an approximately 3% decrease in the ND neutrino spectrum at 5 GeV. Effective monitoring at the near detector will likely only use muon information, so it will take a great deal of time to measure the effect of this on the energy distribution of charged current _νµ_ events. Primary beam monitors will not be sensitive to problems in the horn systems, but there will be an approximately 2% decrease in the flux of 4 GeV muons found in the muon alcove. In order to determine the feasibility of making measurements with the muon monitor, we have conducted a number of Monte Carlo studies of realistic nonoptimal beam conditions such as horn misalignments, beam misalignments, and target density changes. In order to be sensitive to these realistic beam problems, we have determined that we will want to achieve: - 1 to 2 cm sensitivity to changes in the peak position of the muon position just downstream of the hadron absorber. - Approximately 1 to 2% sensitivity to the total signal in a 2 m by 2 m region centered at the nominal beam center - Approximately 2% sensitivity to changes in the muon spectrum at several muon energies (likely around 0, 5, and 8 GeV kinetic energy in the muon alcove - after losing approximately 6 GeV in the absorber). These numbers may be slightly different for threshold detectors. Given the large signal sizes and significant radiation damage expected to detectors, it will be challenging to achieve these goals. ## **2 Are the muon systems required to be able to provide information on the neutrino flux spectrum?** In order to achieve our monitoring goals, measurements that are sensitive to the muon flux will be necessary.Many of the beam conditions that we have simulated generate significant changes to the muon spectrum found downstream of the absorber. In some cases, this will be the most effective observation that we have. In the case of the target density showing an effective reduction of 5% due to aging effects or damage, we find that for a 90 GeV proton beam, the total signal of charged particles in an array of ionization detectors will have a negligible change, but the muon spectrum shows a large increase of higher energy muons and a small decrease in low energy muons. Spectral measurements will be particularly important if the final hadron absorber design resembles the current one, with a mask in the upstream part 2 and sculpted aluminum layers in the core. Such a design makes measurements of position of the muon peak intensity very difficult. ## **3 Are all the types of muon systems needed?** There is already agreement that an array of ionization detectors is necessary in nearly any scenario. Additionally arrays of ionization detectors can be used as threshold detectors to gain spectral information if there are several detector stations with different amounts of shielding. However, our simulations show that some beam conditions are best measured by considering a narrow range of muon energies rather than everything above some set energy threshold. This is not possible with ionization detectors but will be possible with Cherenkov detectors and with stopped muon counters. These two technologies make very different measurements. A Cherenkov detector has a threshold set by the gas pressure in its volume. The current design is a long tube with a mirror directing light to a PMT set far from beam center. The detector response will be quite complicated, as the particle momentum, position, and incident angle all affect the efficiency. However, a Cherenkov detector is very flexible. It can be used to scan over Cherenkov thresholds to build a spectrum and has an easily replaceable target mass. The signals are also very fast, making it useful for timing and studying the beam structure. Stopped muon counters, however, measure signals from muons stopped in the detector inner volume. In order to count these, the detector must look at delayed signals occurring well after the beam pulse is finished. This has the advantage that it will be insensitive to delta rays associated with the beam, but a stopped muon counter will not be capable of precise measurements of timing or beam substructure. The detector stops only low energy muons, so the detector response will be much simpler than for a Cherenkov detector. There is ongoing work studying both Cherenkov counters and stopped muon counters, and it is possible that there are other useful detector types that have not been considered. Because we do not have a good comparison of the performance of the different detector types, it is too early to determine exactly which technology or technologies will be used. In order to ensure that the measurements can be made, we recommend that several alcoves or detector stations be available. ## **4 How do the muon system requirements impact the hadron absorber design?** The current design of the hadron absorber includes several features not included in existing beamlines that will impact the muon signal. The spoiler, mask, and sculpting of the core aluminum pieces creates targets and decay volumes for hadrons impacting the absorber. This can generate muons that will reach the muon monitors that do not originate in the decay pipe. The mask and sculpting 3 also shape the signal. There is significantly less material near the beam center, increasing the muon flux at nominal beam center. Finally, the size of the core also limits how far from beam center useful measurements can be made, since aluminum is less dense than the iron used outside the core. To test how these features affect the signals, we have run simulations with both the standard absorber and with a highly simplified geometry, where (1) the mask and spoiler are replaced with air, (2) the sculpted regions are filled in with aluminum, and (3) the core is expanded. The possible problems with the current design are most evident in beam conditions where the muons are shifted away from the nominal beam center. What we see is that the features of the current design suppress the effects of the beam being directed slightly away from nominal beam center. If the beam is shifted laterally in _x_ on the target by 1 mm, the muon signal shifts by several cm in the _−x_ direction. For the simplified absorber, we see that a Gaussian fit to the muon profile in _x_ with _|y| <_ 7 _._ 5 cm yields a mean position of -1.6 cm for a fit to _x ∈_ [ _−_ 1 _m,_ 1 _m_ ] and -3.8 cm for a fit to _x ∈_ [ _−_ 0 _._ 5 _m,_ 0 _._ 5 _m_ ]. Looking at the same for the current absorber design, the mean positions are -0.47 cm and -0.89 cm, respectively. If we define a left-right asymmetry as ( _R − L_ ) _/total_ , the asymmetry for the simple absorber is _−_ 2 _._ 5% for _x ∈_ [-1 m, 1 m] and _−_ 1 _._ 9% for _x ∈_ [-1 m, 1 m]. For the standard absorber, these two asymmetries are -0.84% and -1.3%. Furthermore, we find that the peak signal position seen in the muon monitor remains at the nominal center for the current absorber even when the mean muon position is well away from the center. A direct measurement of the beam position will be very unreliable, so information will need to be extrapolated from parameters such as the asymmetry or skewness. Without the ability to reliably measure the beam position, the muon systems will then need to rely on the overall signal size and the flux shape to identify problems with the position. This will make it much more difficult to interpret the results. It will be much more important for the near detector to provide this measurement, which may impact the ND design requirements. In order to measure the spatial distribution, we would want the hadron absorber to be as uniform as possible near the beam center. As we are focusing on sensitivity to shifts in the beam position of several cm, we do not expect to need to make measurements much beyond approximately 1 m from nominal beam center. In our simulations, we see that some parameters such as asymmetries are enhanced within 1 m of beam center compared to 0.5 m from beam center, so we would ideally have an approximately constant amount of material in the hadron absorber within 1 m or so from beam center. This would allow us to clearly see the effects of the beam shifting from nominal beam center by small amounts. 4 ## **5 How often do we think a near detector could provide monitoring feedback?** While the near detector group has not done extensive work yet on the topic of monitoring, there are some preliminary thoughts on how this might be done. For the purposes of monitoring the beam, charged-current _νµ_ events will give the highest statistics. The analysis would use events in the fiducial volume, but could be on any material. In the fine grained tracker (FGT) design, there are approximately 3 _×_ 10<sup>4</sup> CC events per day at a beam power of 1 MW. During normal running, this should be sufficient to achieve a 1% uncertainty on the POT-normalized signal (assuming negligible POT counting systematics) for each day.The time needed to gather sufficient statistics for a spectrum measurement will depend on the desired binning. Around the peak (around 1 to 5 GeV, there should be sufficient statistics to achieve a 1% uncertainty roughly every week with 0.5 GeV bins (assuming high efficiency & purity) At higher and lower energies,

In the case of the target density showing an effective reduction of 5% due to aging effects or damage, we find that for a 90 GeV proton beam, the total signal of charged particles in an array of ionization detectors will have a negligible change, but the muon spectrum shows a large increase of higher energy muons and a small decrease in low energy muons. Spectral measurements will be particularly important if the final hadron absorber design resembles the current one, with a mask in the upstream part 2 and sculpted aluminum layers in the core. Such a design makes measurements of position of the muon peak intensity very difficult. ## **3 Are all the types of muon systems needed?** There is already agreement that an array of ionization detectors is necessary in nearly any scenario. Additionally arrays of ionization detectors can be used as threshold detectors to gain spectral information if there are several detector stations with different amounts of shielding. However, our simulations show that some beam conditions are best measured by considering a narrow range of muon energies rather than everything above some set energy threshold. This is not possible with ionization detectors but will be possible with Cherenkov detectors and with stopped muon counters. These two technologies make very different measurements. A Cherenkov detector has a threshold set by the gas pressure in its volume. The current design is a long tube with a mirror directing light to a PMT set far from beam center. The detector response will be quite complicated, as the particle momentum, position, and incident angle all affect the efficiency. However, a Cherenkov detector is very flexible. It can be used to scan over Cherenkov thresholds to build a spectrum and has an easily replaceable target mass. The signals are also very fast, making it useful for timing and studying the beam structure. Stopped muon counters, however, measure signals from muons stopped in the detector inner volume. Striganov, S. Childress, N. Mokhov DUNE Accelerator and Beam Interface Meeting Fermilab January 7, 2016 # Introduction Designs of target station and hadron absorber are connected. About 0.3% of primary beam come through baffle, do not interact with target and create high energy deposition density in the absorber. Therefore, in 2015, a complicated absorber with spoiler and sculpted core has been designed. Long target of the baseline width reduces total energy deposition in absorber, but does not decrease maximal energy deposition, because same number of primary protons misses target. Maximal energy deposition can be radically reduced by adding wings in the upstream end of the long target. How wings change maximal energy deposition? How wings change particle spectra? Striganov DUNE Accelerator and Beam Interface Meeting Fermilab May 5, 2016 ##### Introduction Target collimator has been designed to minimize interaction with proton beam: baffle radius ~ 5 sigma beam. Target horizontal size is ~ 3 sigma beam. About 0.3% of primary beam come through baffle, does not interact with target and creates large density of energy deposition in absorber. We need to consider complicated absorber. Long target with same transverse dimensions reduces total energy deposition in absorber, but does not decrease maximal energy deposition, because same number of primary protons misses target. It is possible radically reduce maximal energy deposition with small wings added to long target. Last upgrades - bug in calculation of nominal case was fixed and neutrino spectra calculation algorithm was improved to get better statistical accuracy. Wings reduce muon neutrino flux less than few percent in region of interest (<5 GeV) 25 # Conclusions Using optimized (long) target with 12-48 cm wings reduces maximal energy deposition in LBNF absorber 6-20 times. It is possible to consider simple absorber without spoiler and sculpted blocks for optimized setup. Such simple absorber can survive even for significantly increased beam power beyond 2.4 MW. Muon neutrino flux decreases a few percent for target with 48 cm wings and less than one percent with 24 cm wings for neutrino energies important for LBNF/DUNE experiment. High energy muon flux after fourth alcove is reduced by factor of 2-3 for long target setup. It significantly decreases ground water activation in rock after absorber. 26 26 Backup

_Images from: Vladimir Sidorov_ Fermilab Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 9 ###### **State of design** - The core is the most challenging part of absorber design, and is where our effort has been concentrated. Its advanced conceptual design is the focus of this review. We believe that the analysis that will be presented shows this to be a very viable design, and is _ready to proceed to detailed mechanical design_ . - Some effort has also been directed at civil construction requirements, to allow cost estimates, and radiological issues that drive the civil construction have been seriously investigated. Some of that will be presented, although not the focus of this review. - The designs of the outer part of the absorber, the water systems, and the monitoring systems are at a conceptual level; real work on those systems will not start until after the core design passes review. They will then be subject to their own reviews after design and optimization efforts occur. - However, the concepts for the absorber protection monitoring follow fairly straightforwardly from NuMI experience, and will be shown in this talk. Fermilab 10 Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 ###### **Conditions used as input to FEA** LBNE will have two phases, 1.2 MW beam, then upgrade to 2.4 MW beam; but because of difficulty to upgrade absorber, design absorber from start for 2.4 MW There will be different configurations of targets and horns in LBNE over its lifetime, in particular: - The current baseline target/horn (using NuMI target/horn design) is financially driven; we know we can improve the beam by re-optimizing components - The current target/horn will only take 1.2 MW; we know we will re-design these components for 2.4 MW Want to leave **_flexibility_** to accommodate those future configurations. Thus we have designed to meet “worst case” scenarios: - Have assumed shortest reasonable target (two interaction lengths) - Giving worst non-interacting proton spot at absorber for normal operation - Have assumed beam can totally miss target, hitting absorber directly - Giving worst accident condition at absorber, although current baffle/target design does not allow such a severe condition - Have assumed tightest focus of beam at absorber (optics + beam-spot-attarget) for accident condition Fermilab 11 Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 **Beam parameters (see LBNE Beamline Operating Parameters LBNE-doc-10095 on review web site for details on phases and energy dependence)** - If not noted, results presented for 120 GeV proton beam (worse than 60 GeV). Will also present results that show design is OK for 60 GeV proton beam. (In fact, absorber could take _MUCH_ higher beam power at 60 GeV). - Beam parameters for various studies were picked for worst case upgrades: – 2.4 MW beam is 1.5e14 POT/spill, 1.2 second repetition at 120 GeV - Beam spot size at target is 1.7 mm RMS for 1.2 MW design, may be up to 3 mm for 2.4 MW designs; used 2.4 mm for accident study since with our optics this gives smallest spot at absorber (7 mm RMS) for beam accident condition - Baffle hole diameter: 17 mm at 1.2 MW, but may be up to 30 mm for 2.4 MW, so have used 30 mm for range of possible beam accidents - Normal operation modeled with fin-type two-interaction-length target where: - 0.3% of beam misses target entirely, giving 9 mm central spot on absorber (7 kW) - 13% of beam protons multiple scatter through target, giving 5 cm central spot on absorber (~300 kW) - The 2.4 MW target will probably include spoiler feature (described later for 1.2 MW target) and be longer, so these beam assumptions are conservative Designing to above parameters leaves **_significant flexibility_** for future configurations Fermilab Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 12 ###### **Using experience with NuMI** - LBNE core (gun-drilled water lines in aluminum blocks) based on NuMI absorber, which has been operating for a decade without any problems. - NuMI upstream decay pipe window is same material (Al 6061-T6) as absorber core, has seen same integrated proton-flux-density as LBNE absorber spoiler will, and has no problems so far. - Remote handling of core blocks based on T-block hanging system used successfully for last decade in NuMI target hall to swap horns and targets. - • Beam Position Monitor (BPM) input to NuMI Beam Permit System, checking that beam is directed toward the target, has been used for last decade. - Thermocouples in absorber core watching for overheating have been an input to NuMI Beam Permit System for last decade. - Muon monitor has been used at NuMI, but not as input to Beam Permit System; some modifications/upgrades required to make this operate smoothly and reliably, and will be discussed. Fermilab 13 Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 ## NORMAL OPERATION Fermilab Jim Hylen | Absorber Introduction & Overview 1/20/2015 14 ###### **Strategy part 1 – keep temperature low** At the previous core review (Nov. 2013), design had peak temperature in Aluminum core of nearly 170 C. Concern was expressed that Aluminum can fatigue, creep, lose temper over time at high temperature, and a more conservative design was desired. ###### **LBNE absorber design features to keep temperature low:** - Spoiler layer initiates particle shower, then air space between it and the rest of the core blocks lets shower spread out, reducing energy density before further showering - Sculpted core blocks (thin at center, thicker at water line) - Provide increased heat transfer conductance to water lines per amount of material at the center - Give more air space for shower to spread out (Aluminum dT < 1 C per pulse) - Water lines are drilled near center of core blocks, reducing transport dT (major contribution) - • Multiple water lines are drilled in each block (also provides redundancy, could run 1 line off) - • Water flows at high enough velocity (2.5 m/s) to give good heat transfer coeff. (dT < 15 C) - • Water flows at high rate (80 gpm /block), gives low water dT in block ( dT max. = 2 C ) • Low temperature water supply (10 C) (will dehumidify air to keep dew point below this) The combination reduces aluminum maximum normal operating temperature to 88 C with the worst target configuration we imagine using. We believe this is a robust design.
